title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning for Practitioners
text:
Preface
This is the practitioner edition of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning. It is for people who build, review and audit machine-learning systems that handle personal data, and who need to know what each result says, when it applies, how to use it and what goes wrong in practice, without working through its proof.
It covers the same topics as the full edition, in the same parts and chapters. Each topic is explained in four steps: the idea and why it works, the result or rule, a worked example with real numbers, and the pitfalls that catch people in practice. Each chapter ends with a cheat sheet and a link to the full edition’s chapter, where every result is derived step by step.

title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning for Practitioners
text:
How this book is organized

Prerequisites collects the mathematics the later parts use: distributions, tail bounds, ways to compare distributions, hypothesis testing, and the basics of information theory, optimization, stability and cryptography.
Threat models and attacks shows how models and data leak: membership inference, attribute and property inference, memorization and extraction, gradient inversion, re-identification, and reconstruction from aggregate statistics.
Differential privacy foundations defines the guarantee those attacks call for, builds its mechanisms, composes them, and says what privacy costs.
Privacy accounting tracks the guarantee through the many steps of private training, and ends with how to choose an accountant and what to report.
Differential privacy in machine learning trains models with the guarantee: where the noise goes, how the knobs of noisy, clipped gradient descent trade privacy for accuracy, what else spends the budget, who pays for the noise, which ε to choose, and how to audit the result.

The numbers in the text are computed by the scripts in the repository’s code/ directory, the same ones the full edition uses, and tests check that the scripts still produce them.

title: Prerequisites
text:
The common thread
This part collects the mathematics that the rest of the book stands on. It contains no privacy yet. Everything here is standard probability, statistics, optimization, information theory and cryptography. What makes it different from a textbook is the selection. Each topic is here because a later part needs it, and each is taken only as far as that need goes.
You need the basics of probability, such as expectation, variance and independence. You need enough machine learning to recognise a loss function and stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and enough Python to read a short script. If you already know a topic, skim its cheat sheet and move on. Each later chapter restates in a sentence what it uses from here, and links back.
The later parts study algorithms whose output is random, and they keep asking the same few questions about them. How far can a random output be from its expected value? How different are the outputs on two inputs that differ in one example, and how well could anyone tell them apart? How much does a trained model depend on a single training example? How much does an observation reveal about something hidden?
Two ideas answer most of these questions. The first is the likelihood ratio: how many times more likely an observation is under one distribution than under another. If you want to know which of two distributions produced an observation, this ratio is all the observation tells you. So every way of comparing two distributions comes back to it. When the ratio can never be large, no single observation is strong evidence either way, and that is the property privacy will later demand.
The second idea is the effect of one input: how far one example can move an average, a trained model or a loss. A quantity that no single input can move much has little room to vary. So a small effect of one input turns into narrow error bars, and in learning, into a model that does as well on new data as on its training data.

title: Prerequisites
section: Why the chapters come in this order
text:
Why the chapters come in this order
The first four chapters build one argument, each on the one before. Probability distributions introduces the few families that model counts and noise. It ends by comparing a noise distribution with a copy of itself moved sideways. The likelihood ratio of normal noise grows without limit far from the centre, while that of Laplace noise stays below a fixed bound.
That raises the question of how often extreme values occur. Concentration inequalities answers it. It turns what you know about a random quantity into an error bar that fails only with a small probability you choose. Divergences then compresses the difference between two distributions into a single number. It shows that there are several such numbers, and that each answers a different question. Hypothesis testing says what those numbers mean for anyone who tries to tell the two distributions apart. It finds the best possible test, draws the curve of its two kinds of error, and explains why a detector should be judged where false alarms are rare.
Information theory follows the same thread from another angle. It asks how much an observation reveals about a hidden value, both on average and for a single best guess. Optimization and Algorithmic stability and generalization take up the second idea. They show how fast training converges, how far its result moves when one example changes, and why a model that depends little on each example generalizes.
Cryptography basics stands somewhat apart. It defines what it means that an efficient observer learns nothing it should not, by asking whether an attacker can tell two worlds apart. You can leave it until a later chapter needs it. Threat models, linkage attacks and trust models are the first chapters that do.

title: Prerequisites
text:
How to read a chapter
Each chapter opens with the practical question it answers and the idea behind the answer. Each section then starts from a problem and reasons its way to a result. Every formula is explained in words first, every condition a result needs is stated with its reason, and a worked example with real numbers shows the result in use. A cheat sheet at the end collects the results on one page.
The chapters contain no proofs. Each one ends with a link to the matching chapter of the full edition, which derives every result step by step and has a script that checks every number quoted.

title: Prerequisites
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
After this part, you will be able to put an error bar on a noisy answer, a measured error rate, or the largest of many noise draws. You will know which inequality gives the narrowest valid error bar, and why.
You will be able to compute the Kullback–Leibler (KL), Rényi, total variation and hockey-stick divergences between two normal or two Laplace distributions. You will also be able to explain why processing data can never increase any of them.
You will know the best test between two distributions and how to read its trade-off curve. You will be able to report a detector by how often it catches positives at a low false-positive rate. You will also be able to size a test set so that the rate you measure is precise enough.
Finally, you will be able to say how fast gradient descent converges and how far a trained model moves when one example changes. You will be able to compute how much an observation leaks about a hidden value, and state a security property as a game between an attacker and two worlds.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.1 Why this matters
Most of the random numbers in a private machine-learning system are either counts or draws of noise. The number of mistakes a model makes on a test set is a count, and so is the size of a randomly sampled minibatch. The noise a system adds on purpose is the other kind, usually drawn from a normal or a Laplace distribution. Before you can trust any of these numbers, you need to know where each one usually lands and how rare its large values are.
A handful of distribution families covers almost every case. They are not unrelated formulas, because each is built from simpler ones. Counting the successes in a series of coin flips gives the binomial, and when each flip rarely succeeds, the binomial becomes the Poisson. Waiting for the first of those rare successes gives the exponential, and placing two exponentials back to back gives the Laplace. Adding many small independent pieces, whatever their own distribution, gives the normal. So each family’s average and spread follow from its pieces, and this chapter explains each fact that way.
The chapter ends with a question that later chapters keep asking. Noise is added to one of two values that differ by a known amount, and an observer sees only the result. How strongly can that result make the observer favour one value over the other? With normal noise, some observations settle the question almost for certain. With Laplace noise, however, no observation can make one value more than a fixed factor more likely than the other. The difference lies in the tails. The normal’s chances fall off much faster far from the centre, and that makes its extreme observations far more telling.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.2 Mean and variance
The mean of a random quantity \(X\), written \(\mathbb E[X]\), is the long-run average of many independent draws of it. It says where a distribution sits, but not how wide it is, and that width is what the variance measures. It squares each draw’s distance from the mean, so that distances on either side count the same, and averages these squares. It is often easier to compute as the mean of the square minus the square of the mean: \[\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb E\big[(X - \mathbb E X)^2\big] = \mathbb E[X^2] - (\mathbb E X)^2. \tag{1.1}\] The standard deviation, written \(\sigma\), is the square root of the variance. It is in the same units as the quantity, so it is the number to compare with the mean. For a fair die, for example, the mean is 3.5 and the variance is about 2.92. Its standard deviation is then about 1.71, which is the typical size of a roll’s distance from the mean.
Three rules cover almost every calculation in this chapter. The first rule says that the mean of a sum is the sum of the means, and it holds even when the quantities depend on each other. That is because an average weighs each outcome by its chance. At each outcome the sum is just the two values added, so the weighted total splits into two separate averages. The second rule says what scaling does to the spread. Multiplying a quantity by a constant \(c\) multiplies every distance from the mean by \(c\), and squaring turns that factor into \(c^2\). So scaling by \(c\) multiplies the variance by \(c^2\).
The third rule says that when a quantity \(X\) is independent of a second quantity \(Y\), their variances add: \[\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y). \tag{1.2}\] In general the variance of a sum has an extra term, the covariance, which measures how much the two quantities tend to move together. Independence makes the covariance zero, which leaves only the two variances. But without independence the rule can fail. Add a quantity to an exact copy of itself, for example, and the sum is twice the quantity. By the second rule its variance is then four times the original, not twice.
The second and third rules together say how fast an average becomes precise. Take some number \(n\) of independent draws and average them. By the third rule, their sum has \(n\) times the variance of one draw, and by the second rule, dividing the sum by \(n\) then divides that variance by \(n^2\). So the average has the variance of one draw divided by \(n\), and its standard deviation is that of one draw divided by \(\sqrt n\). Four times as much data therefore only halves the error.

title: 1  Probability distributions
section: 1.3 Tails and the moment generating function
text:
1.3 Tails and the moment generating function
The mean and the variance describe the bulk of a distribution, but a guarantee that must hold except in rare cases depends instead on the tail. That is the chance \(\Pr[X \ge t]\) that the quantity reaches a threshold \(t\) far from the mean. What matters is how fast the tail shrinks as the threshold grows, and three shapes recur in this book. Take the threshold \(t = 5\), for example. A polynomial decay such as \(1/t^2\) gives 0.04 there. An exponential decay such as \(e^{-t}\) is already down to about \(6.7\times10^{-3}\). A Gaussian decay such as \(e^{-t^2/2}\) falls much further still, to about \(3.7\times10^{-6}\).
The gap widens quickly as the threshold grows, because the exponent of the Gaussian decay grows like \(t^2\) and that of the exponential decay only like \(t\). Among the families defined below, the exponential and Laplace distributions have exponential tails, and the normal distribution has a Gaussian tail.
One function connects a distribution to its tail and also makes sums of independent quantities easy. The moment generating function (MGF) of \(X\) is the average of \(e^{\lambda X}\): \[M_X(\lambda) = \mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda X}\big]. \tag{1.3}\] The number \(\lambda\) is not a parameter of the distribution but a dial that you set. When \(\lambda\) is positive, the weight \(e^{\lambda X}\) grows exponentially with the quantity, so large values dominate the average. So the larger you set the dial, the further into the right tail the MGF looks. A negative dial would look at the left tail instead, so bounds on the right tail use positive values.
A coin shows how an MGF is computed. Take a quantity that is 1 with some probability \(p\) and 0 otherwise. Its weight is \(e^0 = 1\) at the outcome 0 and \(e^\lambda\) at the outcome 1, and the MGF averages these two weights: \[(1 - p) + pe^\lambda = 1 + p(e^\lambda - 1). \tag{1.4}\] The factor \(e^\lambda\), the weight of the outcome 1, will reappear in every count below.
Two properties of the MGF matter in practice. The first is that adding independent quantities multiplies their MGFs: \[M_{X+Y}(\lambda) = M_X(\lambda)\,M_Y(\lambda) \quad\text{when $X$ and $Y$ are independent}. \tag{1.5}\] The reason is that the exponential of a sum is the product of the exponentials, and independence lets the average of that product split into the product of the averages. Without independence the average need not split, and the rule can fail. A standard theorem, which the full edition cites, adds that two distributions whose MGFs are finite and equal for every dial in some interval around zero are the same distribution. Finiteness matters because two different heavy-tailed distributions can both have an infinite MGF at every positive dial, and agreeing there says nothing. So when the MGF of a sum matches a known family’s MGF near zero, the sum belongs to that family.
The second property links the MGF to the tail. For every positive \(\lambda\), \[\Pr[X \ge t] \le M_X(\lambda)\,e^{-\lambda t}. \tag{1.6}\] Because the dial is positive, the weight \(e^{\lambda X}\) grows with the quantity, so whenever the quantity reaches the threshold, the weight is at least \(e^{\lambda t}\). The weight is also never negative, so the other outcomes cannot pull its average below what these outcomes contribute. The MGF is therefore at least \(e^{\lambda t}\) times the chance of reaching the threshold, and dividing both sides by \(e^{\lambda t}\) gives the bound. It follows that if the MGF is finite for some positive dial, the tail shrinks at least exponentially. A heavy-tailed distribution, whose tail shrinks more slowly than every exponential, has an infinite MGF for every positive dial, and then the bound says nothing. Concentration inequalities turns this bound into error bars by choosing the dial well.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.4 Counts: Bernoulli and binomial
The simplest random quantity is a yes-or-no outcome, such as whether a test example is misclassified. A Bernoulli variable is 1 with probability \(p\) and 0 otherwise, so its mean is \(p\). Because it is 0 or 1, it also equals its own square, and the average of its square is \(p\) as well. The variance, the mean of the square minus the square of the mean, is therefore \[p - p^2 = p(1-p). \tag{1.7}\]
Count the yeses over \(n\) independent trials and you get a binomial count, written \(\mathrm{Binomial}(n, p)\). Any one sequence with \(k\) yeses has probability \(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\), because independent trials multiply their probabilities. There are \(\binom nk\) such sequences, one for each choice of which trials say yes. So the count \(S\) equals \(k\) with probability \[\Pr[S = k] = \binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, n. \tag{1.8}\] For the mean and the variance, it is easier to write the count as a sum of \(n\) independent Bernoulli trials and apply the rules for sums. The mean is then \(np\), and because the trials are independent, the variance is \(np(1-p)\). For the same reason, the MGF of the count is the product of \(n\) coin MGFs: \[M_S(\lambda) = \big(1 + p(e^\lambda - 1)\big)^n. \tag{1.9}\]
The variance of one trial, \(p(1-p)\), is zero when the outcome is certain either way and largest at \(p = 1/2\), where it equals a quarter. So in absolute terms, a rate near zero is measured much more precisely than a rate near one half. Hoeffding’s inequality, a bound in Concentration inequalities that knows only that each trial lies between 0 and 1, must assume the worst case of a quarter. It is therefore loose when rates are small.
Every measured rate, such as accuracy or a false-positive rate, is a binomial count divided by \(n\). By the scaling rule, the measured rate has mean \(p\) and variance \(p(1-p)/n\), so its standard deviation is \[\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}. \tag{1.10}\]
Suppose a classifier makes a mistake on each test example independently with probability 0.05. On 2,000 test examples it then makes 100 mistakes on average. The standard deviation of that count is about 9.7, and dividing by the number of examples turns it into about 0.005 for the error rate. So the measured error rate is typically within about half a percentage point of the true 5%.
Now lower the true error rate to 0.001. The same test set then expects only 2 mistakes, with a standard deviation of about 1.4. Relative to the count, that error is now about 70%. The test set can also easily show no mistakes at all, which happens with chance \(0.999^{2000}\). A small chance of failure repeated many times behaves like an exponential, since \((1-p)^n\) is close to \(e^{-np}\) when \(p\) is small. So the chance of a clean test set is about \(e^{-2}\), or one in seven. What sets the relative precision, then, is the expected number of mistakes, not the number of test examples.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.5 Rare events: Poisson
Many counts, such as an accurate model’s mistakes on a large test set, add up many trials that each rarely succeed. Write \(\mu\) for the expected count, which is \(np\). When the trials are many and each success is rare, the binomial depends almost only on \(\mu\). That is because each part of the binomial formula has a simple limit when \(p\) is small. A particular set of \(k\) trials all succeed with chance \(p^k\). When there are many more trials than successes, there are about \(n^k/k!\) such sets, so together they contribute about \(\mu^k/k!\). Meanwhile, all the other trials fail with chance close to \(e^{-\mu}\), because \((1-p)^n\) is close to \(e^{-np}\). Only \(\mu\) survives in either limit.
Holding \(\mu\) fixed as the number of trials grows gives the Poisson distribution \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\). A Poisson count \(N\) equals a whole number \(k\) with probability \[\Pr[N = k] = e^{-\mu}\frac{\mu^k}{k!}. \tag{1.11}\] Figure 1.1 shows how fast the binomial approaches the Poisson.






Figure 1.1: \(\mathrm{Binomial}(n, 5/n)\) for \(n = 10\) and 100 against \(\mathrm{Poisson}(5)\) and its normal approximation. At \(n = 100\) the binomial and the Poisson almost coincide.



A Poisson count has its variance equal to its mean. The reason is that in the binomial variance \(np(1-p)\), the factor \(1 - p\) tends to 1 as the trials become rare, which leaves only \(\mu\). So the standard deviation is \(\sqrt\mu\), and the spread relative to the mean is \(1/\sqrt\mu\), which is small only once you expect many events. With a mean of 4, for example, the standard deviation is 2. A count of 0 or 8, two standard deviations away, is then unremarkable.
The MGF of a Poisson count \(N\) is \[M_N(\lambda) = \exp\big(\mu(e^\lambda - 1)\big). \tag{1.12}\] It is the limit of the binomial MGF \((1 + p(e^\lambda - 1))^n\), for the same reason that \((1-p)^n\) tends to \(e^{-np}\). Multiplying the MGFs of two independent Poisson counts adds their exponents, and the result is again a Poisson MGF. So a sum of independent Poisson counts is a Poisson count whose mean is the sum of their means.
The same MGF also bounds every count of independent yes-or-no outcomes. The line \(1 + x\) touches the curve \(e^x\) at zero, and the curve bends upward away from it, so \(1 + x \le e^x\) everywhere. Putting \(x = p(e^\lambda - 1)\) into this inequality turns its left side into the coin’s MGF. Its right side becomes \(\exp(p(e^\lambda - 1))\), the Poisson MGF with mean \(p\). Now take independent coins, each with its own probability, and let \(\mu\) be the sum of their probabilities. The MGF of their total \(S\) is the product of their MGFs, and each factor is at most its Poisson bound. Multiplying the bounds adds their exponents, so the total’s MGF is at most the Poisson MGF with mean \(\mu\): \[M_S(\lambda) \le \exp\big(\mu(e^\lambda - 1)\big). \tag{1.13}\] The Chernoff bound in Concentration inequalities starts from this fact.
A Poisson count is skewed to the right, since it cannot go below zero but can run far above its mean. For every \(k\), the chance that it equals exactly \(k\) is at most \[\Pr[N = k] \le \Big(\frac{e\mu}{k}\Big)^k. \tag{1.14}\] The reason is that \(k!\) is always at least \((k/e)^k\). Dividing \(\mu^k\) by it therefore gives at most \((e\mu/k)^k\), and the factor \(e^{-\mu}\) only lowers the chance further. This bound says something only once \(k\) exceeds \(e\mu\), where its base drops below 1. Beyond that point it falls faster than any exponential decay, but more slowly than a Gaussian decay with the same variance.
Some training procedures form each minibatch by including each of 60,000 examples independently with probability 0.01. The batch size is then a binomial count with many unlikely trials, so it is very close to \(\mathrm{Poisson}(600)\). Its mean is 600 and its standard deviation is about 24.5. Batch sizes between 550 and 650, about two standard deviations on either side, are therefore typical. Concentration inequalities shows how rarely a batch leaves the range of 600 plus or minus 20%.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.6 Waiting times: exponential
The Poisson counts how many rare events fall in a window of time, while the exponential answers how long you wait for the first one. For this book it is mainly a building block of the Laplace distribution.
The exponential comes from the same construction as the Poisson. Chop time into short slots, and let each slot hold an event independently with a small probability. Write \(b\) for the average time between events, the scale. Write \(m\) for the number of slots per unit of time. Each slot then holds an event with probability \(1/(bm)\), which keeps the expected number of events per unit of time at \(1/b\). Now take a time \(t\), which spans \(tm\) slots. The wait \(T\) exceeds that time when all of them are empty, so these are \(tm\) independent trials that all fail, and together they expect \(t/b\) events. As in the Poisson limit, the chance that they all fail tends to \(e^{-t/b}\) as the slots shrink: \[\Pr[T > t] = e^{-t/b}, \qquad t \ge 0. \tag{1.15}\]
Figure 1.2 shows the limit for a scale of 2. With one slot per unit of time, each slot holds an event with probability one half, so the chance of waiting past \(t\) halves at every whole number. With five slots per unit of time, this staircase already hugs the limiting curve.






Figure 1.2: \(\Pr[T_n > t]\) for the slotted waiting time with \(b = 2\) and \(n = 1\) or \(5\) slots per unit of time, against the exponential tail \(e^{-t/2}\).



The exponential distribution \(\mathrm{Exp}(b)\) is the distribution of this wait, and its density at a waiting time \(y\) is \[f(y) = \frac1b e^{-y/b}, \qquad y \ge 0. \tag{1.16}\] Its mean is the scale \(b\), so \(b\) really is the average wait, and its variance is \(b^2\). Some libraries take the rate \(1/b\) instead, while NumPy’s rng.exponential(b) takes the scale, so check before you trust a noise level.
The exponential’s MGF is finite only for dials below \(1/b\), where it equals \[M_T(\lambda) = \frac{1}{1 - b\lambda}. \tag{1.17}\] The MGF averages the weight \(e^{\lambda y}\) against the density \(e^{-y/b}\). Once the dial reaches \(1/b\), the density no longer shrinks faster than the weight grows, so the average is infinite. An MGF that exists only on part of the line is the mark of an exponential tail.
The exponential also forgets how long you have waited. If you have already waited a time \(s\) without an event, the chance of waiting at least \(t\) more is the same as from scratch: \[\Pr[T \ge s + t \mid T \ge s] = \Pr[T \ge t]. \tag{1.18}\] The slots after time \(s\) are independent of the empty slots before it, so the wait starts afresh. This memorylessness rests on that independence. Suppose instead that a run of empty slots made the next slot more or less likely to hold an event. A long quiet spell would then carry information about the remaining wait, and the exponential would be the wrong model. Among continuous distributions, the exponential is the only one that is memoryless.
A deployed classifier serves 50 requests per second and misclassifies each one independently with probability \(10^{-4}\). Mistakes then arrive at a rate of 0.005 per second, so the time to the first mistake is about exponential, with a scale of 200 seconds. A clean window of ten minutes lasts three scales, which gives it a probability of \(e^{-3}\), about 0.050. And by memorylessness, after 10 clean minutes you still expect to wait 200 seconds for the first mistake.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.7 Laplace
The Laplace distribution is symmetric noise with exponential tails, and one of the two standard noise distributions in later parts of this book. Its density is an exponential density on each side of a centre \(\mu\), mirrored, with each side carrying half the probability. With scale \(b\), written \(\mathrm{Lap}(\mu, b)\), the density is \[f(x) = \frac{1}{2b}e^{-|x - \mu|/b}. \tag{1.19}\] This chapter writes \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) when the centre is zero.
Most facts about the Laplace follow from the exponential. To see why, take the centre to be zero. The density then has the same value at \(x\) and at \(-x\), so the size \(|X|\) of a draw collects the density from both sides. Its density is therefore \(\frac1be^{-x/b}\) for every size \(x \ge 0\), which is exactly the \(\mathrm{Exp}(b)\) density.
The two-sided tail is therefore the exponential tail, \[\Pr[|X| \ge t] = e^{-t/b}, \tag{1.20}\] and each side carries half of it. The average size of a draw is likewise \(b\), the exponential’s mean. For the variance, recall that the average square of a quantity is its variance plus its squared mean, which for the exponential is \(b^2 + b^2 = 2b^2\). A Laplace draw has the same square as its size, and its mean is zero by symmetry, so its variance is also \(2b^2\). Turned around, a Laplace distribution with standard deviation \(\sigma\) has scale \(\sigma/\sqrt2\).
Each side has an exponential tail, so, as for the exponential, the MGF is finite only for \(|\lambda| < 1/b\). There it equals \[M_X(\lambda) = \frac{1}{1 - b^2\lambda^2}. \tag{1.21}\]
The same picture suggests how to build a Laplace draw. Take two independent exponential draws and subtract the second from the first, so that the first supplies the right half and the second, negated, supplies the left half. The MGFs confirm it, because the product \(1/(1 - b\lambda)\) times \(1/(1 + b\lambda)\) is the Laplace MGF. On a million samples, the difference has a cumulative distribution function (CDF) within 0.0006 of the Laplace CDF, and Figure 1.3 shows the fit.






Figure 1.3: Histogram of \(\mathrm{Exp}(1) - \mathrm{Exp}(1)\) samples against the \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) density.



Figure 1.4 puts a Laplace distribution with scale 1 and a normal distribution side by side, both with variance 2. On a linear scale the Laplace has a sharp peak at zero and fatter tails, and a log scale shows why. Taking the logarithm of a density undoes the exponential and leaves the exponent, plus a constant from the factor in front. So the normal’s log density is a parabola, while the Laplace’s log density is two straight lines. Far enough out, a parabola always falls below a line, so the normal’s tails are much lighter. A Laplace draw, for example, lands at least three scales from zero with probability \(e^{-3}\), about 0.050. A normal draw with the same variance gets that far with probability about 0.034, and further out the gap grows quickly.






Figure 1.4: Normal and Laplace densities with variance 2, on linear and log scales. The log of the normal density is a parabola; the log of the Laplace density is two straight lines.



The Laplace also explains absolute-error regression. Suppose each target is a linear function of its features plus independent Laplace noise. Then the logarithm of the likelihood is the sum of the log densities of the errors. Each of these is a constant minus the absolute error divided by \(b\), so the most likely fit is the one with the smallest sum of absolute errors. Normal noise leads in the same way to least squares. With no features, the fit is the median, which ignores how far out an extreme point lies and so resists outliers.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.8 Normal
The normal distribution appears whenever many small independent effects add up, and it is the default model for measurement noise. With mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), the normal distribution is written \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\). Its density is \[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{1.22}\] Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation turns any normal quantity into a standard normal, with mean 0 and variance 1. Write \(\Phi(t)\) for the chance that a standard normal lands below \(t\). Every normal probability reduces to it, since the chance that \(X\) lands below \(x\) is \[\Pr[X \le x] = \Phi\Big(\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\Big). \tag{1.23}\] The function \(\Phi\) has no closed form, so code computes it from the complementary error function, as Section 1.12 shows.
The normal MGF is finite for every \(\lambda\), and it equals \[M_X(\lambda) = e^{\mu\lambda + \sigma^2\lambda^2/2}. \tag{1.24}\] It is finite because, in the exponent, the weight grows along a straight line while the density falls along a parabola, and the parabola always wins.
The exponent of the MGF is quadratic in \(\lambda\), and that makes normal noise easy to combine. Scaling a quantity by a factor \(a\) is the same, inside its MGF, as turning the dial to \(a\lambda\), while adding independent quantities multiplies their MGFs, which adds the exponents. Both operations keep the exponent quadratic, so a weighted sum of independent normal quantities is again normal. Its mean is the weighted sum of the means, and its variance is the sum of the variances, each multiplied by its squared weight: \[\sum_i a_iX_i \sim \mathcal N\Big(\sum_i a_i\mu_i,\ \sum_i a_i^2\sigma_i^2\Big). \tag{1.25}\] Among distributions with finite variance, only the normal keeps every weighted sum of independent copies in its own family, once a shift and a rescaling are allowed. This is a classical result of Lévy. The Laplace, for example, fails the test, because the sum of two independent Laplace draws has the MGF \(1/(1 - b^2\lambda^2)^2\), which is not a Laplace MGF.

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.9 Normal noise in many dimensions
Noise is often added to a whole vector at once, such as a model’s parameters. Such noise is written \(X \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\) when it is a vector of \(d\) independent coordinates, each normal with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\). The identity matrix \(I_d\) in the notation records that the coordinates are independent and alike. Two facts about such a vector are used constantly.
The first fact is that the noise looks the same in every direction. Project the vector onto a fixed direction, given by a unit vector whose squared entries add up to 1. The projection is a weighted sum of independent normal coordinates, so it is normal with variance \(\sigma^2\) times the sum of the squared weights, which is just \(\sigma^2\). So along any direction fixed in advance, the noise is a single draw from \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). The direction must not depend on the noise, though, because along the noise’s own direction the projection is the vector’s full length.
The second fact is that this length is large and predictable. The squared length is a sum of \(d\) independent and alike squared coordinates, each with mean \(\sigma^2\), so its mean is \(d\sigma^2\). By the rules for sums, its standard deviation divided by its mean is \(\sqrt{2/d}\), and taking a square root halves a small relative deviation. So the length itself sits close to \(\sigma\sqrt d\), with a relative spread of about \(1/\sqrt{2d}\). A normal vector in high dimension is almost never near the origin and lives on a thin shell (Table 1.1 and Figure 1.5).

title: 1  Probability distributions
text:
1.10 The central limit theorem
The central limit theorem (CLT) explains why the normal distribution is everywhere. Write \(S_n\) for a sum of \(n\) independent draws from one distribution. Suppose each draw has mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\). The sum then has mean \(n\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\sqrt n\), so subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation gives a quantity with mean 0 and variance 1: \[Z_n = \frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}. \tag{1.26}\] The CLT says that, whatever the distribution of each draw, the shape of this standardized sum approaches the standard normal as \(n\) grows. The variance must be finite, because the standardization divides by it.
The theorem is easiest to see from a badly skewed distribution, such as the exponential. Figure 1.6 shows the standardized sum of \(n\) exponential draws. At \(n = 1\) it is the exponential itself, with a hard wall where the draw is zero, while by \(n = 30\) the curve is close to the standard normal. A small lean remains, though.






Figure 1.6: The standardized sum of \(n\) independent \(\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) variables for \(n = 1, 2, 5, 30\): histogram of 50,000 simulated sums, the exact density from \(\mathrm{Gamma}(n, 1)\), and the \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) density. The skewed exponential becomes a normal step by step.



The leftover lean is measured by the skewness, the average cubed deviation from the mean divided by the cube of the standard deviation: \[\frac{\mathbb E\big[(X - \mathbb E X)^3\big]}{\sigma^3}. \tag{1.27}\] Cubed deviations keep their sign, positive above the mean and negative below it, so a long right tail makes the skewness positive. A normal distribution is symmetric, so its skewness is zero, while one exponential draw with scale 1 has skewness 2. Cubed deviations add over independent draws, just as squared ones do. So a sum of \(n\) draws has an average cubed deviation of \(2n\), while the cube of its standard deviation is \(n^{3/2}\). Their ratio, the skewness of the sum, is \(2/\sqrt n\), which falls only like \(1/\sqrt n\). The largest gap between the sum’s CDF and the normal CDF falls at the same rate (Table 1.2).

Multiply each gap by \(\sqrt n\) and the product settles near 0.133, so the error decays like \(1/\sqrt n\). The Berry–Esseen theorem says that this rate holds in general, provided the average cubed distance of a draw from its mean is finite. Its bound on the gap grows with that cubed distance, so the more skewed the draws, the more of them you need. A common rule of thumb says that the normal approximation to a binomial count is reasonable once its variance \(np(1-p)\) is about 10 or more. The normal curve also fits the Poisson in Figure 1.1. That is because a Poisson count with mean 5 is a sum of five independent Poisson counts with mean 1, so the CLT already applies to it.
The CLT describes the bulk of the distribution, not its far tails. The error it controls is an absolute error of order \(1/\sqrt n\), while a tail probability that a guarantee depends on can be far smaller than that. In the far tail, the normal approximation can therefore be wrong by a large factor. Bounding such tails is the job of Concentration inequalities.

title: 1  Probability distributions
section: 1.11 A density against its shifted copy
text:
1.11 A density against its shifted copy
Suppose you see a noisy measurement \(x\), which is an unknown value plus noise \(X\). The noise has a density, written \(f\), centred at zero, and the unknown value can only be zero or a known shift \(s\). How strongly can one observation favour one candidate over the other?
If the value is zero, the observation has the density \(f(x)\). If the value is \(s\), it has the density \(f(x - s)\), the same curve moved sideways by the shift. The ratio of the two densities at the observation says how many times more likely it is if the value is zero than if it is the shift. Its logarithm is the log ratio: \[L(x) = \ln f(x) - \ln f(x - s). \tag{1.28}\] A positive log ratio favours zero, and a negative one favours the shift. If the log ratio is bounded, no single observation can make one candidate much more likely than the other. If it is unbounded, some observations settle the question almost for certain.
The answer comes from the shapes of the two log densities in Figure 1.4. For normal noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\), the log density is a parabola, and both copies have the same curvature. Subtracting them cancels the squared terms and leaves a straight line: \[L(x) = \frac{s^2 - 2sx}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{1.29}\] A line with a nonzero slope has no bound, so for normal noise the log ratio grows without limit as the observation moves out.
The Laplace’s log density is \(-|x|/b\) plus a constant, so up to the constant it is a distance from the centre divided by the scale. The constant cancels in the log ratio, which leaves the difference of two such distances. Moving the centre by the shift changes the distance from any point by at most the size of the shift. So the log ratio can never exceed \(|s|/b\) in size: \[L(x) = \frac{|x - s| - |x|}{b}, \qquad |L(x)| \le \frac{|s|}{b}. \tag{1.30}\] The bound is reached, not just approached. For a positive shift, every observation outside the stretch between the two centres is exactly \(s\) closer to one centre than to the other. Between the centres, the log ratio falls along a straight line from one limit to the other.
Table 1.3 puts numbers on both formulas, with the shift and both noise scales set to 1. Both log ratios are zero at the midpoint, where the candidates are equally plausible, but further out they part ways. At \(x = 10\) the normal log ratio is \(-9.5\). That makes the observation about 13,360 times more likely under the shifted candidate. The Laplace, by contrast, never says more than about 2.72 times, however far out the observation lies (Figure 1.7).

Unbounded does not mean often large, though, because the extreme ratios sit in tails that carry very little probability. The next three chapters make this precise. Concentration inequalities bounds how rare those observations are, and Divergences averages the log ratio. Hypothesis testing says what an observer can decide from it.

Rules of thumb

Means always add. Variances add only for independent quantities, so an average of \(n\) independent draws has its standard deviation divided by \(\sqrt n\).

For a shift \(s\), the Laplace log ratio is at most \(|s|/b\). The normal log ratio is unbounded, but large only in tails that carry very little probability.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.1 Why this matters
Almost every number in a private system is random. Some are random by design, like the noise a mechanism adds to a count. Others are random because of how they were measured. An error rate depends on which examples happened to land in the test set, and the size of a randomly sampled minibatch changes from one step to the next. Before you rely on any of these numbers, you need to know how far it can stray from the value you actually care about.
A concentration inequality answers that question. It tells you how wide to make an interval around your estimate so that the true value falls outside it only rarely, say once in a thousand runs. This chapter calls that rare event a failure, and the chance of it the failure probability, written \(\beta\). It calls the distance from the estimate to either end of the interval the width, so the interval reaches one width on each side.
How wide the interval must be depends on how much you know about the random quantity. If you know only its variance, the width grows quickly as you ask for a smaller failure probability. If you also know the shape of its distribution far from the centre, the width grows very slowly. For a 95% interval the difference is modest, under a factor of two in the examples below. But later parts of this book often ask for failure probabilities of one in a hundred thousand or less. At one in a million, knowing that shape can make an interval a hundred times narrower. This chapter shows how to use everything you know.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.2 Knowing only the variance: Markov and Chebyshev
text:
2.2 Knowing only the variance: Markov and Chebyshev
Every bound in this chapter starts from Markov’s inequality. It applies only to quantities that cannot be negative, such as a waiting time, a count or a squared error. For such a quantity, knowing the average alone limits how often it can be large. Suppose customers wait 2 minutes at a counter on average. Then at most a quarter of them can wait 8 minutes or more. If more than a quarter did, those customers alone would push the average above 2 minutes, and no customer can have a negative wait that pulls it back down. In general, take a quantity \(X\) that cannot be negative, and write \(\mathbb E[X]\) for its average. For any positive threshold \(a\), Markov’s inequality says that \[\Pr[X \ge a] \le \frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}. \tag{2.1}\] In the example, an average of 2 minutes and a threshold of 8 give the bound of a quarter.
The requirement that the quantity cannot be negative is what makes the argument work. A quantity that can be negative can balance a large value with negative ones, and then its average says nothing about how often it is large. A gain that averages zero, for example, could be large and positive half the time and equally large and negative the other half.
On its own, Markov’s inequality is rarely useful, because it ignores how spread out the quantity is. What makes it useful is that you can apply it to other quantities built from \(X\), and the first of these is the squared distance from the mean. Write \(\mu\) for the mean of \(X\) and \(\sigma^2\) for its variance, the average squared distance from \(\mu\). A squared distance is never negative, so Markov’s inequality applies to it, with \(\sigma^2\) as the average. Now pick a distance \(t\). Being at least \(t\) from the mean is the same as having a squared distance of at least \(t^2\), so the chance of it is at most \(\sigma^2/t^2\). This is Chebyshev’s inequality: \[\Pr[|X - \mu| \ge t] \le \frac{\sigma^2}{t^2}. \tag{2.2}\]
To turn the bound into an interval, set the right side equal to \(\beta\) and solve for \(t\), which gives \(t = \sigma/\sqrt\beta\). So with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the quantity lies within \(\sigma/\sqrt\beta\) of its mean. The same works for an average of \(n\) independent samples. Averaging divides the variance by \(n\), so the width becomes \(\sigma/\sqrt{n\beta}\).
Chebyshev’s bound is weak because it must hold for every distribution with the given variance, including those that hide their spread in a rare spike far from the mean. To cover such spikes, the width has to grow like \(1/\sqrt\beta\) as the failure probability falls. Most noise is better behaved than that, because its tail, the chance of landing far from the centre, falls off quickly. For a quantity whose tail falls off like a normal distribution’s, the width is only \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\beta)}\), and the next section shows where this comes from. Table 2.1 compares the two widths.

At one in a million the gap becomes enormous, since Chebyshev needs 1,000 standard deviations where the normal-shaped tail needs 5.3. So Chebyshev’s inequality is fine for a quick 95% error bar, and useless when failures must be very rare.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.3 Normal and Laplace noise
When you know the distribution of the noise, you don’t need a general inequality. You can read the width directly off the distribution’s tail. The two noise distributions this book uses most are the Laplace and the normal distributions (Probability distributions), both centred at zero.
Laplace noise, written \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\), has a scale \(b\) that sets its typical size. Its tail has an exact formula, which says how likely a draw \(L\) is to land more than a distance \(t\) from zero: \[\Pr[|L| > t] = e^{-t/b}. \tag{2.3}\] Setting this chance equal to \(\beta\) and solving for \(t\) gives the width, so with probability \(1 - \beta\) the noise stays within \(b\ln(1/\beta)\) of zero.
Chebyshev’s inequality would use only the variance of Laplace noise, which is \(2b^2\), and it pays for that. For scale 1 and a 95% interval, it gives a width of about 6.3, while the exact tail gives about 3.0. At a failure probability of one in a million, the gap grows to 1,414 against 13.8. So ignoring the shape of the noise makes the interval a hundred times wider.
Normal noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\) has no simple formula for its tail, but a simple bound on it is enough to compute the width. For a draw \(Z\) of that noise, it says \[\Pr[|Z| > t] \le e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{2.4}\] Solving for \(t\) in the same way gives the width \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\beta)}\) from Table 2.1.
The shapes of the two tails explain why the widths grow at different rates. The Laplace tail falls like \(e^{-t}\), so its width grows like \(\ln(1/\beta)\). The normal tail falls faster, like \(e^{-t^2}\), so only the squared width grows like \(\ln(1/\beta)\). That leaves the width itself growing like the square root of the logarithm, which is very slowly indeed.
Sometimes you add noisy values together, for example to compute a total from several noisy counts. Write \(S\) for the sum of \(k\) independent Laplace draws with scale \(b\). Near its centre the sum looks like a normal distribution, as the central limit theorem (CLT) predicts. Far from the centre, though, its tail keeps the slow decay of a single Laplace draw, like \(e^{-t}\) rather than \(e^{-t^2}\). A bound that is valid everywhere has to describe both regions: \[\Pr[S \ge t] \le \exp\Big(-\min\Big(\frac{t^2}{8kb^2}, \frac{t}{4b}\Big)\Big). \tag{2.5}\] The constants come from the derivation in the full edition. What matters here is the shape. Up to \(t = 2kb\), where the two terms inside the minimum are equal, the first term is the smaller one, and the bound has the normal shape. Beyond that point the second term takes over, and the bound falls only like \(e^{-t}\), as a Laplace tail does.
The difference matters whenever you need a guarantee. Take 10 draws with scale 1, and approximate their sum by a normal distribution with the same mean and variance. That approximation says the sum reaches 20 with probability \(3.9\times10^{-6}\), but simulation gives \(3.4\times10^{-5}\), about nine times more (Figure 2.1). A system that trusted the approximation would therefore fail nine times as often as it promised. The bound above gives \(6.7\times10^{-3}\) at the same point, which is far from the truth but never below it. So when the answer must be a guarantee, use a bound, not the CLT.






Figure 2.1: Empirical tail of a sum of 10 \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) draws, against the bound above and the normal approximation, which badly underestimates the far tail.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.4 Many quantities at once: the union bound
text:
2.4 Many quantities at once: the union bound
Often you need many random quantities to stay close to their targets at the same time. A system might release \(k\) noisy counts and need every one of them to be accurate. The union bound handles this. It says that the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their separate chances. The sum can overcount, because an outcome in which two events happen is counted twice, but it never misses an outcome. So if you want all \(k\) counts to be accurate except with probability \(\beta\), ask each one to fail with probability at most \(\beta/k\).
Dividing the failure probability by \(k\) costs little, because the widths depend on it only through a logarithm, and the logarithm turns the division into an addition: \[\ln\frac{k}{\beta} = \ln k + \ln\frac1\beta. \tag{2.6}\] All \(k\) Laplace draws then stay within \(b\ln(k/\beta)\) of zero, and all \(k\) normal draws within \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(k/\beta)}\). Because the number of quantities enters only through a logarithm, controlling many of them at once is cheap.
The union bound looks crude, but for rare, independent failures it is nearly exact. When the failures are independent and each is rare, two at once are rarer still, so the double counting adds almost nothing. For an example, take 100 Laplace draws with scale 1, and look at the one furthest from zero. With a failure probability of 0.05, the union bound gives the width \(\ln(100/0.05) = 7.60\). In simulation, the draw furthest from zero lands beyond 7.60 in 4.86% of runs, just under the 5% the bound allows (Figure 2.2). The bound is far less exact when the failures are correlated. If all \(k\) events were the same event, the sum would count it \(k\) times.






Figure 2.2: Left: the width \(b\ln(k/\beta)\) for the draw furthest from zero among \(k\) Laplace draws grows like \(\ln k\). Right: the simulated probability that this draw lands beyond the width stays near \(\beta = 0.05\) for every \(k\).

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
text:
2.5 Counts: the Chernoff bound
Many quantities in machine learning are counts, such as the errors on a test set, the examples in a sampled minibatch or the records that match a query. A count adds up many yes-or-no outcomes. When you need a very small failure probability, Chebyshev’s bound for a count is far too loose. The Chernoff bound does much better, with a tail that falls exponentially, by adding one more idea. It assumes that the outcomes are independent of one another, and the calculation below shows where it needs this.
The idea is to apply Markov’s inequality to \(e^{\lambda X}\) instead of to \(X\) itself, where \(\lambda\) is a positive number you are free to choose. The exponential keeps the order of values, so \(X\) is at least \(t\) exactly when \(e^{\lambda X}\) is at least \(e^{\lambda t}\). Markov’s inequality then gives \[\Pr[X \ge t] \le \frac{\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]}{e^{\lambda t}}. \tag{2.7}\] The exponential turns a modest gap between \(X\) and \(t\) into a huge gap between \(e^{\lambda X}\) and \(e^{\lambda t}\). The threshold on the bottom of the fraction is then far above the typical values on top, so the bound becomes small. The bound holds for every positive \(\lambda\), and you pick the one that makes it smallest. For a count, the average on top, \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]\), is also easy to compute, because the exponential of a sum is a product of exponentials. This is where independence comes in. For independent outcomes, the average of that product is the product of the averages, one factor per outcome.
Carrying out this calculation for a count \(S\) gives a bound in terms of two numbers. The first is the expected count, written \(\mu\). The second is the relative deviation you ask about, written \(\delta\), so that \(\delta = 0.2\) means 20% above or below \(\mu\). The two Chernoff bounds are \[\Pr[S \ge (1+\delta)\mu] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{\delta^2\mu}{2+\delta}\Big), \qquad \Pr[S \le (1-\delta)\mu] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{\delta^2\mu}{2}\Big). \tag{2.8}\] The first bounds the chance that the count overshoots its mean by the fraction \(\delta\). The second bounds the chance that it undershoots, and holds for \(\delta\) between 0 and 1. For small \(\delta\), setting either bound to \(\beta\) gives a one-sided width of about \(\sqrt{2\mu\ln(1/\beta)}\).
The exponent contains the expected count \(\mu\), not the number of trials, and this has a cost and a benefit. The cost is that a count of rare events has a small error relative to its mean only once you expect many of them. For example, a million trials that each succeed with probability one in a million expect a single success. That count is far from concentrated, since no success at all and two successes are both common outcomes.
The benefit is that the calculation works with each outcome’s own probability before adding them up into \(\mu\). An outcome that is a yes with probability \(p\) has variance \(p(1-p)\), which is about \(p\) when \(p\) is small. The variance of a count is the sum of its outcomes’ variances, so a count of rare events has a variance of about \(\mu\). The Chernoff bound adapts to that small variance. A bound that knew only that each outcome is 0 or 1 would have to assume the largest variance such an outcome can have, which is 0.25. The next section shows how much that costs.
The overshoot and undershoot bounds also differ. For large \(\delta\), the exponent of the overshoot bound grows like \(\delta\mu\) rather than \(\delta^2\mu\), so the overshoot bound falls more slowly. Counts have long right tails, like the Poisson distribution, so a count can overshoot its mean by a lot far more easily than it can undershoot it.
Here is how the bound is used in practice. A training loop forms each minibatch by including each of 60,000 examples independently with probability 0.01. The batch size is a count with expected value \(\mu = 600\). If your code or your analysis assumes a batch size near 600, you need to know how often that assumption fails. With \(\delta = 0.2\), the overshoot bound says a batch is more than 20% too large with probability at most \(1.8\times10^{-5}\). The undershoot bound gives \(6.1\times10^{-6}\) for a batch more than 20% too small. Adding the two, a single batch leaves the range \(600 \pm 20\%\) with probability about \(2.4\times10^{-5}\). Over 1,000 training steps, the union bound multiplies this by 1,000, so the chance that any batch leaves the range is about 0.024.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.6 Averages of bounded quantities: Hoeffding and Bernstein
text:
2.6 Averages of bounded quantities: Hoeffding and Bernstein
Often you know neither the distribution nor the variance, only the range. A loss clipped to lie between 0 and 1 is one example, and a 0/1 indicator of a mistake is another. Knowing the range already tells you a lot. A quantity confined to an interval cannot have a heavy tail, one that reaches far out with sizable probability, because it cannot go past the ends at all. Its variance cannot be large either. The most spread-out quantity on an interval puts half its probability on each end, like a fair coin, and its variance is a quarter of the squared length of the interval.
Hoeffding’s inequality turns this into a width for an average. Take \(n\) independent quantities, each in the same interval from \(a\) to \(b\). Write \(\bar X_n\) for their average and \(\mu\) for its expected value. Hoeffding’s inequality says that the average has a normal-shaped tail, as if each quantity had the largest variance its range allows. With probability at least \(1-\beta\), \[|\bar X_n - \mu| < (b - a)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{2n}}. \tag{2.9}\] The 2 inside the logarithm appears because the interval has two sides, and each side is allowed half the failure probability. The width shrinks like \(1/\sqrt n\) as you add samples. As you lower the failure probability, it grows only like the square root of a logarithm, as for normal noise.
The most common use is to compare a model’s error on its training data with its true error, its average loss on new data from the same source. For one fixed model, the training error is an average of \(n\) losses between 0 and 1, so Hoeffding’s inequality applies directly. A learner, however, picks its model after seeing the data. The model it picks is the one that looks best on the training data, which makes it the one whose training error is most likely to be too optimistic. So the bound must hold for every model the learner might pick.
Suppose the candidates form a finite set \(H\), and write \(|H|\) for their number. The union bound over all of them puts an extra \(\ln|H|\) inside the logarithm. With probability at least \(1-\beta\), every candidate’s training error is then within \[\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2|H|/\beta)}{2n}} \tag{2.10}\] of its true error. Because the number of candidates enters only through its logarithm, even a huge set of them costs little.
Knowing only the range is Hoeffding’s strength, since there is nothing to estimate. It is also its weakness, because the inequality assumes the largest variance that the range allows. A 0/1 quantity that is rarely 1 has a much smaller variance than that. The gap is therefore widest exactly when you measure small rates, such as a false-positive rate.
Suppose a classifier makes 1 false positive on 1,000 negative examples, and you want a 95% upper bound on its true false-positive rate. An upper bound needs only one side of the interval, so it uses \(\ln(1/\beta)\) in place of \(\ln(2/\beta)\). With \(n = 1{,}000\), this one-sided Hoeffding bound adds about 0.039 to the measured rate, so the added width alone is about 40 times the rate you measured. The culprit is the variance Hoeffding’s inequality assumes, which is 0.25, the variance of a fair coin. A single 0/1 outcome that is 1 with probability near 0.001 has a variance of only about 0.001.
Bernstein’s inequality fixes this by using the variance. Write \(\sigma^2\) for the variance of each quantity, and \(M\) for the largest distance it can be from its mean. Then the one-sided width is about \[\sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2\ln(1/\beta)}{n}} + \frac{2M\ln(1/\beta)}{3n}. \tag{2.11}\] The first term is the normal-shaped width, computed with the true variance. The second term pays for the range, but it shrinks like \(1/n\) instead of \(1/\sqrt n\). For the classifier, take \(M = 1\) and estimate the variance as 0.001. Bernstein’s inequality then adds about 0.0045, against Hoeffding’s 0.039. This calculation is only a heuristic, because the variance was estimated from the same data. A rigorous version, empirical Bernstein, gives a wider interval.
The exact answer comes from the binomial distribution itself, through the Clopper–Pearson interval. Its one-sided 95% upper bound on the rate is 0.0047, a little below the measured rate plus Bernstein’s 0.0045. The same number is the upper end of a two-sided 90% interval, which is how Hypothesis testing computes it.
Figure 2.3 shows the cost of ignoring the variance on a second example. It averages 200 yes-or-no outcomes (Bernoulli variables), each a yes with probability 0.1, and asks how likely the average is to reach 0.15. Hoeffding’s inequality bounds that chance by 0.37. Chebyshev’s inequality does better here, with 0.18, because it uses the variance. At this moderate deviation its \(1/t^2\) has not yet fallen far behind an exponential tail, so knowing the variance counts for more than knowing the tail’s shape. The Chernoff bound uses both and gets 0.135. Even that is far above the true chance of about \(9.6\times10^{-3}\), because a bound must cover every case its assumptions allow.






Figure 2.3: Empirical tail of the mean of 200 Bernoulli(0.1) variables against the Markov, Chebyshev, Hoeffding and Chernoff bounds.

title: 2  Concentration inequalities
section: 2.7 Functions of many inputs: McDiarmid and Azuma
text:
2.7 Functions of many inputs: McDiarmid and Azuma
So far, every quantity was a sum of independent pieces. Two common situations break this. A trained model’s error is a complicated function of its training data, not a sum. And in a sequential procedure, each step can depend on what happened before, so the pieces are not independent. Concentration still holds in both situations, provided that no single input or step can move the result by much.
Start with a function \(f\) of independent inputs \(X_1, \dots, X_n\), and write \(X\) for all of them together. Suppose that changing only the \(i\)-th input, with the others held fixed, moves the result by at most an amount \(c_i\). McDiarmid’s inequality says that the result then concentrates around its average as tightly as a sum of pieces with ranges \(c_i\) would: \[\Pr[f(X) - \mathbb E f(X) \ge t] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_ic_i^2}\Big). \tag{2.12}\]
The reason is easiest to see if you reveal the inputs one at a time and keep a running best guess of the result. Before you see any input, the best guess is the average result. After you see the first input, it is the average over the inputs you have not seen yet, with the first one fixed. Each revealed input updates the guess in this way, and after the last one the guess is the result itself. So the deviation you want to bound is the sum of \(n\) updates.
Two facts about these updates make the sum concentrate. First, an update is zero on average. Before you see an input, you cannot predict which way it will move your guess, or that prediction would already be part of the guess. Second, the \(i\)-th update is small. Changing the \(i\)-th input moves the result by at most \(c_i\), so it moves the guess by at most \(c_i\) too. The updates are not independent, since each one depends on the inputs before it. The next paragraphs explain why the two facts are enough anyway.
For the training error of a fixed model, with losses between 0 and 1, changing one example moves the average by at most \(1/n\). With \(c_i = 1/n\) for every input, McDiarmid’s inequality gives back Hoeffding’s bound. Its real use is for functions that are not averages, such as the error of a model retrained on the data, and Algorithmic stability and generalization uses it that way. The amount \(c_i\) must hold for every possible change to the \(i\)-th input, not just for typical ones, because the argument charges each input its largest possible move. This per-record influence returns in later parts under the name sensitivity.
Hoeffding’s inequality was stated for independent pieces, but its conclusion needs less. It is enough that each piece averages zero given everything before it, and lies in a short interval. A running total whose steps average zero given the past is called a martingale, and Azuma’s inequality bounds how far it drifts. Suppose the \(k\)-th step always lies in an interval of length \(d_k\), and write \(D\) for the total drift. Then the chance that it drifts upward by \(t\) or more is at most \[\Pr[D \ge t] \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_kd_k^2}\Big), \tag{2.13}\] which is McDiarmid’s bound with the step lengths \(d_k\) in place of the influences \(c_i\).
Azuma’s inequality covers procedures that adapt as they go. As an example, flip a coin 200 times, and let each flip depend on the one before. If the previous flip was heads, flip a coin that lands heads with probability 0.7. Otherwise, including for the first flip, use a coin that lands heads with probability 0.3. Because the flips depend on each other, Hoeffding’s inequality does not apply, but you can still bound the drift. To get it, count the heads, and subtract the number of heads you would expect from the coins you chose. Each step of the drift is then the flip’s outcome, 1 or 0, minus the chosen coin’s probability of heads. Given the past, a step averages zero and lies in an interval of length 1. Azuma’s inequality bounds the chance of an upward drift of 20 or more by \(1.83\times10^{-2}\), while simulation gives \(1.12\times10^{-3}\) (Figure 2.4).






Figure 2.4: Empirical tail of the drift in the adaptive coin game against the Azuma bound.



The bound is loose partly for the same reason as Hoeffding’s. It assumes that each step has the largest variance its interval allows, which is 0.25. The true variance of each step is 0.21 for either coin, since \(0.7 \times 0.3 = 0.3 \times 0.7\).

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.1 Why this matters
Many questions in machine learning come down to comparing two distributions. You fit a model to data and want to know how far the fit is from the truth. A feature drifts in production, or an A/B test changes a conversion rate, and you want to know how many samples it takes to see the change. You perturb the data a little and want to know how much a downstream statistic can move. Later parts of this book ask the same questions about the outputs of an algorithm run on two different inputs.
A divergence answers such a question with one number, which is zero when the two distributions are equal and grows as they become easier to tell apart. There are several divergences because there are several questions. Take a die that is either fair or loaded so that a six comes up half the time. You can ask how much one roll tells you, on average, about which die you hold. You can also ask how strongly a single roll can point toward the die you do not hold, or how often the best possible guess from one roll is right. Each question has its own divergence. In general a divergence is not a distance, if only because it can change when you swap the two distributions.
One quantity organizes the whole chapter. Suppose you see an outcome and want to know which of two distributions, call them \(P\) and \(Q\), produced it. Write \(p(x)\) and \(q(x)\) for the probabilities that \(P\) and \(Q\) give to an outcome \(x\). The natural comparison is their quotient, the likelihood ratio \[r(x) = \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, \tag{3.1}\] which says how many times more likely the outcome is under \(P\) than under \(Q\).
The logarithm of the ratio, written \(L(x) = \ln r(x)\), is the evidence that the outcome gives for \(P\). It is positive when the outcome favours \(P\), negative when it favours \(Q\), and zero when the outcome says nothing. The logarithm is there because evidence from independent observations should add up, and a logarithm turns a product of ratios into a sum. With natural logarithms, evidence is measured in units called nats.
On the die, let \(P\) be the loaded die and \(Q\) the fair one. The loaded die gives a six probability 0.5 and each other face probability 0.1, while the fair die gives every face probability \(\frac16\). A six is therefore three times as likely under the loaded die, which gives evidence \(\ln 3 = 1.10\) nats for “loaded”. Any other roll is 0.6 times as likely under the loaded die, so it gives \(\ln 0.6 = -0.51\) nats, weak evidence for “fair”.
Every divergence in this chapter is a summary of the likelihood ratio, and each summary answers one of the questions above. Because they are all built from the same ratio, they obey one shared rule, the data processing inequality, which says that processing the data can never make a divergence grow.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.2 KL divergence
Roll the die many times and add up the evidence from each roll. If the die is loaded, sixes come up often and the sum climbs. If the die is fair, the many small negative terms win and the sum falls. Figure 3.1 shows eight runs of each, and each group drifts along a straight line despite the noise. The slope of the rising line is the average evidence per roll of the loaded die, and it is called the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of \(P\) from \(Q\). It measures how fast data from \(P\) convince you that they are not from \(Q\). The falling line’s slope is the same divergence with the two dice swapped, which comes up below.






Figure 3.1: Cumulative evidence for “loaded”, \(\sum_i\ln r(x_i)\), over 60 rolls. Blue: eight runs with the loaded die, drifting up at \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = 0.294\) nats per roll. Orange: eight runs with the fair die, drifting down at \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P) = 0.243\) nats per roll. Dashed lines are the averages.



Written out, the KL divergence is the average of the evidence over outcomes drawn from \(P\): \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P\left[\ln\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right] = \sum_x p(x)\ln\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}. \tag{3.2}\] Here \(\mathbb E_P\) is the average over an outcome \(X\) drawn from \(P\). For continuous distributions, \(p\) and \(q\) are densities and the sum becomes an integral. On the die, the six and the other five faces each have total probability 0.5 under \(P\), so the KL divergence is \(0.5\ln 0.6 + 0.5\ln 3 = 0.2939\) nats per roll.
The KL divergence is never negative, and it is zero only when \(P\) and \(Q\) are equal. This is Gibbs’ inequality, and it says that data from \(P\) never favour \(Q\) on average. The plain reason is that the logarithm bends downward, so the average of the logarithms of some numbers is at most the logarithm of their average. Apply this to the reversed ratio \(q/p\) under \(P\). Its average adds up the probabilities that \(Q\) gives to the outcomes \(P\) can produce, so it is at most 1. The average of \(\ln(q/p)\) is therefore at most \(\ln 1 = 0\), and the KL divergence, its negative, is at least 0.
The KL divergence is not symmetric, because it averages under its first argument. On the die, the divergence in the reverse direction, written \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)\), is only 0.2426. The difference lies in what each die produces. Rolls of the loaded die produce sixes, which are strong evidence for “loaded”, while rolls of the fair die produce mostly other faces, which are only weak evidence for “fair”. So a loaded die gives itself away faster than a fair one proves its innocence.
The most useful property of the KL divergence is that it adds up over independent observations. The probability of a pair of independent observations is the product of their probabilities, so the likelihood ratio of the pair is a product, and its logarithm is a sum. The averages then add too: \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1\times P_2\,\|\,Q_1\times Q_2) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1\|Q_1) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_2\|Q_2). \tag{3.3}\] Here \(P_1\times P_2\) is the distribution of a pair drawn independently from \(P_1\) and \(P_2\). So \(n\) independent samples from the same distribution carry \(n\) times the KL divergence of one, which is the straight line in Figure 3.1. Independence is a condition here, not a detail. When two observations are correlated, the second can partly repeat what the first already said, and its evidence no longer adds in full.
Additivity tells you how many observations you need. After \(n\) rolls of the loaded die, the total evidence has mean \(0.2939\,n\). Its standard deviation is \(0.8047\sqrt n\), because the evidence of one roll has standard deviation 0.8047 and the variances of independent rolls add. The mean drift grows like \(n\) and the noise only like \(\sqrt n\), so the drift wins in the end. It reaches one standard deviation of noise when \(0.2939\,n = 0.8047\sqrt n\), which happens after \((0.8047/0.2939)^2 = 7.50\) rolls. For other pairs, with a similar spread of evidence per observation, the same argument suggests that the number of observations you need grows like one over the KL divergence. The section on Pinsker’s inequality makes this precise.
The same number measures how well a model fits. Suppose the data come from \(p\) and you model them with \(q_\theta\), a density with parameter \(\theta\). Then \(\ln(p(x)/q_\theta(x))\) is the evidence that an outcome gives for the truth over the model. The KL divergence splits into two parts, and only the second depends on the model: \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q_\theta) = \mathbb E_P[\ln p(X)] - \mathbb E_P[\ln q_\theta(X)]. \tag{3.4}\] So minimizing the KL divergence over \(\theta\) is the same as maximizing the expected log-likelihood \(\mathbb E_P[\ln q_\theta(X)]\). You cannot compute that expectation, because you do not know \(p\), but its sample version, the average of \(\ln q_\theta\) over the data, is exactly what maximum likelihood maximizes. The KL divergence is infinite if the model gives zero probability to an outcome the data can produce, which is why practical models keep every probability positive.
Which direction you minimize matters, because each direction averages over different outcomes. The forward direction, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q_\theta)\), averages over the data, and where the data go but the model puts almost no probability, the evidence \(\ln(p/q_\theta)\) explodes. So the forward fit must cover every region the data visit, and it is called mass-covering. The reverse direction, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_\theta\|P)\), averages over the model instead. Regions the model ignores then cost nothing, but model probability where the data never go is punished heavily. So the reverse fit prefers to sit inside one region of the data and ignore the rest, and it is called mode-seeking. Variational inference, which approximates a hard distribution by a simpler model, minimizes the reverse direction. That direction needs only samples and densities from the model, and the target density only up to a constant.
Figure 3.2 fits a single normal distribution to data from two separated bumps. The forward fit copies the mean and the variance of the data, so it is a wide bump centred in the empty valley between them. The reverse fit sits on one bump and ignores the other, which gives it a forward KL divergence of 15.307 against 0.724 for the forward fit.






Figure 3.2: Fitting one Gaussian to a two-bump density \(p\). Minimizing \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\) matches the mean and variance and covers both bumps; minimizing \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\) locks onto one bump.

title: 3  Divergences
text:
3.3 Rényi divergence
The KL divergence is the average of \(\ln r\) under \(P\). Exponentiating an average of logarithms gives a geometric mean, so \(e^{D_{\mathrm{KL}}}\) is the geometric mean of the likelihood ratio. Nothing forces you to use the geometric mean, though. Other means of the same numbers give large values more weight, or less.
The usual means all belong to one family, the power means. To take the power mean with exponent \(s\), raise each value to the power \(s\), average, and undo the power. The harmonic mean has exponent \(-1\) and the arithmetic mean has exponent 1, while the geometric mean is the limit as the exponent goes to 0. As the exponent grows without bound, the power mean picks out the largest value.
On the die, the likelihood ratio under \(P\) takes two values with equal probability, 0.6 and 3. Table 3.1 lists its means. Each mean gives a larger value than the one before, because each leans harder on the large ratio.

The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\), a positive number you choose, is the logarithm of the power mean with exponent \(\alpha - 1\). Orders 1 and \(\infty\) are defined as limits, which the next paragraph explains. The definition is usually written as an average under \(Q\) rather than under \(P\). That gives the same value, because an outcome with likelihood ratio \(r\) counts that many times as much in an average under \(P\) as in one under \(Q\). So \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_Q\big[r^\alpha\big] = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_x p(x)^\alpha q(x)^{1-\alpha}. \tag{3.5}\] Think of the order as a dial. Near order 1 it gives the typical evidence, and as the order grows, the mean is pulled toward the largest ratio, so you get the worst case.
As the order goes to 1, the power mean tends to the geometric mean, so the Rényi divergence tends to the KL divergence. That is why the KL divergence is also written \(D_1\). A larger exponent leans harder on the large ratios, so power means grow with their exponent, and the Rényi divergence therefore never decreases as the order grows. As the order goes to infinity, the mean is dominated by the largest ratio. The limit is the max-divergence, the strongest evidence that any single outcome can give: \[D_\infty(P\|Q) = \ln\max_x r(x). \tag{3.6}\]
The max-divergence is also the largest ratio that \(P\) and \(Q\) can give to any event, not just to a single outcome: \[D_\infty(P\|Q) = \ln\max_{A:\,Q(A) > 0}\frac{P(A)}{Q(A)}. \tag{3.7}\] Here the maximum runs over every event \(A\) that has positive probability under \(Q\). The reason is that an event’s probability is a sum over its outcomes. So if no outcome is more than some factor as likely under \(P\) as under \(Q\), no sum of outcomes is either.
Like the KL divergence, every Rényi divergence adds up over independent observations. For a pair, \(r^\alpha\) is a product of one factor per observation. When the observations are independent, the average of that product is the product of the averages, and the logarithm turns it back into a sum. This is the same step the Chernoff bound uses in Concentration inequalities, and it needs independence for the same reason.
