Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter, except two that it cites: the Chernoff–Stein lemma and the exception for one-sided composite tests (Karlin–Rubin).

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.1 Why this matters
You often observe one thing and want to know how much it tells you about another thing you cannot see. A word in an email, for example, hints at whether the email is spam. In the same way, a noisy sensor reading carries some trace of the true state of a machine, and a model’s prediction is evidence about the true label. Information theory turns “how much” into a number, and it does so in two different ways, because you might be asking two different questions.
The first question is how many bits the observation saves you, on average, when you describe the hidden value. Shannon entropy and mutual information answer it. That makes them the language of compression, of the cross-entropy loss you train classifiers with, of decision-tree splits and of sending data over noisy links. The second question is how much more likely a single best guess becomes once you have seen the observation. Min-entropy and vulnerability answer that one, so they are the language of password strength, and of anyone who gets only one try.
Every quantity in this chapter is built from the logarithm of a probability. Shannon’s quantities average that logarithm over all the outcomes, while the one-guess quantities look only at the most likely outcome. The two kinds of answer usually agree, but when a rare outcome reveals a lot, they can disagree wildly. One may rank an observation as the less revealing of two, while one guess against it succeeds a million billion times as often. So later parts of the book need to know which one to trust.
Logarithms in this chapter are base 2, so every quantity is in bits. Divergences uses natural logarithms instead, whose unit is the nat, and one nat is about 1.443 bits.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.2 Entropy
A measure of uncertainty should give a fair coin one unit and two fair coins two units, and a coin that always lands heads none at all. Shannon entropy is the measure with these properties, and it is also the average number of bits that the best possible code needs to describe each value.
The construction starts from single outcomes. A rare outcome tells you more when it happens than a common one, so measure the information in an outcome by its surprisal, the logarithm of one over its probability. An outcome of probability one half then has a surprisal of 1 bit, one of probability one quarter has 2 bits, and a certain outcome has none. The logarithm is what makes two independent coins count twice, because their probabilities multiply and the logarithm turns that product into a sum.
Write \(H(X)\) for the entropy of a random variable \(X\), its average surprisal. Writing \(p(x)\) for the probability that \(X\) takes the value \(x\), it is \[H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x), \tag{5.1}\] where an outcome of probability zero adds nothing to the sum. For a coin that lands heads with probability \(p\), the sum has two terms and is called the binary entropy \(h(p)\). As Figure 5.1 shows, it is 1 bit for a fair coin and zero for a coin whose outcome is certain.
The binary entropy is very steep near the ends, which means it climbs quickly as the probability of heads moves away from 0. So even a quite lopsided coin keeps a lot of uncertainty. For example, a coin with an 11% chance of heads still carries \(h(0.11) = 0.4999\) bits, about half a bit.






Figure 5.1: The binary entropy \(h(p)\) against the min-entropy \(-\log_2\max(p, 1-p)\) of the same coin. Both are 1 bit at \(p = \frac12\); the min-entropy is lower everywhere else.



Entropy has a floor and a ceiling. It cannot be negative, because no probability exceeds 1 and so no surprisal is negative, and it is zero only when one value is certain. For the ceiling, write \(\lvert\mathcal X\rvert\) for the number of possible values. The entropy then lies between the two, \[0 \le H(X) \le \log\lvert\mathcal X\rvert, \tag{5.2}\] and it reaches the ceiling only when every value is equally likely. A uniform 4-digit PIN, for example, has \(\log_2 10{,}000 = 13.2877\) bits.
The reason for the ceiling is a comparison with the uniform distribution, under which every value has the same surprisal, \(\log\lvert\mathcal X\rvert\). The ceiling minus the entropy is the average gap between that surprisal and the true one. This average gap is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence from the true distribution to the uniform one. Divergences shows that this divergence is never negative, and zero only when the two distributions are the same.
Entropy depends only on the probabilities, never on the values themselves. Calling the outcomes “red” and “blue” instead of 0 and 1 does not change it.
Two variables need two more quantities. The joint entropy \(H(X, Y)\) is the entropy of the pair, computed from the table of joint probabilities. The conditional entropy \(H(X \mid Y)\) is the uncertainty about \(X\) that remains once you have seen \(Y\). Once you see a particular value \(y\), the uncertainty left is the entropy of the distribution of \(X\) given that value. But before you observe \(Y\), you do not know which value you will see. So the conditional entropy is the average of these entropies, weighted by how likely each \(y\) is: \[H(X \mid Y) = \sum_y p(y)\,H(X \mid Y = y). \tag{5.3}\]
The chain rule links the three. The uncertainty in the pair is the uncertainty in \(Y\), plus whatever uncertainty about \(X\) remains after that: \[H(X, Y) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y). \tag{5.4}\] It holds because the probability of a pair is the probability of \(y\) times the probability of \(x\) given \(y\). Taking logarithms turns this product into a sum of two surprisals, and the average of a sum is the sum of the averages, which here are \(H(Y)\) and \(H(X \mid Y)\). Applied again and again, the rule splits the uncertainty of many variables into one piece per variable, each piece being a variable’s uncertainty given the ones before it.
Learning something should not make you more uncertain, and on average it does not. The conditional entropy \(H(X \mid Y)\) is never larger than \(H(X)\), and the two are equal only when the variables are independent, as the next section explains. But a particular observation can increase the uncertainty, as a spam filter shows.
Let \(X\) be the label of an email, ham or spam, and let \(Y\) say whether it contains the word “offer”. One email in eight is spam, and every spam email contains the word, as does one ham email in seven. Table 5.1 gives the joint probabilities.

Before you read the email, it is spam with probability one in eight, so \(H(X) = h(1/8) = 0.5436\) bits, which is low because most email is ham. If the word is absent, the email is certainly ham and no uncertainty is left. But if the word is present, ham and spam are equally likely, so the uncertainty is a full bit. In that case, seeing the word made you more uncertain than you were before.
On average, though, the word helps. It is absent three times in four, leaving no uncertainty, and present one time in four, leaving 1 bit. So \(H(X \mid Y)\) is 0.25 bits, less than \(H(X)\). The common observation settles the question, while the rare one only muddies it (Figure 5.2). In short, conditioning reduces entropy on average, not for every observation.






Figure 5.2: Entropy of the spam label before observing the keyword, after each of the two possible observations, and on average. The rare observation raises the entropy above \(H(X)\) (dashed line); the average falls below it.



The same table checks the chain rule. The word is present with probability one quarter, so its entropy is \(H(Y) = h(1/4) = 0.8113\) bits. Adding the 0.25 bits that remain about the label gives 1.0613 bits, which is the entropy of the pair, computed directly from the three non-zero cells of the table.
Entropy is also part of the loss you train classifiers with. The cross-entropy loss averages, over the true labels, the surprisal that the model’s predicted probabilities assign to each label. That surprisal splits into two parts, the surprisal under the true label distribution plus the log ratio of the true probability to the predicted one. Averaged, the first part is the entropy of the true labels and the second is a KL divergence from the true distribution to the model’s. No model can remove the entropy, so training can only drive down the divergence.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.3 Mutual information and data processing
How much does observing \(Y\) tell you about \(X\)? A natural answer is the drop in uncertainty that it causes on average, which is called the mutual information and written \(I(X; Y)\).
Mutual information can also be written as a KL divergence \(D\) between two distributions of the pair. The first is the true joint distribution, written \(P_{XY}\). The second is the product \(P_XP_Y\) of the two separate distributions, which is what the joint distribution would be if \(X\) and \(Y\) were independent. The two forms give the same number: \[I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = D\big(P_{XY}\,\big\|\,P_XP_Y\big). \tag{5.5}\] A decision tree calls this quantity the information gain and uses it to choose a split, and many feature-selection methods use it to rank features.
The second form explains how mutual information behaves. It says that \(Y\) helps exactly to the extent that the joint distribution differs from independence. Mutual information is therefore never negative, because a KL divergence is never negative, and that is why the conditional entropy can never exceed \(H(X)\). It is zero only when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent. It is also symmetric, because swapping the two variables changes neither \(P_{XY}\) nor \(P_XP_Y\), so \(Y\) tells you exactly as much about \(X\) as the other way round.
Mutual information measures dependence of any kind, not only linear correlation. Take a variable that is symmetric around zero and can take more than one size, such as a value from −2 to 2, together with its square. Their correlation is zero, yet the square is fully determined by the variable, so their mutual information is positive.
Sometimes you already know \(Y\) and then learn a third variable, written \(Z\). The conditional mutual information \(I(X; Z \mid Y)\) is the further drop in uncertainty about \(X\) that \(Z\) causes. For each value of \(Y\), take the KL divergence between the joint distribution of \(X\) and \(Z\) given that value and the product of their separate distributions given that value. The conditional mutual information is the average of these divergences, so it is never negative.
Revealing two variables one after the other gives a chain rule for mutual information, like the one for entropy. What the pair \((Y, Z)\) tells you about the hidden value is what \(Y\) tells you, plus what \(Z\) adds on top: \[I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y). \tag{5.6}\]
The chain rule leads to the most useful fact in this chapter, the data-processing inequality. Suppose \(Z\) is computed from \(Y\) alone, possibly with fresh randomness of its own. Then once you know \(Y\), also knowing \(X\) tells you nothing more about \(Z\). This condition is written \(X \to Y \to Z\). Then \(Z\) cannot know more about the hidden value than \(Y\) does: \[I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y). \tag{5.7}\] The reason is that the pair \((Y, Z)\) tells you the same amount about \(X\) whichever of the two you reveal first. If you reveal \(Y\) first, \(Z\) adds nothing, because it was computed from \(Y\). But if you reveal \(Z\) first, \(Y\) may still add something. So \(Z\) alone carries at most what \(Y\) carries. The condition is essential, since a \(Z\) that also looked at the hidden value directly could know more about it than \(Y\) does.
The two sides are equal only when \(Y\) adds nothing about \(X\) once \(Z\) is known. Such a \(Z\) keeps everything in \(Y\) that matters for \(X\), and is called a sufficient statistic. An invertible function of \(Y\) is one, because you can compute \(Y\) back from it.
For the spam filter, the word reduced the uncertainty from 0.5436 bits to 0.25 bits on average, so \(I(X; Y) = 0.2936\) bits. Now suppose the word is detected by a sloppy tokenizer that gets the answer wrong 10% of the time, whatever the email. The tokenizer looks only at the word, not at the label, so the condition of the inequality holds. The full edition’s script computes, from the joint table of label and tokenizer output, that the output keeps 0.1668 bits about the label. That is 57% of what the clean feature carries. So a 10% error rate in the detector costs over 40% of the information.
The data-processing inequality says that no function of the data, however clever, can contain more information about the source than the data itself. Denoising, feature extraction and training a model are all processing steps, which can make information easier to use but never larger. So a bound on what the raw observation reveals also covers everything anyone computes from it alone. Divergences gives its own data-processing inequality for KL divergence, and the one here follows from it.
Mutual information has a blind spot, because it is an average over all pairs of values. A small average can hide a few outcomes in which \(Y\) gives \(X\) away completely, because those outcomes carry little weight in the average. Section 5.6 shows how large the gap can be.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.4 Channels and capacity
A channel is a rule that turns an input into a random output. A noisy storage device, a communication link and a lossy sensor are all examples. Any channel can be written as a table, with one row per input, and each row gives the probability of each output for that input, so it sums to 1.
The channel fixes the noise, but you choose how often to send each input, and how much information gets through depends on that choice. The capacity of a channel is the largest mutual information between input and output, over all input distributions \(P_X\): \[\mathcal C = \max_{P_X} I(X; Y). \tag{5.8}\]
Shannon’s channel coding theorem gives capacity a concrete meaning. It involves a code, a scheme that turns each block of data bits into a longer block of channel inputs. That added redundancy lets the receiver correct the noise. Capacity is exactly the highest rate, in data bits per channel use, at which long enough codes can send data with an error rate as small as you like. The full edition cites this theorem rather than proving it.
A basic noisy channel is the binary symmetric channel (BSC), which takes a bit and flips it with a fixed probability \(p\). Its capacity is \[\mathcal C_{\mathrm{BSC}}(p) = 1 - h(p), \tag{5.9}\] and you reach it by sending 0 and 1 equally often, the uniform input. The formula says that the channel carries one bit, the most a binary output can hold, minus the entropy of the noise.
The reason is easiest to see from the symmetric form of mutual information, the uncertainty in the output minus the part of that uncertainty that comes from the noise: \[I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X). \tag{5.10}\] The noise part is \(h(p)\) whatever you send, because each input is flipped with the same probability. So to maximize the mutual information, you only have to make the output as uncertain as possible. A binary output has at most 1 bit of entropy, and the uniform input reaches that bit by making the output a fair coin.
Figure 5.3 shows what the choice of input costs. On the left, each curve is the mutual information as a function of how often you send a 1. Every curve peaks at one half, and away from the peak you lose a lot. With a flip probability of 0.11, for example, sending a 1 only 20% of the time carries 0.3358 bits, against 0.5001 bits with the uniform input.






Figure 5.3: Left: mutual information of a binary symmetric channel as a function of the probability \(q\) of sending a 1, for several flip probabilities; every curve peaks at \(q = \frac12\). Right: the capacity \(1 - h(p)\) against the flip probability \(p\), with the min-capacity of Section 5.5 for comparison.



The right panel shows the capacity against the flip probability. It is zero at one half, where the output is a fair coin flip whatever the input, and it is symmetric around one half. A channel that almost always flips is as good as one that never flips, because the receiver can simply flip every output back.
Here is what this means in practice. A cheap storage medium flips each stored bit independently with probability 0.11, so each stored bit is one use of a binary symmetric channel, with a capacity of 0.5001 bits. That means good error-correcting codes can store about one bit of data in two raw bits, with an error rate as small as you like. No code can do better. At a flip probability of 0.25, the capacity drops to 0.1887 bits, so each data bit needs about five raw bits.
Most channels lack this symmetry, and their capacity has no closed form. The Blahut–Arimoto algorithm computes it numerically instead, by taking turns improving two things until neither changes. One is the input distribution, and the other is, for each output, the receiver’s probabilities of each input given that output. The full edition’s script uses it to confirm Equation 5.9.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.5 Min-entropy and one-guess leakage
Shannon entropy counts the bits needed to describe a value on average. A guesser who gets one try asks something else, namely how likely the best single guess is to be right. The answer is the probability of the most likely value, because no other guess does better. Write \(V(X)\) for that probability, the vulnerability of \(X\). Its negative logarithm puts it on the same bit scale as entropy, and is the min-entropy: \[V(X) = \max_x p(x), \qquad H_\infty(X) = -\log V(X). \tag{5.11}\]
Min-entropy is never larger than Shannon entropy, \[H_\infty(X) \le H(X), \tag{5.12}\] because Shannon entropy averages the surprisals of all outcomes, while min-entropy uses only the surprisal of the most likely outcome. That is the smallest surprisal, and an average is never below its smallest term. The two are equal only when every possible value is equally likely. Min-entropy also has a direct reading. A value with a min-entropy of \(k\) bits is as hard to guess in one try as a uniform string of \(k\) bits, however large its Shannon entropy is.
Both measures belong to one family, the Rényi entropies, in which each member has an order, a number that sets how much weight the most likely values get. As the order grows, the largest probability dominates more and more, and the limit is the min-entropy, while as the order approaches 1, the limit is Shannon entropy. Divergences has the matching family of divergences.
A PIN shows how far apart the two can be. A uniform 4-digit PIN has 13.2877 bits of both entropies. Now suppose that 10% of people choose 1234 and the rest choose uniformly among the other 9,999 PINs. The Shannon entropy barely moves, falling only to 12.4278 bits.
The chain rule says why, by describing the PIN in two steps. The first step says whether the PIN is 1234, and costs \(h(0.1) = 0.4690\) bits on average. The second step is needed only in the 90% of cases where it is not, and says which of the other PINs it is. Averaged over all cases, it costs 11.9588 bits, almost as much as for a uniform PIN, and the two steps add up to 12.4278 bits. The min-entropy, by contrast, falls to 3.3219 bits, because the guess “1234” succeeds one time in ten. So if the guesser gets one try, only the second number matters.
Now let the guesser see an observation \(Y\) before guessing the hidden value \(X\), which this section calls the secret. The observation comes through a channel, written \(C\), whose entry \(C[x, y]\) is the probability of seeing \(y\) when the secret is \(x\). How likely each secret is to begin with is the prior, written \(\pi\). The joint table then has entries \(\pi(x)C[x, y]\), each the probability of the secret times the probability of the observation given that secret.
The best strategy guesses, for each observation, the secret that is most likely given that observation. This is the maximum a posteriori (MAP) guess, and its success probability is the posterior vulnerability. A guess for one observation does not affect the guesser’s success on any other observation. So the guesser can pick the best cell in each column of the joint table separately, and its success is the sum of the cells it picked.
Dividing a column by its total gives the posterior, the distribution of the secret given that observation. Dividing does not change which entry is largest, so the largest entry in each column is the MAP guess. The posterior vulnerability is therefore the sum of these largest entries: \[V(X \mid Y) = \sum_y\max_x \pi(x)C[x, y]. \tag{5.13}\] Its negative logarithm is the conditional min-entropy, \[H_\infty(X \mid Y) = -\log V(X \mid Y). \tag{5.14}\]
The min-entropy leakage, written \(\mathcal L\), compares the two vulnerabilities. It is the logarithm of the factor by which the observation multiplies the chance of a correct first guess: \[\mathcal L = \log\frac{V(X \mid Y)}{V(X)}. \tag{5.15}\] A leakage of 1 bit means the observation doubles the chance of a correct guess, and 2 bits means it quadruples it. An engineer can act on a statement like that. This is why min-entropy is the usual measure in quantitative information flow, the field that studies how much a program’s outputs reveal about its secret inputs.
A small example shows each step. A secret takes four values, the first with prior probability 0.4 and each next value 0.1 less likely. An observation takes three values, through the channel in Table 5.2, and multiplying each row by its prior gives the joint table drawn in Figure 5.4.

Without the observation, the best guess is the first value, which is right with probability 0.4. With it, the guesser picks the boxed cell in each column and wins with probability 0.66, and a million simulated rounds agree, with a win rate of 0.6594. The conditional min-entropy is therefore \(-\log_2 0.66 = 0.5995\) bits. The leakage is 0.7225 bits, which means the observation multiplies the chance of success by 1.65. For comparison, the Shannon leakage of the same table, its mutual information, is 0.6865 bits.
Since only the guesser’s success probability counts, two tempting shortcuts give wrong answers. The first compares channel entries instead of joint entries. On the third observation, that shortcut would pick the fourth secret, because the fourth secret produces that observation more often. But the right guess is the third secret, which is twice as likely to begin with, and that more than makes up the difference.
The second shortcut takes the logarithm too early, by computing the min-entropy of the posterior after each observation and then averaging those values. That gives 0.6548 bits here, against 0.5995 bits for the conditional min-entropy. The correct version averages the success probabilities first and takes the logarithm last.
The two orders differ because the logarithm curves downward, so the logarithm of an average is never below the average of the logarithms. Min-entropy has a minus sign in front, which flips this, so the early version is never smaller than the correct one. More importantly, it is not the logarithm of any guesser’s success rate.
The leakage depends on the prior. A skewed prior already makes the guess without the observation good, so the observation adds less. Often, though, you do not know the prior, and then you want the worst case over all priors. That worst case is the min-capacity, and it has a simple closed form: \[\mathcal{ML}(C) = \log\sum_y\max_x C[x, y]. \tag{5.16}\] It is the logarithm of the sum of the column maxima of the channel itself, with no prior in it.
The reason comes in three steps. First, each entry of the joint table is a prior probability times a channel entry. So each column maximum of the joint table is at most the largest prior times the largest channel entry in that column.
Second, the largest prior is just the vulnerability \(V(X)\) before any observation. Summing the first step over the columns therefore bounds the posterior vulnerability by \(V(X)\) times the sum of the channel’s column maxima, \[V(X \mid Y) \le V(X)\sum_y\max_x C[x, y]. \tag{5.17}\] Dividing by \(V(X)\) shows that the ratio in the leakage is at most that sum, whatever the prior.
Third, a uniform prior loses nothing in the first step, because every prior probability is then the largest one, so the uniform prior attains the bound. For the example, the min-capacity is 1.2630 bits, against a Shannon capacity of 0.8269 bits for the same channel. For the binary symmetric channel with flip probability 0.11, the min-capacity is 0.8319 bits, the dashed curve in Figure 5.3.
The min-capacity is never negative, since an observation never hurts the best guesser. It is also at most the logarithm of the number of observations, because each column maximum is at most 1. It is at most the logarithm of the number of secrets as well. Each column maximum is at most its column’s total, and the totals of all the columns add up to the number of secrets, because each row sums to 1. Finally, computing it needs only one maximum per column, while the Shannon capacity needs an iterative algorithm.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.6 Shannon against min-entropy leakage
The Shannon leakage, which is the mutual information, and the min-entropy leakage both measure how much an observation reveals about a secret. They often agree, as they do for a channel that reveals the same bits on every outcome. When they disagree, though, the disagreement is large and always of one kind, with a channel that reveals the secret completely on a few outcomes and nothing on the rest.
Two families of channels make this concrete. Both act on a uniformly random secret, whose length in bits is written \(n\), and both are deterministic, so their output is a fixed function of the secret. The first family always reveals the lowest \(m\) bits of the secret, and for it both leakages equal \(m\) bits. The second family reveals the whole secret, but only when its lowest \(j\) bits are all zero, which happens with probability \(2^{-j}\). Otherwise it outputs a fixed symbol that says nothing.
For the second family the two leakages part ways, because of where the logarithm sits. Shannon leakage averages the logarithm over outcomes, so the revealing outcome, which carries \(n\) bits but has weight \(2^{-j}\), contributes only about \(2^{-j}n\) bits. Min-entropy leakage instead takes the logarithm of a success probability. The guesser wins whenever the reveal happens, so its success rises from \(2^{-n}\) to just over \(2^{-j}\), and the leakage is close to \(n - j\) bits (Figure 5.5).






Figure 5.5: Shannon leakage against min-entropy leakage for two families of deterministic channels on a uniform 64-bit secret. Revealing the low \(m\) bits gives equal leakages (diagonal). Revealing the whole secret with probability \(2^{-j}\) gives a small Shannon leakage but a min-entropy leakage close to \(64 - j\).



Table 5.3 compares two such channels on a 64-bit secret. Shannon leakage says the second channel leaks more, yet a guesser with one try does better against the first channel by a factor of more than \(10^{15}\). Smith (2009) used a pair of programs like these to argue that Shannon leakage is the wrong measure for one-try guessing. So when the adversary gets one try, use min-entropy.

Min-entropy leakage has its own blind spot. Min-entropy itself looks only at the most likely value, but the posterior vulnerability averages the best guess’s success over the observations. So the leakage, too, is an average over secrets and observations.
Take a channel that reveals a 4-bit secret only when it is all zeros. Its Shannon leakage is 0.3373 bits, while its min-entropy leakage is exactly 1 bit, because the guesser’s chance of success doubles. The guesser wins whenever it sees the reveal, which happens one time in sixteen. Without the reveal, it guesses among the 15 other values and wins one time in fifteen, which adds another one in sixteen overall.
For a 32-bit secret, the Shannon leakage falls to \(7.786\times10^{-9}\) bits, while the min-entropy leakage stays at 1 bit by the same doubling argument. Both numbers are small, yet for the one secret value made of zeros, the channel reveals everything. Any measure that averages over the secret can hide a value that is fully exposed, because that value carries only its small share of the average. Later parts build a measure for the worst case.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.7 Fano’s inequality
Mutual information can also show that a problem is hard, which means that no estimator can beat some error rate. You need such a lower bound to know when to stop looking for a better method, and Fano’s inequality is the basic tool. It says that if the secret is still uncertain after you have seen the observation, every guess must often be wrong. The reason is that a guesser who is usually right leaves little uncertainty about the secret.
Let the secret take one of \(M\) values, and let a guess computed from the observation be wrong with probability \(P_e\). Describing the secret once you know the guess then takes at most two pieces. The first piece says whether the guess was right, and is worth at most \(h(P_e)\) bits. The second piece is needed only when the guess was wrong, and says which of the \(M - 1\) other values is true, which takes at most \(\log(M - 1)\) bits.
The guess sees only the observation, so by the data-processing inequality it knows no more about the secret than the observation does. The uncertainty \(H(X \mid Y)\) that remains about the secret after the observation is therefore at most the uncertainty that remains after the guess, and the two pieces bound it: \[H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log(M - 1). \tag{5.18}\]
The right side grows as the error probability grows from zero, up to the error of a guesser who ignores the observation and picks uniformly. So you can find by bisection the smallest error probability that satisfies the inequality. A weaker form replaces \(h(P_e)\) by its largest value of 1 bit, and \(\log(M - 1)\) by the slightly larger \(\log M\). That form you can solve by hand: \[P_e \ge \frac{H(X \mid Y) - 1}{\log M}. \tag{5.19}\]
Here is how the bound is used. A label is uniform over 8 classes, so it has 3 bits of entropy. Suppose you know the features carry at most 1 bit about it, so that at least 2 bits of uncertainty remain. Then by Fano’s inequality, every classifier, however it is trained, errs at least 0.3730 of the time, while the weak form gives 0.3333.
The same idea shows that estimating a parameter needs many samples. Pick \(M\) candidate values for the parameter that are far apart, so that a good estimate would identify the right candidate. The secret is then which candidate is true, chosen uniformly at random, and if the samples carry little information about it, no estimator can identify it.
Write \(\kappa\) for the largest KL divergence between the sample distributions of two candidates, measured in bits like \(\log M\). One sample then carries at most \(\kappa\) bits about the candidate, because this information is the average KL divergence from each candidate’s distribution to the average of all of them. The average distribution is the closest single reference, so measuring against any one candidate instead can only increase the divergence, and no pairwise divergence exceeds \(\kappa\).
The samples must be independent given the candidate, so that their information adds up to at most \(n\kappa\) bits for \(n\) samples. Dependent samples could reveal the candidate together while each one alone reveals little, and then the count would fail. With independent samples, at least \(\log M - n\kappa\) bits of uncertainty remain, and putting this into the weak form gives \[P_e \ge 1 - \frac{n\kappa + 1}{\log M}. \tag{5.20}\] For example, take 1,024 candidates whose pairwise KL divergences are at most 0.01 bits. With 100 samples, every estimator still errs with probability at least 0.8000, and quadrupling the samples to 400 only brings this bound down to 0.5000. The art of this method lies in choosing candidates that are many and far apart, yet hard to tell apart from samples.
Fano’s bound is tight only when a wrong guess leaves the truth spread evenly over the other values. A symmetric channel does exactly this, because it keeps its input with some probability and otherwise replaces it with one of the other symbols, each equally likely. For example, take 8 equally likely symbols, and a total probability of 0.2 that the channel replaces the input. The bound is then 0.2000, exactly the error of the best guesser (Figure 5.6, left).
When errors go to one neighbour instead, little uncertainty remains after a wrong guess, and the bound becomes loose. Take a channel that shifts each of 8 equally likely symbols to the next one with probability 0.2. The best guesser still errs 0.2000 of the time, but Fano’s bound is only 0.0954 (Figure 5.6, right).
The weak form is worse, because it pays a full bit for \(h(P_e)\). For the symmetric channel it gives 0.0945, and for the shift channel it gives a negative number, which says nothing. In general, the weak form is useless whenever at most 1 bit of uncertainty remains.






Figure 5.6: MAP error against Fano’s lower bound, for \(M = 8\) and a uniform \(X\), as the noise level \(\varepsilon\) grows. Left: on the symmetric channel the bound is exact. Right: on the shift channel, where errors go to a single wrong value, the bound is loose and the weak form is zero.

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.8 Code
Everything about guessing comes from the joint table. This snippet computes the guessing example of Section 5.5:
from math import log2

prior = [0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]
channel = [  # channel[x][y] = probability of observation y given secret x
    [0.8, 0.2, 0.0],
    [0.1, 0.8, 0.1],
    [0.0, 0.5, 0.5],
    [0.0, 0.2, 0.8],
]


def joint(prior: list[float], channel: list[list[float]]) -> list[list[float]]:
    return [[px * c for c in row] for px, row in zip(prior, channel)]


def mutual_information(p: list[list[float]]) -> float:
    """Shannon leakage I(X; Y) in bits, from the joint table p[x][y]."""
    px = [sum(row) for row in p]
    py = [sum(col) for col in zip(*p)]
    return sum(
        pxy * log2(pxy / (px[x] * py[y]))
        for x, row in enumerate(p)
        for y, pxy in enumerate(row)
        if pxy > 0
    )


def posterior_vulnerability(p: list[list[float]]) -> float:
    """Success probability of the best one-shot guess after seeing y: sum of column maxima."""
    return sum(max(col) for col in zip(*p))


p = joint(prior, channel)
v_prior = max(prior)
v_post = posterior_vulnerability(p)
print(f"{v_prior:.4f} {v_post:.4f}")  # 0.4000 0.6600
print(f"{log2(v_post / v_prior):.4f}")  # 0.7225
print(f"{mutual_information(p):.4f}")  # 0.6865
print(f"{log2(sum(max(col) for col in zip(*channel))):.4f}")  # 1.2630
It prints the two vulnerabilities, the min-entropy leakage, the Shannon leakage and the min-capacity. The full edition’s script information_theory.py computes every number in this chapter. Run it from the repository root:
uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/information_theory.py

title: 5  Information theory
text:
5.9 Cheat sheet



Table 5.4: The quantities of this chapter.










Quantity
Formula
Notes




Entropy
\(H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)\)
\(0 \le H \le \log\lvert\mathcal X\rvert\); uniform attains the maximum


Conditional entropy
\(H(X \mid Y) = \sum_y p(y)H(X \mid Y = y)\)
\(\le H(X)\) on average; one observation can raise it


Chain rule
\(H(X, Y) = H(Y) + H(X \mid Y)\)
Extends to any number of variables


Mutual information
\(I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) = D(P_{XY}\,\Vert\,P_XP_Y)\)
Symmetric, \(\ge 0\), zero iff independent


Data processing
\(X \to Y \to Z\): \(I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y)\)
Bound the raw observation


Capacity
\(\max\) of \(I(X; Y)\) over input distributions
BSC: \(1 - h(p)\), at the uniform input


Vulnerability, min-entropy
\(V(X) = \max_x p(x)\), \(H_\infty = -\log V\)
\(H_\infty \le H\); one-guess success


Posterior vulnerability
\(V(X \mid Y) = \sum_y\max_x \pi(x)C[x, y]\)
Success of the MAP guesser


Min-entropy leakage
\(\log V(X \mid Y)/V(X)\)
1 bit doubles one-guess success


Min-capacity
\(\log\sum_y\max_x C[x, y]\)
Worst case over priors, at the uniform prior


Fano
\(H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e\log(M - 1)\)
Lower bound on any estimator’s error; tight when errors spread evenly






Rules of thumb

Shannon quantities average logarithms. Min-entropy quantities take the logarithm of a best-case probability. Use the one that matches how many tries the adversary gets.
Both are averages over the secret. Neither says how exposed a single secret value is.
Processing never adds information. Bound what the raw observation reveals, and the bound covers everything computed from it.
To show that every estimator must fail, bound the mutual information between the unknown and the data, then apply Fano.

text:
5.10 Further reading

Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2nd ed., 2006), ch. 2 and 7: the standard reference for every Shannon result here, including channel capacity and the channel coding theorem.
MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003): the same material with a machine-learning slant, free online.
Smith, “On the Foundations of Quantitative Information Flow” (FoSSaCS 2009): vulnerability, and why Shannon leakage is the wrong measure for one-try guessing.
Alvim et al., The Science of Quantitative Information Flow (2020): the full theory of leakage and capacity.

Derivations. Most results in this chapter are derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter. It cites Shannon’s channel coding theorem, and states a few facts without proof: the limits of the Rényi entropies, the split of the cross-entropy loss, and the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.1 Why this matters
Training a model means finding the parameters that make its average loss over the training set as small as possible. Almost all training in machine learning is done by gradient descent (GD), or by its cheaper and noisier variant, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), and two questions come up every time. The first is how fast these methods get there, how to pick their step size, and how much the noise in SGD slows them down. The second is how much the answer depends on any one training example. If you replace one example and train again, does the best model barely move, or can it jump somewhere else entirely? The first question is about the algorithm and the second about the problem, and the next chapter uses the second to explain when a model generalizes.
Both questions are answered by four constants, three of which describe the loss. The Lipschitz constant \(L\) says how steep the loss can be, and the smoothness constant \(\beta\) says how fast its slope can change. The strong convexity constant \(\lambda\) says how much the loss curves upward at least. The fourth constant belongs to the optimizer rather than the loss. It is the variance \(\sigma^2\) of SGD’s random gradients, which measures how far they scatter around the true gradient. Every result in this chapter is stated in these constants, so knowing which ones a result uses tells you whether it applies to your model.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.2 Convexity, Lipschitz continuity and smoothness
Throughout the chapter, the training set has \(n\) examples, and the model is a vector of parameters \(w\). Write \(\ell(w, z)\) for the loss of the model on an example \(z\), and \(z_1, \dots, z_n\) for the training examples. The empirical risk is the average of these losses over the training set, \[F(w) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(w, z_i), \tag{6.1}\] and training minimizes it. This chapter writes \(w^*\) for a minimizer, a point where the risk is smallest, and \(F^*\) for that smallest value.
The gradient of the risk, written \(\nabla F(w)\), points in the direction in which the risk increases fastest. Write \(\langle a, b\rangle\) for the inner product of two vectors, the sum of the products of their coordinates, and \(\|a\|\) for the length of a vector. An optimizer follows the gradient downhill, so the shape of the loss decides how fast it reaches the minimizer. This section defines convexity and the three constants that describe that shape.
A function is convex when it curves upward everywhere, with no dents. The tangent at a point predicts the value elsewhere by following the slope in a straight line. Convexity says that this prediction never overshoots, so the graph of a function \(f\) lies above every one of its tangents. In symbols, the value of \(f\) at any point \(w'\) is at least the tangent’s prediction from a point \(w\), \[f(w') \ge f(w) + \langle\nabla f(w), w' - w\rangle. \tag{6.2}\] For example, the tangent of \(w^2\) at the point 1 has slope 2. At the point 3 it therefore predicts 5, below the true value there.
This is what makes convex problems easy to optimize. Take the tangent at your current point and use it to predict the risk at the minimizer. Convexity says that this prediction is at most the true smallest value. Rearranged, that says the gradient’s component along the line from the minimizer to your point is at least your current error, the gap between the risk and its smallest value. So a step against the gradient makes progress in proportion to how far from optimal you are.
A function is \(L\)-Lipschitz when it never changes faster than \(L\) per unit of distance, so that for any two points \[|f(w) - f(w')| \le L\|w - w'\|. \tag{6.3}\] For a differentiable function, this means that the gradient never has length more than \(L\).
A function is \(\beta\)-smooth when its gradient changes by at most \(\beta\) per unit of distance. Because the slope cannot change quickly, the tangent stays a good prediction nearby, and its error grows at most like a parabola with curvature \(\beta\). This upper bound is the descent lemma: \[f(w') \le f(w) + \langle\nabla f(w), w' - w\rangle + \frac\beta2\|w' - w\|^2. \tag{6.4}\] The first two terms on the right are the tangent’s prediction, and the last is the parabola that bounds its error.
A function is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, for a constant \(\lambda > 0\), when it lies above each tangent by at least a parabola with that curvature, \[f(w') \ge f(w) + \langle\nabla f(w), w' - w\rangle + \frac\lambda2\|w' - w\|^2. \tag{6.5}\] This is convexity with a margin that grows with the distance from the tangent point. Equivalently, along any straight line the slope grows by at least \(\lambda\) per unit of distance. Now take a differentiable function whose minimizer is not on the edge of a constrained region, so that the gradient there is zero. Moving away from the minimizer, the gradient then grows at least in proportion to the distance. So a point where the gradient is small lies close to the minimizer, within the gradient’s length divided by \(\lambda\), \[\|w - w^*\| \le \frac{\|\nabla f(w)\|}{\lambda}, \tag{6.6}\] and the minimizer is unique.
In practice, strong convexity usually comes from a ridge term \(\frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\), a bowl with curvature exactly \(\lambda\) in every direction. Adding it to a convex function adds that curvature everywhere, which makes the sum \(\lambda\)-strongly convex.
The curvatures can also be read off the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives, since each of its eigenvalues is the curvature along the matching eigenvector. Convex means that no eigenvalue is negative, and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex means that every eigenvalue is at least \(\lambda\). Smooth means that every eigenvalue lies between \(-\beta\) and \(\beta\). The ratio \(\beta/\lambda\) is called the condition number, written \(\kappa\), and it says how much more steeply the function rises in its steepest direction than in its flattest one.
Lipschitz and smooth bound different derivatives, so neither implies the other (Figure 6.1). The absolute value \(|w|\) is 1-Lipschitz but not smooth, because its slope jumps from \(-1\) to \(+1\) at zero. The parabola \(w^2/2\) is 1-smooth but not Lipschitz, because its slope \(w\) grows without bound. Every strongly convex function is like the parabola, since its slope grows at least in proportion to the distance from the minimizer. That is why the SGD results for strongly convex losses below keep the parameters in a bounded set, where the slope stays bounded.
The two constants also do different jobs. The Lipschitz constant bounds the gradient of one step, so it governs SGD on losses that are not smooth, and how far one example can move the minimizer. The smoothness constant instead bounds how far you can trust the tangent. That sets the standard safe step size, \(1/\beta\), at which each step keeps at least half of its progress, and it also drives the analysis of non-convex losses.






Figure 6.1: Left: the slopes of \(|w|\) (bounded, but jumps), \(w^2/2\) (continuous, unbounded) and the logistic loss \(\ln(1+e^{-w})\) (bounded and continuous). Right: the curvature of the logistic loss never exceeds \(1/4\), and that of the non-convex sigmoid loss never exceeds \(1/(6\sqrt3)\).



Logistic regression shows how the constants are found in practice. Take an example with a feature vector \(x\) of length at most 1, and a label \(y\) that is \(\pm1\). The margin, written \(m\), is \(y\langle w, x\rangle\), which is large and positive when the model classifies the example correctly and confidently. The logistic loss turns the margin into a penalty, \[\ell = \ln(1 + e^{-m}). \tag{6.7}\] The sigmoid function maps a number \(s\) to \(1/(1 + e^{-s})\), a value between 0 and 1. Write \(p\) for the sigmoid of the margin, which is the probability the model gives to the correct label.
Differentiating the loss with respect to \(w\) gives its gradient and its Hessian, \[\nabla\ell = -(1 - p)\,y\,x, \qquad \nabla^2\ell = p(1-p)\,xx^\top. \tag{6.8}\] In the gradient, both \(1 - p\) and the length of the features are at most 1, so the loss is 1-Lipschitz. In the Hessian, the matrix \(xx^\top\) has eigenvalue \(\|x\|^2\) along the features and zero orthogonal to them. The factor in front, \(p(1-p)\), is never negative, so the loss is convex. It is also at most \(\frac14\), so the loss is \(\frac14\)-smooth.
The logistic loss is not strongly convex, because it has no curvature orthogonal to the features, and even along them the curvature vanishes for a confidently classified example. The risk averages many examples with different features, so it can still curve in every direction. The full edition’s experiments use a synthetic dataset with 1,000 examples in 5 dimensions, and at its minimizer the smallest curvature of the risk is only \(0.0233\). A ridge term supplies the missing curvature, making the loss \(\lambda\)-strongly convex and \((\frac14 + \lambda)\)-smooth. Its gradient then grows with the parameters, though, so it is Lipschitz only on a bounded set. On the ball of radius \(r\) around zero, for example, the gradient has length at most \(1 + \lambda r\).
The squared loss of least squares, \(\frac12(\langle w, x\rangle - y)^2\), has the Hessian \(xx^\top\), so it is convex and smooth. But it is not Lipschitz, because its gradient is the prediction error times the features, and the prediction error grows with the parameters. Its risk is strongly convex exactly when the average of the matrices \(xx^\top\) is invertible. That fails when there are more features than examples, and the risk then has a whole space of minimizers. A ridge term fixes this, making the risk strongly convex for any data.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.3 Gradient descent and SGD
Gradient descent repeatedly steps against the full gradient of the risk. Write \(w_t\) for the parameters after \(t\) steps, and \(\eta\) for the step size, a positive number you choose. Each step then sets \[w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta\nabla F(w_t), \tag{6.9}\] which costs one gradient evaluation per training example.
SGD replaces the full gradient with the gradient of one example chosen uniformly at random, so each step is cheap. With a minibatch, it averages the gradients of a small random batch instead. Either way, the random gradient is unbiased, meaning that it equals the true gradient on average, and it is the uniform sampling that makes this hold. A scheme that favoured some examples would minimize a reweighted risk instead.
Being right on average does not make the random gradient as good as the true one. To see why, write it as the true gradient plus an error. Its squared length is then the two squared lengths plus twice their inner product, and since the error averages to zero, that cross term averages to zero too. Writing \(g\) for the random gradient, its average squared length is therefore \[\mathbb E\|g\|^2 = \|\nabla F(w)\|^2 + \mathbb E\|g - \nabla F(w)\|^2, \tag{6.10}\] the squared length of the true gradient plus a variance, the average squared length of the error.
Take a training set of three numbers, \((1, 2, 6)\), and the loss \(\frac12(w - z)^2\), where \(z\) is the example. The mean of the data is 3, so the gradient of the risk is \(w - 3\). At the point \(w = 4\), the true gradient is therefore 1. SGD instead picks one example at random and uses its gradient \(w - z\), which takes the three values in Table 6.1.

The three gradients average to the true gradient, but their average square splits into the squared true gradient plus the variance, \(17/3 = 1 + 14/3\). Averaging removed the error from the gradient but not from its square, and every SGD rate in this chapter pays for that variance.
GD, which uses the exact gradient, shows what a fast rate looks like. On a quadratic risk, the gradient is a linear function of the displacement from the minimizer, so each GD step multiplies that displacement by a fixed matrix. With the step \(1/\beta\), the error along a direction of curvature \(h\) shrinks by the factor \(1 - h/\beta\) per step. Along the steepest direction this factor is zero, so that part of the error disappears in one step. The flattest direction shrinks slowest, by the factor \(1 - 1/\kappa\), so the distance to the minimizer shrinks by at least that factor at every step: \[\|w_t - w^*\| \le \left(1 - \frac1\kappa\right)^t\|w_0 - w^*\|. \tag{6.11}\]
This is called linear convergence. Shrinking the error to a fraction \(\epsilon\) of its starting size takes about \(\kappa\ln(1/\epsilon)\) steps, so a large condition number makes GD slow. That is because the step must be small enough for the steepest direction. With that small step, the flattest direction closes only a fraction \(1/\kappa\) of its gap per step. On a test problem with condition number \(9.58\), the bound is nearly exact.
Figure 6.2 shows GD first removing the error along the steep direction, then crawling along the flat valley. SGD with a constant step follows roughly the same route but keeps jittering around the minimizer.






Figure 6.2: Gradient descent (step \(1/\beta\)) and single-example SGD (constant step 0.1) on a two-dimensional least-squares risk with condition number about 10. The grey curves are contours of the risk.



The jitter has a simple cause. Near the minimizer the true gradient vanishes, but the gradients of single examples do not. In Table 6.1, for example, the minimizer is 3, and there the three examples still have gradients 2, 1 and −3. So with a constant step the iterates keep jumping around the minimizer. Averaging the iterates cancels the jumps, and shrinking the step over time makes them smaller, but both give slower rates than GD’s, as the next sections show.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.4 SGD for convex Lipschitz objectives
The cleanest guarantee for SGD needs only convexity and bounded gradients, with no smoothness. It therefore covers losses with kinks, such as the hinge loss, as well as the logistic loss. At a kink, SGD uses a subgradient, any slope whose straight line stays below the graph.
The guarantee runs projected SGD, which keeps the parameters inside a set, such as a ball. Whenever a step leaves the set, the projection pulls it back to the nearest point of the set. The set must be closed, meaning that it contains its boundary, so that a nearest point exists. It must also be convex, so that the segment between two of its points stays inside, and then projection never moves a point farther from anything in the set. So it never undoes progress towards a minimizer inside the set.
The guarantee returns the averaged iterate \(\bar w_T\), the average of the parameter vectors over a run of \(T\) steps, and it needs three conditions. The risk must be convex, because convexity turns the progress of a step into progress on the error. The set must contain the minimizer, or projection could pull you away from it. And the random gradients must have an average squared length of at most a constant \(G^2\), because that bounds how far a step overshoots. Now write \(R\) for the distance from the start to the minimizer, or any upper bound on it. With a constant step size \(\eta\), the averaged iterate satisfies \[\mathbb E[F(\bar w_T)] - F^* \le \frac{R^2}{2\eta T} + \frac{\eta G^2}{2}. \tag{6.12}\]
The two terms pull the step size in opposite directions. The first is the cost of travel, because small steps take long to cover the distance \(R\). The second is the cost of noise, because each step overshoots by an amount that grows with the step size. The step that balances them, and the bound it gives, are \[\eta = \frac{R}{G\sqrt T}, \qquad \mathbb E[F(\bar w_T)] - F^* \le \frac{RG}{\sqrt T}. \tag{6.13}\] A longer run lowers the travel term, so it can afford a smaller step, which lowers the noise term. That is why the best step shrinks like \(1/\sqrt T\). For an \(L\)-Lipschitz loss, every single-example gradient has length at most \(L\), so the bound becomes \(RL/\sqrt T\).
The proof follows the squared distance to the minimizer. On average, by convexity and unbiasedness, each step reduces it by at least a multiple of the current error, and overshoot adds back at most \(\eta^2G^2\). The total reduction over the run cannot exceed the starting value \(R^2\), and that bounds the average error over the run. The last step passes this bound to the averaged iterate. It uses Jensen’s inequality, which says that for a convex function the value at an average of points is at most the average of the values.
So return the averaged iterate, which the bound covers, not the last one. The rate \(1/\sqrt T\) cannot be improved for this class of losses, because some convex Lipschitz functions force an error of order \(RL/\sqrt T\) on any method that only queries gradients. Smoothness does not help either, because the noise term comes from the randomness of the gradient, not from the shape of the loss.
The bound is a worst case, and the full edition measures how loose it is on the logistic dataset. It runs projected SGD on the ball of radius 5 around zero, starting from zero. Since the minimizer is inside the ball, \(R = 5\) bounds the starting distance.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.5 Strongly convex objectives
Strong convexity pulls the iterates towards the minimizer, since the farther you are from it, the larger the gradient pointing back. With matching step sizes and averaging, that turns the \(1/\sqrt T\) rate into a \(1/T\) rate. The setting is the same as before, except that the risk is now \(\lambda\)-strongly convex on the set.
Two schemes work, and both shrink the step like \(1/(\lambda t)\) at step \(t\), a size at which the starting distance cancels out of the argument. The first scheme uses the steps \(1/(\lambda t)\) and the uniform average of the iterates, and after \(T\) steps its expected error is at most \[\frac{G^2(1 + \ln T)}{2\lambda T}. \tag{6.14}\] The second scheme uses the steps \(2/(\lambda(t + 1))\) and weights iterate \(t\) in proportion to \(t\). This removes the \(\ln T\), and the expected error is at most \[\frac{2G^2}{\lambda(T + 1)}. \tag{6.15}\]
The argument is the convex one with an extra term. Strong convexity adds to each step’s progress a term proportional to the current squared distance. With steps \(1/(\lambda t)\), the distance terms of consecutive steps cancel in pairs, which leaves the starting distance with the coefficient zero. Only the noise terms remain, with step \(t\) contributing \(G^2/(2\lambda t)\), and these add up to a harmonic sum of at most \(1 + \ln T\). That is where the \(\ln T\) comes from.
The uniform average pays this price because the early steps are huge, so the early iterates are bad, and yet it gives them full weight. In the weighted scheme, iterate \(t\) has the noise term \(G^2/(\lambda(t + 1))\). Multiplied by its weight \(t\), this is at most \(G^2/\lambda\), so every step contributes at most the same amount and no harmonic sum appears. Averaging only the last half of the iterates also gives the \(1/(\lambda T)\) rate, by dropping the bad early ones.
With a \(1/T\) rate, halving the error takes twice the steps, not four times. The price is the factor \(1/\lambda\), so a weak regularizer gives a fast rate only after many steps. The schedule also needs a value of \(\lambda\) no larger than the true strong convexity. If you overestimate it, the guarantee no longer holds, because the argument counts on more pull than there is. Worse, the steps shrink too fast, and the iterates can stall far from the minimizer.
The constant \(G\) depends on the set, because a strongly convex function has no bound on its gradient over the whole space, which is the reason for the projection. For an \(L\)-Lipschitz loss plus a ridge term, for example, the gradient on the ball of radius \(r\) has length at most \(L + \lambda r\).
Add a ridge term of \(\lambda = 0.1\) to the logistic problem. On the ball of radius 5, this gives \(G = 1.5\). After a run of 10,000 steps, the uniform average has an error of \(9.09\times10^{-5}\), against a bound of \(1.15\times10^{-2}\). The weighted average has an error of \(7.85\times10^{-5}\), against a bound of \(4.50\times10^{-3}\). So both bounds are loose, by factors of about 130 and 60. The main reason is that \(G\) is the worst case over the whole ball, while the actual gradients near the minimizer are much smaller. In the right panel of Figure 6.3, all three iterates fall like \(1/T\), with the weighted average slightly ahead.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.6 Gradient noise and minibatches
Every SGD bound so far pays for the average squared length of the random gradients, which is the squared true gradient plus the variance. That variance comes from sampling examples, but also from low-precision arithmetic or from compressing gradients to send between machines. In later parts, noise is also sometimes added to gradients on purpose. Two practical questions follow. How does the batch size change the variance, and how should the step size change when the gradients get noisier?
Write \(\sigma_1^2\) for the variance of a single-example gradient, the average squared distance of the \(n\) per-example gradients from the true gradient. A batch of \(B\) independent draws divides that variance by \(B\), as for any sample mean. Drawing without replacement does a little better, because the deviations of the per-example gradients from their mean sum to zero. Once you have drawn an example that deviates one way, the rest deviate, on average, slightly the other way, so the draws partly cancel. For the average gradient \(g_B\) over the batch, the variance is \[\mathbb E\|g_B - \nabla F(w)\|^2 = \begin{cases}\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{B} & \text{with replacement,}\\[2ex] \dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{B}\cdot\dfrac{n - B}{n - 1} & \text{without replacement.}\end{cases}. \tag{6.16}\] The extra factor is 1 for a batch of one example, and 0 for a batch of the whole dataset, whose gradient is exact.
On the logistic data, the single-example variance at the minimizer is \(0.1722\), and the formula matches simulated batches of every size. At a batch of 500, half the dataset, the extra factor is about one half, so sampling without replacement halves the variance (Figure 6.4).






Figure 6.4: Minibatch gradient variance at the logistic minimizer against batch size, measured and from Equation 6.16. Without replacement, the variance drops below \(\sigma_1^2/B\) as \(B\) approaches \(n = 1000\).



Larger batches are not free. A batch of \(B\) examples costs \(B\) gradient evaluations and divides the variance by \(B\), so per evaluation the gain is exactly cancelled. Batches help mainly because the evaluations can run in parallel.
Now suppose that each random gradient gets extra noise of mean zero, independent of everything else. Write \(\sigma^2\) for the average squared length of that noise, summed over all coordinates. Its cross term with the gradient averages to zero, so the noise simply adds \(\sigma^2\) to the average squared length of the gradient. The convex Lipschitz bound Equation 6.12 then holds with \(G^2 = L^2 + \sigma^2\), which makes the balanced step and the bound \[\eta^* = \frac{R}{\sqrt{(L^2 + \sigma^2)T}}, \qquad \mathbb E[F(\bar w_T)] - F^* \le \frac{R\sqrt{L^2 + \sigma^2}}{\sqrt T}. \tag{6.17}\]
Noisier gradients call for smaller steps and longer runs. For the bound to reach a fixed accuracy, the number of steps must grow in proportion to \(L^2 + \sigma^2\), so noise multiplies the steps the bound needs by \(1 + \sigma^2/L^2\). Noise of size \(\sigma = 3L\), for example, multiplies them by 10.
The full edition tests this on the logistic problem, adding normal noise to every single-example gradient for 10,000 steps. Table 6.3 compares the bound’s step with the best step on a grid.

title: 6  Optimization
section: 6.7 Non-convex objectives: convergence to stationary points
text:
6.7 Non-convex objectives: convergence to stationary points
The losses of neural networks are not convex, and no method that only uses gradients can promise to find their global minimum. What SGD can still guarantee is a point where the gradient is small, an approximate stationary point. The argument uses smoothness instead of convexity.
Put a GD step of size \(1/\beta\) into the descent lemma Equation 6.4. The tangent term promises a decrease of \(\|\nabla F\|^2/\beta\), and the parabola term, which charges for overshooting, takes back half of that. So each step lowers the risk by at least \[F(w_t) - F(w_{t+1}) \ge \frac{\|\nabla F(w_t)\|^2}{2\beta}. \tag{6.18}\] For SGD the same holds on average, minus a penalty for the noise. Since a risk that is bounded below cannot fall forever, the squared gradients must be small on average over the run.
Each piece of this argument is a condition of the result. The risk must be \(\beta\)-smooth, or the descent lemma does not hold. It must also be bounded below, or it could keep falling while its gradients stay large, and this chapter writes \(\Delta\) for the most it can fall from the start. The random gradients must be unbiased, so that the expected progress of a step depends on the true gradient. And their variance must be at most some \(\sigma^2\), which sets the noise penalty, where \(\sigma^2\) counts the whole variance, from sampling and any added noise together.
Finally, the step size must be at most \(1/\beta\), because such a step keeps at least half of its progress, and the constants of the bound come from that half. A step between \(1/\beta\) and \(2/\beta\) still makes progress, but less, while from \(2/\beta\) on the descent lemma promises none, and a step can raise the risk. Under these conditions, SGD with a constant step size \(\eta \le 1/\beta\) satisfies \[\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E\|\nabla F(w_t)\|^2 \le \frac{2\Delta}{\eta T} + \beta\eta\sigma^2. \tag{6.19}\] The left side is the average squared gradient over the run. Ghadimi and Lan (2013) proved this bound. They return an iterate chosen at random from the run, whose expected squared gradient equals that average.
The two terms are again the cost of travel and the cost of noise, and the best step balances them, up to the cap of \(1/\beta\). Without noise, the step is \(1/\beta\) and the rate is of order \(1/T\), as for GD. With noise, the balanced bound falls like \(1/\sqrt T\), so the gradient’s length falls only like \(T^{-1/4}\). Batches help here as well, since with batches of \(B\) examples the variance becomes \(\sigma^2/B\).
A small gradient is all you get. A stationary point can be a local minimum, a saddle point, or a flat region far from anything good. The convex bounds could say how far the risk is from its smallest value, because convexity links the gradient to the error, but without convexity that link is gone.
The full edition tests the bound on the sigmoid loss, the sigmoid of the negative margin. It is a smooth stand-in for counting mistakes, and it is not convex, because the sigmoid curves up on one side of zero and down on the other. Its curvature is at most \(1/(6\sqrt3) = 0.0962\), which is its smoothness constant (Figure 6.1, right). The loss lies between 0 and 1 and starts at \(\frac12\), so the risk can fall by at most \(\frac12\). Because the features have length at most 1, the gradient has length at most \(\frac14\). The variance is therefore at most its squared length, \(\frac1{16}\).

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.8 Sensitivity of regularized ERM
The previous sections asked how fast an optimizer reaches the minimizer. This one asks how much the minimizer depends on the data. Regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) minimizes the average training loss plus a ridge term, \[J(w; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(w, z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|w\|^2, \tag{6.20}\] where \(D\) is the training set, and \(w^*(D)\) is its minimizer. If you replace one training example and retrain, how far can the minimizer move? The question is about the exact solution, not about the optimizer that finds it.
The answer has two steps. First, replacing one example swaps one of the \(n\) terms of the average. The old loss leaves and the new one enters, each with weight \(1/n\) and a gradient of length at most \(L\). So the gradient of the objective moves by at most \(2L/n\) at every point. The new objective has zero gradient at its own minimizer, so the old objective’s gradient there has length at most \(2L/n\). Second, by strong convexity, a point with a gradient that small lies within the gradient’s length divided by \(\lambda\) of the old minimizer. So for two training sets that differ in one example, \[\|w^*(D) - w^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{6.21}\]
The conditions are that each loss is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz, and that the ridge term is there. The Lipschitz constant caps how much one example can tilt the gradient. Convex losses plus the ridge term make the objective \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, which converts a small tilt into a small move. With subgradients, the argument also covers losses with kinks.
The bound is tight for a loss with no curvature of its own, where the ridge term is the only curvature. For example, take a single parameter \(w\) and labels \(z\) that are \(\pm1\). The linear loss \(zw\) is convex and 1-Lipschitz, and the minimizer of the regularized risk is then the negative mean label divided by \(\lambda\). Flipping one label lowers the mean label by \(2/n\), so the minimizer moves by exactly \(2/(\lambda n)\). With \(\lambda = 0.1\) and a thousand examples, the move is \(0.02\).
The influence of one example shrinks like \(1/n\), because each example carries weight \(1/n\). Regularization buys stability, because its curvature turns a small tilt of the gradient into a small move, and halving \(\lambda\) can double the movement. Since the loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz, the loss on any example then changes by at most \[\frac{2L^2}{\lambda n}. \tag{6.22}\] A bound like this, on how much replacing one example can change the loss anywhere, is called uniform stability. The next chapter, Algorithmic stability and generalization, turns it into a generalization bound, and later parts call the same per-example influence sensitivity.
The bound is loose in two ways. First, it counts only the ridge term’s curvature, while real data add their own. With a larger total curvature, the same argument gives the bound with that curvature in place of \(\lambda\). Second, it assumes that the two examples’ gradients point in opposite directions at full length, which actual examples rarely do.
The full edition measures this on regularized logistic regression, recording the largest movement of the exact minimizer over 20 single-example replacements. The logistic loss is 1-Lipschitz, so the bound is \(2/(\lambda n)\).

Down a column of Table 6.5, ten times the data gives a tenth of the movement, as the \(1/n\) predicts. Across a row, the ratio of observed movement to bound falls from about 0.4 for the strongest ridge term to about 0.1 for the weakest. That is because the weaker the ridge term, the more of the curvature comes from the data, which the bound ignores. So in Figure 6.7, as \(\lambda\) goes to zero the bound blows up, while the observed movement levels off.






Figure 6.7: Left: largest observed movement of the regularized logistic minimizer when one of \(n\) examples is replaced (solid), against \(2L/(\lambda n)\) (dashed), for three values of \(\lambda\). Right: the same at \(n = 1000\) as a function of \(\lambda\).



Convexity alone is not enough, because a convex function can be flat, and on a flat stretch a tiny change in the data can move the minimizer a long way. The absolute loss shows this. It is convex and 1-Lipschitz, and the minimizer of its average is the median. Take an odd number of 0s and 1s, with one more 0 than 1s, so that the median is 0. Replacing one 0 by a 1 then switches the majority and moves the median to 1, however many examples there are. A ridge term would prevent this, since Equation 6.21 caps the move at \(2/(\lambda n)\).
For a non-convex loss, one example can decide which of two valleys is deeper. The full edition shows this with the double-well loss \(\frac14(w^2 - 1)^2 - zw\), where the labels \(z\) are \(\pm1\). Its first term has valleys at \(-1\) and \(+1\), and its second term tilts the risk towards the sign of the mean label. With 11 examples, six of them labelled \(+1\), the minimizer is \(1.0427\). Flipping one label flips the tilt, which moves the minimizer by \(2.0854\) into the other valley (Figure 6.8). With 1,001 examples the move is still \(2.0010\).






Figure 6.8: A double-well empirical risk on 11 examples before (\(D\), six labels \(+1\)) and after (\(D'\), five labels \(+1\)) one label changes. The dots mark the global minimizers, which jump from one well to the other.



A ridge term fixes this only if it makes the whole objective convex. Without strong convexity, the minimizer can jump when the data change slightly, or fail to be unique, and no bound on its movement can hold. So for non-convex models, statements about the influence of one example must be about the algorithm. One such algorithm is a fixed number of SGD steps from a fixed start, and Algorithmic stability and generalization analyses SGD this way for convex losses.

title: 6  Optimization
text:
6.9 Code
The variance split and the minibatch formula are easy to check on the three examples of Table 6.1. This snippet does it with exact fractions.
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import combinations

data = [Fraction(1), Fraction(2), Fraction(6)]
w = Fraction(4)
grads = [w - z for z in data]  # gradient of (w - z)^2 / 2 for each example
true_grad = sum(grads) / len(grads)
second_moment = sum(g * g for g in grads) / len(grads)
variance = sum((g - true_grad) ** 2 for g in grads) / len(grads)
print(true_grad)  # 1
print(second_moment, "=", true_grad**2, "+", variance)  # 17/3 = 1 + 14/3

# Batches of two different examples, drawn without replacement.
pairs = list(combinations(grads, 2))
batch_var = sum(((a + b) / 2 - true_grad) ** 2 for a, b in pairs) / len(pairs)
n, b = len(grads), 2
print(batch_var, variance / b * (n - b) / (n - 1))  # 7/6 7/6
print(variance / b)  # 7/3
The batch variance without replacement, \(7/6\), matches the formula and is half of the \(7/3\) that drawing with replacement would give. The full edition’s script optimization.py runs every experiment in this chapter and draws every figure. Run it from the repository root.
uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/optimization.py

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.1 Why this matters
You train a model and its training loss is low, but what matters is whether its loss on new data will be low too. The difference between the two losses is the generalization gap, and a model with a large gap looks better on its training data than it really is.
The classical way to bound the gap measures how rich a set of models the training algorithm could output. The argument is that a set that is not too rich cannot fit noise. For a large model that set is enormous, so the bound is useless. This chapter takes a different route and looks at the training algorithm itself. Its one idea is that a model generalizes when it does not depend much on any single training example.
That idea gives three results. The first says that the expected gap is exactly the average effect of swapping one training example for a fresh one. The second says that if no single example can move the trained model much, the gap is small on average. If that effect also shrinks fast enough as the data grow, the gap is small with high probability, for the one model you actually trained. The third shows that this per-example effect is controlled by two knobs you already turn, the strength of the regularizer and how long you train with stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Later parts of this book return to how much a trained model depends on a single example, and they reuse the quantities defined here.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.2 Training loss, test loss and the gap
text:
7.2 Training loss, test loss and the gap
Training lowers the loss on the data you have, but you care about the loss on data you will see later. To make this precise, take a training set \(S\) that is a list of \(n\) examples. Its \(i\)-th example is written \(z_i\). Each is drawn independently from the same distribution \(\mathcal D\), the source of all data, past and future. From these examples, a learning algorithm \(A\) returns a model \(A(S)\). Then a loss \(\ell(w, z)\), which is never negative, measures how badly a model \(w\) does on an example \(z\).
The quantity you care about is the average loss on a new example from \(\mathcal D\), called the test loss, or population risk, and written \(R(w)\). You cannot compute it, because you do not know \(\mathcal D\). What you can compute is the average loss over the training set, the training loss or empirical risk, written \(\hat R_S(w)\). The generalization gap of the trained model is its test loss minus its training loss, \[\mathrm{gap} = R(A(S)) - \hat R_S(A(S)). \tag{7.1}\] It is positive when the model looks better on its training data than it is.
For a model fixed before the data were drawn, the training loss is unbiased, meaning that its average over the random draw of the training set equals the test loss. The reason is that each training example is then a typical draw from \(\mathcal D\), as far as that model is concerned. So the model’s average loss on each example is its test loss, and so is the average over all \(n\) examples. This needs the training examples to come from the same distribution as the future data. If they came from a different source, the training loss would estimate the loss on that other source instead.
For a model fitted to the data, the argument breaks, because the algorithm picked the model that does well on these particular examples. From the model’s point of view the training examples are no longer typical draws, so its training loss is biased downward. The gap is this bias. It is not noise that averages out but a systematic error, which comes from using the same data both to choose a model and to judge it.
The running example of this chapter shows the size of the effect. Its features are uniform on the unit sphere in 10 dimensions, and its label is \(+1\) or \(-1\). The label tends to follow the sign of the first feature but is noisy when that feature is near zero. The model is logistic regression with a penalty on the size of its weights, whose strength, written \(\lambda\), is 0.01. With training sets of 50 examples, the average training loss is 0.4603 while the average test loss is 0.5781. The expected gap, estimated as described in Section 7.5, is about 0.119, and with 1,000 examples it shrinks to about 0.006.
The tool for studying the gap is a training set that differs from \(S\) in one example. Write \(z_i'\) for a fresh draw from \(\mathcal D\), independent of \(S\). The replace-one neighbour \(S^{(i)}\) is then the training set with example \(i\) replaced by \(z_i'\). Replacing rather than removing keeps \(n\) examples, all drawn from \(\mathcal D\), so the neighbour is just as typical a training set as the original.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.3 The gap and uniform stability
The first result says the expected gap is exactly an average per-example effect. To see why, measure the test loss in an unusual way.
The test loss of the model \(A(S)\) is its average loss on a point it has not seen. The fresh point \(z_i'\) is such a point, so the average loss of \(A(S)\) on \(z_i'\) is the test loss. Now rename the two points, calling \(z_i\) the fresh one and \(z_i'\) the training example, which turns \(S\) into \(S^{(i)}\). Both points are independent draws from the same distribution, so the renamed situation has exactly the same probabilities as the original one. Single outcomes change, but every average stays the same. After the renaming, the average loss of \(A(S)\) on \(z_i'\) therefore becomes the average loss on \(z_i\) of the model trained on \(S^{(i)}\), a model that never saw \(z_i\).
So the expected test loss is the average loss of each example under a model trained without it. The training loss, by contrast, averages each example’s loss under a model trained with it. Their difference is the expected gap, so for any algorithm, \[\mathbb E[\mathrm{gap}] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E\Big[\ell\big(A(S^{(i)}), z_i\big) - \ell\big(A(S), z_i\big)\Big]. \tag{7.2}\] Each term in the brackets says how much worse example \(i\) does when the model is trained without it. The identity says that this effect, averaged over examples, is the expected gap. In other words, overfitting is dependence on individual examples.
The renaming is the step readers find hardest, so here it is on the smallest possible case. Take a single example \(z_1\) that is 1 with probability 0.3 and 0 otherwise, and a fresh copy \(z_1'\). The algorithm returns half the example, \(w = z_1/2\), and the loss is the squared error \((w - z)^2\). Table 7.1 lists the four possible outcomes.



Table 7.1: Every outcome of the one-example case. The training loss is the model’s loss on \(z_1\), the test loss its loss on \(z_1'\), and the renamed column the loss on \(z_1\) of the model trained on \(z_1'\).
