The rows \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 0)\) are mirror images, holding the same two values with the example and the fresh copy exchanged. They are the only rows where the test and renamed columns differ, and there the renamed column holds the test column’s values with the two rows swapped. Since both rows have the same probability, 0.21, the averages agree.
The renaming needs one condition, that the two points be interchangeable, which holds when they are drawn independently from the same distribution. If \(z_1'\) came from a different distribution, the two mirror-image rows would have different probabilities. The averages would then differ, and the identity would fail.
To bound the gap, bound each term of Equation 7.2. An algorithm is \(\beta\)-uniformly stable if replacing any one training example by any other moves the loss of the trained model by at most \(\beta\), at every test point. In symbols, for every training set \(S\), every index \(i\), every replacement \(z_i'\) and every test point \(z\), \[\big|\ell(A(S), z) - \ell(A(S^{(i)}), z)\big| \le \beta. \tag{7.3}\] So the bound must hold in the worst case, not just on average. The number \(\beta\) often shrinks as \(n\) grows, since each example then carries less weight. For a randomized algorithm such as SGD, the condition applies to the loss averaged over the algorithm’s own randomness.
Figure 7.1 shows the definition at work. When one label is flipped, the fitted model moves a lot under weak regularization and barely under strong regularization.






Figure 7.1: One-dimensional logistic regression trained on 30 points, on \(S\) and on \(S^{(i)}\), where the positive example with the largest feature value is replaced by the same point with its label flipped. Left: \(\lambda = 0.01\). Right: \(\lambda = 1\). The titles compare the change in the weight with the bound \(2L/(\lambda n)\) of Section 7.5.



If the algorithm is \(\beta\)-uniformly stable, every term in the brackets lies between \(-\beta\) and \(\beta\) (for a randomized algorithm, once averaged over its randomness). So does their average, which means the expected gap is at most \(\beta\) in size: \[\big|\mathbb E[\mathrm{gap}]\big| \le \beta. \tag{7.4}\] What makes this bound useful is what it leaves out. No set of models appears in it, so it holds for any algorithm, however rich the set of models it could output. This is why stability gives guarantees for SGD on large models, where measuring that richness gives nothing useful.
The price is that uniform stability is a worst case. The identity averages over examples and data, while \(\beta\) takes the worst training set, replacement and test point, so it can be far above the true gap. Weaker notions of stability that use averages also exist (Bousquet & Elisseeff 2002).
At the opposite end from a stable algorithm sits a memorizing lookup table, which stores the training set. It predicts the stored label at a training point and \(+1\) everywhere else. Score it with the 0-1 loss, which is 1 for a wrong prediction and 0 for a right one. With continuous features, a fresh point almost surely misses the table and gets the prediction \(+1\). In the running example half the labels are \(-1\), so the test error is one half, while the training error is 0, for every \(n\).
Now take a training example whose label is \(-1\), and replace it by a point elsewhere. Because the table no longer stores the old point, the prediction there falls back to \(+1\), and the loss on the old example jumps from 0 to 1. So \(\beta = 1\), and the gap of one half obeys the bound but never shrinks.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.4 High probability: the Bousquet–Elisseeff bound
Equation 7.4 controls the gap on average over training sets. But you train once, on one training set, so you need the gap of your model to be small with high probability. The tool for that is McDiarmid’s inequality from Concentration inequalities. It says that a function of many independent inputs stays close to its average if none of the inputs can move it by much. The chance of a large deviation falls exponentially in the square of its size.
The gap is such a function, since it depends on \(n\) independent examples and uniform stability limits how much one example can move it. Replacing an example moves the test loss by at most \(\beta\), because it moves the loss at every point by at most \(\beta\).
It also moves the training loss, and this is where a second condition enters. The training loss is an average of \(n\) terms, one per example. For the other examples, the term is evaluated at the same point under two models, so stability limits its change. The replaced example’s own term is different, because before the replacement it is a loss at \(z_i\) and after it a loss at \(z_i'\), a different point. Stability compares two models at the same point, so it says nothing about this term, and only a bound on the loss itself limits it. The result therefore assumes that every loss lies between 0 and a maximum \(M\). Without such a bound, one example could move the training loss by any amount, and McDiarmid’s inequality would not apply.
Write \(\delta\) for the failure probability, the chance that the guarantee does not hold. Suppose the algorithm is \(\beta\)-uniformly stable and the loss lies between 0 and \(M\). Then with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over the training set, \[R(A(S)) \le \hat R_S(A(S)) + \beta + (2n\beta + M)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}}. \tag{7.5}\] This is the bound of Bousquet & Elisseeff (2002). They define stability by removing an example rather than replacing it, and the form above restates their bound for replacement. Applying the same argument to the gap with its sign reversed gives a matching lower bound.
The bound adds two things to the training loss you observe. The first is \(\beta\), the bound on the expected gap. The second is a deviation term, which says how far one training set can stray from the average, and together the two make up the bound’s width. Inside the deviation term, the part with \(M\) is what Hoeffding’s inequality gives for one fixed model. That model’s training loss is an average of \(n\) independent losses between 0 and \(M\). Call it the fixed-model term. It falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), and you pay it even without any learning.
The part with \(2n\beta\) is the price of learning. Multiplied out, it equals \(\beta\sqrt{2n\ln(1/\delta)}\), so it goes to zero only if \(\beta\) shrinks faster than \(1/\sqrt n\) as the training set grows. Figure 7.2 shows three cases. When \(\beta\) falls like \(1/n\), as for regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) below, the width falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), only a constant factor above the fixed-model term. When \(\beta\) falls like \(n^{-3/4}\), the width still falls, but only like \(n^{-1/4}\). And when \(\beta\) falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), the width does not fall at all, so the bound is useless, although Equation 7.4 still says the expected gap is at most \(\beta\).






Figure 7.2: Width of the high-probability bound, Equation 7.5, with \(M = 1\) and \(\delta = 0.05\), for stability \(\beta = 1/n\), \(n^{-3/4}\) and \(n^{-1/2}\), against the Hoeffding width for a single fixed model.



The bound is loose because McDiarmid’s inequality charges every example the full worst case, while in reality the effects of different examples largely cancel. Later work removed most of this slack. Feldman & Vondrák (2018) proved a bound that is useful whenever \(\beta\) goes to zero, at any rate. Two later papers went further for losses between 0 and 1 (Feldman & Vondrák 2019; Bousquet, Klochkov & Zhivotovskiy 2020). Their bound is \(\beta\), multiplied by logarithmic factors, plus the fixed-model term. With it, a \(\beta\) of order \(1/\sqrt n\) also gives a gap of order \(1/\sqrt n\), up to logarithmic factors.
For a sense of scale, apply Equation 7.5 to regularized logistic regression with 10,000 examples and \(\delta = 0.05\). With features of size 1, the next section shows that \(\beta\) is \(2/(\lambda n)\). The logistic loss has no upper limit in general, since it grows as a prediction gets more confidently wrong. Here it is bounded, because the penalty keeps the weights at size at most \(1/\lambda\), as the next section also shows. With features of size 1, no prediction can then be more wrong than \(1/\lambda\) allows, so the largest loss \(M\) is \(\ln(1 + e^{1/\lambda})\). That is 1.313 for \(\lambda = 1\) and 10.000 for \(\lambda = 0.1\).
With \(\lambda = 1\), the bound adds 0.065 to the training loss, and with \(\lambda = 0.1\) it adds 0.614. In both cases the stability term \(2n\beta\) makes up three quarters or more of the width. The expected gap itself is far smaller. For \(\lambda = 1\) it is already \(2.53\times10^{-4}\) with 1,000 examples, a tenth as many, and it keeps falling like \(1/n\).

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.5 Regularized ERM is stable
The bounds above need an algorithm with small \(\beta\). The first such algorithm is regularized ERM, which covers ridge regression, regularized logistic regression and support vector machines. It picks the weights that minimize the training loss plus a penalty on their size, \[w_S = \arg\min_w \Big(\hat R_S(w) + \frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\Big). \tag{7.6}\]
Stability gives a new reading of the regularizer. With a convex loss, the penalty makes the objective a bowl whose curvature is at least \(\lambda\) everywhere. Replacing one example changes only one term of the objective, a term that carries weight \(1/n\). Such a small change can only tilt a steep bowl a little, so the bottom of the bowl moves only a little.
Two properties of the loss turn this picture into a number, and Optimization defines both. A loss is \(L\)-Lipschitz when its gradient never exceeds \(L\) in size, so that moving the weights changes the loss by at most \(L\) times the distance moved. A loss is convex when its curvature is never negative. If the loss is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz for every example, then replacing one example moves the minimizer by at most \(2L/(\lambda n)\). The loss at every test point then moves by at most \(L\) times that, which gives \[\beta = \frac{2L^2}{\lambda n}. \tag{7.7}\]
Each condition has a job. The Lipschitz bound limits how hard the one changed term can tilt the bowl, since its gradient changes by at most \(2L/n\). It also turns a movement of the weights into a change of the loss. Convexity of the loss keeps the whole objective a bowl with curvature at least \(\lambda\). Without it, the data term can cancel the curvature of the penalty. For example, Optimization shows a non-convex loss with two valleys where flipping one label makes the minimizer jump from one valley to the other, however large \(n\) is. Squared loss is convex but not Lipschitz everywhere, yet you can still use the result for ridge regression when the features and labels are bounded. The minimizer then lies in a bounded region, and the squared loss is Lipschitz there.
The same reasoning bounds the size of the weights. At the minimizer the gradient of the objective is zero, which says that \(\lambda w_S\) equals minus the average gradient of the losses. That average has size at most \(L\), so \(\|w_S\|\) is at most \(L/\lambda\). With bounded features this also bounds every prediction, which is how the previous section found the largest loss \(M\) of regularized logistic regression.
Because \(\beta\) falls like \(1/n\), faster than \(1/\sqrt n\), both the expected-gap and the high-probability bounds go to zero as the training set grows. Regularization buys stability linearly, since doubling \(\lambda\) halves \(\beta\). But it is not free, because a larger \(\lambda\) also pulls the weights towards zero and away from the best fit. The test loss is therefore U-shaped in \(\lambda\), with too little regularization overfitting and too much underfitting.
The running example tests the bound. The gradient of the logistic loss is the feature vector scaled by a probability, a number between 0 and 1. With features of size 1 its size is at most 1, so the loss is 1-Lipschitz and \(\beta = 2/(\lambda n)\). The script fits the model on \(S\) and then on \(S^{(i)}\) for 10 random examples, each replaced by the same point with its label flipped. It records the largest change in the weights and in the loss. To find the test point where the loss changes most, it checks 2,000 random test points and the points that lie in the direction the weights moved.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.6 SGD is stable if you stop early
text:
7.6 SGD is stable if you stop early
Large models are not trained to an exact minimizer but by SGD, for a number of steps. At each step \(t\), SGD picks one training example \(z\) uniformly at random and moves the weights against the gradient of its loss, scaled by a step size \(\eta_t\), \[w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta_t\nabla\ell(w_t, z). \tag{7.8}\] The sum of the step sizes over all steps is the total step size. Hardt, Recht & Singer (2016) showed that SGD itself is stable, with a \(\beta\) that grows with the total step size. This turns “train for fewer epochs” into a guarantee.
The idea is to run SGD twice, once on \(S\) and once on \(S^{(i)}\), with the same starting point and the same sequence of random picks. Sharing the picks is allowed, because stability compares the average loss of each run, and sharing does not change either average. The two runs can then drift apart only on the steps that pick example \(i\), since only there do they step on different examples.
The other steps must not push the runs apart, which needs three conditions. The loss must be convex, because on a non-convex loss a gradient step can push two points apart. It must also be \(\rho\)-smooth, meaning that its gradient changes by at most a constant \(\rho\) per unit of distance. (Optimization writes this constant as \(\beta\), but here \(\beta\) is the stability.) Finally, every step size must be at most \(2/\rho\), for the reason the next paragraph shows. Under these conditions, a gradient step on the same loss never moves two points farther apart than they were.
A one-dimensional loss shows why the step size matters. For the parabola \(\frac\rho2w^2\), a gradient step with step size \(\eta\) multiplies every distance by \(|1 - \eta\rho|\), a factor that is at most 1 exactly when \(\eta\) is at most \(2/\rho\). A larger step overshoots the minimum and blows differences up.
The steps that pick example \(i\) need a fourth condition, that the loss be \(L\)-Lipschitz, so that its gradient has size at most \(L\). Such a step moves each run by at most \(\eta_t L\), so it pushes the runs apart by at most \(2L\eta_t\). Because the picks are uniform, it happens with probability \(1/n\), so on average the distance grows by at most \(2L\eta_t/n\) per step. Adding up the steps and multiplying by \(L\) to turn distance into loss gives \[\beta \le \frac{2L^2}{n}\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t, \tag{7.9}\] where \(T\) is the number of steps. The bound holds on average over the random picks. Many implementations instead shuffle the data once per epoch, and the argument as stated does not cover them.
Figure 7.4 shows this as a staircase. A single run jumps when example \(i\) is picked, which happens about once per epoch, and otherwise does not grow. In practice, a gradient step on a curved loss often brings two points closer together, so single runs also shrink between jumps.






Figure 7.4: Distance between coupled SGD runs on \(S\) and \(S^{(1)}\) (\(n = 100\), \(\eta = 0.25\)), for three single runs and the average over 200 runs, against the bound \((2L/n)\sum_t\eta_t\). Single runs jump when example 1 is drawn and contract otherwise. Dotted lines mark epochs.



Stability therefore degrades with training time. Take a constant step \(\eta\) and train for a number of epochs \(E\), which is \(En\) steps with a total step size of \(\eta En\). Equation 7.9 then becomes \[\beta \le 2L^2\eta E. \tag{7.10}\] The \(n\) cancels, so for a fixed number of epochs more data does not improve the bound, and one pass over the data gives \(\beta \le 2L^2\eta\).
This makes early stopping a trade-off rather than a trick. Training longer lowers the optimization error, the excess of the training loss over that of the best weights. But it also raises \(\beta\), and the excess test loss pays for both. To see the balance, take averaged SGD, which outputs the average of the weights along the way rather than the last ones. For convex Lipschitz losses, its optimization error falls like one over the total step size \(\eta T\), while the stability bound grows like \(\eta T/n\). Balancing the two puts the best total step size at order \(\sqrt n\). There the bound on the expected excess test loss falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), plus a term proportional to the step size. Training much longer buys optimization accuracy that the growing stability term gives back.
The running example shows the trade-off without regularization, using 100 examples and a constant step \(\eta = 0.25\). The logistic loss with features of size 1 is \(\frac14\)-smooth, so the condition \(\eta \le 8\) holds, and with \(L = 1\) the loss bound is \(0.5E\). The script averages over 100 pairs of runs, with the first example replaced by a fresh draw.

The size of the bound, however, is far off. After one epoch the bound is 14 times the measured gap, and after 40 epochs it is 165 times. The reason is that the argument uses only the fact that a step does not push points apart. In fact the distance between the runs levels off near 0.4, while the bound grows linearly.
Convexity is the condition that fails for neural networks. Without it, a gradient step can push two points apart. Hardt, Recht & Singer still get a bound in that case, but it grows polynomially in the number of steps rather than linearly in the total step size.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.7 An unstable algorithm: 1-nearest neighbour
Seeing an algorithm without stability makes clear what stability rules out. The nearest neighbour (NN) rule with one neighbour, 1-NN, predicts the label of the closest training point. It fits every training example using that example itself, which is exactly the dependence that stability forbids.
Its training error is 0, since each training point is its own nearest neighbour when the points are distinct. Its \(\beta\) under the 0-1 loss is 1, the largest possible value. To see this, replace a training example by the same point with the opposite label. The prediction at that point flips, so the loss there changes from 0 to 1.
Its gap does not close when the labels are noisy. Write \(p(x)\) for the probability that the label at the point \(x\) is \(+1\). As the training set grows, the nearest neighbour of a test point lies almost on top of it, so its label is an independent draw with the same probability \(p(x)\). The two labels then disagree with probability \(2p(x)(1 - p(x))\), and the average of this over \(x\) is the limit of the test error (Cover & Hart 1967). Since the training error is 0, this limit is also the limit of the gap.
1-NN is still a reasonable classifier. The best possible classifier, the Bayes classifier, predicts the more likely label at each point, and the limiting error of 1-NN is at most twice its error. But the training error of 1-NN says nothing about how close it gets to that best error. With a majority vote over more neighbours, a prediction rarely changes when one example is replaced. Its uniform stability is still \(\beta = 1\), though, because replacing one neighbour can flip a vote that is split as evenly as possible. Average-case notions of stability explain it instead (Devroye & Wagner 1979).
In the running example the best possible error is 0.250, and the 1-NN limit is 0.338. Table 7.5 compares 1-NN with the regularized logistic regression, averaging over 10 training sets and measuring the 0-1 error on 2,000 test points.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
section: 7.8 Overfitting is memorization of individual examples
text:
7.8 Overfitting is memorization of individual examples
The identity of Section 7.3 says which examples carry the gap. Each term of Equation 7.2 is the self-influence, or memorization score, of one example. It is the example’s loss under the model trained without it, minus its loss under the model trained with it: \[\mathrm{mem}_i(S) = \ell\big(A(S^{(i)}), z_i\big) - \ell\big(A(S), z_i\big). \tag{7.11}\] The expected gap is the average of these scores, and each score can be measured directly, by retraining with the example replaced. Feldman (2020) uses the same idea with accuracy in place of loss and with the example removed rather than replaced.
The script checks the identity on training sets of 40 examples. It fits the model, then for each example replaces it by a fresh draw, refits, and records the score. It repeats this over 100 training sets and reports each average with its standard error, written after a ± sign. At \(\lambda = 0.01\) the measured gap is \(0.1482 \pm 0.0073\) and the average self-influence is \(0.1422 \pm 0.0025\). At \(\lambda = 0.1\) the two are \(0.0420 \pm 0.0017\) and \(0.0416 \pm 0.0003\). In both cases they agree within their errors, as the identity requires.
The scores are uneven, and the reason is redundancy. A typical example is fitted well whether or not it is in the training set, because its neighbours carry the same information. An atypical example, such as a mislabelled point or a member of a rare subgroup, is fitted only if it is there itself. So the atypical examples carry most of the gap.
The running example makes this visible, since about a quarter of its examples have a label that goes against the trend. At \(\lambda = 0.01\) their average self-influence is 0.284, three times the 0.097 of the other examples, while at \(\lambda = 0.1\) the two are 0.055 and 0.037. Regularization flattens the profile, because it limits how far any one example can pull the weights, and atypical examples pull hardest (Figure 7.7).






Figure 7.7: Self-influence \(\ell(w(S^{(i)}), z_i) - \ell(w(S), z_i)\) of each training example against \(y_ix_{i1}\), which measures how typical its label is, for \(n = 40\) and two values of \(\lambda\). Examples whose label goes against the trend have the largest self-influence. The dashed line is the average, which equals the expected gap.



A small average leaves room for a few heavily memorized examples, because the expected gap needs only the average score to be small. Uniform stability is a stronger requirement, since it caps every score at \(\beta\).
Memorization is not always a defect. Feldman (2020) shows that it can be necessary when the data have a long tail of rare subpopulations, each seen about once. On such data, an algorithm that does not memorize those rare examples loses accuracy on the tail, so a large gap can come with good test accuracy. The empirical evidence points the same way. Zhang et al. (2017) found that deep networks fit even randomly relabelled training data perfectly. Later, Feldman & Zhang (2020) measured memorization scores on image benchmarks and found the highest scores on atypical and mislabelled examples. In practice, expect the rarest examples to be the most memorized, and measure them rather than only the average.

title: 7  Algorithmic stability and generalization
text:
7.9 Code
There is no snippet, because every number here comes from retraining models. The full edition’s script stability.py runs every experiment and draws every figure in this chapter. Run it from the repository root.
uv run python code/part01-prerequisites/stability.py
Its results support four lessons. The \(1/(\lambda n)\) scaling of regularized ERM holds, but the measured changes and gaps sit between 4 and more than 30 times below the bound. The gap identity, unlike the bounds, is exact. The SGD bound gets the direction right and the size wrong. And 1-NN has training error 0 and test error 0.35, while the training and test errors of regularized logistic regression meet.

0-1 loss
\(\beta = 1\); training error 0






Rules of thumb

A gap bound from stability needs \(\beta\) to go to zero. The Bousquet–Elisseeff bound needs \(\beta\) to fall faster than \(1/\sqrt n\).
Regularization strength and training time are the two stability knobs. For ERM, \(\beta\) is proportional to \(1/\lambda\), and for SGD to \(\eta T\).
A training error of 0 is a warning, not a result. The model may depend entirely on individual examples.
The examples a model memorizes most are the atypical ones.

text:

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.1 Why this matters
Some computations must hide something, such as the message in an encrypted file, or a value split among several holders that no single holder may learn. To build or review such a system, you need a precise answer to one question. What does it mean that an observer learns nothing it was not supposed to learn?
Against unlimited computing power, a key shorter than the message cannot hide it perfectly, because seeing the ciphertext rules some messages out. Perfect hiding is possible, but it needs a key as long as all the data. Practical cryptography therefore asks for less, namely that every attacker with realistic computing power learns almost nothing. This chapter makes “realistic” and “almost nothing” precise, and shows the few tools that prove such statements.
The whole subject rests on one idea, which is that security is a game. A challenger secretly flips a fair coin to pick one of two worlds, for example one world where it encrypts one message and one where it encrypts another. The challenger shows the result to an adversary, whose task is to guess which world it is in. An adversary who learns nothing from what it sees is right half the time, whatever it answers, so only a win rate above one half shows that something leaked. A scheme is secure when no efficient adversary beats the coin by more than a tiny amount, where “efficient” means roughly “feasible in practice” and is defined below. Proofs reach that conclusion in small steps, each of which changes one thing in what the adversary sees, and the rest of the chapter shows how.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.2 Advantage
The simplest adversary sees one sample and answers with a single bit. It is called a distinguisher, written \(A\), and its answer 1 means “I think this sample came from the second world”. Let \(X\) be the distribution of the sample in the first world, and let \(Y\) be its distribution in the second. A distinguisher that is any good then says 1 more often on samples from \(Y\) than on samples from \(X\). Its advantage is the gap between how often it says 1 in the two worlds. To write this in symbols, let \(\Pr[A(X) = 1]\) be the probability that it says 1 when its sample comes from \(X\), and likewise for \(Y\). The advantage is then \[\mathrm{Adv}_A(X, Y) = \big|\Pr[A(X) = 1] - \Pr[A(Y) = 1]\big|. \tag{8.1}\]
The absolute value also credits a distinguisher whose answers point the wrong way, since flipping its answers turns it into one that points the right way. A distinguisher that ignores its sample says 1 equally often in both worlds, so its advantage is 0, while one that is always right has advantage 1.
The advantage and the chance of winning the coin game measure the same thing. The distinguisher wins when it says 1 in the second world or 0 in the first. Since each world comes up half the time, its chance of winning is the average of these two success rates: \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \tfrac12\Pr[A(Y) = 1] + \tfrac12\Pr[A(X) = 0] = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\big(\Pr[A(Y) = 1] - \Pr[A(X) = 1]\big). \tag{8.2}\] So a distinguisher whose answer 1 points to the second world wins with probability one half plus half its advantage. For example, let the first world be a fair coin and the second a coin that lands heads with probability 0.6. A distinguisher that says 1 on heads says 1 with probability 0.6 in the second world and 0.5 in the first. Its advantage is therefore 0.1, and it wins the game with probability 0.55, which is one half plus 0.05.
You already know distinguishers from machine learning, since a classifier trained to tell real images from generated ones is one. If it outputs 1 for “real”, it says 1 on real images at its true positive rate and on generated images at its false positive rate. Its advantage is therefore the difference between the two rates. In statistics, deciding which of two distributions produced a sample is a hypothesis test, the subject of Hypothesis testing.
How large can the advantage be? Some outcomes are more likely under one distribution than under the other. A distinguisher, even a randomized one, can only choose for each outcome how often to say 1 on it. Saying 1 on an outcome that is more likely under \(Y\) widens the gap, while saying 1 on one that is more likely under \(X\) narrows it. So the best distinguisher says 1 exactly on the outcomes that are more likely under \(Y\), however long it may run. Its advantage is then the extra probability that \(Y\) puts on those outcomes, compared with \(X\). That quantity is the total variation (TV) distance between the two distributions, which Divergences studies. It is 0 when the two distributions are equal, and 1 when they never produce the same outcome.
This limit splits security into three levels. If the TV distance is 0, the two worlds look identical and no adversary has any advantage, which is perfect security. If the TV distance is tiny, even an adversary with unlimited time gains almost nothing, which is statistical security. The third level, computational security, is the main business of cryptography. There the TV distance can be large, as long as no efficient adversary can find the outcomes where the two worlds differ. A short key cannot make the two worlds identical, but it can make their difference too hard to find, and that is how a short key protects a long message.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.3 Efficient adversaries and tiny advantages
No key resists every attacker, but the key’s length decides how much an attack costs. An attacker who tries keys one after another finds a 40-bit key quickly and a 256-bit key never. Security is therefore a statement about how fast the attacker’s success shrinks as the key grows. Cryptographers measure the size of the key with a security parameter, written \(\lambda\), which you can think of as the key length in bits.
The asymptotic view describes what happens as \(\lambda\) grows, and it needs two definitions. The first says which attackers count as efficient, namely those whose running time grows at most like a polynomial in \(\lambda\), such as the cube of \(\lambda\). Such an attacker may also flip coins as it runs. It is therefore called probabilistic polynomial time (PPT), probabilistic because of the coins and polynomial time because of the bound on its running time.
The second definition says which advantages count as tiny. Think of the adversary’s advantage as a function of \(\lambda\). That function is negligible if it falls below one over every polynomial in \(\lambda\) once \(\lambda\) is large enough, and stays below it for all larger \(\lambda\). For example, \(2^{-\lambda}\) is negligible, because \(2^\lambda\) outgrows every polynomial. But \(\lambda^{-10}\) is not, because it never falls below \(\lambda^{-11}\). A scheme is secure if every PPT adversary has a negligible advantage.
The two definitions fit together because of repetition. An efficient attacker can repeat its attack a polynomial number of times, and the union bound from Concentration inequalities limits what that buys. It says that the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their chances. So the chance that at least one try succeeds is at most the number of tries times the chance per try. A negligible chance per try falls below one over any polynomial, including the number of tries times any other polynomial you pick. Multiplying it by the number of tries therefore still leaves it below one over that other polynomial, so repetition does not help.
A small chance that is not negligible does not survive repetition. Suppose an attack succeeds with probability \(\lambda^{-3}\) on each try, and the tries are independent. Independence lets the chances of failure multiply, so \(\lambda^4\) tries all fail with probability at most \(e^{-\lambda}\), and the attack almost surely succeeds.
Brute force shows why the best one can ask for is “negligible”, never zero. Suppose an attacker tries \(t\) different keys against a key drawn uniformly from all \(2^\lambda\) keys. Each try is right with probability \(2^{-\lambda}\), so the attacker succeeds with probability \(t/2^\lambda\). That chance is negligible when \(t\) is a polynomial in \(\lambda\), but it is never zero.
The weakness of these definitions is that “negligible” describes a limit, not a value at the key length you actually use. Table 8.1 evaluates four functions at \(\lambda = 128\). The negligible \(2^{-\sqrt\lambda}\) is still \(3.9\times10^{-4}\) there, far larger than the non-negligible \(\lambda^{-10}\). It drops below \(\lambda^{-10}\) for good only from \(\lambda = 20{,}520\) (Figure 8.1). A statement that holds “for all large enough \(\lambda\)” does not tell you whether 128 is large enough.

Real systems fix the key length. A block cipher encrypts data in blocks of fixed size under a key, and the standard one, AES, uses keys of 128 bits or more. Concrete security therefore replaces “efficient” and “negligible” by explicit numbers, naming the attacker’s resources and bounding the advantage they can buy. Those resources are the attacker’s running time and the number of questions it may ask an oracle. An oracle is a box the game lets it query, such as one that encrypts messages of its choice. The benchmark is brute force. A scheme has \(\kappa\)-bit security, where \(\kappa\) is a number of bits, if no attack does better than brute force over \(2^\kappa\) keys. In other words, an attacker that runs for time \(t\) gets an advantage of at most about \[\frac{t}{2^\kappa}. \tag{8.3}\]
Here is what 128-bit security buys. Suppose an attacker tests \(10^{18}\) keys per second for a whole year, which comes to about \(2^{84.7}\) keys. Against a 128-bit key, that attack succeeds with probability only \(9.3\times10^{-14}\). At that rate, trying all \(2^{128}\) keys would take \(1.08\times10^{13}\) years.
Security proofs are reductions. A scheme is built from a primitive, a simpler building block such as a block cipher. Its security proof turns any adversary who breaks the scheme into one that breaks the primitive. Read in reverse, this says that if the primitive is hard to break, so is the scheme. But the conversion usually loses something. Suppose a reduction turns an advantage against the scheme into one \(2^{20}\) times smaller against the primitive. Then, if the primitive has 128-bit security, the scheme has only about 108 bits. A tight reduction loses almost nothing, while a loose one forces larger keys for the same guarantee.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.4 Hybrid arguments
Proofs rarely compare the two worlds of a game directly. They walk from one to the other through intermediate worlds called hybrids, and each world differs from the next in one thing. Write \(m\) for the number of steps and \(H_i\) for the world reached after \(i\) steps. Then \(H_0\) is the first world of the game and \(H_m\) is the second.
Look at how often a distinguisher says 1 in each world along the way. The gap between the two ends is the sum of the gaps between neighbours, since every intermediate frequency is added once and subtracted once. The size of a sum is at most the sum of the sizes, so the advantages add up: \[\mathrm{Adv}_A(H_0, H_m) \le \sum_{i=1}^m\mathrm{Adv}_A(H_{i-1}, H_i). \tag{8.4}\] So any gap between the two ends must show up in at least one step of the chain.
The most common use is for many samples. Suppose that one sample from \(X\) cannot be told from one sample from \(Y\). To compare \(m\) independent samples from each, walk from all samples drawn from \(X\) to all drawn from \(Y\), swapping one sample at a time. Each step changes a single sample, so it is a one-sample problem, and the total advantage is at most \(m\) times the one-sample advantage.
The argument needs two conditions. First, the number of samples \(m\) must be a polynomial in \(\lambda\), because otherwise \(m\) times a negligible advantage need not be negligible, and the bound says nothing. Second, both distributions must be efficiently samplable, because of how the proof works. It turns an attack on \(m\) samples into an attack on one sample. That attack places its one sample at a random position, and fills the other positions with samples it draws itself, from \(Y\) before that position and from \(X\) after it. If drawing samples were slow, the one-sample attack would no longer be efficient.
The factor \(m\) is safe but pessimistic, because it reflects how the proof is organized, not how the best attacker works. Take a coin that lands heads with probability 0.51, so that its bias, written \(\delta\), is 0.01, and compare \(m\) of its flips with \(m\) fair flips. One flip gives an advantage of at most \(\delta\), so the hybrid bound for \(m\) flips is \(m\delta\). Table 8.2 compares it with the best possible advantage and with a simple test, majority vote, which says 1 if more than half the flips are heads.

The hybrid bound is exact for one flip but useless by 100 flips. To see why, note that the best attacker counts the heads, and its advantage depends on how far apart the two average counts are compared with their random spread. The average counts differ by \(m\delta\), while each count spreads by about \(\sqrt m/2\) around its average. Their distance in units of the spread is therefore \(2\delta\sqrt m\), so the best advantage grows like \(\delta\sqrt m\), not like \(\delta m\) (Figure 8.2). To reach a constant advantage, such as one half, the attacker needs about \(1/\delta^2\) flips, while the hybrid bound would allow it after \(1/\delta\).






Figure 8.2: Advantage of telling \(m\) flips of a coin with bias \(\frac12 + 0.01\) from fair flips: majority vote (simulation), the best possible distinguisher (exact TV distance), and the hybrid bound \(m\delta\).



At 10,000 flips, majority vote reaches an advantage of only 0.481, while the best possible is 0.683. The trouble is its threshold of half the flips, which sits at the centre of the fair coin’s count. For many flips, the biased count lands above that threshold almost always, but the fair count still lands above it about half the time. So the advantage of majority vote can never exceed about one half. The best test puts its threshold halfway between the two average counts instead. A reasonable-looking test can thus be far from the best one, which is why security is measured against every adversary.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.5 Pseudorandom generators and functions
Truly random bits are expensive to produce and to share, while a short random key is cheap. Two tools stretch a short key into a lot of randomness that looks real to any efficient observer.
A pseudorandom generator (PRG) is a fast, deterministic procedure that stretches a short random seed into a longer string. It is secure if no efficient distinguisher can tell its output from truly random bits of the same length.
A PRG can never be statistically secure. Suppose its output is at least one bit longer than its seed. Then there are at most half as many seeds as output strings, so at most half of all strings of that length are outputs of the PRG. A distinguisher that says 1 exactly on those outputs always says 1 on the PRG’s output, and at most half the time on random bits. Its advantage is therefore at least one half. But checking whether a string is an output means trying every seed, which takes exponential time. That is why pseudorandomness is only a promise against efficient distinguishers.
PRGs exist if one-way functions exist, which are functions that are easy to compute but hard to invert. In practice, a stream cipher such as ChaCha20 encrypts by combining the data with a long keystream generated from a short key. Designers treat stream ciphers as PRGs, which means assuming that no efficient distinguisher can tell the keystream from random bits.
A random function is a table that gives each input its own independent, uniform output. A table on 128-bit inputs has \(2^{128}\) entries, so nobody can store one.
A pseudorandom function (PRF) is a keyed function, written \(F_k\) for the key \(k\), whose outputs look like those of a random function to anyone without the key. Its game uses an oracle, a box that a fair coin fills either with \(F_k\) under a freshly drawn random key or with a truly random function. The adversary may ask the box for its output on any inputs it likes, each one chosen after seeing the earlier answers. The PRF is secure if no efficient adversary can tell which function is in the box. In practice, the hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) is assumed to be a PRF.
A PRF can be built from any PRG whose output is twice as long as its seed, with a construction called the GGM tree, after Goldreich, Goldwasser and Micali. It grows a binary tree of keys with the secret key at the root, and the PRG applied to a node gives two halves, which become its two children. To evaluate the PRF, each bit of the input picks the left or the right child, and the leaf reached at the end is the output.
The proof of the GGM tree is a chain of hybrids that replaces the tree by random values, one level at a time. Write \(n\) for the number of input bits, which is also the number of levels, and \(q\) for the number of queries the adversary makes. At each level the \(q\) queries touch at most \(q\) nodes, so each step of the chain costs at most \(q\) times the PRG’s advantage. Write \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}\) for that advantage and \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}\) for an efficient adversary’s advantage against the PRF. Over the \(n\) levels, the steps add up to \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}} \le nq\cdot\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}. \tag{8.5}\] The full edition sketches this proof and cites the complete one.
In proofs, both tools play the same role, since they let you replace “pseudorandom” by “truly random” at the cost of a small advantage.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.6 The birthday bound
Many arguments about random values fail only if two of the values happen to coincide, and the birthday bound says how likely that is. Draw \(q\) values independently and uniformly from a set of size \(N\). They form about \(q^2/2\) pairs. Each pair coincides with probability \(1/N\), because whatever the first value is, the second matches it with probability \(1/N\). So collisions become likely once the number of pairs approaches \(N\), which happens after about \(\sqrt N\) draws, far fewer than \(N\). Precisely, \[1 - e^{-q(q-1)/(2N)} \le \Pr[\text{collision}] \le \frac{q(q-1)}{2N}. \tag{8.6}\]
The upper bound is the union bound over all pairs. The lower bound instead comes from the exact chance of no collision, which multiplies the chances that each new value misses all earlier ones. The two bounds are close. The full edition shows that, while the upper bound is below 1, it overstates the true chance by a factor of at most about 1.6. It also computes that a collision becomes as likely as not at about \(1.18\sqrt N\) draws.
The bound needs the values to be uniform and independent, because that is what makes each pair coincide with probability \(1/N\). Values that are not uniform coincide more often, so the upper bound can then fail.

The birthday bound also limits how much data one key may protect, and the reason runs through block ciphers. A block cipher is a keyed permutation, which never maps two different inputs to the same output. It is modelled as a pseudorandom permutation (PRP), a keyed function that no efficient adversary can tell from a random shuffle of the inputs. Many proofs, such as the encryption proof in the next section, are written for a PRF instead, whose outputs on different inputs are independent. But a permutation’s outputs are not quite independent, since they can never repeat.
The only visible difference between a random function and a random permutation is that the function sometimes repeats an output and the permutation never does. So an adversary can tell them apart only about as often as the answers collide, and this observation is the switching lemma. Write \(n\) for the number of bits in a block, so that there are \(2^n\) possible blocks. Treating a PRP as a PRF then costs an extra advantage, on top of its advantage as a PRP. After \(q\) queries, the lemma bounds that extra advantage by \[\frac{q^2}{2^{n+1}}, \tag{8.7}\] which is the birthday bound for \(2^n\) values. The bound is tight, because an adversary that says 1 when it sees a repeated answer has an advantage equal to the exact chance of a collision.
So a bound in terms of queries is really a limit on data. Take blocks of 128 bits, so that \(2^{32}\) blocks hold 64 GiB of data. That much data costs an extra advantage of at most \(2^{-65}\). At \(2^{48}\) blocks the bound has grown to \(2^{-33}\). By \(2^{64}\) blocks it reaches one half and says nothing, because the guarantee degrades with the square of the data under one key. That is why you should change keys long before that point. Ciphers with 64-bit blocks fare much worse. To keep the extra advantage below \(2^{-20}\), they can process only about 6 million blocks under one key.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.7 Encryption
An encryption scheme has perfect secrecy if the ciphertext’s distribution is the same for every message. Seeing the ciphertext then does not change how likely any message is.
The one-time pad achieves this with a key \(K\) that is a uniformly random string as long as the message \(m\). The ciphertext is \(m \oplus K\), where \(\oplus\) is the bitwise exclusive or (XOR), which flips each bit of the message where the key has a 1. For a fixed message, each key gives a different ciphertext, and each ciphertext comes from exactly one key. A uniform key therefore gives a uniform ciphertext, whatever the message is. Table 8.4 shows this for 2-bit messages.

Perfect secrecy has a price, because it needs at least as many keys as messages. Fix a ciphertext that occurs. Because decryption must recover the message, each key decrypts it to one message, so it can come from at most as many messages as there are keys. With fewer keys than messages, some message could never produce that ciphertext, and seeing it would rule that message out. The pad must also be used only once, because combining two ciphertexts under the same pad with XOR cancels the pad and reveals the XOR of the two messages.
Practical schemes use short keys, so they settle for computational security. The standard goal is security under chosen-plaintext attack (CPA), defined by a game. The adversary may ask an oracle for encryptions of any messages it likes, at any time. It then submits two messages of equal length, receives the encryption of one of them, chosen by a fair coin, and must guess which one it got. The lengths must be equal because a ciphertext usually reveals the length of its message. The encryption oracle models reality, since an attacker can often get chosen data encrypted, such as a request it sends or a value it plants in a database. Passing this game is equivalent to a scheme hiding everything an efficient adversary could compute about the message, apart from its length.
The game has a consequence that surprises many programmers, which is that encryption must be randomized. To see why, suppose encrypting the same message always gives the same ciphertext. The adversary can then ask for the encryption of its first message and compare it with the challenge. That works because two different messages never share a ciphertext, since decryption could not then tell which one to return. So if the two ciphertexts match, the adversary got the first message, and otherwise the second. Since it is always right, its advantage is 1, and the full edition’s script measures exactly 1.000.
The same weakness shows up without any game. Deterministic encryption of a column of labels maps equal labels to equal ciphertexts, so the frequency of each ciphertext reveals the frequency of each label.
The fix is to use a fresh pad for every encryption. To encrypt, draw a random value \(r\), called a nonce, uniformly from a set of possible values, written \(\mathcal R\). The PRF’s output on \(r\), \(F_k(r)\), then serves as a one-time pad, and \(r\) is sent along so that the receiver can rebuild the pad. The ciphertext is the pair \[(r,\ m \oplus F_k(r)). \tag{8.8}\]
This scheme can fail in only two ways. Either the PRF can be told from a random function, or the challenge reuses a nonce that the adversary has already seen. A reused nonce is fatal because the adversary already knows its pad. Each encryption it requested showed it a nonce together with the ciphertext of a message it chose, and combining the two with XOR reveals the pad for that nonce. So if the challenge reuses that nonce, the adversary removes the pad and reads the message.
The bound adds the two failures. Write \(q\) for the number of encryptions the adversary requests, and \(\lvert\mathcal R\rvert\) for the number of possible nonces. By the union bound, the challenge’s nonce matches one of the \(q\) earlier ones with probability at most \(q/\lvert\mathcal R\rvert\). Writing \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}\) for the PRF’s advantage, the scheme’s advantage is then at most \[2\,\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}} + \frac{q}{\lvert\mathcal R\rvert}. \tag{8.9}\] The factor 2 comes from converting a win probability into an advantage, by the rule in Section 8.2.
The second term is real, not a weakness of the proof. Take 8-bit nonces and 16 encryptions, for example. Then an attacker who waits for a repeated nonce wins with advantage 0.0607, against a bound of 0.0625. This matches the simulation, which measures 0.0605. With 128-bit nonces, though, the same attack has an advantage below \(2^{-124}\).
The proof needs only the challenge’s nonce to differ from the earlier ones, and that costs at most \(q/\lvert\mathcal R\rvert\), which grows in proportion to \(q\). Over the life of a key, though, any two nonces may repeat, and each repeat reuses a pad. By the birthday bound, repeats become likely after about \(\sqrt{\lvert\mathcal R\rvert}\) encryptions, so size the nonce set for that.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.8 Simulation and secret sharing
Encryption hides everything. Many procedures instead run among several participants, each holding its own input, and must reveal something to each of them, such as the final result, and nothing else. “Nothing else” is hard to state directly, because a participant may combine what it sees in clever ways. Simulation sidesteps the problem. Suppose a participant could have faked everything it sees from what it is allowed to learn. Then what it sees contains nothing more.
A participant’s view, written \(\mathrm{View}(x)\), is everything it sees during a run, which depends on all the inputs \(x\) and on the procedure’s randomness. Write \(L(x)\) for what it is allowed to learn, such as its own input and the output. A simulator, written \(S\), is an efficient procedure that receives only \(L(x)\) and produces a fake view. The procedure reveals nothing beyond \(L(x)\) if the fake view has the same distribution as the real one, for every input \(x\): \[S(L(x)) \equiv \mathrm{View}(x). \tag{8.10}\] This exact equality is perfect security. If the two distributions are only close in TV distance, the security is statistical, and if no efficient distinguisher can tell them apart, it is computational.
The definition captures “nothing else” because anything the participant could compute from its real view, it could compute equally well from the simulator’s output. That output was made from \(L(x)\) alone, so whatever the view reveals, \(L(x)\) already revealed. The simulator must be efficient, because in computational security an unbounded simulator could compute things the participant cannot. The definition would then accept views that reveal facts that are easy to read from the view but hard to compute from \(L(x)\). Finally, the definition compares the view only with \(L(x)\), so it says nothing about whether revealing \(L(x)\) itself is acceptable. That is decided when you choose \(L\).
Additive secret sharing is the simplest example. It works with the integers from 0 to \(p - 1\), where \(p\) is the modulus and arithmetic wraps around mod \(p\). To split a secret \(x\) among \(h\) holders, draw the first \(h - 1\) shares, written \(s_1\) to \(s_{h-1}\), independently and uniformly at random. The last share is \(x\) minus the sum of the others, \[s_h = x - (s_1 + \dots + s_{h-1}) \bmod p, \tag{8.11}\] so that all the shares add up to \(x\). Suppose two secrets are shared among the same holders, and each holder adds its share of one to its share of the other. The results are shares of the sum of the secrets, so the holders can compute a sum without ever putting their shares together.
Any \(h - 1\) of the shares look like independent uniform numbers, whatever the secret is, because the one missing share is what ties them to \(x\). The reason is that subtracting a uniform number mod \(p\) wraps around and hits every value equally often. Table 8.5 shows this for two holders and \(p = 5\). As the random first share \(r\) runs through all five values, the second share \(x - r\) takes each value exactly once, for either secret. The simulator for a group of \(h - 1\) holders therefore just outputs uniform random numbers, and its fake view has exactly the real distribution, so the security is perfect.

Suppose the group of \(h - 1\) holders also learns the secret, for example because it is published later. The simulator then receives \(x\) as well. It draws the group’s \(h - 1\) shares uniformly, and these shares together with \(x\) fix the one missing share as \(x\) minus their sum, exactly as in the real sharing. This is the typical form of a simulator, random where the view is random and consistent with the leakage where the leakage pins the view down.
The wrap-around is a condition of the result, not a detail, because without it the share’s range moves with the secret. For example, suppose the mask \(r\) is uniform on the 16 values from 0 to 15, and the share \(x - r\) is not reduced. Call the number of possible masks, here 16, the mask width \(W\). The share then lies in a window of 16 values that ends at the secret itself. So the window for the secret 7 starts seven places above the window for the secret 0. Seven of the 16 values in each window are therefore impossible under the other secret, which makes the TV distance \(7/16 = 0.4375\). A simulation with 100,000 shares for each secret measures 0.4423 (Figure 8.4).
For comparison, the simulation also draws \(r\) uniformly from 0 to 10 and reduces the share \(x - r\) modulo 11. The measured TV distance is then 0.0045, which is sampling noise, since the exact distance is zero. In general, for two secrets \(x\) and \(x'\) whose difference is smaller than the mask width \(W\), the TV distance between their shares without the wrap-around is \[\frac{\lvert x - x'\rvert}{W}. \tag{8.12}\] A much wider mask makes it tiny, which gives statistical rather than perfect security.






Figure 8.4: Histograms of the second share for secrets \(x = 0\) and \(x = 7\). Left: reduced mod \(p = 11\), both are uniform. Right: over the integers with \(r < 16\), the support shifts with the secret.

title: 8  Cryptography basics
text:
8.9 Learning with errors
Every tool so far is defined by a property, such as looking random, and works with any primitive that has it. Learning with errors (LWE) is instead a specific hard problem, with three attractions. Under a condition on its errors, it is as hard as worst-case problems on lattices, regular grids of points in many dimensions. No efficient quantum attack on it is known. And encryption built on it lets you add ciphertexts without decrypting them.
LWE hides a secret vector behind linear equations whose right-hand sides are slightly wrong. Here the secret \(s\) is a vector of numbers mod \(p\), and its length \(d\) is called the dimension. The problem gives out samples, each of which pairs a uniformly random vector \(a\) with a number \(b\). To compute \(b\), take the inner product \(\langle a, s\rangle\), the sum of the products of matching entries. Then add the error \(e\), a small random integer drawn fresh for each sample, and reduce mod \(p\) to get \[b = \langle a, s\rangle + e \bmod p. \tag{8.13}\]
The search version of the problem asks for \(s\), while the decision version asks whether a list of pairs consists of LWE samples or of uniform random pairs.
The errors are what make the problem hard. Without them, the samples form a linear system, and Gaussian elimination solves it from \(d\) independent equations. With them, elimination solves the wrong system exactly, because undoing the equations multiplies the small errors by large numbers mod \(p\), which scrambles the answer. The full edition’s script shows this with a 16-dimensional secret and \(p = 4096\). Elimination recovers all 16 coordinates when there are no errors, but none of them once small errors of \(-1\), 0 or 1 are added.
Hardness holds under a condition on the errors. Regev proved it for errors drawn from a normal distribution rounded to integers, with a standard deviation large enough relative to \(\sqrt d\). For such errors, solving LWE is at least as hard as worst-case lattice problems. His proof used a quantum algorithm, though later work gave classical proofs. Other small error distributions, such as the uniform errors in the toy below, need separate arguments, and the full edition cites these results rather than proving them.
Regev encryption of a single bit uses LWE directly. It is a secret-key scheme, in which the same secret \(s\) encrypts and decrypts. Picture the numbers mod \(p\) as a clock with \(p\) positions, where \(p\) is even. To encrypt a bit \(m\), take a fresh LWE sample and move its \(b\) halfway round the clock if the bit is 1, so that the ciphertext is \[\big(a,\ \langle a, s\rangle + e + m\cdot\tfrac p2 \bmod p\big). \tag{8.14}\] Whoever knows \(s\) subtracts \(\langle a, s\rangle\), which leaves the error plus the encoded bit. That is near 0 for the bit 0 and near halfway for the bit 1, and decryption reads off whichever is closer. It is correct as long as the error is smaller than a quarter of the clock, \[\lvert e\rvert < \frac p4. \tag{8.15}\] A larger error could push the value past the boundary between the two halves.
Without the key, the sample looks uniform, by the decision version of LWE, so the bit is added to something that looks uniform, which works like a one-time pad. That is why the scheme is secure against chosen-plaintext attack, provided that decision LWE is hard.
Adding ciphertexts entry by entry adds everything inside them. The bits add, and two half-turns round the clock make a full turn, so the sum decrypts to the XOR of the bits. Two half-turns make exactly a full turn only when \(p\) is even, which is why the scheme needs an even \(p\). The errors add as well. Suppose every error lies between \(-B\) and \(B\), where \(B\) is the error bound. A sum of \(k\) ciphertexts then has an error of at most \(kB\), and it decrypts correctly whenever \[k < \frac{p}{4B}. \tag{8.16}\] With \(p = 4096\) and \(B = 32\), the budget guarantees that sums of fewer than 32 ciphertexts decrypt correctly.
That guarantee is a worst case, which assumes every error is as large as possible and all have the same sign. Independent errors with mean zero mostly cancel instead. Their variances add, so the summed error has a standard deviation that grows like \(\sqrt k\), not like \(k\). Table 8.6 compares a simulation with a normal approximation built on this fact.



Table 8.6: Decryption failure rate of a sum of \(k\) Regev ciphertexts, \(p = 4096\), errors uniform on \(\{-32, \dots, 32\}\) (20,000 trials).

Take a sum of 1,024 ciphertexts as an example. The full edition computes the standard deviation of the summed error from the variance of the individual errors, and gets about 600. A quarter of the clock is 1,024, or about 1.7 standard deviations. A normal value lands that far from zero with probability about 0.088. Overall, failures become measurable only for sums of around 256 ciphertexts, eight times the guaranteed 32 (Figure 8.5).






Figure 8.5: Decryption failure rate of a sum of \(k\) Regev ciphertexts (\(p = 4096\), errors uniform on \(\{-32, \dots, 32\}\)): simulation against the normal approximation. The dashed line is the worst-case guarantee \(k < p/(4B) = 32\).



But the budget is still finite. Once the error is comparable to a quarter of the clock, the decrypted value is spread round the whole clock, and decryption becomes a coin flip. A larger modulus, relative to the error, buys more additions. That trade-off sets the parameters of every LWE-based scheme that computes on ciphertexts.
A Regev ciphertext carries one bit in \(d + 1\) numbers, which is wasteful. Practical lattice schemes use structured variants of LWE, such as ring-LWE and module-LWE, which pack many values into each ciphertext and compute faster. Module-LWE underlies ML-KEM, the standardized scheme for sending a fresh shared key, published as FIPS 203 in 2024.

text:

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter, with a few exceptions. It cites the existence of PRGs, the hardness of LWE, and the equivalence between passing the CPA game and hiding everything an efficient adversary could compute. It also only sketches the proof for the GGM tree.

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
The common thread
This part teaches you to break models before the rest of the book teaches you to protect them. Every defence is measured against an attack. A guarantee is only as meaningful as the strongest adversary it stops, and an evaluation is only as honest as the attack it runs. So the book starts with the adversaries: what they see, what they want, and how well the best of them can do.
You need the Prerequisites, or their content. This part leans hardest on three of them. It uses hypothesis testing, especially reading a test at a low false-positive rate, the total variation distance, and the link between stability and generalization. The defence that most of the book is about, differential privacy, arrives only in the next part. It is designed against exactly the games defined here. The only privacy definitions in this part are the older ones of its second-to-last chapter, such as k-anonymity, and they appear as targets.
Every attack in this part has the same shape. A challenger trains a model or releases data, and what it releases depends on a hidden secret. An adversary then guesses the secret from whatever the threat model lets it see. Writing an attack this way, as a game, makes it precise enough to score and to compare with other attacks. What changes from chapter to chapter is the secret. It can be one bit saying whether a record was used, a person’s sensitive attribute, a string the model memorized, a fact about the whole training population, a client’s input to federated training, a person’s name, or the entire dataset.
Two ideas run through all the chapters. The first is that an attack is a hypothesis test. When the secret is a single bit, the adversary must decide which of two worlds produced what it sees. The best possible attack is then the likelihood-ratio test from Hypothesis testing, and no attack can beat the ceiling that test sets. That ceiling is what lets you say how well the best attack could do, not just how well the attack you tried did.
The second idea is that the worst case is not the average case. Attacks succeed first on outliers, on strings repeated many times, on people with a rare combination of attributes, and on the one example in a batch that a neuron singles out. An average over all records can look harmless while a few records are fully exposed. That is why attacks are reported by how many members they catch at a very low false-positive rate. It is also why the defence of the next part has to protect every record, not just the typical one.
A third idea closes the part. Answering too many statistics too accurately gives the data away, however cleverly the answers are computed. This is the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery. It means some noise is unavoidable, and the question becomes how little noise is enough.

title: Threat models and attacks
section: Why the chapters come in this order
text:
Why the chapters come in this order
Threat models and privacy games comes first, because it fixes the vocabulary that the other chapters use without redefining it. That vocabulary covers the challenger and the adversary, what the adversary sees, and how an attack is scored. Then the part splits in two.
The first half attacks trained models, from the smallest secret to the largest. Membership inference asks whether one record was in the training set, and it is the reference attack the next chapters build on. Building on it, Attribute inference asks whether the model reveals a person’s sensitive attribute beyond what the population already does. Property inference asks whether a model reveals a fact about its training population that no single record reveals. Memorization and extraction asks when a model can be made to emit its training text. Gradient inversion shows that a gradient computed on private data can give the data back exactly. After membership inference, these chapters can be read in any order.
The second half attacks released data, from the weakest protection to the strongest. Linkage and re-identification shows why removing names does not hide whose record is whose. Syntactic anonymity starts from that linkage game and asks what hiding records in crowds guarantees, and which attack gets past each version. Reconstruction attacks shows that even exact aggregate statistics, with no records released at all, can rebuild a whole dataset. Read these three in order. The attacks on syntactic anonymity are the requirements that the next part’s definition is built to meet. The reconstruction results return there as limits on what any private release can achieve.

title: Threat models and attacks
text:
How to read a chapter
Each chapter states its attack as a game, reasons its way to the best possible attack and its ceiling, and measures both on an experiment. The experiments are small enough to run in seconds: logistic regression on synthetic data, a small neural network, a language model built from letter counts with planted secrets. Each is chosen so that the best attack can be computed exactly and compared with the practical one. Where the published experiment needs a large training pipeline, the chapter describes that pipeline in words and reports what it found.
The chapters contain no proofs. Each one ends with a link to the matching chapter of the full edition, which derives every result and has a script that checks every number quoted.

title: Threat models and attacks
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
After this part, you will be able to state any privacy attack as a game, name its threat model and its baseline, and bound how well any attack could do. You will be able to run a membership attack and report it properly, by the members it catches at a false-positive rate of one in a thousand or lower.
You will be able to tell what a model reveals about a person from what the population already reveals about them. You will also know how a property of the training population can leak when no single record does. You will know when a language model memorizes a string well enough to emit it, and why averaging gradients over a batch does not hide the inputs.
On the data side, you will be able to estimate how many people a set of attributes makes unique. You will also be able to run a linkage attack like the one that de-anonymized the Netflix Prize data. You will be able to say what k-anonymity, l-diversity and t-closeness each guarantee and which attack breaks each one. Finally, you will be able to explain why answering many statistics accurately lets an attacker rebuild the data behind them.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a model on patient records and offers it to doctors through a web service. The question whether the model is private has no answer until you say against whom. One attacker can only read predicted labels, while another holds the weights. One knows the other patients in the training set, while another knows only the population, and one may slip crafted records into the training data. They also want different things, from learning that one person was a patient to rebuilding the whole table. A threat model pins all of this down. Without one, “the model leaks” and “the model is safe” are both claims nobody can test, and two attack results cannot be compared.
Once the threat model is fixed, an attack can be written down as a game, as cryptographers do for encryption. One party, the challenger, runs the training pipeline with a hidden secret, such as whether one patient’s record was used. It hands the adversary what the threat model allows it to see, and the adversary guesses the secret. An attack is good only if it guesses better than someone who never saw the model.
That is the one idea of this chapter: an attack is a guess about a hidden secret. When the secret is a single yes-or-no answer, such as whether this patient was in the training set, the game is a hypothesis test. Everything in Hypothesis testing then carries over, including a limit on how well any attack can guess. The chapter also shows that what matters is how many people an attack identifies while almost never accusing the wrong person. And tests on typical records can badly understate the risk to the most exposed person.
crumbs: 9  Threat models and privacy games

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.2 Scoring an attack
The simplest games ask the adversary to guess one hidden bit. Before anything else happens, the challenger picks one of two worlds at random, and the bit records which. It is 1 in the world where the target’s record is used for training, which makes the target a member, and 0 in the world where it is not. Write \(b\) for this bit. The adversary sees what the threat model allows, which this chapter calls its view, and then guesses whether \(b\) is 1 or 0. The view includes everything the adversary knew beforehand.
Two numbers describe how an attack behaves. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of members that it flags as members. Its false positive rate (FPR) is the fraction of non-members that it wrongly flags. Each rate is measured inside one world, so neither depends on how often the challenger picks that world.
How often the attack wins does depend on that, though. Write \(\pi_1\) for the probability that the challenger picks the member world, and \(\pi_0 = 1 - \pi_1\) for the other. The attack wins a member game when it says “member”, and a non-member game when it says “not a member”. So its chance of winning is the weighted sum of its success in the two worlds: \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0\,(1 - \mathrm{FPR}). \tag{9.1}\]
Table 9.1 makes this concrete for an attack whose TPR is 0.6 and whose FPR is 0.2.

The attack wins more often in the second row, but only because most games are played in the world where saying “not a member” is easy. Always saying “not a member”, with no attack at all, would win 900 of those games. So a win rate alone cannot tell a good attack from simply knowing which world is more common. Every game in this chapter is therefore scored against a baseline, the best score of a guess that never looks at the view.
Most evaluations use a fair bit, so that half the targets are members. An adversary who ignores its view then wins exactly half the time, whatever it answers. Putting one half for both priors in Equation 9.1 gives \(\frac12\mathrm{TPR} + \frac12(1 - \mathrm{FPR})\), which is one half plus half the difference between the two rates. That difference is the attack’s advantage: \[\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}. \tag{9.2}\] In a fair game the attack therefore wins with probability \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\).
The advantage measures how much more often the attack says “member” when the target is a member than when it is not. An attack that ignores its view, such as “always say member”, says “member” equally often in both worlds, so its advantage is 0. A perfect attack has advantage 1, and the attack of Table 9.1 has advantage \(0.6 - 0.2 = 0.4\). Because both rates are measured inside one world, the advantage does not change with the prior. That solves the problem of the second row, where an attack that ignores its view wins 0.9 of the games but still has advantage 0.
How large can the advantage be? Write \(P\) for the distribution of the view when the target is not a member, and \(Q\) for its distribution when it is. For a particular view \(x\), write \(p(x)\) for its probability in the non-member world. Its probability in the member world is \(q(x)\), and for a continuous view both are densities. An attack that says “member” on a set of views gains \(q(x)\) in TPR and \(p(x)\) in FPR from each view it includes. Each view therefore adds \(q(x) - p(x)\) to the advantage, and the best attack includes exactly the views where this is positive, those more likely in the member world. Its advantage is the sum of those positive differences, which is the total variation (TV) distance between \(P\) and \(Q\) (Divergences). No attack in a two-world game can have a larger advantage, whatever it does.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.3 Threat models
An attack’s reported number means nothing until you know what the attacker was assumed to see, know and do. A threat model fixes these assumptions by answering five questions.

Goal: what is the secret? A membership attack asks whether a record was in the training data, and an attribute attack seeks a sensitive field of a known record. A reconstruction attack seeks the records themselves, and a property attack a statistic of the whole dataset.
Access: what does the adversary observe? The weakest is label-only access, the model’s decisions on inputs the adversary chooses, such as a predicted class. Next is black-box access to the model’s scores, such as confidences or losses. Then comes white-box access to the parameters. The strongest is the transcript, everything training exposed along the way, such as per-step gradients.
Behaviour: does it follow the rules? An honest-but-curious adversary follows the protocol and only analyses what it legitimately sees. A malicious adversary may deviate, for example by choosing its queries adaptively or by inserting crafted records into the training data, which is called poisoning.
Trust: who sees the raw data? In the central model a trusted curator, a party that holds everyone’s raw data, runs the training, and the adversary sees only what is released. In the local model nobody is trusted, so each person’s data are protected on their own device, for example by adding noise, before the collector sees them. Distributed settings sit in between.
Side information: what does it know already? It may know the population, a public dataset, some or all of the other records, or the target’s non-sensitive fields.

Of these questions, access has the most natural order, and the reason is a general fact about views. Suppose the adversary throws information away, or adds noise of its own. Then it cannot do better, because whoever holds the original view could have done the same processing and run the same attack. For instance, if a service returns a confidence score and you look only at whether it exceeds 0.5, you can do no better than someone who sees the score itself. This is the data processing inequality of Divergences, seen from the attacker’s side.
The fact has one condition. Any randomness the adversary adds must be independent of the hidden bit. Randomness that depended on the secret would carry information about it, and then the processed view could reveal more than the original.
Each level of access lets the adversary compute the level below it. A label is a function of the scores when the service computes it from them, and a score is a function of the weights and the input. The final weights are the last entry of the transcript. So every attack with less access can be copied, with the same TPR and FPR, by an adversary with more access. For the same model and the same side information, the best advantage can therefore only grow along the chain \[\text{labels} \;\le\; \text{scores} \;\le\; \text{weights} \;\le\; \text{transcript}. \tag{9.3}\]
Since the copies keep both rates, the same chain holds for the best TPR at every fixed FPR. Side information is ordered in the same way, because an adversary can always forget what it knows. Behaviour is ordered too, since an honest adversary is a malicious one that chooses not to deviate. And an output tweak, such as noising the returned scores, is processing the adversary could have done itself, so it can only lower the best advantage, perhaps not by much.
Table 9.2 places four common deployments on all the axes. Its last row is federated learning, where clients train on their own data and a server that collects their updates holds the transcript, the setting of Gradient inversion. The same trained model can sit in several rows at once, and its risk is set by the most exposed of those rows.
