Trust works differently from the other axes, because it decides who the adversary is rather than how strong it is. In the central model the threat is whoever sees the released model, and the curator is outside the threat model. In the local model the curator is inside it, so protection has to be applied before the data leave the user. Local, shuffle and distributed trust models in Part 3 compares the two.
Side information is the hardest axis to bound, because the defender usually does not know what the adversary knows. That is why a privacy guarantee, such as the one Part 3 defines, should survive the strongest assumption, an adversary who knows every record except the target’s (Section 9.6).
The chain compares the best attack at each level, not the attacks people actually run, and the gap inside one access level can be larger than the gap between levels.
A security team fits the simplest anomaly detector there is, whose parameters \(\theta\) are the mean of the training records. Write \(n = 100\) for the number of training records. Each record is drawn from a standard normal distribution with \(d = 50\) features. A point \(x\) gets the anomaly score \(\|x - \theta\|^2\), its squared distance from the mean. The detector flags the point when the score exceeds a threshold, written \(\tau\) and set to \(d\), roughly the score a typical point gets. The adversary holds a target record \(z\) and plays the membership game, in which \(z\) is either a training record or a fresh draw.
Training on a record pulls the mean a little towards it, so a member sits a little closer to \(\theta\) than it otherwise would. With the weights, the best attack compares how likely this exact \(\theta\) is in the two worlds. That ratio is the likelihood ratio, and by the Neyman–Pearson lemma of Hypothesis testing no attack catches more members at a given FPR than one that thresholds it. Here the likelihood ratio depends on the weights only through the quantity \(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2\), which grows when training has pulled the mean towards \(z\).
A black-box adversary sees only the score of \(z\). A simple attack says “member” when that score is low, and the table below calls it the raw-loss attack. It is confused by targets that are simply far from the mean, because they have a high score whether or not they were used. So the raw score mixes how unusual a record is with whether it was a member.
A better black-box attack uses the calibrated score \(\|z\|^2 - \|z - \theta\|^2\). Expanding the square shows that this is exactly \(2\langle z, \theta\rangle - \|\theta\|^2\), the quantity the white-box likelihood ratio needs. The likelihood ratio also contains a term that depends only on the length of \(z\). Leaving it out moves the attack’s cut-off a little from one target to the next, so the calibrated attack is almost, but not exactly, the white-box one. A label-only adversary sees only the flag, and says “member” when \(z\) is not flagged.

Table 9.3 respects the chain, but the large gap is inside the black-box level, between two attacks on the same view. Calibrating each target against its own typicality multiplies the advantage by about seven, so “the attack we tried failed” proves little. That is the idea behind the per-example attacks of Membership inference. Sablayrolles et al. (2019) prove a general version, on condition that training draws the parameters with a probability that decreases exponentially in the training loss. Under that condition, the best membership attack depends on the parameters only through the target’s loss, so white-box access adds little.

9.4 Privacy games
The same name, such as “membership inference”, is used for attacks with different assumptions and scoring. Salem et al. (2023) write each attack in the literature as a game with the same four steps. The challenger draws a secret, and a dataset whose distribution may depend on it. It trains a model and gives the adversary the view the threat model allows. The adversary guesses and earns a gain, usually 1 for a correct guess and 0 otherwise. Finally, the gain is compared with the baseline, the best gain of a guess made from the side information alone. Figure 9.2 draws the membership game. Table 9.4 lists the others, including the distinguishing game, in which the adversary picks the two datasets itself.

Figure 9.2: The membership game. The challenger trains on a dataset, flips a bit that decides whether the target was in it, and shows the adversary the target and a view of the model. The adversary’s guess is scored by its advantage.



The baseline is part of the game, not an afterthought. A model that lets an attacker guess a rare diagnosis “with 90% accuracy” reveals nothing if 90% of people do not have that diagnosis. So what does the best attack look like when the secret bit is not equally likely to be 0 or 1?
The formula below assumes that 1 is the rarer value, so that \(\pi_1\) is at most one half. Only then is guessing 0 the best blind guess, and if 1 is the more likely value you swap the labels. This default already wins with probability \(\pi_0\). Saying 1 on a view instead wins games in proportion to \(\pi_1 q(x)\) and loses them in proportion to \(\pi_0 p(x)\). So the view should overturn the default only where it is strong evidence for 1. Write \(\gamma = \pi_0/\pi_1\) for the prior odds against the bit being 1. The view should then be more than \(\gamma\) times as likely in the world where the bit is 1. With \(\pi_1 = 0.1\), that means 9 times as likely.
On each such view, the net gain \(\pi_1 q(x) - \pi_0 p(x)\) equals \(\pi_1\) times the excess \(q(x) - \gamma\,p(x)\). Adding up these excesses over the views where they are positive gives the hockey-stick divergence of Divergences, written \(E_\gamma(Q\|P)\) with the rarer world first, as on that page. So the best attack wins with probability \[\max_{\text{attacks}}\Pr[\text{win}] = \pi_0 + \pi_1\,E_\gamma(Q\|P), \qquad \gamma = \frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}. \tag{9.4}\] The first term is the baseline of always guessing 0, and the second is everything the view adds. A randomized attack does no better, because it only mixes the choices of flagging a view or not. With a fair bit, the factor \(\gamma\) is 1, the hockey-stick divergence is the total variation distance, and the formula gives back the fair-game ceiling of Section 9.2.
Attribute inference needs particular care, because it has two possible baselines that answer different questions. Comparing with a guess from the population asks whether the model helps at all. Comparing members with non-members asks whether it helps because this person was in the training data, and only that is a breach of the person’s privacy. An attack that is right 75% of the time on members, and just as often on non-members, infers the attribute from the population, not from the person’s participation. Attribute inference and model inversion develops this.
The games also differ in where the data come from. Drawing the data from the population gives an average over datasets and targets, while letting the adversary choose them gives a worst case (Section 9.6).
One released number can be attacked in all three of the first games. A data team publishes how many people in a dataset have a sensitive condition, with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 1 added. The adversary knows every record except the target’s, so it knows the rest of the count.
In the membership game, the target has the condition. Without the target, the released count is a bell curve centred on the known rest. With it, the curve is the same but shifted right by one. The best attack says “member” on counts more likely in the member world, those above the crossing point half a unit above the known rest. It is right whenever the noise does not push the count more than half a unit towards the other world, which happens with probability 0.6915.
In the attribute game with a fair prior, the target is known to be in the dataset, and its bit is the secret. The view has the same two distributions, so the best guess is again right with probability 0.6915. Now make the condition rare, with \(\pi_1 = 0.1\), so that always guessing “no” already wins with probability 0.9. The hockey-stick divergence at \(\gamma = 9\) is only 0.0134, and Equation 9.4 weights it by the prior. The best accuracy is therefore \(0.9 + 0.1 \times 0.0134 = 0.9013\), about a tenth of a percentage point above the baseline. One record shifts the count by just one standard deviation of noise, which rarely yields evidence strong enough to overturn 9-to-1 odds.
In the reconstruction game, release instead the exact count of \(m\) independent bits, each 0 or 1 with equal chance. Given the count, every arrangement of that many ones is equally likely, so each bit is 1 with probability equal to the count divided by \(m\). The best guess for every bit is therefore the majority value, which beats a coin flip only by as much as the count strays from half of \(m\), and that margin shrinks like \(1/\sqrt m\). With 10 bits, the best reconstruction recovers a fraction 0.6230 of them. With 100 bits the fraction falls to 0.5398. With 1,000 bits it is only 0.5126, barely better than a coin flip. Many aggregates are a different matter. Reconstruction attacks shows how a few times as many noisy subset counts as there are bits give away almost every bit.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
section: 9.5 Advantage, total variation and the trade-off curve
text:
9.5 Advantage, total variation and the trade-off curve
A two-world game is a test of “not a member” against “member”, so everything Hypothesis testing says about tests becomes a statement about attacks. The first, the total-variation ceiling on the advantage, appeared in Section 9.2.
The second ceiling goes further. It bounds the attack’s TPR at every FPR, not just at the one point where the advantage is largest. It comes from the trade-off function of the two view distributions \(P\) and \(Q\), written \(T(P, Q)\). For each false positive rate \(\alpha\), the value \(T(P, Q)(\alpha)\) is the smallest fraction of members that any attack with that FPR must miss. An attack can catch at most the rest. So for every attack in a two-world game, \[\mathrm{Adv} \le \mathrm{TV}(P, Q), \qquad \mathrm{TPR} \le 1 - T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR}). \tag{9.5}\] Both ceilings are reached by likelihood-ratio attacks. Such an attack flags views in decreasing order of the likelihood ratio until the FPR reaches its budget, so each false positive it spends buys the most members.
The plot of an attack’s TPR against its FPR, as its threshold varies, is its receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. The advantage is the height of that curve above the diagonal. The total variation distance is the largest such height, and it says nothing about what happens where false positives are rare. Yet that end of the curve is where privacy breaks. An attack that flags 1% of members with no false alarms has an advantage of only about 0.01, but it identifies those members with certainty. An attack that flags 55% of members and 45% of non-members has advantage 0.1. But almost as many of the people it flags are non-members, so it identifies nobody with confidence.
A person who is flagged cares about a third quantity, the chance that the verdict “member” is true. A fraction \(\pi_1\) of targets are members, and the attack flags a fraction TPR of them. The other targets, a fraction \(\pi_0\), are not members, and the attack flags a fraction FPR of those. The precision is therefore the members’ share of everyone flagged: \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{flagged}] = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR} + \pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{9.6}\] When members are rare, non-members far outnumber them, so even a small fraction of non-members flagged swamps the true positives. If only one target in a hundred is a member, even a good attack produces mostly false alarms (Jayaraman et al., 2021). Only a small FPR keeps the precision high. Carlini et al. (2022) argue from this that membership attacks should be reported by their TPR at a low FPR, such as \(10^{-3}\), on ROC curves with log axes. The rest of this part does so.
The two ceilings depend only on \(P\) and \(Q\), so they bound every attack, including attacks nobody has invented yet. That is what makes them the right target for a defence. A mechanism, any procedure that turns data into a release, defeats every attack at once if its trade-off curve stays close to the diagonal for every target.
Take the noisy count again, with the other 100 records known. Say 50 of them have the condition, so the count is centred on 50 without the target and on 51 with it. The best attack says “member” when the count is above 50.5, where the two curves cross, and its advantage is the total variation distance, 0.3829.
Now hold the FPR at \(10^{-3}\) instead. The attack still flags large counts, but it has to raise its threshold until only one non-member in a thousand passes it, which happens at 53.09. A member’s count, centred one higher, passes that threshold with probability 0.0183. That is the TPR, and by the Neyman–Pearson argument above it is the best possible at this FPR. The attack now catches fewer than 2% of members. But when it fires at a fair prior, it is right with precision 0.948. If only one target in a hundred is a member, the precision drops to 0.156, so state the prior whenever you report a precision.
The black curve in Figure 9.3 is this ROC curve on log axes, and the green one is the next section’s adversary, who does not know the other records.






Figure 9.3: Left: the released count in the two worlds when the other 100 records are known (solid) and unknown (dashed). Right: the membership ROC curves of the best attacks on log axes, exact (lines) and from 100,000 simulated games per world (dots). The dotted diagonal is random guessing.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.6 Average case and worst case
A membership game can be scored in two ways. In the average case, the data and the target come from the population, which is all the adversary knows, so the advantage is an average over that randomness. In the worst case, the adversary knows, or even picks, the rest of the data and the target, so the advantage is the largest one over those choices. Evaluations of real models usually measure the first, but privacy guarantees have to control the second.
The two differ because not knowing something works like extra noise. Often the adversary’s view depends on something it does not know, such as the other records in the dataset. Then it sees an average of several possible situations, and averaging two distributions can only blur the difference between them. An adversary who knows the unknown removes that blur, and one who may choose it picks the situation where the two worlds differ most.
A tiny case shows how much the unknown can hide. Let there be one other record, whose bit is 0 or 1 with equal chance. The mechanism releases the exact sum of that bit and the target’s bit \(b\). An adversary who knows the other bit subtracts it and reads off \(b\), so its best advantage is 1. An adversary who does not know it sees a sum of 0 or 1 when \(b\) is 0. When \(b\) is 1 it sees 1 or 2, each with equal chance. A sum of 1 could come from either world, so the best advantage drops to one half.
In general, the unknown part of the game is everything the average-case game draws at random and a worst-case adversary may fix, such as the other records and the target. The best advantages of the three adversaries are ordered: \[\text{does not know it} \;\le\; \text{knows it} \;\le\; \text{chooses it}. \tag{9.7}\] The first step holds because averaging blurs, as above. The second holds because the adversary who knows the unknown gets, on average, the advantage of each situation, and an average is at most its largest term.
Both gaps can be as large as possible. Release the exact count of the target’s bit plus \(m\) other bits. An adversary who knows the other bits reads off the target’s bit, so its advantage is 1. For one who does not, the advantage equals the largest single probability of the unknown count, which tends to 0 as \(m\) grows. The random-record release below shows the second gap.
Now return to the noisy count, with noise of standard deviation 1 and a target who has the condition. This time the \(m = 100\) other bits are fresh random draws that the adversary does not see. In the two worlds the count has the same shape, shifted by one. That shape is a binomial count plus normal noise, and for shapes of this kind, called log-concave, a larger count is always more evidence of membership. The best attack is still a threshold on the count, at 50.5. Table 9.5 compares the adversaries of Equation 9.7, and adds the case where the target’s own condition is random.

Not knowing the crowd cuts the advantage by a factor of five. Each unknown bit has variance one quarter, so together they act as extra noise with variance \(m/4\), which is 25 here, on top of the released noise. A normal approximation with that combined variance gives 0.0781, close to the exact 0.0779. When the target’s own bit is random, the count does not depend on membership for the half of targets whose bit is 0. The advantage therefore halves, to 0.0390.
The gap shows up at a low FPR too. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) the average-case attack has a TPR of 0.0019, while the adversary who knows the rest reaches 0.0183 (Figure 9.3). Figure 9.4 shows the average-case advantage falling as the crowd grows, while the worst case does not move.






Figure 9.4: Best membership advantage on the noisy count against the number \(m\) of other records the adversary does not know, for three noise levels (solid), and the same mechanism against an adversary who knows them (dashed). Dots: the exact count, \(\sigma = 0\), whose worst case is 1.



Averaging over datasets hides the target in a crowd, but only from an adversary who does not know the crowd. A defence that relies on that blur fails against an adversary who knows the other records, or who planted them, as a malicious adversary can. If it controls every other record, it knows the rest of the count, and the advantage goes back to 0.3829.
Averaging over targets hides the worst-treated person in the same way. A mechanism publishes one record of a dataset, chosen at random among \(n = 1000\) records that are all different, and the attack says “member” if the published record is the target. A member is published with probability \(1/n\), so the TPR is 0.001. A non-member is never published, so the FPR is 0. By the average-case measure the advantage is therefore 0.001, and the mechanism looks almost perfectly safe. Yet every run exposes one person completely, because when the attack fires its precision is 1. For the person whose record is published, the attack is always right, so the worst-case advantage is 1.
Privacy is a promise to each person, so the number that matters is the advantage against the most exposed one, usually an outlier or a duplicated record (Membership inference). Average-case numbers still measure the risk a typical record faces, and they are what an audit can estimate from data. But they are lower bounds on the worst case, never upper bounds. An audit that reports an advantage of 0.01 on random examples shows only that the worst case is at least 0.01. Audits narrow the gap by playing the adversary who chooses the target. They plant canaries, records built to be as exposed as possible, and measure the attack on those (Memorization and training-data extraction).
This is where the book is heading. The definition of differential privacy in Part 3 is a guarantee for every pair of datasets that differ in one record. It therefore bounds the worst case of Equation 9.7 for every game in this part whose two worlds differ in one record. Games whose worlds differ in many records, such as the property games of Property inference, are bounded only through a weaker guarantee for groups, which degrades as the group grows.

title: 9  Threat models and privacy games
text:
9.7 Code
When the attack’s score is standard normal for non-members and shifted for members, the best TPR at any FPR takes a few lines. A shift of 1 is the noisy count with the other records known, whose curves cross at 0.5.
from statistics import NormalDist

Z = NormalDist()


def tpr_at_fpr(fpr: float, shift: float) -> float:
    """Best TPR at a given FPR when the attack score is N(0, 1) for non-members, N(shift, 1) for members."""
    return 1 - Z.cdf(Z.inv_cdf(1 - fpr) - shift)


def precision(tpr: float, fpr: float, prior: float) -> float:
    """Fraction of 'member' verdicts that are right when a fraction `prior` of targets are members."""
    return prior * tpr / (prior * tpr + (1 - prior) * fpr)


advantage = 2 * Z.cdf(0.5) - 1  # best TPR - FPR for a shift of 1: the total variation distance
tpr = tpr_at_fpr(1e-3, 1.0)
print(f"{advantage:.4f}")  # 0.3829
print(f"{tpr:.4f}")  # 0.0183
print(f"{precision(tpr, 1e-3, 0.5):.3f}")  # 0.948
print(f"{precision(tpr, 1e-3, 0.01):.3f}")  # 0.156
The full edition’s script, threat_models.py, computes every number in this chapter and checks it by simulation.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a model to predict a disease and publishes it. You hold one patient’s record. Was that record in the training set? If it was, you have learned that the patient was treated at that hospital for that disease, even though the model never output a diagnosis. This question, the simplest and most common one an attacker can ask about a trained model, is called membership inference.
Membership inference is also the standard measure of leakage, because an attacker that cannot even tell whether a record was used can do little else with it. Leaking membership is therefore the first sign of a leak, not the worst one. The later chapters of this part show what more a model can leak.
The one idea of this chapter is that membership inference is a test about one record. Some records are predicted well whether or not the model trained on them, and their outputs reveal almost nothing. Others are predicted well only if the model trained on them, and their outputs can reveal membership with confidence. An attack that applies the same rule to every record mixes the two kinds, and it identifies almost no member with confidence. The strong attacks compare the model’s output on a record with how that same record fares under models trained with and without it. The records they expose are the outliers.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.2 Membership as a test about one record
text:
10.2 Membership as a test about one record
Membership inference is scored as a game (Threat models and privacy games). A challenger trains a model and flips a fair coin. On heads it hands the attacker a record from the training set, and on tails a fresh record from the same population. The attacker then guesses whether the record is a member. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of members it calls members, and its false positive rate (FPR) is the fraction of non-members it wrongly calls members.
An attack’s advantage is the TPR minus the FPR. Half the games have a member, which the attacker wins with probability TPR. The other half have a non-member, which it wins with probability one minus the FPR. So the attacker wins a share \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\) of the games, where \(\mathrm{Adv}\) is the advantage. An attack that ignores the model has advantage 0 and wins half the games, so any win rate above one half comes from what the model reveals.
Now fix one target record, which this chapter calls \(z\). Train a model on data that contains \(z\), and look at the model’s output on \(z\), such as its loss or its confidence in the true label. Train another on data without \(z\), and look again. Training is random, because each run draws the rest of the training data afresh, and the starting weights and the order of the examples also change. So each case gives a distribution of outputs rather than a single value. Call them the IN distribution and the OUT distribution of \(z\). The attacker sees one output and must say which of the two it came from.
That is a test between two fully specified distributions, and the Neyman–Pearson lemma says how to do it best (Hypothesis testing). Compute the likelihood ratio, the density of the observed output under IN divided by its density under OUT, and say “member” when it is above a threshold. For any FPR you allow, no test flags more members. The reason is a budgeting argument. Every output you call “member” has a cost, its OUT probability, which adds to the false positives. It also has a gain, its IN probability, which adds to the true positives. With a fixed budget of false positives, you gain the most by spending it first on the outputs with the best ratio of gain to cost. That ratio is the likelihood ratio.
The IN and OUT distributions differ from record to record, as the introduction said. They nearly coincide for a typical record and lie far apart for an atypical one, and the rest of the chapter follows from taking that difference seriously.
Most of the chapter reduces to one simple case. Suppose the attacker turns the output into a single number, its score, and that this score is normal with standard deviation 1 for members and for non-members alike. For non-members its mean is 0. For members, it is the same bell curve shifted to the right by an amount \(s\), called the separation. A large separation means that the two curves barely overlap. The log of the likelihood ratio then works out to the score times \(s\), minus \(s^2/2\), so the ratio grows with the score. The best test therefore says “member” when the score is above a cut-off, set by the FPR you allow, which this chapter writes \(\alpha\).
Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF), so that \(\Phi(t)\) is the chance that a standard normal draw falls below \(t\). To flag a fraction \(\alpha\) of non-members, the cut-off must be \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha)\), the point a standard normal draw exceeds with probability \(\alpha\). A member’s score is shifted by \(s\), so it passes that cut-off with probability \[\mathrm{TPR}(\alpha) = 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - s\big). \tag{10.1}\] This is the Gaussian trade-off curve of Hypothesis testing, written as the TPR against the FPR. It gives the most members any test can catch at each FPR.
Take an FPR of \(10^{-3}\). A standard normal draw exceeds 3.0902 one time in a thousand, so that is the cut-off. With a separation of 0.5, a member’s score must still clear 2.59 standard deviations above its own mean. Its TPR is then only 0.0048, barely five times the chance rate of 0.001. With a separation of 4, the cut-off sits below the member mean, so most members pass and the TPR is 0.8185.
Every number in this chapter comes from one experiment, small enough to run in seconds. Its pool has 1,000 labelled points with 100 features each. The 950 typical points have labels that follow their first feature, with some noise. The 50 outliers have feature vectors with five times the length, and a label drawn by a fair coin. So a model can get an outlier’s label right only by fitting that point itself.
Each model is logistic regression with a penalty that keeps its weights small, trained on a random half of the pool. The models come in complementary pairs, one trained on a random half and the next on the rest, so every point is a member of exactly half the models. The attacker attacks 128 such target models. It knows the pool and the training recipe but not which half each target used. It also trains 64 models of its own, the shadow models of a later section. Asking one target model about one pool point is one game, which gives 64,000 member games and as many non-member games. This is the setup of Carlini et al. (2022), scaled down from an image classifier to a linear model.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.3 The loss attack and the generalization gap
text:
10.3 The loss attack and the generalization gap
A model is fitted to its training data, so its loss on a training point is usually lower than on a fresh one. Yeom et al. (2018) turned this into an attack that says “member” when the loss is low, which needs no shadow models. They also showed that its advantage is exactly the generalization gap divided by the range of the loss. The gap is the model’s average loss on fresh data minus its average loss on its training data. For this attack, overfitting and membership leakage are the same number.
The cleanest version turns the loss directly into a probability of saying “member”. It needs the loss to have a known range, from 0 to some maximum \(B\), because otherwise the rule below is not a probability. The bounded-loss attack says “member” with probability one minus the loss divided by \(B\), so it always says “member” at loss 0 and never at loss \(B\). Its TPR is then one minus the average member loss divided by \(B\), and its FPR is the same with the average non-member loss. The advantage is their difference, which is the gap between the two average losses divided by \(B\): \[\mathrm{Adv} = \frac{\text{expected test loss} - \text{expected training loss}}{B}. \tag{10.2}\]
The two averages are the expected training and test losses. A member target is a random training point, and a non-member target is a fresh draw that the model never saw. The randomized rule makes only these averages matter, because its chance of saying “member” falls in a straight line as the loss grows. A plain threshold would give an advantage that depends on the whole distribution of the loss.
The most familiar case is the 0-1 loss, which is 0 on a correct prediction and 1 on a wrong one. With \(B = 1\) the rule becomes deterministic. It says “member” exactly when the model classifies the record correctly. Its advantage is then the test error minus the training error.
In the running example, averaged over the target models, the training error is 0.1495 and the test error is 0.2663. “Member if correctly classified” flags the members it gets right, so its TPR is 0.8505. It also flags the non-members it gets right, so its FPR is 0.7337. Its advantage is 0.1168, exactly the gap between the two errors.
The logistic loss has no maximum, so the bounded-loss attack needs it clipped, here at \(B = 2\). The mean clipped loss is then 0.4158 on members and 0.5433 on non-members. Equation 10.2 predicts an advantage of 0.0638, and simulating the randomized rule gives 0.0639. Yeom et al. also propose a deterministic version, which says “member” when the loss is below the mean training loss. It has an FPR of 0.4834 and an advantage of 0.1102.
These advantages mean winning between 53% and 56% of the games, and none of the three attacks identifies anyone with confidence. The two deterministic attacks, for example, flag about half of the non-members or more. Figure 10.1 shows why. It plots \(\phi\), the log of the odds that the model gives to the true label, which rises as the loss falls and so carries the same information. The distributions of \(\phi\) over members and over non-members are shifted, but they almost entirely overlap.






Figure 10.1: Distribution of \(\phi\), the logit of the target model’s confidence in the true label, over member pairs and non-member pairs of the 128 target models. The dashed line is Yeom’s threshold: the attack says “member” to its right, where the loss is below the mean training loss.



The first lesson is that overfitting implies leakage. Any model with a generalization gap leaks membership through its loss, by at least the gap divided by the loss range. You can read this off from the training and test errors alone, without running any attack.
The converse fails, because of what the gap averages. Algorithmic stability and generalization shows that the expected gap equals the average self-influence of the training records. The self-influence of a record is how much its own loss rises when it is left out of training and replaced by a fresh one. So the loss attack’s advantage is the average, over records, of how much each one is memorized, and an average hides who is memorized. When a lower loss always makes membership more likely, a threshold on the loss is the best attack that ignores the record’s identity, as the next section shows. But an attack that uses the identity of the record can beat it by a wide margin. Yeom et al. even construct models that leak membership with no generalization gap at all. A small gap does not mean a private model.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.4 Shadow models
A better rule than “low loss means member” requires knowing what members’ outputs look like, and the attacker cannot see them because it does not know the target’s training set. Shokri et al. (2017) solved this with shadow models, which the attacker trains itself to imitate the target. They use the same architecture and recipe, and data from the same population. For its own models the attacker knows who was a member. It labels their outputs on members “in” and on non-members “out”, and trains an attack model, one per class, to tell the two apart.
With enough shadow data and a flexible enough attack model, it learns the best rule available from the output alone. Trained with the usual cross-entropy loss, a classifier learns to predict, at each output, the true fraction of members among the shadow pairs with that output. If those pairs look like the real game, that fraction is the probability that a record is a member given its output. With a fair coin, Bayes’ rule makes the odds of membership given the output equal to the likelihood ratio. So a threshold on the attack model is a threshold on the likelihood ratio, and by the Neyman–Pearson lemma no attack that sees only the output does better.
That the shadow pairs look like the real game is a condition of the result. It assumes that each shadow model is trained exactly as the target is, on data from the same population. If the shadow data came from a different hospital, or the shadows used a different recipe, the attack model learns the membership probability for the wrong game. The attack is not useless, because “lower loss means member” usually still holds, but thresholds set on the shadows no longer give the intended FPR on the target.
The attack model is optimal, but for the wrong question. “Sees only the output” means that its input is the output, not the identity of the record that produced it. So the likelihood ratio it learns is pooled over all records, and it is the best attack only among those that treat all records alike. In the running example, that pooled ratio rises with \(\phi\), so the attack reduces to the loss attack with a threshold for each class. It cannot know that a given value of \(\phi\) is high for one record and low for another.
What shadow models really buy is calibration. They let the attacker set a threshold that gives a chosen FPR on the real model, without knowing any member of the real training set. The attacker picks the threshold at which the desired fraction of its own shadow non-members pass, and then trusts that the real non-members behave the same way. LiRA, in the next section, keeps shadow models for exactly this job. The imitation can also be crude. Salem et al. (2019) found that one shadow model is often enough, and that shadow data from another distribution still works.
In the running example, the labels have two classes, and each class’s attack model is a logistic regression on \(\phi\), trained on about 32,000 shadow pairs. In both classes, its predicted chance of “in” rises with \(\phi\). An attack’s area under the curve (AUC) summarizes how well its score separates members from non-members. It equals the chance that a random member gets a higher score than a random non-member. The attack model’s AUC is 0.577, the same as the loss attack’s (Table 10.3).
Calibration works here. Setting the threshold on the shadow models for an FPR of 1% gives an FPR of 0.0095 on the target models, which the attacker never saw. But the TPR at that threshold is 0.0098, no better than the fraction of non-members flagged. At a low FPR, a threshold on \(\phi\) shared by all records has nothing to work with.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.5 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per example
text:
10.5 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per example
The pooled attacks compare a record’s output with everyone else’s outputs. The right comparison is with the same record’s output under models that did and did not train on it. Carlini et al. (2022) built the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) on that idea. For each target record, the attacker estimates the IN and OUT distributions from shadow models trained with and without it, and computes the likelihood ratio of the target model’s output.
The output LiRA uses is \(\phi\), the logit of the confidence. If \(p_y\) is the probability the model gives to the true label, then \(\phi\) is the log of the odds the model gives to that label: \[\phi = \ln\frac{p_y}{1 - p_y}. \tag{10.3}\]
As decision rules, the confidence, the loss and \(\phi\) are interchangeable, because the confidence and \(\phi\) rise together and the loss falls as they rise. A threshold on one is a threshold on the others. They differ only when a statistic is combined across models, as when LiRA fits a distribution to it.
For fitting, \(\phi\) is the right scale. A confidence of 0.9 gives a \(\phi\) of 2.197. Raising the confidence to 0.999 raises \(\phi\) to 6.907, so the confidence crowds against 1 while \(\phi\) keeps spreading the values out. For logistic regression, \(\phi\) is the margin, which measures how far the point lies on the correct side of the decision boundary. The margin is a linear function of the weights, and the trained weights are close to normal over retrainings, because they solve an equation that averages many independent terms. So \(\phi\) is close to normal too, and for deep networks Carlini et al. found the same.
Write \(\phi_z\) for a model’s \(\phi\) on the record \(z\). The attacker has only a few dozen shadow values of \(\phi_z\), so it summarizes each set by a normal distribution. Write \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{in}}\) for their mean and standard deviation over the shadow models that trained on the record. Write \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{out}}\) for the same over the shadow models that did not. In the running example, each fit uses 32 values, because each point is in exactly half of the 64 shadow models.
Online LiRA asks how much more likely the target model’s \(\phi_z\) is under the IN fit than under the OUT fit. Its score is the log of that ratio, where \(\mathcal N(\phi; \mu, \sigma^2)\) denotes the normal density at \(\phi\): \[\ln\Lambda_z = \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{in}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{in}}^2\big) - \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{out}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{out}}^2\big). \tag{10.4}\] It says “member” when this score exceeds a threshold that is the same for every record.
One threshold for all records is optimal because the attacker knows which record it is testing. Its observation is a pair, the record and the model’s output on it, and the Neyman–Pearson lemma applies to the pair. The likelihood ratio of the pair has two factors. The first is the chance of being handed this record, which cancels because the challenger draws it the same way whether or not it ends up in training. The second is the record’s own ratio. So the best test of the whole game puts one common threshold on each record’s own ratio. When the normal fits are exact, no attack that sees the record and its output has a higher TPR at any FPR.
The condition that the record is drawn the same way in both worlds matters. If members were drawn from one hospital and non-members from another, the record alone would reveal the answer.
Offline LiRA uses only OUT models. These can be trained before the target record is known, and then reused for every query. Without IN models it cannot compute an IN density. It asks instead how far above its usual OUT value the observed output lies, measured in OUT standard deviations, again with one threshold for all records: \[\frac{\phi_z - \mu_{\mathrm{out}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{out}}}. \tag{10.5}\] This works as a one-sided test because training on a record raises its \(\phi_z\), as the model moves to fit the record.
When do the two scores agree? Suppose the two fits have the same width. Write \(t_z\) for the offline score of a record, and \(s_z\) for the distance between its IN and OUT means in units of that width. Then \(t_z\) is standard normal under OUT and shifted by \(s_z\) under IN, which is the simple case of Section 10.2. As there, the online score of Equation 10.4 simplifies to \[\ln\Lambda_z = s_zt_z - s_z^2/2. \tag{10.6}\] For one record, the separation is a fixed positive number, so both scores rank that record’s outputs the same way. Across records they differ. Online LiRA multiplies \(t_z\) by \(s_z\), so it treats a given offline score as strong evidence when the separation is large and as weak evidence when it is small.

A population with two kinds of record shows what each step buys (Table 10.1). Now set three attacks, a single threshold on \(\phi\), offline LiRA and online LiRA, so that each flags one non-member in a thousand, counting all non-members together.
One threshold on \(\phi\) is the loss attack. Typical non-members score high, and they are 95% of the non-members, so the threshold must sit high, at \(\phi = 6.075\). Atypical members score around 2 and almost never reach it. Only typical members occasionally do, and the TPR is 0.0048.
One threshold on the offline score gives every record its own FPR of \(10^{-3}\). Each kind then gets its own best TPR from the table. The overall TPR is their average weighted by the shares, which is 0.0455.
Both per-record tests catch about ten times as many members as the single threshold on \(\phi\). One threshold on the online score does slightly better than the offline one, with a TPR of 0.0503. That is the best possible at this FPR, because one common threshold on each record’s own ratio is the best test of the game. It gets there by moving the false-positive budget between the kinds, so that typical records get an FPR of \(5.90\times10^{-4}\) and atypical ones get 0.0088. The trade pays because a typical record’s extra false positives buy almost no true positives, while an atypical record’s buy many.






Figure 10.2: The logit \(\phi\) of one point over the 64 shadow models, split into the 32 that trained on it (IN) and the 32 that did not (OUT), with the fitted Gaussians. Left: a typical point, whose two distributions overlap. Right: an outlier, which the models predict wrongly unless they trained on it.



Figure 10.2 shows the two distributions for a typical point and an outlier of the running example. The choice between online and offline LiRA is a choice about cost. Online LiRA needs models trained with each target record, so attacking a new record means training new shadow models. Offline LiRA’s OUT models are trained once and reused, which is why it matters in practice, at some cost in power.
In practice LiRA can fail through its fits. Each record’s variance is estimated from half the shadow models, and with few shadow models these estimates are noisy. If a record’s spread is underestimated, its OUT curve is drawn too narrow, and an ordinary output looks far out in the tail. Its likelihood ratio is then inflated, and it becomes a false positive exactly at the strict thresholds that matter. Carlini et al. recommend one global variance, shared by all records, when shadow models are few. It is estimated from every record’s values at once, so it is stable (Figure 10.3).






Figure 10.3: TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) of four LiRA variants on the 128 target models, as the attacker uses the first 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 of its shadow models. The variants are online and offline LiRA, each with per-example or global variances. With a global variance the attack is strong even with few shadow models; with per-example variances it needs many. The dotted line is the loss attack, which needs no shadow models.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.6 Evaluating attacks: TPR at a low FPR
text:
10.6 Evaluating attacks: TPR at a low FPR
Older papers on membership inference report the attack’s accuracy and its AUC, which both average over all members and non-members. A privacy breach is not an average. It happens when an attacker can say with confidence that a particular person was in the data, and that requires a low FPR. So Carlini et al. (2022) argued that attacks should be reported by their TPR at a fixed low FPR, such as \(10^{-3}\). They should also be shown by their full receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve on log axes. That curve plots the TPR against the FPR as the threshold moves from strict to lenient.
Two constructed attacks show what an average can hide. Attack A recognizes a fraction \(q\) of members with certainty, here 5%, and gives every other record, member or not, the same random score. Its AUC is 0.525. The recognized members always win the comparison with a non-member, and the others win only half the time, because their scores have the same distribution as the non-members’. Attack B gives every member a score slightly higher than a non-member’s on average, using normal scores with a shift of 0.0887. That shift is chosen to give B the same AUC as A.

Table 10.2 compares them, and their best advantages differ by only about 0.015. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), though, A catches 38 times as many members as B. At any FPR \(\alpha\), A’s TPR is \(q + (1 - q)\alpha\), because the recognized members always pass and the others pass as often as non-members. B is barely above chance, because a tiny shift moves almost no member past a strict cut-off. So A is a severe breach for one person in twenty, and B a negligible one for everyone, and only the low-FPR end of the ROC curve shows the difference.






Figure 10.4: ROC curves of attacks A and B. Left, linear axes: the two curves are indistinguishable from each other and from the diagonal. Right, log axes: A identifies 5% of members at every FPR, B is barely above chance. The dashed line marks FPR \(10^{-3}\).



Log axes are how you see that end. On linear axes, every FPR below 0.01 is squeezed into a narrow strip at the left edge (Figure 10.4). On log axes, chance is the diagonal at every scale, and a useful attack stays well above it.
Measuring a low FPR takes many non-members, because an FPR is estimated by counting false positives. A count of \(k\) events has a relative error of about \(1/\sqrt k\). Seeing \(k\) false positives at an FPR \(\alpha\) takes about \(k/\alpha\) non-members. That is why the running example evaluates many target models, whose 64,000 non-member pairs give about 64 false positives at an FPR of one in a thousand.
The precision of an attack is the fraction of its “member” verdicts that are right. When members and non-members are equally many, the precision is \(\mathrm{TPR}/(\mathrm{TPR} + \mathrm{FPR})\), because the right verdicts are proportional to the TPR and the wrong ones to the FPR. At a TPR of 0.05 and an FPR of one in a thousand, that is 0.98. Real targets are rarely members with probability one half, and Threat models and privacy games shows how the prior changes the precision.

By AUC the attacks are close, at 0.577 against about 0.63, and by best advantage offline LiRA even looks the strongest. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), though, they are not close at all. The loss and shadow attacks are at chance there, since their TPRs are no higher than the FPR. Online LiRA finds 952 of the 64,000 members. Its TPR is 17.0 times the loss attack’s, although both use the same statistic \(\phi\), so comparing each record with itself is the whole gain.
How precise are these numbers? The Clopper–Pearson interval is an exact 95% confidence interval for a rate estimated from a count (Hypothesis testing). For online LiRA’s TPR it runs from 0.0140 to 0.0158. The FPR is far less certain, because it rests on only 64 false positives. Its interval runs from 0.00077 to 0.00128, which is as wide as the square-root rule above predicts.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.7 Why outliers are most exposed
The two-kinds example already shows that the low-FPR end of the ROC curve is made of the records whose IN and OUT distributions are far apart. This section asks which records those are.
For one record, the best test is the simple case of Section 10.2, so its best TPR is set by its own separation. Suppose the record’s IN and OUT distributions are normal with a common width \(\sigma_z\). Its separation \(s_z\) is then the distance between the two means, measured in units of that width. The best TPR of any test on that record alone, at an FPR \(\alpha\), is \[\mathrm{TPR}_z(\alpha) = 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - s_z\big), \qquad s_z = \frac{\mu_{\mathrm{in}} - \mu_{\mathrm{out}}}{\sigma_z}. \tag{10.7}\] The numerator of \(s_z\) is the record’s self-influence, measured with \(\phi\) instead of the loss. It is the average amount by which training on the record raises the model’s \(\phi\) on that record. That is the mirror image of the earlier definition, in which the loss rises when the record is left out.
Which records have a large self-influence? If the rest of the data already predict a record’s label, its OUT mean is high, and training on it adds little. If the rest of the data predict the opposite label, its OUT mean is low, and the model must move toward the record to fit it. The regularization penalty limits how far one record can move the weights (Algorithmic stability and generalization). Within that limit, a long feature vector can pull the weights harder, and it also turns a given change in the weights into a larger change in its own margin. The outliers of the running example have both an unpredictable label and a long feature vector.
So leakage is concentrated. The loss attack’s advantage is the average self-influence. The low-FPR end of the ROC curve is governed by the largest ones, because a strict threshold is passed only by the records with the largest separations. A model can have a small generalization gap and still expose a few records completely.

Table 10.4 splits the running example by kind of point, and it shows first that the outliers carry the generalization gap. Their mean loss self-influence is 2.0999, against 0.0897 for typical points. The average over all points is 0.1902. Although outliers are only 5% of the pool, they supply a share of 0.552 of it.
The outliers are also the true positives. At a pooled FPR of one in a thousand, online LiRA flags 26% of outlier members and 0.2% of typical members. Counting its flags on the target models, a share of 0.873 of the members it finds are outliers. As in the two-kinds example, the likelihood ratio gets there by moving FPR budget to the outliers (Table 10.4).
Not every outlier is exposed. An outlier’s label is a coin flip, so about half the time it happens to agree with the trend in the first feature. Those outliers are predicted correctly without being seen, and they are no more exposed than typical points (Figure 10.6). It follows that two records with the same loss under the target model can be exposed very differently. A low loss is normal for an easy record and strong evidence for a hard one.






Figure 10.6: Each pool point’s separation \((\mu_{\mathrm{in}} - \mu_{\mathrm{out}})/\sigma\) against \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}}\), the mean \(\phi\) of the shadow models that did not train on it. Outliers (triangles) whose label the rest of the data contradict have the largest separations.



Memorizing outliers can be what makes a model accurate. Feldman (2020) shows that on long-tailed data, where many subpopulations are rare, a subpopulation seen only once in training must be memorized for good test accuracy. The next example from it will look like that one. So the records a model needs to memorize are the ones it exposes.
Removing the outliers does not fix the problem. Carlini et al. (2022b) removed the most exposed records and retrained, and the next layer of records became exposed. They call this the onion effect. Exposure is relative to the rest of the dataset, because a record’s OUT distribution depends on what the other records predict about it.
This is the gap between average-case and worst-case games of Threat models and privacy games, seen from the data. A score averaged over records is never more than the score on the worst record, and it can be far less. So a guarantee that protects every record has to bound the self-influence of the worst record, not the average. That is what differential privacy does, in Part 3.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.8 The full-size pipeline: LiRA on CIFAR-10
text:
10.8 The full-size pipeline: LiRA on CIFAR-10
The usual full-scale experiment trains an image classifier on CIFAR-10, a standard benchmark of small colour images in ten classes. It runs LiRA with 16 shadow models and reports the TPR at an FPR of 0.1%. That takes hours of GPU time, so this book runs the same protocol with logistic regression in place of a deep network.

Split the data. Take the 50,000 CIFAR-10 training images as the pool. For each of \(N + 1\) models, where \(N\) is the number of shadow models, choose a random half of the pool. One model plays the target and the others are shadows, and rotating the target gives many pairs to evaluate.
Train every model with the same recipe, including the architecture, optimizer, number of epochs and data augmentation. Augmentation, for example, changes how strongly the model fits each image, and so it changes the IN mean and the variances.
Compute the statistic. For each model and image, compute the model’s outputs on the image and on a few augmented copies. Convert each to \(\phi\) directly from the logits \(f\), the raw class scores the network produces before the softmax: \[\phi = f_y - \ln\sum_{y' \ne y}e^{f_{y'}}. \tag{10.8}\] This equals \(\ln\frac{p_y}{1 - p_y}\) but never forms \(1 - p_y\), which rounds to 0 for a confident model.
Fit IN and OUT normal distributions for each image over the shadow models, a multivariate one over the augmented copies, so that each copy adds evidence.
Score each pair of target model and image with the online score Equation 10.4, or the offline score Equation 10.5.
Evaluate. Pool all pairs, sweep one threshold, and plot the ROC curve on log axes. Report the TPR at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), with the number of non-member pairs it rests on.

With 16 shadow models, use a global variance. Each image is then in about half the shadows and out of the other half, and variances estimated from 8 values are too noisy for the low-FPR end. In the running example with 16 shadow models, for instance, online LiRA reaches a TPR of only 0.0023 at an FPR of one in a thousand with per-record variances. With a global variance it reaches 0.0151.
Carlini et al. report that online LiRA is about ten times more powerful than earlier attacks at a low FPR on CIFAR-10. They also find that the loss attack is close to chance there, which is what Table 10.3 shows in miniature. The exact TPR depends on the model, its training length and the augmentations. A single target model with 25,000 non-member images allows only 25 false positives at an FPR of one in a thousand. Rotating over several target models multiplies that count and tightens the interval.
The auditing part of the book reuses this pipeline, with a privately trained model as the target and inserted canaries as the members. Canaries are records chosen to be as exposed as possible, such as mislabelled or unusual images, so that the attack measures the worst case rather than the average.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.9 Code
The snippet below reproduces the two-kinds example. The last two lines score a typical record’s output that lies 3.244 OUT standard deviations above its OUT mean. Its online score is 1.497, which is exactly online LiRA’s threshold in the two-kinds example.
from math import log, pi, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist

Z = NormalDist()


def log_normal_pdf(x: float, mu: float, sd: float) -> float:
    return -0.5 * ((x - mu) / sd) ** 2 - log(sd * sqrt(2 * pi))


def lira_online(phi: float, mu_in: float, sd_in: float, mu_out: float, sd_out: float) -> float:
    """Log of how much more likely the target's phi is under the IN fit than under the OUT fit."""
    return log_normal_pdf(phi, mu_in, sd_in) - log_normal_pdf(phi, mu_out, sd_out)


def lira_offline(phi: float, mu_out: float, sd_out: float) -> float:
    """How many OUT standard deviations the target's phi lies above its OUT mean."""
    return (phi - mu_out) / sd_out


def tpr_at_fpr(fpr: float, separation: float) -> float:
    """Best TPR at a given FPR for a record whose IN and OUT scores are unit normals `separation` apart."""
    return 1 - Z.cdf(Z.inv_cdf(1 - fpr) - separation)


typical, atypical = tpr_at_fpr(1e-3, 0.5), tpr_at_fpr(1e-3, 4.0)
print(f"{typical:.4f}")  # 0.0048
print(f"{atypical:.4f}")  # 0.8185
print(f"{0.95 * typical + 0.05 * atypical:.4f}")  # 0.0455
print(f"{lira_offline(6.244, 3.0, 1.0):.3f}")  # 3.244
print(f"{lira_online(6.244, 3.5, 1.0, 3.0, 1.0):.3f}")  # 1.497
The full edition’s script, membership_inference.py, trains every model of the running example, runs every attack and prints every number in this chapter. It runs in about ten seconds:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/membership_inference.py

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter, except two kinds. Some come from earlier chapters: the Neyman–Pearson lemma and confidence intervals for counts from Hypothesis testing, and the gap as an average self-influence and the limit on how far one record moves the weights from Algorithmic stability and generalization. Others are findings cited from the literature: Yeom et al.’s models that leak with no generalization gap, Salem et al.’s results on crude shadow models, Carlini et al.’s finding that \(\phi\) is close to normal for deep networks, their use of augmented copies and their CIFAR-10 results, Feldman’s memorization result and the onion effect.

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a model that predicts whether a patient will develop a lung disease from their age band and whether they smoke. It puts the model behind an interface that anyone can query. An insurer knows your age and, from a claim, that you have the disease. Can it use the model to find out whether you smoke?
It can make a better guess than it could without the model, but that alone is not a privacy failure. If smokers get the disease more often, the insurer learns something about every person with the disease, whether or not their record was used for training. A published study saying that smoking causes the disease would allow the same guess. The question that matters for you is a different one. Does the model reveal more about your attribute because your record was in its training data?
Attribute inference tries to recover one sensitive field of a record, such as smoking status, a genotype or an income band. The attacker uses the record’s other fields and access to a model that takes the sensitive field as one of its inputs. Model inversion is the classic way to do it. You query the model once for each possible value of the sensitive field. Then you keep the value whose prediction best explains the person’s outcome, such as the diagnosis, which you already know.
This chapter compares the attack with a guesser who never sees the model but knows the population perfectly. That separates what the attack learns about you from what it learns about everyone. No attack can beat the guesser on people outside the training data, so any excess on people inside it is a leak about individuals. Measuring that leak turns attribute inference into a membership question.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.2 The attribute inference game
“The attack recovered 78% of smoking statuses” sounds alarming, but the number means nothing on its own. You also need to know how often the attribute could be guessed without the model, and how often the attack succeeds on people who were not in the training set. Yeom et al. (2018) made this precise with a privacy game. As in Threat models and privacy games, a challenger sets up a hidden situation, the adversary sees only what the rules give it, and its guess is scored.
The game needs a little notation, because a record has three fields that play different roles. The sensitive attribute \(s\) is the field the adversary wants, and it takes a few values, such as smoker or non-smoker. The public features \(x\) are what the adversary already knows about the person, such as the age band. The label \(y\) is what the model predicts, such as the disease. Records are drawn from a population, and the training set consists of records drawn independently from it.
The game runs in three steps. First, the challenger draws a training set and trains a model on it. Second, it flips a fair coin. On heads it picks the target uniformly at random from the training set, so the target is a member. On tails it draws a fresh target from the population, so the target is a non-member. Third, the adversary receives the target’s \(x\) and \(y\), but not \(s\), together with access to the model and whatever it knows about the population. It outputs a guess of \(s\). The coin models nothing an attacker does, and only lets the two success rates be compared under one set of rules.
The score measures how much better the attack does on people in the training data than on others. The attribute advantage is the success rate on members minus the success rate on non-members: \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attr}} = \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{member}] - \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{non-member}]. \tag{11.1}\] The subtraction is what makes this a measure of privacy. Some success comes from patterns that hold across the population, such as “people with the disease tend to smoke”. This chapter calls that population inference. It helps members and non-members equally, so it appears in both terms and cancels. What is left is what the model knows about its own training records. Because the advantage hides the success the two groups share, report the two success rates as well.
The advantage also turns any attribute attack into a membership attack, which sees a whole record and the model and says whether the record was in the training set. As Membership inference explains, its true positive rate (TPR) is the chance that it says “member” for a member. Its false positive rate (FPR) is the chance that it says “member” for a non-member, and its advantage is TPR minus FPR. If an attribute attack is right more often on members, then being right is itself evidence of membership. So a membership attack can run the attribute attack, compare its guess with the true \(s\) in the record, and say “member” exactly when the guess is right. Its TPR is then the attribute attack’s success on members, and its FPR the success on non-members. Its advantage is therefore the attribute advantage.
This reduction gives every attribute attack a ceiling. Picture everything a membership attack could look at, the target record together with the model. Run the game many times, and this view follows one distribution when the target is a member and another when it is not. No test can tell two distributions apart with an advantage above their total variation distance, half the total absolute difference between their probabilities (Hypothesis testing). The membership attack built above obeys this ceiling, so every attribute attack does too.
So a model that reveals nothing about membership, where the two distributions are equal, gives no attribute advantage to anyone. The opposite direction fails, because a membership leak need not come with an attribute leak. Suppose the sensitive attribute has no bearing on the label. A model can then memorize its training records through their features and labels while its predictions ignore \(s\), and no attribute attack gains anything on members.
The membership test built this way is also weak. It outputs one bit, so a “member” verdict can only shift the odds that the target is a member by the ratio of its TPR to its FPR. An attack that is right on most people, members or not, has a ratio close to 1, so its verdict barely shifts those odds. Dedicated membership attacks are judged by their TPR at a low FPR, where each verdict is strong evidence. There, a test built from an attribute attack is much weaker than the attacks of Membership inference.
The toy experiment of this chapter (Section 11.6) shows how small the advantage can be behind a large success rate. It trains a logistic regression on 100 records, 200 times over. Each time, a model inversion attack, explained in Section 11.4, guesses a two-valued sensitive attribute for the 100 members and for 100 fresh records. The attack is right on 0.7832 of members and on 0.7262 of non-members. The attribute advantage is therefore only 0.0569. Like every difference on this page, it is computed from the unrounded rates, which is why it is not 0.0570. Its standard error over the 200 models is 0.0045. Read as a membership test, being right is only 1.08 times as likely for a member as for a non-member. Most of the attack’s 78% success would be there even if the person had never been in the training data.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.3 The imputation baseline
The game removes population inference by subtracting it. Measuring it directly is just as useful, because it tells you how much success any model of the same population would give, or any published statistic about it. Statisticians call filling in a missing field from the others imputation. The imputation baseline is the success rate of the best possible guess of \(s\) from \(x\) and \(y\), made by a guesser who knows the population exactly. Jayaraman & Evans (2022) found that many published attribute inference attacks do no better than imputation from similar data. This baseline is the one an attack must beat.
The best possible guess is easy to describe. Whatever a guesser answers after seeing \(x\) and \(y\) is right exactly when the true \(s\) equals its answer. So for each pair, the best answer is the value of \(s\) that is most probable together with it. This is the maximum a posteriori (MAP) guess, “a posteriori” because it is made after seeing the observation.
Write \(p(s, x, y)\) for the probability that a record from the population has these three values. For a given pair of \(x\) and \(y\), the MAP guess is right on the records with that pair and the guessed value of \(s\). Their total probability is \(\max_s p(s, x, y)\), and adding over all pairs gives the success rate of the MAP guess: \[V(S \mid X, Y) = \sum_{x, y}\max_s p(s, x, y). \tag{11.2}\] Information theory calls this success rate the vulnerability, hence the letter \(V\). The capital letters stand for the fields as random quantities.
The ceiling for non-members comes from one more fact. An observation that is independent of the record, such as a coin flip, cannot change which value of \(s\) is most likely, so it cannot raise the best success. A model trained without the target is such an observation. A non-member is drawn afresh, separately from the training set, and the model depends only on the training set and on the randomness of training. So the best any adversary can do on a non-member is the best guess from \(x\) and \(y\) alone. This is the non-member ceiling. For every adversary in the game, \[\Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{non-member}] \le V(S \mid X, Y). \tag{11.3}\] The ceiling rests entirely on that independence. A member’s record was used to train the model, so for a member the model is not an independent observation, and the ceiling does not apply.
Attacks that never look at the model cannot tell members from non-members at all. The member target is one record of the training set, chosen at random, and each training record is an independent draw from the population. If you ignore the model, a member is therefore just a record drawn from the population, like a fresh one. An attack that uses only \(x\) and \(y\) has the same success in both worlds, and zero advantage. The MAP guess made with the population’s true probabilities, called Bayes imputation, is such an attack, and it reaches the ceiling for members and non-members alike. The game guarantees this by drawing the training set and the fresh target from the same population. Without that, members would differ from non-members before anyone looked at the model.
A worked population makes this concrete. Let \(s = 1\) mean “smoker”, let \(x\) be the age band, young or old, and let \(y = 1\) mean “has the disease”. Smokers make up 30% of the population. They also tend to be older, since a fraction 0.6 of them is old, against 0.4 of non-smokers. The chance of the disease rises with both age and smoking, so for non-smokers it is 0.1 when young and 0.3 when old. For smokers it is higher, 0.4 when young and 0.7 when old.
To get the probability of a full record, multiply three chances. They are the chance of its smoking status, the chance of its age band given that status, and the chance of its disease outcome given both. The result is the joint table, Table 11.1. For example, an old smoker with the disease has probability \(0.3 \times 0.6 \times 0.7 = 0.126\).

The last row divides each column’s smoker entry by the column total, which gives the chance that a person in that column smokes. With no observation, the best guess is “non-smoker”, which is right 70% of the time. Age alone changes the odds but not the decision. Adding the two columns of each age band shows that a young person smokes with probability 0.2222, and an old person with probability 0.3913. Since both are below one half, the guess stays “non-smoker” in both age bands, and the success stays at 0.7.
With age and disease together, the chance of smoking crosses one half in the two disease columns (Figure 11.1), so the MAP guess becomes “smoker” there. Its success is the sum of the bold entries, the largest in each column, which gives a vulnerability of 0.748. In the terms of Information theory, this gain over the blind guess is a min-entropy leakage of 0.0957 bits. That is the base-2 logarithm of the ratio of the two success rates.






Figure 11.1: The posterior probability of smoking in each cell of the smoking table, with each cell’s probability in brackets. Red bars cross \(\frac12\), where imputation guesses “smoker”; together they add 0.048 to the 0.7 of the blind guess.



Every one of these numbers comes from the population, not from any model. A model trained on 10,000 patients from this population, if it predicts well, lets an insurer reach 0.748 on anyone drawn from it. The ceiling says that nobody outside the training set can be attacked more successfully. Dwork & Roth (2014) make the same point about a study showing that smoking causes cancer, which discloses a fact about the world, not about its participants. A privacy definition that forbade this would forbid learning anything from data.
That does not make population inference harmless, since being guessed to be a smoker hurts whether or not the guess used your record. But no defence that limits what any single record contributes to a model can prevent it, because the harm would remain with your record removed. It is a question for policy and fairness, not for the attacks of this part.
The ceiling is also a property of the population, not of the model, and it can be high. If the public features and the label nearly determine the sensitive attribute, every model and every statistic “reveals” it. That is why attacks should be reported relative to the ceiling.
