title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.4 Model inversion: the MAP attack
The imputation guess needs the probability of the label given the other two fields, \(p(y \mid x, s)\), which the adversary usually does not know. But a model that predicts \(y\) from \(x\) and \(s\) is an estimate of exactly that link. Fredrikson et al. (2014) used this to infer patients’ genotypes from a warfarin dosing model, given their demographics and dose. They called the attack model inversion, because it runs the model backwards from its output to an input. A model’s confidences are the probabilities it predicts for each label. Fredrikson, Jha & Ristenpart (2015) showed that releasing them makes the attack much stronger.
The attack is Bayes’ rule. Write \(f_y(x, s)\) for the model’s confidence in the label when it is fed the public features and a candidate value of the sensitive attribute. Bayes’ rule says that the most likely value of \(s\) maximizes the product of two factors. The first factor, \(p(s \mid x)\), says how plausible \(s\) is for someone with these features. The adversary supplies it from what it knows about the population. The second factor says how likely the known label is if the attribute were \(s\), and the adversary gets it by querying the model at each candidate. The MAP inversion attack guesses \[\hat s(x, y) = \arg\max_s\; p(s \mid x)\, f_y(x, s). \tag{11.4}\]
Bayes’ rule also divides by the probability of the label given \(x\), but that is the same for every candidate, so it cannot change which one wins. Fredrikson et al. used the overall frequency \(p(s)\) in place of \(p(s \mid x)\), which treats the attribute as independent of the public features. That throws away what \(x\) says about \(s\), and can lose success even when the model’s confidences are exactly right.
Everything the attack does well or badly comes from how the model’s confidences differ from the population’s probabilities. A model whose confidences equal those probabilities is called calibrated. Take a calibrated model and an adversary that uses the population’s true \(p(s \mid x)\). Both factors are then the true ones, so inversion is imputation and reaches the ceiling. The attack queries the model, but it only reads off probabilities that a guesser who knows the population already has. It therefore behaves like a model-free attack, with the same success on members and non-members.
Take an old patient with the disease. From the population, the adversary knows that an old person smokes with probability 0.3913, and so does not with probability 0.6087. A calibrated model, queried at both values of \(s\), returns a disease probability of 0.7 for a smoker and 0.3 for a non-smoker. So “smoker” scores \(0.3913 \times 0.7 = 0.2739\). “Non-smoker” scores \(0.6087 \times 0.3 = 0.1826\), and the attack guesses “smoker”. Normalized, the smoker score is 0.6000, the posterior in Table 11.1, so the attack is imputation.
A trained model differs from the population in two ways, one for members and one for non-members. On members, the model is too sure of the truth. Training lowers the loss on each training record, which is small when the model gives the record’s label a high confidence. It does this at the record’s true value of \(s\), so the confidence there rises towards 1. The other value of \(s\) was never paired with this record, so the model’s confidence there is like its confidence on a fresh record. The ratio of the two scores is therefore tilted towards the truth for members. This tilt is the generalization gap of Membership inference, the difference between a model’s loss on its training records and on fresh ones, seen through the sensitive attribute.
On non-members, the second difference shows. An overfit model’s confidences carry the noise of a small training set rather than the population’s exact probabilities, so its guesses fall below the ceiling.
The toy experiment shows both effects. Its population has a sensitive attribute that is 1 with probability 0.3, ten public features, and a label from a logistic model whose weights depend on the attribute. Each trained model has one weight vector per value of \(s\), so a training record never touches the weights used at its other value. The mean log-loss is 0.2965 on members and 0.6690 on non-members. On a million fresh records, guessing from \(x\) alone is right 0.7045 of the time, and Bayes imputation reaches the ceiling of 0.7517.
Over the models of the game, imputation does as well on members as on non-members, up to sampling noise, as the model-free argument predicts. MAP inversion with the trained model is right on 0.7832 of members, which is 0.0315 above the ceiling. But on non-members it is right only 0.7262 of the time, 0.0254 below the ceiling. In this experiment, then, measuring the attack only on fresh records would understate what it achieves on members.
No knowledge of the population could produce success on members above the ceiling. Figure 11.2 shows where it comes from instead: for members, training has removed most of the cases where the model strongly prefers the wrong value.






Figure 11.2: The evidence of MAP inversion for the true attribute, the log of the score of the true value over the other, for members and non-members of 50 models trained on 100 records each. The attack is right when the evidence is positive; members have far fewer large negative values.



More data closes both gaps, members above the ceiling and non-members below it. As the training set grows, the model approaches the population’s probabilities, and both success rates approach the ceiling (Figure 11.3). With 25 training records the advantage is 0.1610. It falls to 0.0111 with 400 records. With 1,600 records it is only 0.0052.






Figure 11.3: Success of MAP inversion on members and non-members against the training-set size \(n\), 40 models per point. Members start above the Bayes imputation ceiling and non-members below it; both converge to the ceiling as the model approaches the population.



The same idea can invert a whole input rather than one field. Fredrikson, Jha & Ristenpart (2015) ran gradient descent on an image to find the input that a face recognition model most confidently assigns to one person. They recovered a blurred but recognizable image of that person. What such an attack recovers is a typical input of the class, which is population inference about the class. It is a privacy problem because here the class is a single person.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.5 Confidence masking
If confidences make inversion stronger, why release them? Fredrikson, Jha & Ristenpart (2015) suggested rounding the confidences that an interface returns, and many deployed interfaces return only the top label. Such confidence masking is cheap and leaves the predicted label unchanged. Does it close the leak?
Masking can never help the best attacker, because it only coarsens what the attacker sees. Whoever holds the full answers can apply the mask themselves and then guess. So any rule that guesses from the masked answers is also a rule on the full answers, and the best rule on the full answers is at least as good. This is the guessing version of the data processing inequality.
To write this down, let \(F\) be the list of answers the adversary gets by querying the model at every candidate value of \(s\). Each answer is the model’s vector of confidences over the labels. Let \(g\) be any masking function applied to these answers, such as rounding, keeping only the top label, or adding noise. Then the best attack on the masked answers does no better than the best attack on the full ones: \[V\big(S \mid X, Y, g(F)\big) \le V\big(S \mid X, Y, F\big). \tag{11.5}\] This holds on members and on non-members separately, since the argument never used which world the target came from. Added noise is no exception, because an adversary with the full answers could draw the noise itself.
The inequality is about the best attacker in each world separately. It says nothing about the difference between members and non-members, which is the leak. Masking can only lower the best success in each world, by amounts that depend on the mask and on how the confidences of members and non-members differ. Nothing forces the two drops to be equal, so the gap can shrink or grow.
Labels alone still leak, for the same reason confidences do. With only the top label, the adversary still sees, for each candidate \(s\), whether the predicted label equals the known label \(y\). On a member, the model usually predicts the training label at the true \(s\), because it fit that record. At the other value it predicts as it would for a fresh record, which matches \(y\) less often. So “the label matches at only one candidate” points to that candidate, and on members it usually points to the truth. Non-members rarely get this help. The model fit neither value for them, so its two predicted labels usually agree, and the attack falls back on the guess from \(x\) alone. Label-only membership inference (Choquette-Choo et al. 2021) exploits the same asymmetry.

0.0650






Rounding to one decimal changes almost nothing. The attack only compares the scores of the two candidates, and most confidences are far enough from the rounding boundaries that the comparison keeps its sign. With labels only, non-member success drops to 0.7092, close to the 0.7045 of guessing from \(x\) alone. Member success drops less, to 0.7741, which is still 0.0224 above the imputation ceiling. So the advantage grows, from 0.0569 to 0.0650 (Figure 11.4). Masking has hurt population inference more than the individual leak. The interface now leaks less about the population, and as much as before about the people in the training set.






Figure 11.4: MAP inversion success on members and non-members through three interfaces, for models trained on 100 records. The dashed line is Bayes imputation, the dotted line the guess from the public features alone.



Small changes mean little either way. MAP inversion with an overfit model is not the best possible attacker, so a mask can raise its success slightly, as rounding does for members here, without contradicting the inequality.
Above all, masking is obfuscation, not a guarantee. It removes one attack’s input without bounding what any attack can learn about a member. So don’t count a drop in overall attack success as a privacy gain, and check the gap between members and non-members instead. Less overfitting, for example from more training data, shrinks that gap. Part 3 introduces differential privacy, which bounds the gap itself, for every attacker and every output format.

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.6 Code
The imputation baseline and the inversion scores of the smoking example take a few lines with the standard library:
from itertools import product
from math import log2

P_SMOKER = 0.3
P_OLD = {0: 0.4, 1: 0.6}  # Pr[old | s]
P_DISEASE = {(0, 0): 0.1, (0, 1): 0.3, (1, 0): 0.4, (1, 1): 0.7}  # Pr[disease | s, old]


def joint(s: int, old: int, disease: int) -> float:
    """Probability of the record (smoker s, old, disease) in the population."""
    p_s = P_SMOKER if s else 1 - P_SMOKER
    p_x = P_OLD[s] if old else 1 - P_OLD[s]
    p_y = P_DISEASE[(s, old)] if disease else 1 - P_DISEASE[(s, old)]
    return p_s * p_x * p_y


def best_guess_success(sees_age: bool, sees_disease: bool) -> float:
    """Success of the MAP guess of s for a guesser who knows the population and sees the chosen fields."""
    cells: dict[tuple[int, int], list[float]] = {}
    for s, old, disease in product((0, 1), repeat=3):
        key = (old if sees_age else -1, disease if sees_disease else -1)
        cells.setdefault(key, [0.0, 0.0])[s] += joint(s, old, disease)
    return sum(max(cell) for cell in cells.values())


def inversion_scores(old: int, confidence: dict[int, float]) -> dict[int, float]:
    """MAP inversion: prior of s given the age band, times the model's confidence in the known label at s."""
    prior = {s: (P_SMOKER if s else 1 - P_SMOKER) * (P_OLD[s] if old else 1 - P_OLD[s]) for s in (0, 1)}
    total = sum(prior.values())
    return {s: prior[s] / total * confidence[s] for s in (0, 1)}


v0, vx, vxy = best_guess_success(False, False), best_guess_success(True, False), best_guess_success(True, True)
print(f"{v0:.4f} {vx:.4f} {vxy:.4f}")  # 0.7000 0.7000 0.7480
print(f"{log2(vxy / v0):.4f}")  # 0.0957
scores = inversion_scores(old=1, confidence={0: 0.3, 1: 0.7})  # a calibrated model, queried for an old patient with the disease
print(f"{scores[1]:.4f} {scores[0]:.4f}")  # 0.2739 0.1826
print(f"{scores[1] / (scores[0] + scores[1]):.4f}")  # 0.6000
The full edition’s script, attribute_inference.py, plays the game on the toy model and prints every number in this chapter. Each run trains a regularized logistic regression with one weight vector per value of \(s\). It then attacks the members and the same number of fresh records with MAP inversion, Bayes imputation and the guess from \(x\) alone. The whole run takes a few seconds:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/attribute_inference.py

Success on non-members \(\le V(S \mid X, Y) = \sum_{x, y}\max_s p(s, x, y)\)

Equal success on members and non-members; imputation reaches \(V(S \mid X, Y)\)
Ignoring the model, a member is a population record

\(\hat s = \arg\max_s p(s \mid x)\,f_y(x, s)\)

\(V(S \mid X, Y, g(F)) \le V(S \mid X, Y, F)\), but the member/non-member gap can grow

Rules of thumb

Report success on members, on non-members, and the imputation baseline. One success rate says nothing about privacy.
Success up to the imputation baseline is population inference, and any model or statistic of the population gives it.
Success on members beyond what non-members get is the individual leak. It comes from overfitting and shrinks as the training set grows.
An attribute attack is a membership test that outputs one bit, and it is weak at low false positive rates.
Rounding confidences or returning labels only changes the attack, not what the model memorized.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.1 Why this matters
A hospital trains a readmission model on its 1,000 patients and shares it with a research partner. Suppose you have checked that no attack on the model can tell, much better than a coin flip, whether any one patient was in the training set. The partner can still learn whether 45% or 55% of the hospital’s patients are over 65, and be right almost every time. A company that shares a fraud model may reveal the share of its customers in a market it has not announced. A model trained on data from a lab’s machines may reveal whether those machines had been patched.
None of these secrets is about a single record. Each is a property of the training set as a whole, a statistic of the dataset such as the fraction of records that belong to some subgroup. Property inference is the attack that recovers such a statistic from a trained model. Ateniese et al. (2015) introduced it, with attacks that learned whether a speech recognizer had been trained on speakers with a particular accent. Ganju et al. (2018) carried the attack to neural networks.
How can a model hide every record and still give away the mix of records? Think of the model as an average over its training records, and write \(n\) for the number of records. Changing one record moves an average by about \(1/n\). The training set is a random sample, and the luck of the draw moves an average by about \(1/\sqrt n\), the usual size of the error of an average. That is much larger than \(1/n\) when \(n\) is large.
A single record is therefore lost in the sampling noise, and that is why membership inference gets harder with more data. Changing the subgroup’s share is different, because it changes a fixed fraction of the records at once. The small effects of those records add up to a shift that does not shrink as \(n\) grows, while the noise does shrink. So property inference gets easier with more data. This chapter makes that argument precise, and shows how an attacker turns it into a working test by training models of its own. It ends with neural networks, whose raw weights hide the property unless the attacker describes the network in a way that ignores the order of its units.

title: 12  Property inference
section: 12.2 The property game and its ceiling
text:
12.2 The property game and its ceiling
Threat models and privacy games writes every attack as a game. A challenger trains a model with a hidden secret, and an adversary, the attacker, tries to guess the secret. In the property game the secret is one bit about the population that produced the training set. The records come from a population that mixes a majority group and a subgroup. The subgroup’s share of that population is one of two values, written \(t_0\) and \(t_1\), and the attacker knows both. Suri & Evans (2022) call this game distribution inference.
The game runs in four steps. First, the challenger flips a fair bit \(b\), which is 0 or 1 with probability one half each. Second, it draws \(n\) records independently from the population in which the subgroup’s share is \(t_b\), and trains a model on them. Third, the attacker receives either the model’s parameters, called white-box access, or only its answers to queries, called black-box access. The attacker also knows how records from each group are distributed, the dataset size, the two shares and the training algorithm. Fourth, the attacker outputs a guess of \(b\), and it wins if the guess is right. Because the bit is fair, an attacker who learns nothing wins exactly half the time.
The secret belongs to a group, not to a person, and that changes how the attack is scored. In Membership inference the attacker faces many target records, and a few records exposed with high confidence matter even if most are not. So there you report the true positive rate (TPR), the chance of saying 1 when the bit is 1. You report it at a low false positive rate (FPR), the chance of saying 1 when the bit is 0. Here each dataset carries a single secret, so the natural score is the accuracy, the probability that the guess equals \(b\).
Accuracy is tied to the advantage of Threat models and privacy games, the TPR minus the FPR. With a fair bit, half the games have \(b = 1\), and the attacker wins those with probability equal to the TPR. The other half have \(b = 0\), and the attacker wins those with probability one minus the FPR. Averaging the two halves gives an accuracy of \(\frac12(1 + \text{advantage})\). An attacker who ignores the model says 1 equally often in both worlds, so its advantage is 0 and its accuracy is one half. That is the coin-flip baseline.

12.2.1 The most any attacker can win
The attacker sees a view, such as the trained parameters. The view has one distribution when the bit is 0, written \(P\), and another when the bit is 1, written \(Q\). Some views are more likely in one world than in the other, and that difference is all the attacker has to go on. The best attack says 1 exactly on the views that are more likely under \(Q\), because saying 1 on such a view raises the TPR more than the FPR. This attack is the likelihood-ratio test.
Its advantage is the total variation (TV) distance between the two distributions. For each view \(x\), write \(p(x)\) for its probability when the bit is 0, and \(q(x)\) for its probability when the bit is 1. The TV distance is half the total absolute difference between the two, summed over all views, \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \tfrac12\sum_x|p(x) - q(x)|. \tag{12.1}\] For continuous views, such as parameters, the sum becomes an integral over densities. Hypothesis testing explains why no attack does better, and with a fair bit the best accuracy any attacker can reach is \(\frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{TV}(P, Q)\).
The attacker sees the model, not the data, and the model is computed from the data. Anyone holding the data could train the model themselves, with the same algorithm and fresh random choices, and run the attacker’s test on it. So no test on the model can beat the best test on the data. This is the data processing inequality of Divergences, which says that passing a view through a channel cannot increase its TV distance. A channel here is any random procedure that does not use the secret. It holds under one condition. The training algorithm’s own random choices, such as its initialization and the order of its minibatches, must not depend on the secret bit. A training run that could see the bit could write it into the weights, and then the model could reveal more than the data do.
Put together, the two facts give a ceiling that holds for every attacker: \[\text{advantage} \le \mathrm{TV}\big(\text{model under } t_0, \text{model under } t_1\big) \le \mathrm{TV}\big(\text{data under } t_0, \text{data under } t_1\big). \tag{12.2}\] The first inequality says that no attack on the model beats the likelihood-ratio test. The second says that training cannot add information about the share.


12.2.2 When the group is visible: the count
The right-hand side of Equation 12.2 becomes a number you can compute under one more condition, that each record shows which group it comes from. Each record is a subgroup record with probability equal to the share, and the features of a record from either group are drawn the same way in both worlds. So when you compare how likely a dataset is under the two shares, the features cancel, and only the number of subgroup records makes a difference. Call that count \(S\).
The count carries everything in the data that bears on the share, so it is called a sufficient statistic for the share (Divergences). Nothing else in the data helps to tell the shares apart. So the TV distance between the two distributions of the dataset equals the one between the two distributions of the count. The records are drawn independently, so the count is binomial. For every model trained on the data, \[\text{advantage} \le \mathrm{TV}\big(\mathrm{Bin}(n, t_0), \mathrm{Bin}(n, t_1)\big). \tag{12.3}\]
So releasing the count is the worst case. The count already carries everything the data say about the share, so no model trained on the data can leak more, and releasing the count itself reaches the ceiling. A model that never sees the group leaks less, by an amount you can measure. Deleting the group column does not break the bound, because a dataset without the column is computed from the dataset with it. The bound may just no longer be reached.
The game also says what the attacker needs. It hands the attacker the two groups’ distributions and the training algorithm. In practice this means auxiliary data from both groups, and the ability to train models the way the victim does. This is the same assumption that makes shadow models work in Membership inference, where the attacker trains copies of the victim’s pipeline on data it controls.
You may ask whether this is an attack at all. Learning that smokers get more lung cancer is the purpose of a medical study, not a breach. Property inference is a harm only when the property describes the data owner rather than the world. The share of a company’s customers in a region is such a property, and so are the demographics of one hospital’s patients. When the dataset is a small sample from a public population, its property is public knowledge anyway.
The game has variants. The secret can be a real number to estimate, or whether any record with a given feature is present. Some games fix the number of subgroup records instead of drawing it at random. With a visible group, the ceiling is then 1, because the count itself reveals the bit, and only training noise and a hidden group make the attack hard. A stronger attacker, one who can add a few records of its own to the training set, can make a property far easier to infer (Mahloujifar et al. 2022).
Return to the hospital’s secret about its patients over 65. If age group is part of each record, Equation 12.3 caps the advantage of every attack on every model trained on the data at 0.9985. The count has mean 450 in one world and 550 in the other. Its standard deviation is about 15.7, so the two means are more than six standard deviations apart and the two distributions barely overlap. An attacker who can read the count off the model reaches this ceiling, and with a fair bit it is right more than 99.9% of the time.
With only 100 patients, the two means of the count are only 10 apart and its standard deviation is about 5. The distributions then overlap much more, and the ceiling falls to 0.6827.

title: 12  Property inference
section: 12.3 Why a property leaks when no record does
text:
12.3 Why a property leaks when no record does
The simplest model of all is a training algorithm that releases the count of subgroup records. Two attackers can look at the same release. One asks whether a target record, a member of the subgroup, is in the data. The other asks whether the data were drawn with share \(t_0\) or \(t_1\). For a count, both best advantages can be computed exactly, and they move in opposite directions as \(n\) grows. This makes the argument of the opening section exact.
Start with membership. The dataset holds \(n - 1\) records from a population with subgroup share \(t\), plus one more, which is either the target or a fresh record. Write \(X\) for the count of subgroup records among the \(n - 1\) others. The target always adds 1 to the count, while a fresh record adds 1 only when it comes from the subgroup, a fraction \(t\) of the time. In that fraction the count is \(X + 1\) in both worlds, so only the remaining fraction \(1 - t\) of games carries any signal, and the advantage is scaled down by that factor. In those games the attacker must tell \(X\) from \(X + 1\).
A binomial distribution has a single peak. For such a distribution, the TV distance between a count and the same count shifted by one equals the probability of the most likely value. The single peak is needed, because a count that took only the values 0 and 2 would not overlap with its shift at all. With many records the binomial is close to a normal distribution, so its most likely value has probability about \(1/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,s)\), where \(s\) is its standard deviation (Probability distributions). So the best membership advantage is \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{mem}} = (1 - t)\max_k\Pr[X = k] \approx \frac{1 - t}{\sqrt{2\pi(n - 1)t(1 - t)}}. \tag{12.4}\] It falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), because one extra record is measured against a spread that grows like \(\sqrt n\).
Now the property. Under the two hypotheses, the fraction of subgroup records centres on \(t_0\) or on \(t_1\). Its standard deviation is about \(\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)/n}\), where \(\bar t = \frac{t_0 + t_1}2\) is the midpoint share. Using the midpoint’s spread for both hypotheses is an approximation that is good when the gap between the shares is small.
Approximate both distributions of the fraction by normals with that common spread. Two normals with the same spread are best told apart by a threshold halfway between their means. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function, the chance that a standard normal draw is at most a given value. If the threshold lies \(z\) standard deviations from each mean, the test’s TPR is \(\Phi(z)\) and its FPR is \(1 - \Phi(z)\), so its advantage is \(2\Phi(z) - 1\). Here \(z\) is half the distance between the two centres, which gives \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{prop}} = \mathrm{TV}\big(\mathrm{Bin}(n, t_0), \mathrm{Bin}(n, t_1)\big) \approx 2\Phi\Big(\frac{\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|}{2\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}}\Big) - 1. \tag{12.5}\] The argument of \(\Phi\) is that \(z\), and it grows like \(\sqrt n\), so the advantage rises towards 1. Because \(n\) and the gap enter only through \(\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\), doubling the gap has the same effect as multiplying \(n\) by 4.
Table 12.1 puts numbers on both formulas. The property attacker tells share 0.45 from share 0.55, and the membership attacker faces a population share of one half. The approximations are close even at 100 records.

At 10,000 records, the attacker who asks about one patient has an advantage of 0.0040. With a fair bit, it is right with probability 0.502. The attacker who asks about the share of patients over 65, by contrast, is never wrong to four decimals. The data, the release and the attacker’s knowledge are the same, and only the question differs. Figure 12.1 shows both advantages against \(n\). The membership advantage falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), while the property advantage climbs to 1, sooner for a larger gap between the shares.






Figure 12.1: Left: the released fraction \(S/n\) at \(n = 1{,}000\) under \(t = 0.45\) and \(t = 0.55\), and under \(t = 0.5\) with and without one target from the subgroup; the last two curves are indistinguishable. Right: the best property advantage for two gaps, and the best membership advantage of one record, against \(n\).



Neither argument is special to counts. An estimator is any quantity computed from the data, such as a model’s parameters, and most estimators behave like averages. Each record pulls an average by its own contribution, called its influence, divided by \(n\). So one record’s pull shrinks like \(1/n\), while the sampling noise shrinks only like \(1/\sqrt n\). A change of share moves the centre of the estimate by a fixed distance instead, so measured in units of the noise its shift grows like \(\sqrt n\).
Put plainly, a property is a group of records. Moving from share \(t_0\) to share \(t_1\) changes about \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records, which for the hospital is 100 of its 1,000 patients. A protection measured one record at a time says little about a change to 100 records at once. Differential privacy, the defence of Part 3, protects one record at a time. Its group-privacy property covers a group only with a guarantee that weakens as the group grows (Properties of differential privacy). So hiding the property means hiding the population’s mix itself. Only a released statistic that is noisy on the scale of \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records, not of one record, pushes the property advantage down. That much noise also destroys what the statistic was for.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.4 Shadow models and meta-classifiers
For a real model, nobody can write down the distribution of the trained parameters, so the likelihood-ratio test is out of reach. Ateniese et al. (2015) gave the recipe that every later attack uses: if you cannot compute the two distributions, sample from them. The attacker draws many datasets with each share from its auxiliary data, and trains a shadow model on each, exactly as the victim trains. It then trains a classifier, the meta-classifier, to tell the two shares apart from the shadow models’ parameters, and applies it to the victim’s model. This is the shadow-model idea of Membership inference, with whole models as the data points.
That leaves two questions, which meta-classifier to train and how accurate it can be. Both have an answer when the trained parameters are approximately normal, as they are for many models.

12.4.1 When the parameters are normal, the best test is linear
Suppose the parameters are normal under both hypotheses, with the same covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) but different means. To see how hard the two distributions are to tell apart, start with a single parameter, where the answer depends on how far apart the means are in standard deviations. For many parameters, the noise can be larger in some directions than in others. A shift along a noisy direction then counts for less than the same shift along a quiet one, because more of it is hidden by the noise. The Mahalanobis distance measures the shift between the means \(m_0\) and \(m_1\) in exactly this way: \[\Delta = \sqrt{(m_1 - m_0)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(m_1 - m_0)}. \tag{12.6}\] For a single parameter, it is the distance between the means divided by the standard deviation.
Because the covariance is shared, the log-likelihood ratio of the two normals turns out to be a linear function of the parameters, as the full edition shows. So the likelihood-ratio test is a linear discriminant. It says 1 when the parameters lie on \(m_1\)’s side of a flat boundary halfway between the two means, and the direction across that boundary is \(\Sigma^{-1}(m_1 - m_0)\). As for a single parameter, its accuracy with a fair bit depends only on the Mahalanobis distance: \[\Phi(\Delta/2). \tag{12.7}\] The condition of a shared covariance matters, because with different covariances the log-likelihood ratio keeps a quadratic part, and the best test is curved rather than flat.
Are trained parameters normal? A model fitted by minimizing an average loss over its records is called an M-estimator, and for large \(n\) its parameters are approximately normal. Write \(\theta(t)\) for the population fit, the model that infinitely many records with share \(t\) would give. At the fitted parameters the average gradient of the loss is zero. Near the population fit the gradient is close to linear in the parameters. So the fitted parameters differ from the population fit by about a fixed matrix times the average of the per-record gradients, each taken at the population fit. That average is approximately normal by the central limit theorem, because the records are independent. The parameters therefore scatter normally around \(\theta(t)\), with a covariance that shrinks like \(1/n\), written \(\Sigma_1(t)/n\).
Here \(\Sigma_1\) is the covariance the fit would have with a single record, and two matrices set it. The first is the average curvature of the loss at the population fit, written \(H\). A sharply curved loss pins the minimizer down, so more curvature means less noise. The second is the covariance of the per-record gradients there, written \(G\), which measures how much each record pulls in its own direction. The fixed matrix of the previous paragraph is the inverse of \(H\), up to sign, and applying it on both sides of the gradients’ covariance gives \(\Sigma_1 = H^{-1}GH^{-1}\). This is called the sandwich covariance, because \(G\) sits between two copies of \(H^{-1}\). These are large-\(n\) results. When \(n\) is small, or training stops before the average gradient reaches zero, the parameters can be skewed, and the linear meta-classifier is then no longer the best one.


12.4.2 The accuracy of the attack and the scaling law
Under the two hypotheses the parameters are approximately normal around \(\theta(t_0)\) and \(\theta(t_1)\). When their covariances are close, use one shared covariance for both. Write \(\bar\Sigma_1\) for the average of the two per-record covariances, so that the shared covariance is \(\bar\Sigma_1/n\). The best attack is then a linear discriminant, and its accuracy is \(\Phi(\Delta/2)\), where the Mahalanobis distance is now \[\Delta = \sqrt{n\,\big(\theta(t_1) - \theta(t_0)\big)^\top\bar\Sigma_1^{-1}\big(\theta(t_1) - \theta(t_0)\big)}. \tag{12.8}\] The factor \(n\) appears because the noise shrinks like \(1/n\) while the shift between the population fits stays fixed.
For a small gap between the shares, the population fit changes almost linearly with the share. Its shift is then about its slope \(\theta' = d\theta/dt\) at the midpoint share, times the gap. This gives the scaling law \[\text{accuracy} \approx \Phi\big(\kappa\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|/2\big), \qquad \kappa = \sqrt{\theta'^\top\Sigma_1^{-1}\theta'}. \tag{12.9}\] The constant \(\kappa\) is how fast the model moves with the share, measured in units of its per-record noise, with both evaluated at the midpoint share. For the released count, \(\kappa\) is \(1/\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)}\), which is 2 at a midpoint of one half. With that \(\kappa\), the accuracy \(\Phi(\Delta/2)\) becomes the advantage of Equation 12.5, since advantage is twice the accuracy minus 1.
Two numbers set the leak. The slope \(\theta'\) says how much the property moves what the model learns, and \(\Sigma_1\) says how noisy that is. If the property does not change what the model fits, the slope is zero and, to first order, nothing leaks, however large \(n\) is. If it does, the leak is a side effect of fitting the data well, and no amount of care in the training code removes it.
The constant also compares any model with the count. The accuracy depends on \(\kappa\sqrt n\), so a model with a smaller \(\kappa\) on \(n\) records leaks as much as the count would on fewer records. Matching the two values of \(\kappa\sqrt n\) shows that the count needs only a fraction \((\kappa\sqrt{\bar t(1 - \bar t)})^2\) of them. Suri & Evans (2022) measure leakage in exactly these units, as the number of records an attacker would need to see directly to learn as much as the model reveals.


12.4.3 Example: a logistic regression that never sees the group
Each record has two features drawn from a standard normal distribution, and a label. In the majority, the chance of a positive label rises with both features, while in the subgroup it rises with the first feature and falls with the second. Think of a symptom that raises risk in most patients and lowers it in a minority. The group is never a feature, so a logistic regression sees only the two features and the label. It fits an intercept, a weight \(w_1\) for the first feature and a weight \(w_2\) for the second. It is trained by Newton’s method with a tiny ridge penalty, a small cost on large weights that keeps the fit stable.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.5 Permutation invariance
A logistic regression has one parameter vector per function, because different weights give different predictions. A neural network has many. Swap two hidden units, together with their incoming and outgoing weights, and the network computes exactly the same function. Ganju et al. (2018) observed that a meta-classifier fed the flattened weights then does poorly. It must learn the same pattern in every position of the weight vector, called a slot, and in every order.
Take a network with one hidden layer of units that use the tanh activation, and write \(h\) for the number of hidden units. For the unit numbered \(j\), collect its incoming weights, its bias and its outgoing weight into a vector \(u_j\). The function tanh is odd, which means that it turns a negated input into a negated output. Flip the signs of a unit’s incoming weights and bias, and its activation flips sign. Flip its outgoing weight too, and the unit’s contribution to the output flips back, so the network’s function is again unchanged. Reordering the units and flipping signs therefore gives a typical network \(h!\,2^h\) parameter vectors for the same function. For four units that is \(4! \times 2^4 = 384\).
The symmetry of the function carries over to the distribution of the trained weights under two conditions. The first is that the random initialization treats every reordering and sign flip alike, as it does when the entries are drawn independently from a distribution symmetric about zero. The second is that training is gradient descent. The loss is unchanged by the symmetry, so gradient descent from a transformed start ends at the transformed end. A transformed result is therefore as likely as the original one, under either hypothesis.
The property shows in which units the network has, not in which slot holds which unit, and this has three consequences. First, each slot holds a unit chosen at random from the network’s units, with a random sign, so averaging slot by slot washes the property out. Second, a unit and its sign-flipped copy are equally likely, so every raw parameter has mean zero under both hypotheses. The linear discriminant puts weight on a feature only where the means differ, so on raw weights it can use nothing except the output bias, which no symmetry touches. Third, features that combine all units alike are unchanged by any reordering or sign flip, and they keep information that the raw means lose. An example is the matrix \(\sum_ju_ju_j^\top\), which adds up, over the units, the products of every pair of entries within each unit.
The sign argument needs tanh to be odd. A network of ReLU units has no sign symmetry, only the reorderings. The reorderings force every unit slot to have the same mean, but that common mean can differ between the two shares, so the raw means need not vanish.
There are three ways to undo the symmetry, and with raw weights as the baseline they give four representations to compare. A canonical form picks one parameter vector per function. It flips each unit so that its outgoing weight is positive, and then sorts the units by that weight. Ganju et al. propose sorting, and since their networks use ReLU units, sorting alone gives them the canonical form, which beats raw weights in their experiments. Sorting is fragile, because two units with nearly equal outgoing weights swap places from one network to the next.
A set representation passes each unit’s parameters through the same function, adds the results, and applies a second function to the sum. The sum does not depend on the order of the units. Ganju et al. use this form, from DeepSets (Zaheer et al. 2017), with both functions learned. The matrix \(\sum_ju_ju_j^\top\) is a case of it, with each unit mapped to \(u_ju_j^\top\), and it is also unchanged by sign flips because \((-u_j)(-u_j)^\top = u_ju_j^\top\). A linear meta-classifier on the plain sum \(\sum_ju_j\) would fail for tanh networks, because every \(u_j\) has mean zero and so does their sum. Deeper networks have the same problem at each layer, so a set representation is applied layer by layer.
Probe outputs, the network’s answers on fixed inputs, need no correction. A function does not depend on how it is written down, so these features are unchanged by any symmetry automatically, and they need only black-box access.
Table 12.4 compares the four representations on tanh networks with four hidden units, each trained on 200 records. The two shares are 0.2 and 0.8. On each side, 150 shadow networks fit the linear discriminant, and the same number of fresh target networks measure its accuracy. To see which features carry signal, the table also reports each representation’s largest standardized mean gap. For each feature, this is the difference of its means under the two shares, divided by its pooled standard deviation.

So a meta-classifier at chance on raw weights says that the representation is wrong, not that the model is safe. The table also corrects an intuition about access. Whoever holds the weights can compute any query answer, so white-box access is never weaker for the best attack. That says nothing about a fixed simple attack, for which the representation can matter more than the access. Here black-box probes beat raw weights. A model served only through an API is therefore not safe from property inference, and Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko (2021) attack properties through queries alone.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.6 Code
The ceiling of Equation 12.3 and the two advantages of Section 12.3 take a few lines:
from math import erf, exp, lgamma, log, sqrt

def binom_pmf(n: int, t: float) -> list[float]:
    """Pr[Bin(n, t) = k] for k = 0..n, in log space so that large n does not overflow."""
    return [exp(lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(k + 1) - lgamma(n - k + 1) + k * log(t) + (n - k) * log(1 - t)) for k in range(n + 1)]

def property_ceiling(n: int, t0: float, t1: float) -> float:
    """Best advantage of any property attack when the group is visible: TV(Bin(n, t0), Bin(n, t1))."""
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(p - q) for p, q in zip(binom_pmf(n, t0), binom_pmf(n, t1)))

def property_normal(n: int, t0: float, t1: float) -> float:
    """The normal approximation 2 Phi(sqrt(n) |t1 - t0| / (2 sqrt(tbar (1 - tbar)))) - 1."""
    tbar = (t0 + t1) / 2
    z = sqrt(n) * abs(t1 - t0) / (2 * sqrt(tbar * (1 - tbar)))
    return erf(z / sqrt(2))  # equals 2 Phi(z) - 1

def membership_best(n: int, t: float) -> float:
    """Best advantage for one subgroup record from the same count: (1 - t) max_k Pr[Bin(n - 1, t) = k]."""
    return (1 - t) * max(binom_pmf(n - 1, t))

print(f"{property_ceiling(100, 0.45, 0.55):.4f} {property_normal(100, 0.45, 0.55):.4f}")  # 0.6827 0.6827
print(f"{property_ceiling(1000, 0.45, 0.55):.4f} {property_normal(1000, 0.45, 0.55):.4f}")  # 0.9985 0.9984
print(f"{membership_best(100, 0.5):.4f} {membership_best(10000, 0.5):.4f}")  # 0.0398 0.0040

Rules of thumb

Property inference gets easier with more data, and membership inference harder. What matters for a property is \(\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\).
A property changes about \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records at once, so defences sized for one record do not cover it.
Removing the group column does not remove the property, because whatever correlates with the group still moves the model.
Train the meta-classifier on a representation that respects the network’s symmetries, such as canonical order, sums over units or probe outputs.
Report accuracy for property attacks, and when the population is known well enough to compute \(\kappa\), the predicted accuracy next to it.

text:
12.8 Further reading

Ganju, Wang, Yang, Gunter & Borisov, “Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations” (CCS 2018): the practical attack on neural networks, neuron sorting and the DeepSets meta-classifier.
Suri & Evans, “Formalizing and Estimating Distribution Inference Risks” (PoPETs 2022): the property game as a test between two training distributions, and leakage measured in records.
Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko, “Leakage of Dataset Properties in Multi-Party Machine Learning” (USENIX Security 2021): black-box property inference, including properties of attributes that were removed from the training data.
Mahloujifar, Ghosh & Chase, “Property Inference from Poisoning” (IEEE S&P 2022): how a few injected records make a property far easier to infer.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter, except that the approximate normality of trained parameters is derived only in outline there, citing van der Vaart (1998) for its conditions, and the results of Ateniese et al. (2015), Ganju et al. (2018), Zaheer et al. (2017), Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko (2021), Suri & Evans (2022) and Mahloujifar et al. (2022) are cited.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1 Why this matters
A language model trained on scraped text sees phone numbers, addresses, keys and private messages. Ask it to continue “Anna Smith’s phone number is”, and it may finish the sentence with the real number. Nobody queried a database, and no breach leaked anything. The number is stored in the model’s weights, and it comes out through the model’s normal interface. This is training-data extraction. Membership inference asks whether a record was in the training set, and the attacker needs the record in hand to ask. Extraction goes further, because the attacker gets the record itself, often without knowing that it existed.
This chapter first asks what it means for a model to memorize a string, since several definitions exist and they assume different attackers. It then asks which strings get memorized, and finds that repetition in the training data and the size of the model decide it. Finally it shows how an auditor measures memorization and how an attacker finds memorized strings in practice.
One idea runs through all three answers. A language model gives every possible string a probability. Fix the context in which a secret appears, say “my pin is”. Then list every possible filler, here all five-digit pins, from the most likely to the least likely under the model. The rank of the true secret is its position in that list. It is also the number of guesses an attacker needs if it tries the fillers in that order. Memorization means that the model puts a training string far above the other strings that could have stood in its place. A low rank therefore means that the model has done most of the attacker’s work. Every measure in this chapter reads that rank in its own way.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.2 How a language model scores a string
text:
13.2 How a language model scores a string
Every experiment in this chapter uses one small example that runs in seconds. The training set is a contact list. Each line is a made-up name of three syllables, a space, and a five-digit pin, such as toneka 14524. The list has 5,000 background lines, each seen once. Its 600 secret lines, whose pins the experiments try to recover, come in six groups of 100. All the lines of a group are repeated equally often, from once in the first group, doubling each time, to 32 times in the last. Counting the copies, the training set has 11,300 lines.
A language model never scores a whole string at once. It answers a smaller question many times: given everything written so far, how likely is each possible next symbol? To score a whole string after a prompt, the model multiplies these one-step probabilities, which is the chain rule of probability. For the pin 16430 after the prompt “migule” and a space, the model multiplies five numbers. The first is the probability of 1 after the prompt, the second that of 6 after the prompt and 1, and so on to the last digit.
Taking the logarithm turns this product into a sum of per-symbol log-probabilities. The negative base-2 logarithm of the product is the string’s log-perplexity, in bits. It measures how surprised the model is by the string, and each extra bit means the model finds the string half as likely. Every score in this chapter is built from this sum.
The model in the example is a character \(n\)-gram model, the simplest language model there is. An \(n\)-gram model of order \(n\) predicts the next character from the last \(n - 1\) characters, which it calls the context. When this chapter writes out a context, _ stands for a space, so gule_ is the five characters before the first digit of migule 16430.
Training such a model is nothing more than counting. Write \(c\) for a context and \(w\) for a possible next symbol. For every such pair, the model stores the number of times the symbol followed the context in the training text, written \(N(c, w)\). These counts are the model’s parameters, and a higher order stores more of them, because it tells apart more contexts. The order therefore plays the role of model size.
The natural prediction would be the fraction of times \(w\) followed \(c\). But that gives probability 0 to every symbol never seen after \(c\), and one zero in the chain rule makes a whole string impossible. Add-\(\alpha\) smoothing avoids the zeros by pretending that every symbol was seen \(\alpha\) extra times in every context. Write \(V\) for the number of symbols in the alphabet and \(N(c)\) for the total count of context \(c\). The smoothed probability is \[p(w \mid c) = \frac{N(c, w) + \alpha}{N(c) + \alpha V}. \tag{13.1}\]
Three consequences of this formula drive the whole chapter. The first is that training on \(k\) copies of a line adds \(k\) to the count of every pair of context and next symbol that the line passes through. It changes no other count.
The second is that smoothing does not change which symbol is most likely. In a fixed context, every count gets the same extra \(\alpha\), and every symbol shares the same denominator. So the symbol with the largest count still has the largest probability. Greedy decoding, which writes out the most likely next symbol at each step, therefore just follows the largest counts.
The third concerns a context that occurs only in the copies of one line. Suppose a line has been inserted \(k\) times, and one of its contexts appears nowhere else. In that context the line’s own next symbol has count \(k\), and every other symbol has count 0. The true symbol is then \((k + \alpha)/\alpha\) times as likely as any other symbol. The size of the alphabet does not matter, because it sits in the denominator that all symbols share. The example uses \(\alpha = 0.1\) and an alphabet of 39 symbols, so one copy makes the true symbol 11 times as likely as each rival, a ratio worth \(\log_2 11 = 3.46\) bits. That is the mechanism of memorization in this example: a context that belongs to one training line alone, followed by that line’s next symbol.
Ranks need one more convention. Candidates tied with the secret count in its rank, because the attacker may have to try them all first. Information theory measures how hard a secret is to guess with its min-entropy, the negative logarithm of the chance that the best single guess is right. A uniformly random five-digit pin has 16.61 bits of it, and this is the scale on which exposure, later in the chapter, measures memorization.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.3 Verbatim, approximate, discoverable, extractable
“The model memorized its training data” can mean several things. A model that completes a famous quotation has memorized it, but nothing private leaked, while a model that emits a phone number seen once in training has leaked it. Some definitions assume that the attacker knows the beginning of the training string, and others ask whether any prompt at all brings it out. The numbers differ by orders of magnitude between these notions, so a report must say which one it measures.
All the definitions use greedy decoding from a prompt. A string is extractable (Carlini et al. 2021) if some prompt, any prompt at all, makes greedy decoding begin with that string. A string is \(k\)-eidetically memorized if it is extractable and appears in at most \(k\) documents of the training data. Here \(k\) counts documents, much as it counts copies in the example. A small \(k\) is the dangerous case, because it describes a secret seen once and given back.
The next definition assumes more of the attacker. Suppose the training data contain a prefix followed by a suffix. The suffix is discoverably memorized (Carlini et al. 2023, named by Nasr et al. 2023) if prompting with that same prefix makes greedy decoding produce the suffix. Discoverable implies extractable, because the training prefix is one of the prompts that extractability allows. The converse fails. An extractable string may come out after a prompt that is not its training prefix, while its own prefix leads somewhere else.
The definitions also differ in how close the output must be. The three above are verbatim, which means the output must match exactly. A suffix is approximately memorized (Ippolito et al. 2023) if greedy decoding from its prefix comes within a chosen distance of it, such as a number of wrong characters. In this chapter’s example, a pin with at most one wrong digit counts. A verbatim match is also an approximate one, since an exact match has distance 0.
Each definition fits a different threat model. Discoverable memorization assumes an attacker who holds the training prefix. That is a strong assumption, but it makes memorization easy to measure, because you can prompt with every training prefix and compare the output with the true suffix. Extractable memorization fits the real attacker, who has only the model. It is hard to measure, because you would have to search over all prompts. So papers report discoverable rates on open models, and attacks then show how much of that an outsider can actually reach.
Verbatim matching is a weak notion of leakage, because it misses near copies. A model that emits a phone number with one digit changed has still leaked it to anyone who reads it. Ippolito et al. (2023) show that a filter blocking verbatim training text is easy to bypass with prompts that change the style, while the approximate copies still come out. A verbatim rate is therefore a lower bound on the leak, not a measure of it.
Greedy decoding is a convenience for measurement, and deployed systems sample instead. A sample at temperature 1 uses the model’s probabilities unchanged, drawing each next symbol with exactly the probability the model gives it. By the chain rule, the chance that one sample writes out a string \(x\) after a prompt is then the model’s probability of \(x\) after that prompt, written \(p\). Write \(m\) for the number of samples. The budget below assumes that the samples are drawn independently. Then the chances of missing multiply, so all \(m\) samples miss with probability \((1 - p)^m\), which is at most \(e^{-mp}\). Asking for this to be at most a small failure probability \(\beta\) gives a budget: \[m \ge \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{p} \quad\text{samples suffice to extract } x \text{ with probability at least } 1 - \beta. \tag{13.2}\] The budget is inversely proportional to the string’s probability. For example, take a string with probability \(10^{-3}\) after its prefix, and ask for 99% confidence, \(\beta = 0.01\). The budget is then about 4,600 samples.
Sampling gives a graded version of memorization. For the secret migule 16430, inserted 4 times, greedy decoding from its prefix gets the pin wrong at orders 3 to 5 and right from order 6 on. At order 5, a single sample reproduces a secret’s pin with probability \(1.4 \times 10^{-3}\) on average over the secrets inserted 4 times, and with probability 0.142 over those inserted 32 times. For a 99% chance of extracting the pin, the first group needs 3,252 samples and the second only 31. Repetition turns a needle in a haystack into the model’s favourite answer.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.4 Duplication and model size: the copies a string needs
text:
13.4 Duplication and model size: the copies a string needs
Carlini et al. (2023) measured discoverable memorization on a family of open models. They found that it grows log-linearly with three things, the number of times a string is repeated, the size of the model and the length of the prompt. Log-linear means that the rate rises by about the same amount each time one of these is multiplied by a fixed factor. Kandpal, Wallace & Raffel (2022) found that a sequence repeated 10 times is generated about 1,000 times more often than a sequence seen once. The \(n\)-gram example shows where both effects come from, using nothing but its counts.
The explanation is a vote. Greedy decoding follows the largest count at each step. Each copy of a line adds a vote for its own next symbol in every context it passes through. The line comes out when, at every step, these votes beat the strongest rival symbol.
To make this precise, look at one step of the line’s suffix and count only the rest of the training set, without the line’s copies. Write \(c_t\) for the context at step \(t\) and \(x_t\) for the true symbol there. Write \(N_-(c_t, w)\) for the number of times a symbol \(w\) follows that context outside the line’s copies. The gap at that step is how far the strongest rival symbol is ahead of the true symbol in these counts.
With \(k\) copies, the true symbol wins the step when \(k\) is larger than the gap, that is when \(k\) is at least the gap plus one. Greedy decoding stays on the line’s path only while every step wins, because one wrong symbol puts it in a different context. So the number of copies the line needs, written \(k^*\), is set by the step where the rival is furthest ahead: \[k^* = \max_{t}\Big[\max_{w \ne x_t}N_-(c_t, w) - N_-(c_t, x_t)\Big] + 1. \tag{13.3}\] Apart from ties, greedy decoding from the prefix emits the suffix if and only if the number of copies is at least \(k^*\). At some steps a tie with the rival already wins, because of how greedy decoding breaks ties, and such a step needs one copy fewer.
The statement needs a condition. Each context must occur only once within the line, so that a copy adds a vote to the true symbol and to no rival. Without it, a copy could also add a vote to a rival at the same context, and the copies would no longer close the gap one vote at a time. A line breaks the condition only if it repeats the same stretch of \(n - 1\) characters, and in the example almost no line does.
Figure 13.1 draws the vote for one line. A line whose contexts all belong to it alone has no rival votes at any step, so every gap is 0 and \(k^* = 1\). Such a line is memorized from a single copy. Over a population of lines, the fraction memorized at \(k\) copies is the fraction of lines whose \(k^*\) is at most \(k\).






Figure 13.1: For one secret line inserted once, an order-5 model: at each step of its pin, the count of the true next digit (blue) and of its strongest rival (orange) in the rest of the training set. The label is the gap plus one, the copies that step needs. The line needs as many copies as its hardest step.



Model size works by splitting the vote. A longer context divides the training positions into finer groups, since fewer positions share any one context of 7 characters than of 2. So the rival counts in a longer context are smaller, while the line’s own \(k\) votes stay with it in every context it passes through. In the limit every line has contexts of its own, and \(k^* = 1\) for every line. This is the example’s version of “larger models memorize more”. A larger model has enough counts to give rare strings contexts of their own.
The secret migule 16430 shows how the two effects trade off. Its \(k^*\) depends only on the rest of the corpus, not on the 4 copies it actually has. At order 3 it would need 151 copies, and at order 4 it would need 43. At order 5 it needs 9, so its 4 copies lose, and greedy decoding writes 14032, with three wrong digits. From order 6 on it needs only 1, because an order-6 model reads five characters of context. From the first digit on, its contexts are gule_, then ule_1, and so on, and they occur in this line and nowhere else. Shorter contexts, such as the four characters ule_ that an order-5 model reads, are shared with other lines, whose digits can outvote the four copies.
For the same reason, rare data are exposed first. A line whose name shares few syllables with other names reaches a context of its own sooner. Algorithmic stability and generalization found the same pattern for self-influence, how much a model’s loss on a training example rises when that example is left out of training. Nothing else in the data predicts an atypical example, so a model can fit it only by memorizing it, and such examples have the largest self-influence.
Deduplication is the cheapest defence, because it lowers the number of copies of every repeated string. Lee et al. (2022) found that models trained on deduplicated data emit memorized text about ten times less often, without losing quality. Kandpal et al. (2022) found that it sharply lowers the success of extraction attacks. It does nothing for a string seen once in a high-capacity model, though, because there a single copy is already enough.
To measure discoverable memorization in the example, the script prompts each of the 600 secrets with its true prefix, the name and the space. It then decodes five symbols greedily and compares them with the pin. It also computes \(k^*\) for every secret. The predicted fraction with \(k^*\) at most \(k\) matches the measured verbatim rate exactly in all 36 combinations of order and copies. The formula is not an approximation, but a restatement of what greedy decoding does with counts.
The main run shows both effects. Along the copies, at order 5, the verbatim rate climbs from 0 at one copy to 0.70 at 32 copies. Along the orders, a line seen once is safe at orders up to 5. At order 6 it is memorized 8% of the time, and the share climbs to 70% at order 7 and 98% at order 8. The order-8 model has memorized its training set almost completely, and its memorized singletons are 1-eidetic, seen in one document and given back. Figure 13.2 plots the same measurement for a second, independent draw of the training set.






Figure 13.2: Discoverable memorization against copies of the secret in the training set, for \(n\)-gram models of order 3 to 8, on an independent draw of the corpus. Left: greedy decoding reproduces the pin exactly. Right: at most one digit is wrong. Both rise with duplication and with order, and the approximate rate is only slightly higher.



The approximate rates are barely above the verbatim ones. A pin in this example either sits in contexts of its own and comes out whole, or it loses an early vote and wanders off in the wrong context. Natural text, with its many near-ties such as synonyms, is where approximate memorization adds the most (Ippolito et al. 2023).
Carlini et al. (2023) ran the same measurement on GPT-Neo and GPT-J models from 125 million to 6 billion parameters. All were trained on the Pile, a large public collection of web and book text. They prompted each model with 50 tokens of a training sequence, decoded 50 tokens greedily and counted exact matches. The largest model reproduced at least 1% of its training data this way.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.5 Canaries and the exposure metric
Discoverable memorization is all or nothing, since the secret either comes out or does not. An auditor wants a graded answer: how much closer to the secret does the model bring an attacker? Carlini et al. (2019) proposed planting canaries in the training data. A canary is a random secret of a fixed format, such as “my pin is” followed by five random digits. After training, you measure where the model ranks the planted secret among all secrets of the same format. Because you drew the canary at random and planted it yourself, you know the right answer and the number of possible values, so you can measure memorization exactly.
Write \(\mathcal R\) for the set of values that can fill the hole in the format, here the \(10^5\) pins, and \(|\mathcal R|\) for their number. The canary’s value, written \(\hat r\), is drawn uniformly from \(\mathcal R\), and the line is inserted \(k\) times. Before seeing the model, an attacker faces all \(|\mathcal R|\) candidates, which is \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\) bits of search. After seeing it, the attacker faces only the canary’s rank, which is \(\log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r)\) bits. The exposure is the difference, the number of bits of search that the model saves the attacker: \[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r). \tag{13.4}\]
The rank lies between 1 and \(|\mathcal R|\), so the exposure lies between 0 and \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\). It reaches its maximum when the canary is the model’s top candidate. Each bit of exposure halves the number of guesses the attacker needs.
What makes exposure an audit tool is that you know how it behaves when nothing was memorized. Suppose the model does not depend on the canary’s value, for instance because the canary was never inserted. Then the model’s scores are fixed before the canary’s value is drawn, so a uniformly drawn value lands at a uniformly random position in their order. Pick a threshold of \(t\) bits. An exposure of at least \(t\) bits means a rank in the top fraction \(2^{-t}\) of the list. A canary that was never inserted lands there with probability at most that fraction: \[\Pr\big[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) \ge t\big] \le 2^{-t}. \tag{13.5}\] Ties among the scores do not break this bound, because a tie can only push the canary’s rank up, which lowers its exposure.
The same argument gives the average exposure of a canary that was never inserted. Its rank is uniform, and the average of \(\log_2\) of a uniform rank falls a little short of \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\). When no two candidates tie, the shortfall, which is the average exposure, tends to \(\log_2 e = 1.4427\) bits as the space grows, where \(e\) is the base of the natural logarithm. For the \(10^5\) pins of the example it is already 1.4426 bits.
A space of four candidates makes the null concrete. A canary that was never inserted has each of the four ranks with probability one quarter. Its exposure is then 2 bits at rank 1, 1 bit at rank 2, 0.415 bits at rank 3 and 0 at rank 4. So an exposure of at least 1 bit has probability one half, from the top two ranks. An exposure of 2 bits has probability one quarter, from rank 1 alone. In this example, the bound is exact at whole-number exposures.
The null distribution makes exposure a membership test. “Was this canary inserted?” is a membership question (Membership inference). Consider a test that says “inserted” when the exposure is at least \(t\) bits. Its false positive rate (FPR), the chance of saying “inserted” about a canary that was not, is at most \(2^{-t}\). Put another way, the chance that a canary never inserted would look at least this memorized is a p-value, and \(2^{-\text{exposure}}\) is an upper bound on it. Membership inference calibrates its tests with shadow models, extra models trained with and without a record. Exposure needs none, because the canary’s own randomness does the calibration.
Exposure is also guessing work saved. Before seeing the model, the attacker faces a canary with \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\) bits of min-entropy. After seeing it, an attacker who guesses in the model’s order needs only as many tries as the canary’s rank. Carlini et al. (2019) note that an exposure close to \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\) means the secret can actually be extracted. One way is a shortest-path search that finds the most likely pin digit by digit, without listing every pin.
For a large space, exposure must be estimated, because nobody can score every 9-digit number. The first estimator is sampling. Score \(m\) random candidates and count the share of them that score at least as high as the canary. That share estimates the canary’s rank as a fraction of the whole space. It cannot resolve exposures above \(\log_2 m\) bits, because a canary that beats all \(m\) sampled candidates only tells you that its rank fraction is below about \(1/m\). The second estimator is extrapolation. Fit a distribution to the sampled scores and read off how much of it lies beyond the canary’s score. Carlini et al. (2019) fit a skew-normal, a normal distribution with an extra parameter that lets one tail be heavier than the other. The fit is only as good as its tail, and the tail is exactly the part that sampling cannot reach.
In the example, the script estimates an order-3 canary’s exposure from 10,000 random pins. Counting is accurate there, because every exposure is well below 13.3 bits, the most that 10,000 samples can resolve. Fitting a plain normal distribution instead overestimates the exposure by up to 3 bits. The scores have a heavier right tail than a normal, so the fit puts too few pins above the canary, and the canary’s rank looks smaller than it is. This is why Carlini et al. (2019) fit a skewed distribution.
Ties can also hide memorization. In a context that the model has never seen, every count is 0, so smoothing gives every symbol the same probability, one over the alphabet size. All candidates then tie, so every rank is \(|\mathcal R|\) and every exposure is 0, whatever the model has learned elsewhere. On this corpus, the order-8 model without a canary gives every pin exactly the same probability after “my pin is”, so every pin there has exposure 0.
Canaries also test defences, by comparing two training runs that differ in one thing, such as training with and without deduplication. Under a differentially private algorithm (Part 3), an exposure near the null mean says the planted secrets were not memorized. Carlini et al. (2019) found that private training kept their canaries at the exposure of canaries never inserted. Measuring exposure before and after an unlearning method tests that method. Auditing differentially private training uses the same tool, with canaries designed to be as exposed as possible.
The example plants “my pin is 58745” and computes its exact exposure by scoring all \(10^5\) pins (Table 13.1). The jump from no copies to one copy depends on whether a digit of the canary sits in a context that only the canary’s copies fill. No background line contains s_, an s followed by a space, because every name ends in a vowel.

The orders differ in which digits get a context of their own. At order 2 the first digit’s context is a single space, which all 11,300 lines share. So one copy is one vote among thousands, and it moves the exposure by only 0.01 bits. At order 3 the first digit’s context is s_, which only the canary fills. One copy then makes that digit 11 times as likely as its rivals, a factor worth 3.46 bits. The exposure rises by 3.16 bits, a little less, because the rank also depends on how the other pins’ scores are spread. At order 4 the first two digits have contexts of their own, and the exposure rises by 6.22 bits, a little under twice 3.46. The remaining digits share their contexts with the background pins, and they move only as the copies outvote those pins.

The null also holds in the example, where every pin that was never inserted plays the part of an uninserted canary. At orders 2, 3 and 4 their mean exposure is 1.443 bits, against the 1.4426 bits predicted for \(10^5\) candidates. A fraction \(1/32 = 2^{-5}\) of them has an exposure of at least 5 bits, exactly on the bound.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.6 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
text:
13.6 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
The attacker in the definitions section held the training prefix, but a real attacker has only the model. Carlini et al. (2021) showed how such an attacker extracts training data from GPT-2. It generates many samples, ranks them by how likely each is to be memorized, and checks the top of the ranking against public sources. The hard step is the ranking.
A model can find a string likely for two different reasons. The string may be ordinary, the kind of text any model of the language finds likely. Or the model may have memorized it from its training set. Only the second is a leak, so ranking is a test between two explanations. To score them you need a model of each. A reference model, trained on data from the same source but not on the target’s training set, stands in for ordinary text. The target model itself stands in for memorization. Write \(p_\theta(x)\) for the target’s probability of a string \(x\), and \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) for the reference’s. The evidence for memorization is how much more likely the target finds the string than the reference does, which on a log scale is a difference: \[\Lambda(x) = \ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x). \tag{13.6}\]
This is the best possible ranking, by the Neyman–Pearson lemma of Hypothesis testing. Among all tests that flag the same fraction of ordinary strings, the test that thresholds the likelihood ratio flags the largest fraction of memorized ones. The reason is a budget argument. Flagging a string costs false positives in proportion to its reference probability and gains true positives in proportion to its target probability. For a fixed budget of false positives you catch the most by flagging the strings with the largest ratio first. Membership inference made the same move when it compared a record’s loss under the target with the loss that models trained without the record give it.
Ranking by the target’s likelihood alone is the same as treating the reference probability as constant, as if every string were equally common in advance. That assumption is wrong exactly for strings that any model finds likely, such as software licences, news boilerplate and number sequences. These are in the training data, but extracting them reveals nothing, and they are the strings that raw likelihood puts first. The reference model knows them too, so their ratio is close to 1 and they cancel in Equation 13.6.
The reference can be crude. Carlini et al. (2021) used a smaller model of the same family and the target’s own likelihood on the lowercased text. They also used the length of the text after compression with zlib, a general-purpose compressor. Each gives a different idea of ordinary text, and each catches strings that the others miss.
An attacker who checks the top 100 candidates by hand cares about precision, how many of those candidates are real training data. It does not care about recall, how many of all memorized strings it eventually finds. Flagging only a few strings keeps the FPR tiny. If most of the flagged strings are real training data, the attack catches members at that tiny FPR, which is the operating point that matters in membership inference too.
In the example, the attacker draws 20,000 lines from the order-6 model, starting each at the beginning of a line. To make the ranking realistic, the target’s training set also contains 50 public lines, repeated 100 times each, standing in for a published directory. The attacker’s reference model is trained on an independent contact list of 5,000 lines, generated the same way as the target’s background lines, which also contains the public lines. A generation counts as a hit if it is a private training line, one that is in the target’s training set and is not public.
Of the 20,000 samples, 14,852 are distinct. Among them are 197 private training lines and all 50 public lines. The samples contain no secret inserted fewer than 8 times. Above that the share climbs fast, to 11% at 8 copies, 86% at 16 and all of them at 32. With the prefix in hand, by contrast, 8% of the singletons and 65% of the lines seen twice come out at order 6 (Section 13.4). Without the prefix, a sample must first produce the right name before it can produce the pin, and only heavily repeated lines make their names likely enough. This attack extracts much less than is discoverable.
The ranking makes a large difference (Figure 13.4). Among the top 100 distinct generations by target likelihood, 45 are private training lines. Most of the rest are the public lines, which are the most likely strings the model knows because each was repeated 100 times. Ranked by Equation 13.6, 85 of the top 100 are private training lines, because the reference model also finds the public lines likely and cancels them.






Figure 13.4: Fraction of the top-ranked distinct generations that are private training lines (solid) or public lines (dashed), from 20,000 samples of an order-6 model trained with 50 public lines repeated 100 times. Ranking by likelihood puts the public lines first. Ranking by the likelihood ratio to a reference model trained on other data puts the private lines first.



Nasr et al. (2023) carried extraction to production language models. On closed models, whose training data are unknown, they counted matches against 9 terabytes of public web text as a lower bound.
The aligned chat model ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) rarely emitted training data in normal use. Alignment is a later training stage, and it had taught the model to answer as an assistant rather than continue documents. Their divergence attack asked it to repeat one word forever. The model eventually fell back to emitting text that looked like pretraining documents, and emitted about 150 times more training data than in normal use. About 200 US dollars of queries extracted over 10,000 unique memorized examples, including personal contact details. The attack follows this chapter’s structure. It generates with a prompt that escapes the aligned behaviour, verifies the output against a corpus, and estimates from what it found how much the model has memorized in total.
