Rules of thumb

Memorization is a rank: the secret placed above the strings it could have been.
Duplication is a vote in every context a string passes through, and the most contested context decides.
Larger models split contexts and give rare strings their own parameters, so they memorize more and from fewer copies.
Deduplicate first. It is cheap and helps, but not for singletons in a high-capacity model.
Report exposure, not just extraction, because it is graded and has a known null.
Rank generations against a reference model, never by raw likelihood.
An attacker without the prefix gets less than the discoverable rate suggests, but production attacks show that “less” can still be thousands of records.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.1 Why this matters
A phone keyboard learns from what its users type, and the raw text never leaves the phones. Instead, a server sends the current model to each phone. The phone computes the gradient of the loss on its own few examples and sends back only that gradient. The server averages the gradients of many phones and takes a training step. This is the setting of federated learning (FL), and it is often described as private because “the data stay on the device”. Later parts study FL itself. This chapter asks one question about it: what does a single client’s gradient reveal about the client’s data?
The answer is often everything. A gradient is not a summary chosen to hide the data. It holds one derivative of the loss for every parameter of the model, often millions of them, and many of those derivatives are simple functions of the input. This chapter reads the data back out in four ways, from an exact division to a search. It then asks how much the client gains by averaging the gradient over a batch, and the answer is much less than you might hope.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.2 The attacker and the experiments
The attacker in this chapter is the server. It is honest-but-curious in the sense of Threat models and privacy games, so it follows the protocol and only analyses what it receives. It sees each client’s own update, not just the final model, which is the strongest level of access in that chapter, the transcript. It also knows the architecture and every parameter of the model, since it chose them.
A client holds a batch of \(B\) labelled examples. Example number \(i\) in the batch has an input \(x_i\) and a label \(y_i\). The client’s training loss is the average of the losses on its examples. It sends the gradient of that average, which lists how fast the loss changes as each parameter changes (Optimization). The derivative of an average is the average of the derivatives, so the update is the average of the gradients of the single examples: \[g = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i, y_i). \tag{14.1}\] In this formula, \(\theta\) stands for all the parameters of the model, and \(\ell(\theta; x_i, y_i)\) is the loss on example \(i\).
All the experiments use \(8\times8\) grey-scale images of four shapes: a horizontal bar, a vertical bar, a diagonal and a square outline. Each image is shifted at random and has pixel noise. The network has one hidden layer. A fully connected layer turns the 64 pixels into one number per hidden unit, and an activation function is applied to each unit. It is either the ReLU, which passes positive values and replaces negative ones by 0, or the sigmoid, which squashes every value smoothly into the range from 0 to 1. A second fully connected layer turns the hidden units into one score per class, called a logit.
The softmax turns the logits into probabilities that are all positive and add up to 1. The loss is the cross-entropy, minus the log of the probability the model gives to the true label. The network has 32 hidden units and sits at its random initialization, as in the first round of training. Counting the weights and biases of both layers, it has 2,212 parameters, so the gradient has 2,212 entries.
The attack plays the reconstruction game of Threat models and privacy games on one client. A challenger draws the batch from the population and keeps the inputs secret, and the attacker sees the model and the update \(g\). It outputs one reconstruction per example, scored by its relative error, the length of the mistake as a fraction of the length of the input. An error of 0 is a perfect reconstruction, and an error of 1 is a mistake as large as the image itself. Each true example is matched to its closest reconstruction, because an average does not change when the examples are reordered, so the gradient keeps no record of their order. The baseline is a guess from the population alone, such as the average image of a shape.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.3 Three facts about gradients
Every attack in this chapter rests on three facts about how a gradient is computed. The first explains why a gradient contains the input at all.
A fully connected layer gives one output per unit. Each unit multiplies every input by a weight of its own, adds up the products and adds a bias. Write \(a_j\) for the output of unit number \(j\). The weight that this unit gives to the input \(x_k\) is written \(W_{jk}\). So a small change in the weight \(W_{jk}\) changes \(a_j\) by \(x_k\) times that change. How much that moves the loss depends on everything after the layer. The rate at which the loss responds to \(a_j\) is called the backward signal \(\delta_j\) of unit \(j\).
The chain rule multiplies the two rates, so the loss changes with the weight \(W_{jk}\) at the rate \(\delta_jx_k\). The bias is added to \(a_j\) directly, so the loss changes with it at the rate \(\delta_j\) alone. Collected into a matrix with the shape of the weights \(W\) and a vector with the shape of the biases \(b\), these rates are \[\nabla_W\ell = \delta\,x^\top, \qquad \nabla_b\ell = \delta. \tag{14.2}\] A matrix built this way, with the product \(\delta_jx_k\) in row \(j\) and column \(k\), is called the outer product of the two vectors. Its row \(j\) is the input \(x\) multiplied by the single number \(\delta_j\). The backward signals depend on everything after the layer, including the loss and the label, but the input depends on none of it. So whatever the rest of the network does, it can only rescale the rows of the weight gradient, and the layer’s input sits in every row.
The second fact concerns the last layer, where the softmax turns the logits into probabilities and the cross-entropy scores them. Write \(z\) for the vector of logits and \(p\) for the vector of predicted probabilities. Write \(e_y\) for the one-hot vector of the label \(y\), which has a 1 at the label’s position and 0 elsewhere. The backward signal at the logits is the difference of the two: \[\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z} = p - e_y. \tag{14.3}\] The softmax never gives a probability of exactly 0 or 1, because it is built from exponentials, which are always positive. So the entry at the true label, \(p_y - 1\), is negative, and every other entry is a positive probability. This sign pattern is what label recovery uses.
The third fact gives the backward signals of the first layer. Write \(\delta_2\) for the vector of backward signals at the logits, which the second fact says is \(p - e_y\), and \(\delta_1\) for the vector of backward signals of the hidden units. Backpropagation computes \(\delta_1\) from \(\delta_2\). Each hidden unit feeds every logit through a weight of the second layer, so it collects the logits’ signals weighted by those connections. It then multiplies by the slope of the activation function \(\sigma\) at that unit: \[\delta_1 = (W_2^\top\delta_2)\odot\sigma'(a). \tag{14.4}\] Here \(W_2\) is the weight matrix of the second layer, and \(\sigma'(a)\) holds the slope of the activation at each hidden unit. The symbol \(\odot\) multiplies two vectors entry by entry.
For the ReLU the slope is 1 if the unit is switched on and 0 if it is switched off. So a unit that is switched off on an input has a backward signal of 0, and by the first fact its row of the weight gradient is all zeros.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.4 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
text:
14.4 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
Is there any computation, short of a search, that gives back the client’s input from its gradient? For the most common first layer of all, a fully connected layer with a bias, there is one division. The observation goes back at least to Phong et al. (2018), who made it for this federated setting.
Suppose the client sends the gradient of a single example, and the first layer is fully connected with a bias. Write \(\delta_{1,j}\) for the backward signal of hidden unit \(j\). By the first fact, row \(j\) of the weight gradient is the input scaled by \(\delta_{1,j}\), and entry \(j\) of the bias gradient is that same number. Dividing the row by the bias entry cancels the scale and leaves the input. This works for every unit whose bias gradient is not zero: \[x = \frac{(\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j}. \tag{14.5}\] The top of the fraction is row \(j\) of the first layer’s weight gradient, and the bottom is entry \(j\) of its bias gradient. Since every row is a multiple of the same vector, the weight gradient also has rank one: all its rows lie on a single line, the line through \(x\).
The depth of the network, the activations above, the loss and the label all sit inside the number \(\delta_{1,j}\), and that number cancels. So a network with twenty layers above the first one and a custom loss leaks its input in exactly the same way. The attack needs no optimization, no prior knowledge of what the data look like and no knowledge of the label. It also checks itself, because every usable unit must give the same answer, so ratios that agree tell the attacker it has the input. Applied at a deeper fully connected layer, the same division gives that layer’s input, an intermediate feature vector.
Table 14.1 works through a network small enough to compute by hand. It has three inputs, two ReLU units and two classes. Its first layer has weights \(W_1\) and bias \(b_1\), and its second layer has weights \(W_2\): \[W_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0.4 & -0.2 & 0.1\\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.4\end{pmatrix},\quad b_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0.1\\ -0.1\end{pmatrix},\quad W_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ 0.5 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}. \tag{14.6}\] The second layer has no bias. The example is \(x = (0.5, 1, 0.2)\), and its label is the first class. In the table, \(h\) is the vector of hidden values after the ReLU.

The server sees only the gradients, whose two rows are visibly the same vector at two scales, and each division gives back the input. Middle: the weight gradient, one row per hidden unit and one column per pixel (blue positive, red negative), next to the bias gradient. Every nonzero row is the image times the matching bias entry, and switched-off units give zero rows. Right: one row divided by its bias entry, which is the input exactly.



Two things weaken the division without stopping it. With the ReLU, a unit switched off on \(x\) has a backward signal of 0 and gives nothing. But a single active unit is enough, and a random network almost always has one. Without a bias there is no denominator. Every row still points along \(x\), though, so \(x\) is known up to one number, and a one-dimensional search finds it.
What stops the division is a convolutional first layer. A convolution applies the same small filter to every patch of the image, the small square of pixels under the filter at one position. The filter’s weights are used at every position, so their gradient adds up one outer product per patch, and no division separates the sum. That is why images fed to convolutional networks need the search of Section 14.6. A batch of several examples also turns the gradient into a sum, which defeats the division for some examples but not all (Section 14.7).

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.5 Label recovery from the last layer
text:
14.5 Label recovery from the last layer
The gradient depends on the label too, and the label is often the most sensitive part of an example, such as a diagnosis. Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen (2020) noticed that the label can be read off the last layer without any search. The rules below need a last layer that uses the softmax with the cross-entropy loss, and each comes from the sign pattern of the second fact.
The first rule needs a bias in the last layer, and works on a single example. By the first fact, the last layer’s bias gradient equals the backward signal at the logits, which the second fact says is \(p - e_y\). Every entry is a positive probability except the one at the true label, where subtracting 1 makes it negative. So the label is the position of the smallest entry, the only negative one: \[y = \arg\min_k(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.7}\]
The second rule reads the last layer’s weight gradient instead. By the first fact, its row \(k\) is entry \(k\) of the backward signal times the vector \(h\) of hidden values. If those values cannot be negative and are not all zero, as for the ReLU and the sigmoid, the multiplication keeps the sign of the backward signal. So the row of the true label is the only one with no positive entries, and the only one with a negative sum. An activation that can be negative, such as tanh, can flip the signs, and then this rule as stated fails.
For one example, both rules make no errors as long as their conditions hold. The model’s quality does not matter, because the sign argument holds at any point of training. On 1,000 random images and random networks, both rules named the label correctly every time. The one weakness is floating point. A confident model gives the true label only a tiny negative entry, and if \(p_y\) rounds to exactly 1, the sign is lost. That is one reason these attacks are run on models early in training.
A batch hides which example has which label, but not how many examples there are of each class. Its last-layer bias gradient is the average of the vectors \(p_i - e_{y_i}\), one per example. The one-hot parts add up to the label histogram, whose entry \(n_k\) is the number of examples of class \(k\). The probability parts add up to the model’s total predicted probability for each class. Write \(p_{ik}\) for the probability the model gives class \(k\) on example \(i\). Multiplying the bias gradient by \(B\) and solving for the histogram gives \[n_k = \sum_{i=1}^Bp_{ik} - B\,(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.8}\]
The server knows the bias gradient and \(B\), so the only thing it lacks is the total predicted probability for each class. It can estimate that total well, because it knows the model. It runs the model on data of its own from the same population, averages the predictions and multiplies by \(B\). The true counts are integers, so rounding gives them exactly whenever every estimate is off by less than one half. A cruder guess assumes that the model spreads its predictions evenly over the \(K\) classes. It does worse, because even an untrained network is not uniform.
Table 14.2 reads the counts of one batch of 16 images off the bias gradient of the 32-unit ReLU network. Here there are \(K = 4\) classes, and the true counts are \((4, 2, 4, 6)\).

With the averaged guess, every estimate is within one half of the truth, so rounding fixes it. With the uniform guess, the first class is off by 1.88, and rounding cannot help. Figure 14.2 shows the same comparison on another batch of 16.






Figure 14.2: Labels from the last-layer bias gradient. Left: for one example, the bias gradient has a single negative entry, at the true label (red). Right: for a batch of 16, the counts estimated with the model’s average prediction on the attacker’s own images (green) are close to the true counts (grey). With a uniform guess (orange) they are further off, by up to about half an example, which is enough for rounding to miss one class.



Larger batches make rounding miss more often. Over 200 random batches and networks per batch size, the averaged guess got every count exact in all batches of 4. That share was 0.975 for batches of 16 and 0.525 for batches of 64. The uniform guess got 0.925 of batches of 4 right, but only 0.095 of batches of 16. The error of the estimate is a sum of \(B\) deviations, one per example. They do not cancel exactly, so the chance that some class is off by more than one half grows with \(B\). With the averaged guess, even inexact counts stay close.
Knowing the labels also helps the search of the next section. In its original form (Zhu et al. 2019), that search looked for the input together with a soft label, a probability vector standing in for the unknown label. This joint search often failed. With the labels fixed, the search runs over the input only.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.6 Deep Leakage from Gradients
The division of Section 14.4 needs a fully connected layer with a bias. Most image models start with convolutions, and many architectures have normalization layers, attention, or no biases at all. Zhu, Liu & Han (2019) gave a general attack that needs none of these, called Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG). It guesses an input, computes the gradient that input would produce, and moves the guess until that gradient matches the one observed.
To search for a match, the attack needs one number that says how badly a guess matches. DLG uses the matching loss, written \(R\). It is the squared distance between the gradient that the guessed batch would produce and the observed update \(g\), summed over every entry of the gradient. The labels come from Section 14.5. For a batch that section gives only the counts. But the gradient ignores the order of the examples, so the attacker can hand those labels to the guesses in any order. DLG then looks for the guesses \(x'_1, \dots, x'_B\) that make \(R\) smallest: \[\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_B = \arg\min_{x_1', \dots, x_B'}R(x'), \qquad R(x') = \Big\lVert\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i) - g\Big\rVert^2. \tag{14.9}\] It starts from random noise and repeatedly moves the guess a little downhill on \(R\), as gradient descent does. A squared distance is never negative, and the true batch reproduces the observed gradient exactly, so the true batch has \(R = 0\), the smallest possible value.
Moving downhill needs the slope of \(R\) with respect to the guess. The matching loss is built from gradients of the network, so its slope is made of second derivatives. Automatic-differentiation libraries compute it by running backpropagation through the backward pass itself, which is called double backpropagation.
Second derivatives are also why Zhu et al. replaced the ReLU by the sigmoid, and the experiments here do the same. The ReLU’s slope is 0 or 1, constant on each side of zero. So the factor \(\sigma'(a)\) in Equation 14.4 does not change as the guess moves, and the search gets no signal through it. The sigmoid’s slope varies smoothly.
The search has no guarantee of finding the input, because \(R\) is not convex. As Optimization explains, a gradient method on such a function can stop at a stationary point, where the surface is flat but which need not be the true minimum. The final value of \(R\) tells the attacker which case it is in. A loss that reaches rounding error means an exact match. A loss that has stopped falling above that means the search is stuck, and the remedy is a restart from a new random guess.
A match is the input only if no other input produces the same gradient. That is plausible when the equations outnumber the unknowns, and matching the gradient gives one equation per parameter, 2,212 here, against 64 unknown pixels per image. Section 14.4 proves it in one case, a single example and a fully connected first layer with a bias, where the gradient determines the input.
DLG is a general recipe, since any automatic-differentiation library can differentiate the gradient with respect to the input. So it works for convolutional networks and on real images, where no closed form exists. Zhu et al. recover pictures from the CIFAR-100 image dataset and tokens of text from the gradients of single examples. A failed run is an optimization failure, not a lack of information, and the attacker can retry with restarts, better optimizers or knowledge of what images look like. Geiping et al. (2020) compared gradients by direction only and penalized differences between neighbouring pixels. With these changes they recover recognizable images from trained networks and from batches.
Table 14.3 follows one run on one image, with the sigmoid network of 32 hidden units. The run starts from uniform noise and takes 600 steps of the Adam optimizer. Adam is a variant of gradient descent that scales each pixel’s step to the size of that pixel’s recent gradients.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.7 Batches and averaging
Clients rarely send the gradient of one example. They send the average over a batch, or the change in the parameters after several local training steps. Averaging is often said to protect the individual examples, because the gradient now describes the batch and not anyone in it. Averaging does break the division of Equation 14.5, and it does make DLG harder, but much of the structure survives.
Take a batch of \(B\) examples and a fully connected first layer, and write \(\delta_{1,i}\) for the first-layer backward signal of example \(i\). The batch gradient is the average of the per-example gradients, and by the first fact each of those is an outer product. Each outer product has rows that are multiples of its own input. So every row of the average is a weighted combination of the \(B\) inputs, and it lies in their span, the set of all such combinations. Adding \(B\) matrices of rank one also gives a matrix of rank at most \(B\): \[\nabla_{W_1}\ell = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\delta_{1,i}\,x_i^\top, \qquad \operatorname{rank}\nabla_{W_1}\ell \le B. \tag{14.10}\]
The span leaks even when nothing else does. From the rows of the gradient, the server learns a set of at most \(B\) directions that every example is built from. When \(B\) is much smaller than the number of pixels, that already rules out almost every input. A further search, such as DLG, then has only \(B\) unknowns per example instead of one per pixel.
The division of Equation 14.5 now gives a weighted average. Row \(j\) of the weight gradient is a sum of different inputs with different scales, and entry \(j\) of the bias gradient is the sum of those scales. Dividing gives each input a weight equal to its share of the total. The result equals one input exactly when only that example contributes to unit \(j\). For the ReLU, that happens when unit \(j\) is switched on for that example and off for every other example of the batch. The unit then isolates the example, and the division recovers it exactly.
How often is an example isolated? The simplest model assumes that each ReLU unit switches on for each example independently with probability one half, like a fair coin. Under that assumption, one unit isolates a given example with probability \(2^{-B}\), the chance of one particular pattern of \(B\) coin flips. The example is missed only if every unit misses it. Write \(m\) for the number of hidden units. If the units are also independent of each other, each example is recovered exactly with probability \[P_{\text{iso}}(B, m) = 1 - (1 - 2^{-B})^m. \tag{14.11}\]
The coin-flip model is exact for a single unit when the first-layer bias is zero and the inputs are independent and symmetric about zero, like Gaussian noise. Across units it is only approximate, because different units look at the same inputs. Real images are not symmetric, and images of the same kind are correlated, which matters a great deal, as the experiments below show.
The formula falls exponentially with the batch size and rises with the number of units. Among \(m\) units, on average \(m2^{-B}\) isolate a given example, so the formula is near 1 when that number is large and near 0 when it is small. Under the coin-flip model, an even chance of isolating each example of a batch of 10 needs 710 units. Real first layers have thousands of units, so batches of 10 are not safe from this attack.
Singular values make this structure visible. They measure how much of a matrix lies along each of its independent directions, so the number that are not zero is the rank. Take a batch of 4 images through the 32-unit ReLU network. Its first-layer gradient has four nonzero singular values, so its rank is four. Every row lies in the span of the four images, up to rounding error. The unit ratios recover all four images exactly, while Equation 14.11 predicts 0.873 per example. Table 14.4 tests the formula more widely, with 20 random networks and batches for each row.

For Gaussian inputs the formula matches to within the noise of the simulation. It slightly overestimates the recovered fraction in seven of the eight rows, because units that share inputs are not fully independent. For images, however, the formula is far too optimistic about privacy at large batches. In the largest network and a batch of 16, it predicts that 1.6% of the batch is exposed, but in fact 69.1% is (Figure 14.4).
Correlated data are easier for the attacker, not harder. With images, a unit tends to fire on many examples of a batch or on few. So the number of examples it fires for is more spread out than coin flips would make it. Statisticians call this overdispersion. It makes units that fire on just one example much more common at large batch sizes, and isolation decays much more slowly than the formula says. It cuts both ways, though. At small batches it makes “on for all” and “on for none” common, and such units isolate nothing. That is why, in a batch of 4, the smallest network recovers fewer images than the formula predicts, 0.838 against 0.984.

Every single image is recovered to rounding error, and so are most examples in batches of two. From a batch of 4, the median run gets stuck. Its matching loss stalls near \(10^{-5}\), far above that of a successful run, and the reconstructions are blends of the batch (Figure 14.5). Averaging has made the search harder, not the information smaller. The gradient still supplies 2,212 equations, against only 256 unknown pixels in a batch of four. And on a ReLU network of the same width, the isolation attack recovered all four images of such a batch.

Left: relative error of the closest reconstruction for every example (dots) and the median (red), on a log scale; the dotted line marks an error of 0.05. Sending the parameter change after several local steps does not protect a single example either. Every step’s first-layer gradient is an outer product with the same input, and only the backward signal changes from step to step. So every row of the total change in the first-layer weights is still a multiple of \(x\), and Equation 14.5 still recovers \(x\) exactly.
Everything so far assumes an honest server that sends random weights. A malicious server that chooses the weights does better still. It can plant first-layer units that fire on rare inputs only, which Boenisch et al. (2023) call trap weights. Or it can add units that sort inputs into narrow bins by a feature such as brightness, so that few examples share a bin (Fowl et al. 2022). Either way, most examples of even a large batch are isolated by design.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.8 Code
The snippet below runs the hand example of Section 14.4, the label rule of Section 14.5 and the isolation formula, in plain Python. It indexes classes from 0, so label 0 is the first class.
from math import ceil, exp, log

Vector = list[float]
Matrix = list[Vector]


def client_gradient(w1: Matrix, b1: Vector, w2: Matrix, x: Vector, y: int) -> tuple[Matrix, Vector, Vector]:
    """What a client sends for one example: the gradients of W1, b1 and b2 (one ReLU layer, softmax, cross-entropy)."""
    a = [sum(wk * xk for wk, xk in zip(row, x)) + bj for row, bj in zip(w1, b1)]
    h = [max(aj, 0.0) for aj in a]
    z = [sum(wk * hk for wk, hk in zip(row, h)) for row in w2]
    total = sum(exp(zk) for zk in z)
    delta2 = [exp(zk) / total - (1.0 if k == y else 0.0) for k, zk in enumerate(z)]  # p - e_y
    delta1 = [sum(delta2[k] * w2[k][j] for k in range(len(w2))) * (1.0 if a[j] > 0 else 0.0) for j in range(len(a))]
    grad_w1 = [[dj * xk for xk in x] for dj in delta1]  # outer product delta1 x^T
    return grad_w1, delta1, delta2  # the bias gradients equal the backward signals


def recover_input(grad_w1: Matrix, grad_b1: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Exact recovery: a row of the weight gradient divided by its bias entry."""
    j = next(j for j, g in enumerate(grad_b1) if g != 0.0)
    return [g / grad_b1[j] for g in grad_w1[j]]


def recover_label(grad_b2: Vector) -> int:
    """The only negative entry of the last-layer bias gradient is the label."""
    return min(range(len(grad_b2)), key=lambda k: grad_b2[k])


def isolation(batch: int, units: int) -> float:
    """Chance that some ReLU unit fires for one given example of the batch only, under the coin-flip model."""
    return 1 - (1 - 2.0**-batch) ** units


def width_for_even_odds(batch: int) -> int:
    """Smallest number of units that isolates each example with probability at least 1/2."""
    return ceil(log(2) / -log(1 - 2.0**-batch))


w1 = [[0.4, -0.2, 0.1], [0.3, 0.5, -0.4]]
b1 = [0.1, -0.1]
w2 = [[1.0, -1.0], [0.5, 0.5]]
gw1, gb1, gb2 = client_gradient(w1, b1, w2, x=[0.5, 1.0, 0.2], y=0)
print([round(v, 4) for v in recover_input(gw1, gb1)])  # [0.5, 1.0, 0.2]
print([round(v, 4) for v in gb2], recover_label(gb2))  # [-0.6559, 0.6559] 0
print(f"{isolation(4, 32):.3f}")  # 0.873
print(width_for_even_odds(10))  # 710
The full edition’s script runs every attack in this chapter on the image network, including DLG with a hand-written double backpropagation, in about half a minute:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/gradient_inversion.py

Rules of thumb

A gradient is a sum of outer products of backward signals with forward inputs. Any layer whose input you can isolate, you can read.
When there is no closed form, match gradients. The final matching loss tells you whether the match worked.
Batching and local steps help against search but not against structure. The label histogram and the span of the batch leak, and every example isolated by a single unit leaks exactly.
An honest server can already do all of this. A malicious server that chooses the weights can do it for large batches by design.

14.10 Further reading

Zhu, Liu & Han, “Deep Leakage from Gradients” (NeurIPS 2019): the gradient-matching attack, with reconstructions of images and text.
Geiping, Bauermeister, Dröge & Moeller, “Inverting Gradients — How easy is it to break privacy in federated learning?” (NeurIPS 2020): cosine matching with an image prior, and attacks on trained networks, local steps and batches.
Huang, Gupta, Song, Li & Arora, “Evaluating Gradient Inversion Attacks and Defenses in Federated Learning” (NeurIPS 2021): how attack strength depends on assumptions such as known labels and untrained models. Read it before trusting a published attack number.
Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen, “iDLG: Improved Deep Leakage from Gradients” (arXiv 2020): label recovery from the sign of the last-layer gradient, and the search with the label fixed.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter, except the published attacks it only cites: the reconstructions of Zhu et al. on real images and text, the improvements of Geiping et al., and the malicious-server attacks of Boenisch et al. and Fowl et al. Four results are worked out in the full edition’s exercises rather than its text: the search for the scale when the first layer has no bias, the condition under which rounding gives the exact label counts, overdispersion, and several local steps.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.1 Why this matters
A hospital wants to share its discharge records with researchers. It deletes the names, the addresses and the insurance numbers. It keeps what the research needs, which is the postcode, the date of birth, the sex and the diagnosis. Nobody’s name is in the file. Is anyone in it identifiable?
Usually, yes. Most people are the only person with their combination of postcode, birth date and sex. Anyone who holds a second table with names and those same three columns, such as a voter roll, can join the two tables on them. The join puts a name back on most rows. This is a linkage attack, and putting a name back on a “de-identified” record is re-identification. The attack needs no model and no queries, only the release and some auxiliary data about the people in it. The other chapters of this part attack trained models, while this one attacks the data itself. This chapter explains why removing names was never the same as anonymizing.
The idea that runs through the chapter is that identifying information can be measured in bits, and that bits add up. Write \(n\) for the number of people in a population. Picking one of them takes \(\log_2 n\) bits of information, because each bit can halve the number of candidates and you have to halve \(n\) down to 1. Singling out one of the 248.7 million people counted in the United States in 1990 takes 27.9 bits. For the world’s 8 billion people it takes 32.9 bits.
Each attribute you learn about someone carries bits too. An attribute with \(v\) equally likely values carries \(\log_2 v\) bits, so a person’s sex carries 1 bit. A birth date is one of about 29,200 days in 80 years, worth about 14.8 bits. When attributes are independent, their bits add. The reason is that the chance of a combination of values is then the product of the chances of each value, and a logarithm turns that product into a sum. For correlated attributes the sum overstates the bits, as a later section explains.
Once the bits that an adversary knows exceed \(\log_2 n\) by a few, almost everyone is unique. The rest of the chapter makes that sentence precise. It does so for tidy tables, for sparse data such as movie ratings, and for releases that contain only a sample of the population.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.2 Quasi-identifiers and the linkage attack
Data protection practice sorts the columns of a table into three kinds. Direct identifiers name a person on their own, like a name, a social security number or an email address. Sensitive attributes are what the release is about and what must not be tied to a person, such as a diagnosis or a salary. Quasi-identifiers are the columns in between. None of them names anyone alone, but in combination they often single out one person, and they also appear in other datasets next to names.
ZIP code, birth date and sex are the classic example of quasi-identifiers. The most common form of “de-identification” removes the direct identifiers and keeps the quasi-identifiers, and the linkage attack is aimed at exactly that gap.
Threat models scores an attack with a game, in which a challenger sets a task and the adversary wins or loses. In this section, \(n\) is the number of records in the release, one per person. In the linkage game, the challenger draws a target uniformly at random from those records and gives the adversary the target’s quasi-identifiers. The adversary wins if it outputs the target’s record.
Because the target is drawn from the release, the adversary knows that the target is in it. The result below needs this condition. It fits a curious neighbour, or an insurer with a list of patients, who knows that a particular person was treated at the hospital. Without it, a unique match may belong to someone who shares the target’s quasi-identifiers but is not in the release. The last section of this chapter asks how much that uncertainty protects anyone.
Group the records of the release into equivalence classes, the sets of records with identical quasi-identifiers. Write \(J\) for the number of classes, which is the number of distinct combinations in the release. A target alone in its class is found for sure. A target in a class of \(k\) records is found one time in \(k\), because the adversary can only pick one of the look-alikes at random. Now think of the whole class. The target lands in it \(k\) times as often as in a class of one record, but the adversary is right only one time in \(k\) when it does. So each class adds one record’s worth of wins whatever its size, and averaging over the target gives the success probability \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n}. \tag{15.1}\]
No adversary that sees only the quasi-identifiers can do better than this. Within a class, the records differ only in their sensitive attribute, which the adversary does not know, so the target is equally likely to be any of them. Every guess inside the class therefore wins with the same chance, and a guess outside it never wins.

Join the hospital release in Table 15.1 with the voter roll in Table 15.2 on the three shared columns. Ana, Carla and Dan each match exactly one record, so their diagnoses come out with certainty. Ben matches two records, so the adversary gets diabetes or hypertension and is right half the time. The game, though, draws its target from every record of the release, including the women born on 1990-01-01, who would appear on a fuller voter roll. Ana’s, Carla’s and Dan’s records each form a class of one, and Ben’s record and its look-alike form a class of two. The three women form a fifth class. With 5 classes among 8 records, Equation 15.1 gives a success of \(5/8 = 0.625\).
This is, in miniature, how the computer scientist Latanya Sweeney re-identified the governor of Massachusetts in the late 1990s. The state had released the hospital records of its employees and their families without names. On the Cambridge voter roll, which Sweeney bought for twenty dollars, six people shared the governor’s birth date, and three of them were men. Only one of those lived in his ZIP code.
Sweeney also measured how common such uniqueness is. From the 1990 census tables, she estimated that 87% of the US population was likely unique on ZIP code, birth date and sex. The figure was 53% with the city in place of the ZIP code, and 18% with the county.
For this adversary, uniqueness is the whole story. Each unique record is a certain win, and no class adds more than one win. So the fraction of unique records is a lower bound on the success, which is why the next section is about predicting uniqueness. The formula also shows what a defence would have to do. If every class holds at least \(k\) records, there are at most \(n/k\) classes, and the success is at most \(1/k\). That guarantee holds against this adversary only. If all the records of a class share one diagnosis, the adversary learns the diagnosis without knowing which record is the target’s. Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks studies such releases and the attacks they leave open.
Now count the bits of Sweeney’s three attributes, treating each one as uniform over its values (Figure 15.1). This gives an upper bound, because an attribute carries the most bits when its values are equally likely. There are about 40,000 ZIP codes, which are worth 15.3 bits. With the birth date’s 14.8 bits and the 1 bit of sex, the three attributes carry at most 31.1 bits. That is more than the 27.9 bits above that single out one American.






Figure 15.1: The three classic quasi-identifiers, in bits, against the bits needed to single out one person in the US population of 1990 and in the world population. The bits are upper bounds that treat each attribute as uniform over its values.



There are about 2.34 billion combinations of ZIP code, birth date and sex, which leaves about 0.106 people per combination. Suppose everyone fell into a combination at random, all of them equally likely. A person then has a combination to themselves with probability about \(e^{-0.106} = 0.899\), as the next section explains. Sweeney’s 87% is a little lower because people are not spread evenly. ZIP codes range from a few residents to tens of thousands, and birth years are not equally common, so people crowd into the popular combinations. A later study, Golle (2006), redid the estimate with the next census and found 63%.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
section: 15.3 How many people are unique? A birthday calculation
text:
15.3 How many people are unique? A birthday calculation
You can count the unique records of a release you hold, but only because you hold the data. As at the start of the chapter, write \(n\) for the number of people in the population. A count says nothing about a release you have not made yet, or about a different choice of columns, and a model of the population answers both questions. Call a person’s combination of attribute values their cell. Number the cells, and write \(p_c\) for the probability that a person falls in cell \(c\). The model says that each person falls in a cell independently of everyone else.
The question is the birthday problem of Cryptography basics asked the other way round. The birthday problem asks whether any two people share a birthday, while here you ask how many people share their cell with nobody. Write \(U\) for that number, the number of unique people. Its average is the sum of each person’s chance of being unique, because the average of a sum is the sum of the averages. This rule, linearity of expectation, holds even though one person’s uniqueness changes the chance that another is unique.
So take one person in cell \(c\). That person is unique when each of the other \(n - 1\) people lands outside cell \(c\). Each of them does so with probability \(1 - p_c\). Because people fall in cells independently, these chances multiply, and all of the others avoid the cell with probability \((1 - p_c)^{n-1}\). Without independence the product would no longer give that chance. Averaging over the person’s own cell, which is \(c\) with probability \(p_c\), gives the expected fraction of unique people, \[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} = \sum_c p_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}. \tag{15.2}\]
The formula turns into the bits picture when all cells are equally likely. Write \(M\) for the number of cells. Every term then has \(p_c = 1/M\), so the fraction unique is \((1 - 1/M)^{n-1}\). For \(M\) in the thousands or more, this is very close to \(e^{-n/M}\), where \(n/M\) is the average number of people in a cell. Now count the cells in bits, writing \(b\) for the number of bits, so that \(M = 2^b\). Since \(n = 2^{\log_2 n}\), the average occupancy is \(2^{\log_2 n}/2^b = 2^{\log_2 n - b}\), and \[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} \approx \exp\big(-2^{\log_2 n - b}\big). \tag{15.3}\]
This fraction depends only on \(b - \log_2 n\), the bits beyond those needed to name one person. The curve is therefore the same for a town and for the planet, as the right panel of Figure 15.2, further down, shows. It is also steep, because each extra bit halves the average occupancy. Solving the formula for the bits that give a chosen fraction, half the people are unique at only 0.53 bits beyond \(\log_2 n\). Ninety per cent are unique at 3.25 bits beyond it, and 99% at 6.64 bits.
This corrects a popular rule. The claim that “33 bits identify anyone” rests on 33 bits being just above the bits that single out one of 8 billion people. With \(2^{33}\) equally likely cells, the average cell then holds 0.93 people. Only a fraction 0.394 of people are unique. Thirty-three bits are enough to give everyone a distinct label, but labels drawn at random collide often, and for 99% of the world to be unique you need 39.5 bits.
Real attributes are skewed, and skew usually lowers uniqueness. When a few values are common, such as a big city or a common occupation, many people crowd into a few cells and are not unique. The rare cells that could have held a unique person mostly stay empty. This is a tendency, not a theorem. Suppose there are far fewer cells than people. Spread evenly, every cell holds many people and nobody is unique. With skew, a few rare cells may hold a single person each, and those people are unique.
The exact formula needs the probability of every cell, and there can be billions of cells, but a floor on uniqueness needs much less. The collision probability \(\sum_c p_c^2\) is the chance that two people, drawn independently, land in the same cell. For any cell probabilities, \[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} \ge \Big(1 - \sum_c p_c^2\Big)^{n-1}. \tag{15.4}\]
The floor uses one number for everybody. Instead of the probability of each person’s own cell, it uses the average of that probability over people, which is the collision probability. As a function of a cell probability \(x\), the chance \((1 - x)^{n-1}\) bends upward, which is called being convex. Replacing the input of a convex function by its average can only lower the average output, which is Jensen’s inequality. The floor is exact when all cells are equally likely, since then there is nothing to average. It is loose when a few crowded cells hold most of the people, because they make the collision probability large even though the people in rare cells are still unique.
The floor is cheap to compute for independent attributes. Two people share a cell exactly when they agree on every attribute, and for independent attributes those agreements are independent events. The collision probability is then the product, over attributes, of each attribute’s own collision probability. So the floor needs only each attribute’s own frequencies, its marginals.
A third shortcut uses the entropy \(H\), the average number of bits that a person’s cell carries (Information theory). The entropy rule pretends that the real cells are \(2^H\) equally likely cells, and so predicts a fraction \(e^{-n2^{-H}}\) of unique people. It is a rule of thumb, not a bound, and the exact value can sit on either side of it. The collision floor never exceeds the entropy rule, apart from a difference between \(n\) and \(n - 1\) in the exponent. The reason is that the collision probability is never below \(2^{-H}\), which the full edition shows with Jensen’s inequality.
Correlated attributes need more than marginals. If age and number of children go together, the second attribute partly repeats the first, so a model that multiplies their frequencies overstates the bits. The prediction then needs a model of the joint distribution. Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye (2019) fit a Gaussian copula. This model keeps each attribute’s own frequencies and ties the attributes together through the correlations of a multivariate normal distribution. The last section of this chapter uses their results.
Equation 15.2 gives an expectation, which is an average over many imagined populations, but you have only one population. One population turns out to be enough. Moving a single person to another cell changes the number of unique people by at most 2, since only the cell they leave and the cell they join change. McDiarmid’s inequality (Concentration) says that a function of many independent inputs stays close to its average when no single input can move it by much. Here the inputs are the people’s cells, so it needs the same independence as before. For every positive distance \(t\), it gives \[\Pr\Big[\Big|\frac Un - \frac{\mathbb EU}{n}\Big| \ge t\Big] \le 2e^{-nt^2/2}. \tag{15.5}\]
Set the right side equal to a failure probability \(\beta\) and solve for \(t\). With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the fraction unique in your population is then within \(\sqrt{2\ln(2/\beta)/n}\) of its expectation. For 10,000 people and \(\beta = 0.05\), that distance is 0.0272. The bound is loose, because it charges every person the worst case, a change of 2 in \(U\), while most moves change it by 0 or 1.
The full edition’s script tests all of this on a synthetic census of 10,000 people. It reveals eight independent attributes, made up but shaped like real ones, one at a time. title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
section: 15.4 Sparse, high-dimensional data: the Netflix attack
text:
15.4 Sparse, high-dimensional data: the Netflix attack
In 2006, Netflix released about 100 million movie ratings for a public competition. They came from 480,189 subscribers, whose names were replaced by random numbers, and some ratings and dates were perturbed. Each record is a set of films with a rating and a date, 209 films on average out of 17,770. There are no quasi-identifier columns to join on, and what an adversary knows about a person (“she watched these films around these dates and liked them”) is partial and noisy.
Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) showed that none of this protects the subscribers. In sparse data, a handful of approximate facts about a person typically matches one record far better than any other. They matched some Netflix records to public reviews on the Internet Movie Database, which carry names or pseudonyms. This section explains why a score that favours rare items works, and when to trust its answer.
Since no record will match exactly, the attack scores how well each record agrees with what the adversary knows. Write \(\mathrm{aux}\) for the adversary’s auxiliary information, a few items \(i\), such as films, each with an approximate value \(\mathrm{aux}_i\), such as a rating.
For a record \(r\), write \(r_i\) for its value on item \(i\). The agreement \(\mathrm{Sim}(\mathrm{aux}_i, r_i)\) is 1 if the record rated item \(i\) within one star of \(\mathrm{aux}_i\), on Netflix’s scale of one to five stars, and 0 otherwise. The score adds up the agreements, each with a weight \(w_i\): \[\mathrm{Score}(\mathrm{aux}, r) = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{aux}} w_i\,\mathrm{Sim}(\mathrm{aux}_i, r_i). \tag{15.6}\]
The weights favour rare items. An agreement on a film that half the subscribers rated says little, while an agreement on an obscure film says a lot. Narayanan and Shmatikov used the weight \[w_i = \frac{1}{\ln\lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert}, \tag{15.7}\] where the support \(\lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert\) of item \(i\) is the number of records that rated it.
On Netflix, eight ratings identified 99% of records, even with 2 of them completely wrong. That held with dates known only to within 14 days. With dates known to within 3 days, two ratings were enough for 68% of records.
The weights can also be derived. For each record, the adversary weighs two explanations, “this record is the target” and “this record belongs to someone unrelated”. The standard way to weigh them is the likelihood ratio, the probability of what you observed under the first explanation divided by its probability under the second. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Hypothesis testing), thresholding it accepts the true target most often among all tests that wrongly accept an unrelated record equally often.
The ratio takes the form of Equation 15.6 under two assumptions. The first gives each item \(i\) a probability \(s_i\) that an unrelated record agrees on it. The target’s own record agrees with probability \(1 - \varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the chance that the auxiliary information about the item is wrong or stale.
The second assumption is that agreements on different items are independent, so the probability of a pattern of agreements is a product over items and its logarithm is a sum. Each disagreeing item adds a fixed amount to that sum, and an agreeing item swaps it for another. So the log of the ratio is a constant, the same for every record, plus a sum over the agreeing items with the weights \[w_i = \ln\frac{1 - s_i}{s_i} + \ln\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon} \approx \ln\frac{1}{s_i} + \ln\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}. \tag{15.8}\] The approximation uses \(1 - s_i \approx 1\), which holds for rare items. The first term rewards rarity, as the weight of Narayanan and Shmatikov does. The second term, the same for every item, is the evidence from agreeing at all.
The top-scoring record is also the best single guess. Suppose the target is one of the \(n\) records, each equally likely in advance. Suppose also that the records’ agreement patterns are independent once you know which record is the target. The probability of all the patterns together is then a product with one factor per record. Whichever record is the target, all the others contribute their “unrelated” factors, so the candidates differ only through their likelihood ratios \(\mathrm{LR}(t)\). Bayes’ rule then gives \[\Pr[\text{target} = t \mid \text{data}] = \frac{\mathrm{LR}(t)}{\sum_j\mathrm{LR}(j)}. \tag{15.9}\] The most probable record is therefore the one with the largest likelihood ratio, which is the one with the top score.
Rare items carry the attack because each one is worth many bits. A false match is an unrelated record that happens to agree on every item the adversary knows. Take the clean case, in which the auxiliary information is never wrong and exact agreement is required. Write \(I\) for the set of items the adversary knows. Since agreements on different items are independent, an unrelated record agrees on all of them with probability \(\prod_{i \in I} s_i\), so among \(n\) records the expected number of false matches is \[n\prod_{i\in I}s_i = 2^{\log_2n - \sum_{i\in I}\log_2(1/s_i)}. \tag{15.10}\] Each item contributes \(\log_2(1/s_i)\) bits, so the false matches vanish once the items’ bits exceed \(\log_2 n\), the same picture as for census tables. For example, a film that 1% of subscribers rated carries 6.64 bits. Three such films therefore carry 19.9 bits, just over the 18.9 bits needed to single out one Netflix subscriber.
Sparsity is the vulnerability. Most items are rated by few people, so each item in a record is worth many bits, and nobody’s record is close to anyone else’s. Noise in the auxiliary information costs little, because the score adds up evidence rather than demanding a perfect match. With one wrong item, the target loses one term of its score, while unrelated records rarely gain one. What decides success is whether the auxiliary information carries more bits than \(\log_2 n\), and the exact weights matter much less, as the experiment below shows.
The full edition checks this on a synthetic ratings matrix of 5,000 users and 4,000 items. Item popularity is very uneven, and the density of 0.0102 is close to Netflix’s 0.0118. The adversary knows a few items from the target’s record, with the rating off by one star half the time, which still counts as agreement. In the noisy setting, a quarter of the items are replaced by random items. The target has almost never rated these, because each user rates only a small share of the items.
Table 15.4 compares three weightings. The first gives every item the same weight, and the second is the Narayanan–Shmatikov weight. The third is the likelihood-ratio weight \(\ln(1/s_i)\), with \(s_i\) the fraction of the users who rated the item. With \(n\) users, that is the table’s \(\ln(n/\lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert)\). The script sets \(\varepsilon = \frac12\), which makes the constant term zero, so the weight reflects rarity alone.

Read the table with the bits in mind. An item carries a median of 5.83 bits. Singling out one of 5,000 users takes 12.29 bits. So two items carry about 11.7 bits, a little under what is needed, and they re-identify about 43% of targets. Four items carry about 23 bits and re-identify 93%. Because 5.83 is a median, half of the items carry fewer bits, so for some targets four items still fall short. Now make a quarter of the 8 items wrong. The rarity weightings still re-identify 98–99% of targets, close to what Narayanan and Shmatikov found on Netflix with a quarter of the ratings wrong. Equal weights fall to 94%, because a wrong popular item helps many unrelated records score. The two rarity weightings differ by less than two standard errors.






Figure 15.3: Left and centre: the scores of all 5,000 records for one target’s auxiliary information (8 items, 2 wrong), on a log scale. When the target is in the release its record stands far out; when it is not, the best score is the edge of the crowd. Right: re-identification rate against the number of auxiliary items, for three weightings, and for the likelihood-ratio weights when a quarter of the items, rounded down, are wrong.



The top score is the best guess only if the target is in the release. When it may not be, the adversary also has to decide whether to trust the guess. A real match should stand out, with a score well above the second-best one. The eccentricity test measures this gap in units of the spread of all the scores. Write \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) for the two largest scores, and \(\sigma\) for the standard deviation of all scores. The test declares a match only if the gap clears a threshold \(\varphi\), \[\frac{S_1 - S_2}{\sigma} \ge \varphi, \tag{15.11}\] and otherwise says “no match”.
Figure 15.3 (left and centre) shows why the threshold needs calibration. When the target is not in the release, the top score is the edge of a long tail. How often it stands out by chance depends on the shape of that tail. So the threshold has to be set on records known not to be the target, and read at a small false positive rate, as for any attack (Hypothesis testing).
The full edition’s script measures this with 400 outsiders, people drawn from the same model who are not in the release, so any match declared for them is false. Take 8 items, 2 of them wrong, and Narayanan and Shmatikov’s threshold of 1.5. The test then re-identifies 94.8% of insiders correctly, but it also “matches” 26.3% of outsiders to someone. To hold false matches to 1% of outsiders, the threshold must rise to \(\varphi = 4.83\). That threshold still re-identifies 73.0% of insiders. Figure 15.4 shows the whole trade-off as the threshold varies.






Figure 15.4: True against false positive rates of the eccentricity test as the threshold \(\varphi\) is swept, for 4, 6 and 8 auxiliary items with 1, 1 and 2 of them wrong. The dots mark \(\varphi = 1.5\). A false positive rate of 0 is drawn at the left edge.



Equation 15.9 also gives a principled alternative to the eccentricity test. Write \(q\) for the prior probability that the target is in the release, so that each record is the target with prior probability \(q/n\). Add a third explanation, “the target is not in the release”, with prior probability \(1 - q\), under which every record is unrelated. Bayes’ rule then gives the probability that record \(t\) is the target as \[\frac{q\,\mathrm{LR}(t)}{q\sum_j\mathrm{LR}(j) + (1 - q)n}. \tag{15.12}\] The factor \(n\) appears because each record’s prior is \(q/n\), and the formula multiplies top and bottom by \(n\). The adversary declares a match when this probability clears a level it chooses. Even the top record stays unlikely unless its likelihood ratio is large compared with \((1 - q)n/q\).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.5 Does releasing a sample protect?
Statistical agencies often release only a sample, such as 1% of a census. The argument is plausible deniability. A record that is unique in the sample need not be unique in the population. The person you have in mind may share their attributes with someone who was not sampled. Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye (2019) measured how much this argument is worth. Their copula model predicted that 99.98% of Americans would be correctly re-identified in any dataset with 15 demographic attributes, and that releasing a sample changes that very little.
Suppose each of the \(n\) people in the population is in the release with probability \(\pi\), the sampling fraction, independently of everyone else and of their cell. Consider a cell with probability \(p\), and write \(\lambda = (n - 1)p\) for the expected number of other people in it. The adversary can attack from either side, starting from a person or from a record.
Start from a person. The adversary knows the target’s cell and finds exactly one record in it. Either the target was sampled and none of the others in the cell were, and the match is right. Or the target was not sampled and exactly one of the others was, and the match is wrong. Swapping who was sampled between the target and one other person leaves the probability unchanged. So each other person in the cell gives a wrong match as likely as the right one. Because the release shows no second record, those others were all left out of the sample, and the cell is expected to hold about \(\lambda(1 - \pi)\) of them, not \(\lambda\). Putting this expected count in place of the actual one, for a rare cell a match is correct with probability “right over right plus all the wrong ones”, \[\kappa = \Pr[\text{correct} \mid \text{one match}] \approx \frac{1}{1 + \lambda(1 - \pi)}. \tag{15.13}\]
Now start from a record that is alone in its cell in the release. Look the cell up in a register of the whole population, such as a voter roll. The record is identified if nobody other than its owner is in the cell in the population either. Nobody else in the cell was sampled, so the only people who could be there are unsampled ones, about \(\lambda(1 - \pi)\) on average. For a rare cell, the chance that there are none is \[\xi = \Pr[\text{population-unique} \mid \text{sample-unique}] \approx e^{-\lambda(1 - \pi)}. \tag{15.14}\] Both formulas are approximations for a small cell probability \(p\).
Sampling enters both formulas only through the factor \(1 - \pi\), which multiplies \(\lambda\). Because that factor is at most 1, both probabilities are at least their values for a vanishingly small sample. So for every sampling fraction, the chance \(\kappa\) that a match from a person is correct is at least \(1/(1 + \lambda)\). Likewise, the chance \(\xi\) that a sample-unique record is unique in the population is at least \(e^{-\lambda}\). Sampling helps only when the cell is crowded.

Table 15.5 shows both probabilities for three crowding levels. Shrinking a 50% sample to a 1% sample lowers \(\kappa\) by only 0.04 for a rare cell, and by 0.16 for a crowded one. Matching from a person is also more forgiving than matching from a record. For the same crowding and sample, \(\kappa\) is never below \(\xi\), because \(e^x \ge 1 + x\). A match from a person can be right even when the target is not unique in the population, if the others in the cell were not sampled.
Averaged over a whole release, the fraction of sample-unique records that are also unique in the population is \[\frac{\sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}}{\sum_cp_c(1 - p_c\pi)^{n-1}}. \tag{15.15}\] The top counts records that are unique in the population, which makes them unique in the sample too. The bottom counts sample-unique records, for which each other person must be outside the cell or unsampled, which fails with probability \(p_c\pi\). As the sample shrinks, each term of the bottom tends to \(p_c\), and the probabilities \(p_c\) add up to 1. So the ratio tends to the population’s uniqueness rate from Equation 15.2, and at a full release it is 1.
So a small sample gives plausible deniability only to the people who were not unique in the population anyway. With enough attributes, that is almost nobody. The full edition’s script draws a population of 100,000 people with the first seven attributes of Table 15.3, and 82.8% of them are unique. In a 1% sample, Equation 15.15 says that 0.8301 of the sample-unique records are unique in the population. The simulation agrees, at 0.8334. For a 50% sample the fraction rises to 0.9235.
The adversary can also tell which matches to trust. The crowding \(\lambda\) depends on the cell, and a sample is a fair picture of the population. So the adversary can estimate each cell’s probability from the sample itself and compute \(\xi\) record by record. The script does this from a separate 1% sample with 993 sample-unique records, multiplying each attribute’s estimated frequencies. In that sample, the mean prediction is 0.817, against an actual 0.824. The predictions also sort the records well (Figure 15.5). Among the 415 records rated above 0.95, 99.3% are unique in the population. Among the 119 rated below 0.5, only 30.3% are.






Figure 15.5: Left: the fraction of sample-unique records that are unique in a population of 100,000, against the sampling fraction, for 5 to 8 attributes; lines are Equation 15.15, dots are simulations. As \(\pi \to 0\) each curve levels off at the population’s uniqueness rate. Right: the adversary’s predicted probability that a sample-unique record is unique in the population, estimated from a 1% sample, against the observed fraction, in bins of width 0.1.



Removing names, perturbing values and sampling all failed in the same way, because each left enough bits in every record and relied on what the adversary did not know. A defence has to hold whatever auxiliary data exist. Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks tests the classic attempts, k-anonymity and its successors, against that requirement. The definition of differential privacy gives a guarantee that meets it.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.6 Code
Three numbers summarise the linkage risk of a release you hold. They are the success \(J/n\), the fraction of unique records and the smallest class size. For a planned release, the uniform-cells formula and Equation 15.13 give quick estimates.
from collections import Counter
from math import exp, log2


def linkage_report(rows: list[tuple[str, ...]]) -> tuple[float, float, int]:
    """Linkage success J/n, fraction of unique records, and smallest class size of a release."""
    sizes = Counter(rows).values()  # one count per distinct quasi-identifier combination
    n = len(rows)
    return len(sizes) / n, sum(1 for k in sizes if k == 1) / n, min(sizes)


def uniform_unique(n: float, cells: float) -> float:
    """Expected fraction of n people who are unique when they fall in `cells` equally likely cells."""
    return exp(-n / cells)


def match_correct(lam: float, pi: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """In a sample of fraction pi, with lam expected others in the cell: (kappa, xi)."""
    return 1 / (1 + lam * (1 - pi)), exp(-lam * (1 - pi))


release = [
    ("02138", "1961-03-14", "F"), ("02138", "1972-11-02", "M"), ("02138", "1972-11-02", "M"),
    ("02139", "1958-06-21", "F"), ("02139", "1990-01-01", "F"), ("02139", "1990-01-01", "F"),
    ("02139", "1990-01-01", "F"), ("02141", "1983-09-30", "M"),
]
success, unique, k = linkage_report(release)
print(f"{success:.3f} {unique:.3f} {k}")  # 0.625 0.375 1
cells = 40_000 * 365 * 80 * 2  # ZIP code x birth date over 80 years x sex
print(f"{log2(cells):.1f} {uniform_unique(248.7e6, cells):.3f}")  # 31.1 0.899
kappa, xi = match_correct(0.1, 0.01)
print(f"{kappa:.3f} {xi:.3f}")  # 0.910 0.906
The full edition’s script, linkage.py, computes every number in this chapter:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/linkage.py

text:
15.8 Further reading

Sweeney, “Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely” (2000): the 87% estimate and its variants with coarser geography.
Narayanan & Shmatikov, “Robust De-anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets” (IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2008): the scoring algorithm, the eccentricity test and the Netflix experiments.
Rocher, Hendrickx & de Montjoye, “Estimating the success of re-identifications in incomplete datasets using generative models” (Nature Communications, 2019): per-record re-identification risk from a copula model, and why sampling does not protect.
Golle, “Revisiting the Uniqueness of Simple Demographics in the US Population” (Workshop on Privacy in the Electronic Society, 2006): the same estimate from the 2000 census, and how it depends on the granularity of the attributes.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter, except the findings of Sweeney, Golle, Narayanan and Shmatikov, and Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye, which it cites from their papers.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.1 Why this matters
Linkage and re-identification showed that deleting names does not anonymize a table. The columns that remain, such as age, ZIP code and sex, are called quasi-identifiers. None of them names anyone, but together they single out most people. Anyone who holds a list of names with the same columns, such as a voter roll, can join it to the released table and name most rows.
Between 1998 and 2008, data custodians and researchers answered with a family of definitions that constrain the released table itself. The first, k-anonymity, hides every record in a crowd of at least \(k\) records that look alike, where the custodian chooses the crowd size \(k\). The second, l-diversity, asks each crowd to hold several different sensitive values, such as diagnoses. The third, t-closeness, asks each crowd to look like the whole table.
They are called syntactic because each is a property of the published table that you can check by reading it, whatever produced the table. Statistics offices, regulators’ guidance and anonymization tools such as ARX still use them, so you need to know where their promise ends. Their failures are also the list of requirements that differential privacy, the subject of the next part, is built to meet.
Each definition was proposed to answer an attack on the one before, and a last attack, which combines two releases, defeats all three. The reason is what they share. Each is a property of one table, and it protects only against an adversary whose knowledge is fixed in advance. Give the adversary one piece of knowledge the definition did not anticipate, and the guarantee says nothing.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
section: 16.2 What the adversary believes about a class
text:
16.2 What the adversary believes about a class
Take a released table of \(n\) records. Each record has quasi-identifiers and one sensitive attribute, written \(S\), such as a diagnosis. To protect it, the custodian applies a generalization, which replaces each quasi-identifier by a coarser value, so that an age becomes a range and a ZIP code becomes a prefix. Records that end up with the same generalized quasi-identifiers form an equivalence class, or class for short.
The adversary knows the target’s quasi-identifiers and that the target is in the release, so it can find the target’s class, which we write \(E\). All the records in the class look the same, so if the adversary knows nothing else about the target, each one is equally likely to be the target’s.
The adversary’s belief about the target’s sensitive value after it has seen the release is called its posterior. When the adversary knows nothing else, the posterior is just the share of the class that has each value. Write \(\lvert E\rvert\) for the number of records in the class, and \(n_E(v)\) for the number of them whose sensitive value is \(v\). The posterior that the target has value \(v\) is then \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert} = P_E(v). \tag{16.1}\] We call this share \(P_E(v)\) the class’s distribution of the sensitive attribute. The same share computed over the whole table is written \(P(v)\).
Background knowledge breaks the condition that the adversary knows nothing else, and it works by elimination. In a class with the diagnoses cancer, cancer and flu, the posterior for cancer is \(\frac23\). An adversary who knows that the target did not have flu crosses out the flu record, and its posterior for cancer becomes 1. Every attack on the sensitive attribute in this chapter is this calculation.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.3 k-anonymity
Sweeney and Samarati proposed the first answer to the linkage attack in 1998. A release is k-anonymous if every class has at least \(k\) records, so that every combination of quasi-identifier values in the release is shared by at least \(k\) people. A custodian gets there by generalizing, so that an exact age becomes a five-year range and a ZIP code keeps only its first three digits. It also uses suppression, which deletes the few records that still stand out.
To see what this buys, recall the linkage game of Linkage and re-identification. There the adversary must pick out the record of a target drawn at random from the release. Within a class it can only guess, so its best chance of winning is \(J/n\), where \(J\) is the number of classes. When every class needs at least \(k\) records, the \(n\) records cannot fill more than \(n/k\) classes. So the chance of winning the linkage game is capped: \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n} \le \frac1k. \tag{16.2}\]
This guarantee is about names only. It says nothing about the sensitive attribute, which is the very thing the release must protect. The sections on l-diversity and t-closeness below attack exactly that gap.
The guarantee also needs the adversary to know the quasi-identifiers and nothing more. A neighbour who already knows the target’s diagnosis can pick out the target’s record whenever that diagnosis appears only once in the class, with no linkage at all.
Which columns count as quasi-identifiers is a judgment, and in sparse data every column is one. Sparse data has many columns, each filled for few people, such as a matrix of movie ratings. Linkage and re-identification showed that a handful of rare ratings single out a subscriber. To make such a matrix k-anonymous, you would have to generalize thousands of columns until little is left (Aggarwal, 2005).
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.4 What k-anonymity costs
Coarse quasi-identifiers protect more but say less, so the practical question is how coarse they must be. The uniform-cells model of Linkage and re-identification answers it. The generalized quasi-identifiers split the population into \(M\) cells, and each of the \(n\) people falls into a cell independently, every cell equally likely.
Fix one person, and count the others who share that person’s cell. Each of the other \(n - 1\) people lands there with probability \(1/M\). When there are many people and each has a small chance, this count is close to a Poisson count (Probability distributions). Its mean is \((n - 1)/M\), which is about \(n/M\), the average number of people per cell.
A person violates k-anonymity when their class has fewer than \(k\) records. The class holds the person plus the others in the cell, so this happens when at most \(k - 2\) others share it. Every person has the same chance of this, so the expected fraction of people in classes that are too small equals that chance: \[\Pr[\mathrm{Poisson}(n/M) \le k - 2]. \tag{16.3}\]
Suppose you allow a small fraction \(\alpha\) of records, for example 1%, to violate the definition. More people per cell make small classes rarer, so the fraction falls as the average \(n/M\) grows. Write \(\lambda_k\) for the average at which the fraction equals \(\alpha\). The release then stays within the allowance as long as \(n/M\) is at least \(\lambda_k\), so there can be at most \(n/\lambda_k\) cells.
Counting in bits lets you compare this budget with what each published column costs. A quasi-identifier with \(M\) equally likely values carries \(\log_2 M\) bits about a person, so the quasi-identifiers may carry at most \(\log_2 n - \log_2 \lambda_k\) bits.
You might expect 2-anonymity to need 2 people per cell on average. But cell sizes vary around their average, and the unlucky small cells are the ones that violate the definition, so \(\lambda_k\) is larger than \(k\). For \(k = 2\), a person violates the definition when nobody else is in their cell, which for a Poisson count with mean \(\lambda\) has probability \(e^{-\lambda}\). Setting that probability to 1% gives \(\lambda_2 = \ln 100 = 4.61\), more than twice \(k\). Table 16.1 gives \(\lambda_k\) for larger \(k\), in a population of 10,000 people.

k-anonymity is the mirror image of uniqueness, and counting in bits makes the comparison exact. In the same model, a person is unique when nobody else is in their cell, which has probability \(e^{-n/M}\). For 99% of people to be unique, there must be about 100 cells per person. That takes \(\log_2 100 = 6.64\) bits beyond \(\log_2 n\) (Linkage and re-identification). Hiding 99% of records in classes of at least 2 needs the opposite, and Table 16.1 shows that it takes 2.20 bits below \(\log_2 n\). So the window between “almost everyone is unique” and “almost everyone is hidden” is about 9 bits wide, and every attribute you publish uses some of it.
Real tables are not uniform, so real anonymizers search for a generalization that works on the data at hand. The full edition’s script builds a synthetic hospital table of 10,000 patients, with age, ZIP code and sex as quasi-identifiers. 16.5 Homogeneity, background knowledge and l-diversity
Machanavajjhala and colleagues (2006) pointed out that k-anonymity hides who a record belongs to, but not what the record says. Table 16.3 is a 3-anonymous release.
