Alice is 26 and lives in ZIP code 13053, so she is in the first class. Every record there says heart disease, so by Equation 16.1 her posterior for heart disease is 1. This is the homogeneity attack, and it discloses her diagnosis without re-identifying her record. Bob is 35 and lives in ZIP code 13068, which puts him in the third class. Two of its three records say cancer, so his posterior for cancer starts at \(\frac23\). But his neighbour saw him at work through the whole flu season, and so can rule out flu. Crossing out the flu record leaves only cancer, and the posterior rises to 1. This is the background knowledge attack.
Both attacks work because one value dominates the class, either from the start or after a few values are ruled out. To stop them, l-diversity asks each class to hold enough different values, and its three versions differ in how they measure “enough”. The simplest is distinct \(\ell\)-diversity, which asks each class to hold at least \(\ell\) different values. A release is \(\ell\)-diverse when every class is.
The second version, entropy \(\ell\)-diversity, measures how evenly the values are spread. A class with \(\ell\) equally common values has an entropy of exactly \(\log_2\ell\) bits. The condition asks every class for at least that much, so each is at least as spread out as \(\ell\) equally common values.
Neither version limits the share of the most common value directly, so either can leave the adversary fairly sure. A class can hold three values and still have one value in almost all of its records, and entropy helps only a little. A class over eight values can be entropy 3-diverse with one value in 73% of its records, because the remaining records, spread over seven values, add enough entropy.
The third version targets the background knowledge attack directly. Sort a class’s value counts from largest to smallest, so that \(r_1\) is the count of the most common value. Set aside the \(\ell - 1\) largest counts, and call the total of the rest the tail. A class is recursive \((c, \ell)\)-diverse if its top count is less than \(c\) times the tail, for a constant \(c\) that the custodian chooses. In symbols, with \(r_\ell\) the \(\ell\)-th largest count, \[r_1 < c\,(r_\ell + r_{\ell+1} + \dots). \tag{16.4}\]
The tail is what survives the background knowledge attack. An adversary who rules out \(\ell - 2\) values cannot make any remaining count larger. Whichever values it removes, the counts that remain besides the top one still add up to at least the tail. So the top value still holds less than \(c\) parts for every one part held by the rest. Every remaining value therefore has a posterior below \(c/(1 + c)\): \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}, \text{background}] < \frac{c}{1 + c}. \tag{16.5}\] The guarantee stops at \(\ell - 2\) ruled-out values, because ruling out one more can leave a class with a single value.
So l-diversity protects against certainty, not against likelihood. The cap \(c/(1 + c)\) is already a half at \(c = 1\), and it climbs towards 1 as \(c\) grows, so even recursive diversity lets the adversary be fairly sure. The guarantee also fixes in advance how much the adversary may know. It does not cover one who rules out more values, or who knows something softer such as “probably not flu”.
Some tables cannot be made diverse at all. The table’s distribution is a mix of its classes’ distributions, and mixing distributions can only spread the values out further. So if every class had entropy at least \(\log_2\ell\), the whole table would too. A table dominated by one value, with entropy below \(\log_2\ell\), therefore has no entropy \(\ell\)-diverse split into classes.
In Table 16.3, the third class counts for only 1.89 equally common values when measured by entropy, because its two values are unevenly spread. The release as a whole is only 1-diverse, because of Alice’s class.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.6 Measuring what a release teaches
In the hospital table, the “certain disclosure” column of Table 16.2 counts the patients in classes with a single diagnosis. At \(k = 2\) it is 28.0% of all patients. At \(k = 5\) it falls to 2.3%. That still means the release states 232 diagnoses outright. Knowing a patient’s age and the population’s patterns never gives that certainty, since at no age does the population give any diagnosis a probability above 0.705.
A posterior has to be read against what the adversary would believe with no release. A posterior of 0.6 is not a leak if the population already gives 0.6 to people of the target’s age. The right comparison is the imputation baseline of Attribute inference and model inversion. It is the most likely value of the sensitive attribute given the target’s own quasi-identifiers, under the true population distribution, computed with no release at all. Success up to the baseline comes from what the population reveals, and only success beyond it tells the adversary something about the individual.
The “guess accuracy” column of Table 16.2 needs this comparison (Figure 16.1, right). Guessing the most common diagnosis of the whole table is right for 18.5% of patients. Here diagnosis depends on age, so imputation guesses the most likely diagnosis for each patient’s exact age. It is right for 53.6% with no release at all. A 5-anonymous release is right for 59.3%. So most of what the release teaches is the pattern linking age to diagnosis, which any useful study would report. The excess over imputation, 0.057 at \(k = 5\), comes from the small classes, and it almost vanishes by \(k = 20\).

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.7 Skewness, similarity and t-closeness
Li, Li and Venkatasubramanian (2007) found two attacks that l-diversity does not see. In the skewness attack, 1% of the table has HIV. A class that is half HIV is 2-diverse by every definition. Yet by Equation 16.1 it raises the belief that a member has HIV fifty-fold, to 50%. In the similarity attack, a class holds three different diagnoses, gastric ulcer, gastritis and stomach cancer. It is 3-diverse, and the adversary still learns that the target has a stomach disease.
So counting values is the wrong yardstick. What matters is how far a class’s distribution is from what the adversary would believe anyway, the distribution of the whole table. A release is t-close if every class’s distribution is within a distance \(t\) of the table’s, for a chosen measure of distance.
The first choice of distance is the total variation (TV) distance (Divergences). It is half the total absolute difference between the two distributions’ probabilities, summed over the values. It also equals the largest difference that the two distributions can show in the probability of any set of values.
The second form is what t-closeness relies on, because by Equation 16.1 the adversary’s belief about a target in class \(E\) is the class’s distribution \(P_E\). Write \(P_E(A)\) for the probability that a value drawn from the class lands in a set of values \(A\), and \(P(A)\) for the same probability under the table. A bound \(t\) on the total variation between the two distributions then bounds every question the adversary can ask about the target’s value. For every class and every set \(A\), \[\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert \le t. \tag{16.6}\] Taking \(A\) to be a single value shows that no value’s share in a class exceeds its share in the table by more than \(t\). So guessing the most common value of the target’s class is right with probability at most \(\max_v P(v) + t\), the best guess from the table alone plus \(t\).
The bound is additive, and an additive bound protects rare values badly. It lets a value held by 1% of the table rise to \(1\% + t\). At \(t = 0.15\) that is 16%, a sixteen-fold increase for the people who most need protection. In the skewness attack, a class with 10% HIV passes a threshold of 0.1, yet it makes HIV ten times as likely for its members (Figure 16.2). A guarantee for rare values has to bound the ratio of the adversary’s beliefs with and without the release, not their difference. Differential privacy, in the next part, has that shape.






Figure 16.2: The skewness attack: a table in which 1% of patients have HIV, and a class of it that is half HIV. The class is 2-diverse but at total variation 0.49 from the table.



Total variation treats every pair of different values as equally far apart, so it does not see the similarity attack. Li and colleagues chose the earth mover’s distance (EMD) instead, under which similar values are close. Think of each distribution as piles of sand on the values. The EMD is the least work needed to reshape one set of piles into the other, when moving sand costs the distance it travels. If the distances come from a tree that groups diagnoses by organ, gastritis and gastric ulcer are close, and a class full of stomach diseases fails.
Values with a natural order, such as salary bands, have a closed form. Number the \(m\) ordered values from 1 to \(m\), spaced evenly so that the two ends are distance 1 apart. On a line, sand can cross a gap only by passing through it, so the least work adds up the net sand that must cross each gap: \[\mathrm{EMD}(P_E, P) = \frac{1}{m - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\Big\lvert\sum_{j \le i}\big(P_E(j) - P(j)\big)\Big\rvert. \tag{16.7}\] The index \(i\) numbers the gap between values \(i\) and \(i + 1\). The inner sum is the extra share of the class, over the table, at or below value \(i\), which is the net sand crossing that gap. The factor \(1/(m - 1)\) is the length of each gap.
t-closeness also fights the purpose of the release. If age predicts diagnosis, a class of similar ages differs from the whole table, so making every class t-close means mixing ages until the pattern is gone. But that pattern is a fact about the population, not a secret about any one patient.
Even the toy release is far from close. Alice’s class is all heart disease, which makes up only four ninths of the table, so the release is t-close only for \(t\) of at least 0.556. On the hospital table, Table 16.5 adds t-closeness in total variation to \(k = 5\).

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.8 The composition attack
Every definition so far is about one release, and Ganta, Kasiviswanathan and Smith (2008) asked what happens when there are two. Suppose two hospitals in one city publish properly k-anonymous or \(\ell\)-diverse tables without coordinating. A patient treated at both then appears in a class of each release.
The adversary keeps only the diagnoses that appear both in the target’s class in release A, written \(E_A\), and in its class in release B, written \(E_B\). These candidates are \[\{v : n_{E_A}(v) > 0\} \cap \{v : n_{E_B}(v) > 0\}. \tag{16.8}\] The true value is always among them, because the target’s own record carries it in each class. So when only one candidate is left, the diagnosis is pinned down. Each release satisfies its definition, yet together they can reveal the diagnosis outright.
How often this happens depends on the size of the classes. To see how, suppose the other members of the target’s classes are independent draws from the population’s distribution of diagnoses, which gives each value \(v\) a probability \(p_v\). The target is pinned exactly when no wrong value turns up in both classes. Each extra member is another chance for the two classes to share a wrong value, so larger classes are pinned less often.
To compute the chance, fix the true value \(v\), and write \(W_v\) for the set of wrong values found among the other members of the class in release A. Each of the \(k_B - 1\) other members of the class in release B, a class of \(k_B\) records, avoids those values independently. Averaging over the true value and over the random set gives \[\Pr[\text{pinned}] = \sum_v p_v\,\mathbb E\big[(1 - p(W_v))^{k_B - 1}\big], \tag{16.9}\] where \(p(W_v)\) is the total probability of the values in \(W_v\). A simpler union bound, which charges each wrong value separately, is exact for classes of 2 but turns negative from classes of 5. It fails there because two classes of 5 already share more than one wrong value on average.
In the model, with the diagnosis distribution of the hospital table, two classes of 2 pin down the diagnosis with probability 0.8734. For classes of 5 it is 0.1615, and by classes of 10 it has fallen to 0.0015. Simulation agrees (Figure 16.3, left).
The script then runs the attack on a city of 15,000 people drawn from the model of the hospital table. Two hospitals each treat a random 10,000 of them, so 6,649 people are treated at both, and each hospital publishes a 5-anonymous Mondrian release of its own patients. Table 16.6 gives what the adversary learns about the 6,649.

Together, the two 5-anonymous releases pin down the diagnosis of 9.9% of the shared patients, more than three times what either release pins alone. With distinct 3-diversity, no single release pins anyone down. The two together still pin down 18 patients, or 0.27% of those treated at both.






Figure 16.3: Left: the probability that two releases pin down the diagnosis, against the class size, when the other members of each class are drawn from the population: exact (Equation 16.9), simulated, and the union bound. Right: the number of diagnoses still possible for a patient treated at both hospitals, from either 5-anonymous release alone and from their intersection.



The model understates the risk. In the 5-anonymous release of Table 16.2, a patient’s class has 6.8 records on average. For classes of 7 the model predicts that only 2.9% are pinned, far fewer than the 9.9% the real releases pin. A real class collects people of similar age, who share diagnoses more often than random draws, so each class holds fewer distinct wrong values.
None of the three definitions survives composition, because each is a condition on one table, and the intersection of two tables is a table that neither custodian checked. Checking its own table more carefully does not help. To rule the attack out, a custodian would need to know the other hospital’s classes, and every other release in which its patients appear.
That points to what a better definition must do. First, it must compose, so that the leak of two releases together is at most a known function of the leak of each. Second, it must hold whatever the adversary knows, since another release is just auxiliary information. Third, as the rare values under t-closeness showed, it must bound the ratio of the adversary’s beliefs rather than their difference. The definition of differential privacy starts from these requirements.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.9 Code
An auditor can check every definition of this chapter by grouping the rows. The snippet audits Table 16.3, and its third line shows the entropy-equivalent \(\ell\) of each class. It also checks recursive \((2, 2)\)-diversity and each class’s total variation from the table.
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from math import log2


def classes(rows: list[tuple[str, str, str]]) -> list[Counter[str]]:
    """Group (ZIP, age, diagnosis) rows by their quasi-identifiers; count the diagnoses in each class."""
    groups: defaultdict[tuple[str, str], Counter[str]] = defaultdict(Counter)
    for zip_code, age, diagnosis in rows:
        groups[(zip_code, age)][diagnosis] += 1
    return list(groups.values())


def entropy_l(counts: Counter[str]) -> float:
    """2 ** entropy: the number of equally common values with the same spread."""
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return 2 ** -sum(c / total * log2(c / total) for c in counts.values())


def recursive_diverse(counts: Counter[str], c: float, l: int) -> bool:
    """Recursive (c, l)-diversity: the top count is below c times the counts from the l-th largest on."""
    r = sorted(counts.values(), reverse=True)
    return r[0] < c * sum(r[l - 1 :])


def tv_to_table(counts: Counter[str], table: Counter[str]) -> float:
    """Total variation between a class's distribution and the whole table's."""
    nc, nt = sum(counts.values()), sum(table.values())
    return sum(abs(counts[v] / nc - table[v] / nt) for v in table) / 2


rows = [
    ("130**", "<30", "heart disease"), ("130**", "<30", "heart disease"), ("130**", "<30", "heart disease"),
    ("148**", "4*", "cancer"), ("148**", "4*", "flu"), ("148**", "4*", "heart disease"),
    ("130**", "3*", "cancer"), ("130**", "3*", "cancer"), ("130**", "3*", "flu"),
]
table = Counter(diagnosis for _, _, diagnosis in rows)
found = classes(rows)
print(min(sum(e.values()) for e in found))  # 3
print(min(len(e) for e in found))  # 1
print(" ".join(f"{entropy_l(e):.2f}" for e in found))  # 1.00 3.00 1.89
print(all(recursive_diverse(e, 2, 2) for e in found))  # False
print(" ".join(f"{tv_to_table(e, table):.3f}" for e in found))  # 0.556 0.111 0.444
The full edition’s script, syntactic_anonymity.py, computes every number in this chapter and draws every figure. It implements Mondrian with any criterion on a class, the uniform-cells calculation, the attacks on the sensitive attribute and the composition attack. Tools such as ARX play Mondrian’s part on real data. From the repository root:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/syntactic_anonymity.py

Rules of thumb

k-anonymity protects names, not attributes. Ask what a class’s sensitive values reveal, not just how big the class is.
Measure attribute disclosure against imputation from the population, or you will count the study’s findings as leaks.
A rare sensitive value needs a bound on the ratio of beliefs, not on their difference.
Assume another release exists. A guarantee that is only about one table is not a guarantee about a person.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.1 Why this matters
A hospital keeps one sensitive bit for each patient, recording whether that patient tested positive. It never releases the bits. It only answers counting questions such as “how many of the patients on this list tested positive?”, and to be safe it adds a little noise to every answer. Dinur and Nissim (2003) showed that this is not safe unless the noise is large. Each answer is a linear equation whose unknowns are the patients’ bits. A table of counts is therefore a system of equations, and enough equations with small enough errors determine the unknowns.
Threat models and privacy games set this up as the reconstruction game. The secret is a whole column of the dataset, and the attacker is scored by the fraction of entries it recovers. For bits that are equally likely to be 0 or 1, the baseline is one half, the score of guessing at random. That chapter showed that a single exact count barely beats this baseline. The count tells you which value is in the majority, but nothing about who holds it. This chapter shows what happens when the attacker gets many counts.
The only thing standing between the attacker and the solution is the error in the answers, and that protection can fail in two ways. The first is error that is too small. To hide a wrong guess, the error has to be as large as the amount by which that guess changes the answers. A randomly chosen question picks up each wrong bit of the guess only about half the time, like a coin flip. So when the guess is wrong on a sizable share of the people, the change behaves like a sum of coin flips. It is then about the square root of the number of people.
The second failure is too many answers. Errors that are independent from one answer to the next, and do not grow with the number of questions, are averaged away as the attacker asks more. Dwork and Roth call this the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery: overly accurate answers to too many questions destroy privacy. If you run or audit a system that answers aggregate queries, you have to check both halves of the law.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.2 Counts are linear equations
Write the secret as a list of bits \(d = (d_1, \dots, d_n)\), one per person, where \(n\) is the number of people. A subset-sum query names a set of people and asks how many of them have bit 1. You can write the query as a vector \(q\) of zeros and ones, with a 1 for each person in the set. Its true answer is the inner product \(\langle q, d\rangle\), which adds up the bits of the people in the set. Table 17.1 shows six of the 16 possible queries about four people whose secret is \((1, 0, 1, 1)\).

The party that holds the secret and answers the queries is called the curator. The attacker asks \(m\) queries, and they form the rows of a query matrix \(A\) with one row per query and one column per person. The true answers are then the entries of \(Ad\). The curator publishes the answers \(a = Ad + e\), where the error vector \(e\) holds one error per query. Write \(E\) for a bound on the size of every error, so that every published answer is within \(E\) of the true one.
With exact answers there is nothing to attack. In the example, the four queries about a single person reveal the four bits directly. More generally, any \(n\) queries whose vectors are linearly independent determine the secret, because Gaussian elimination solves the system. Everything interesting in this chapter is about answers with error.
Linearity also tells the attacker how to rule out a wrong guess. Suppose the attacker considers a candidate secret \(c\). On any query, the candidate’s answer differs from the true answer by the subset sum of the difference \(c - d\) over the same set. The candidate is ruled out if this gap between the two answers is larger than the curator’s error could explain. Every attack below is a way of finding such a query for every candidate that is far from the truth.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.3 The exponential attack
Start with the strongest attacker, who may ask all \(2^n\) subset sums. How large must the curator’s error be before this attacker can no longer pin the secret down? The answer is an error that grows in proportion to \(n\), and the reason takes only a few steps.
The attacker cannot know the secret, but it can throw away every candidate that contradicts an answer. Call a candidate consistent if each of its subset sums is within \(E\) of the published answer. The true secret is always consistent, so at least one candidate survives, and the attacker outputs any consistent candidate.
The people on whom a consistent candidate \(c\) is wrong fall into two sets. One set holds the people whose bit is 1 but whom the candidate sets to 0. The other holds the people whose bit is 0 but whom the candidate sets to 1. The attacker has asked about both sets, since it asked about every set. On the first set, the true secret sums to the size of the set and the candidate sums to zero. Both sums are within \(E\) of the same published answer, so they are within \(2E\) of each other, and the set holds at most \(2E\) people. The same argument limits the second set to \(2E\) people. The number of bits on which \(c\) and \(d\) differ is called their Hamming distance, and it therefore satisfies \[\mathrm{dist}(c, d) \le 4E. \tag{17.1}\]
The bound is tight. Flip about \(2E\) of the secret’s ones to zeros and as many zeros to ones. Within any set, the flips to zero lower the candidate’s sum and the flips to one raise it. They partly cancel, so the two sums differ by at most \(2E\). A curator that answers halfway between them is within \(E\) of both and keeps the candidate. It is wrong on \(4E\) bits when \(2E\) is a whole number and the secret has enough ones and zeros to flip.
The argument assumes nothing about how the curator picks its errors except that each is at most \(E\). The errors may be chosen by an adversary, even one that has seen the attacker’s candidate. By Equation 17.1, a curator whose error is a smaller and smaller fraction of \(n\) as \(n\) grows lets the attacker recover all but a vanishing fraction of the bits. Dinur and Nissim call such a curator blatantly non-private. For example, take a million people with every answer off by up to 1000. The attacker then gets at most 4,000 bits wrong, only 0.4% of them.
The bound is a worst case over curators, so a particular curator can leak far more than it suggests. A curator that rounds every answer to a multiple of 4 has error at most 2, but the rounding is a known function of the true sum. An attacker who applies the same rounding to each candidate’s sums therefore recovers the secret exactly. A distortion that the attacker can simulate is not noise.
The proof uses only two queries, the two sets of wrong bits. The attacker does not know these sets in advance, because it does not know which bits it got wrong, and that is why it needs every answer. It also has to check \(2^n\) candidates against \(2^n\) answers, so the attack is far too slow to run on real data.
Table 17.2 runs the attack on ten people whose secret has four ones, checking all 1024 candidates against all 1024 subset sums. It counts, for each error, the candidates that some curator with that error can make consistent, and finds the farthest of them from the secret.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.4 The linear-programming decoder
Asking \(2^n\) questions is not realistic. Dinur and Nissim showed that a number of random queries only slightly larger than \(n\) is enough, with a decoder that runs in polynomial time. Each random query includes each person independently with probability one half. Their proof asks for \(n(\log n)^2\) queries, and the version in the full edition needs a constant times \(n\log n\).
The decoder makes the search easier by allowing fractions. Instead of checking every list of bits, it lets each unknown be any number between 0 and 1. It then looks for a vector whose answers are all within \(E\) of the published answers. This search is a linear program, a problem of finding a point that satisfies a list of linear inequalities. Each requirement that an answer be within \(E\) is a pair of such inequalities. Linear programs can be solved in time polynomial in the number of unknowns and inequalities. The true secret meets every requirement, so a solution exists, and the decoder rounds each entry of it to the nearest bit.
The price of using random queries is that the curator’s error must now be smaller, well below \(\sqrt n\) instead of well below \(n\). The reason is that a random query cannot aim at the wrong bits. Suppose a candidate differs from the secret on \(k\) bits. A query aimed at exactly those bits, which the exponential attacker could ask, would move the answer by \(k\). A random query picks up each of those bits with probability one half, so its sum over them behaves like a sum of \(k\) coin flips. Such a sum fluctuates by about \(\sqrt k\), not by \(k\). A consistent candidate’s answers differ from the true answers by at most \(2E\) on every query, so an error well below \(\sqrt k\) cannot hide that fluctuation. When the candidate is wrong on a fixed share of the bits, \(\sqrt k\) grows like \(\sqrt n\).
The proof has to show that this fluctuation really happens with a decent probability, whatever the signs of the differences. A random query catches a bad candidate only when the subset sum of the difference is far from zero. So the proof needs a lower bound on how often a quantity is large. Markov’s inequality (Concentration inequalities) gives the opposite, an upper bound: a quantity that cannot be negative is rarely far above its mean.
A lower bound cannot hold for every quantity. One that is 0 most of the time and huge once in a while has a large mean, and it is still usually 0. What rules this out is a second moment, the average of the square, that is not much larger than the squared mean. A rare huge value would make the average square enormous.
The Paley–Zygmund inequality makes this precise. Like Markov’s inequality, it applies only to a quantity \(W\) that cannot be negative, and it needs a finite second moment so that the right side below is defined. Without the first condition, being above a fraction of the mean would not mean being away from zero. A subset sum whose terms cancel can have a mean of zero and still be large in either direction. That is why the attack applies the inequality to the square of the sum. For any fraction \(\theta\) from 0 up to (but not including) 1, the inequality says that \[\Pr\big[W > \theta\,\mathbb E W\big] \ge (1 - \theta)^2\frac{(\mathbb E W)^2}{\mathbb E[W^2]}. \tag{17.2}\] The right side is large when the average square is close to the squared mean, which is exactly the case where \(W\) cannot hide its mass in rare spikes. A lower bound like this, on how often a quantity stays away from zero, is called anti-concentration.
The attack takes \(W\) to be the square of a random subset sum, so the average of \(W^2\) is the average fourth power of the sum. The inequality is useful when that fourth moment is not much larger than the squared second moment. A random subset sum passes this test, because it is built from independent fair coins and has no heavy tails. Its fourth moment is at most 3 times the square of its second moment, the same ratio as for a normal distribution.
Putting these facts together gives the lemma the decoder rests on. Think of a vector \(z\) as the difference between a bad candidate and the secret. Write \(\beta\) for a fraction of wrong bits, not a failure probability as in the concentration chapter. Suppose \(z\) has at least \(\beta n\) entries of size at least one third. That is less than the one half by which a wrong bit differs, because the proof leaves room for a rounding step described below. Then a random subset sum of \(z\) lands far from zero with at least a constant probability, whatever the signs of the entries: \[\Pr\left[|\langle q, z\rangle| > \frac{\sqrt{\beta n}}{12}\right] \ge \frac{3}{16}. \tag{17.3}\] Here “far” is measured on the scale \(\sqrt{\beta n}\), the square root of the number of large entries, as the coin-flip picture predicts.
The hard case is a difference whose entries cancel. If all the large entries of \(z\) have the same sign, a random subset sum has a large average and escapes any small band around zero almost always. If half are positive and half negative, the sum is centred at zero, and only its fluctuation can carry it out of the band. The lemma covers both cases, because its proof ignores the average and relies on the fluctuation alone. Figure 17.2 shows both cases for the band of half-width \(\sqrt{\beta n}/12\) from Equation 17.3. In the figure’s example, a random sum escapes the band about 62% of the time even in the balanced case, far above the lemma’s guarantee of 0.1875.






Figure 17.2: A random subset sum of a difference vector \(z\) with \(\beta n = 100\) entries of size \(\frac13\) (\(n = 1000\)), over 20 000 random subsets, against the band \(|\langle q, z\rangle| \le \sqrt{\beta n}/12 = 0.83\) (red). Left: half the entries \(+\frac13\) and half \(-\frac13\), so the sum is centred at 0, yet it still leaves the band most of the time. Right: all entries \(+\frac13\), so the sum is centred far from the band. The lemma guarantees at least \(\frac3{16} = 0.1875\) in both cases.



The theorem turns the lemma into a guarantee for the decoder. A query catches a bad candidate when the candidate’s answer differs from the true one by more than the error can explain. The theorem’s condition on \(E\) below makes every gap beyond the lemma’s threshold such a catch. So each query catches a bad candidate with probability at least \(\frac{3}{16}\). The queries are independent, so the candidate escapes all \(m\) of them with probability at most \((13/16)^m\), which shrinks exponentially as \(m\) grows.
The proof also has to handle the infinitely many points the program can return, because the union bound needs a finite list. It rounds them to a grid of at most \((n + 1)^n\) points. The union bound (Concentration inequalities) over that grid then sets the number of queries below.
Theorem (Dinur–Nissim, in the form the full edition proves). Fix the secret, a fraction \(\beta\) of wrong bits and a failure probability \(\eta\). Suppose that the curator’s error \(E\) satisfies \(2E + \frac12 \le \sqrt{\beta n}/12\), and that the number of independent random queries satisfies \[m \ge \frac{n\ln(n + 1) + \ln(1/\eta)}{\ln(16/13)}. \tag{17.4}\] Then, with probability at least \(1 - \eta\) over the queries, every solution of the linear program rounds to a vector with at most \(\beta n\) wrong bits, whatever errors the curator chose.
The condition on the error is the lemma’s threshold with room for two things. A consistent candidate and the secret are each within \(E\) of every answer, so their sums can differ by up to \(2E\). Rounding to the grid adds up to \(\frac12\) more. The guarantee holds for every curator at once, because whether a bad grid point escapes depends only on the queries, not on the errors. If the error grows more slowly than \(\sqrt n\), the condition holds for smaller and smaller \(\beta\) as \(n\) grows. In words, the attacker then recovers all but a vanishing fraction of the bits in polynomial time, from a number of random queries of order \(n\log n\).
The proved constants are poor, but the scaling is right. Take a thousand people and a target of 10% wrong bits. The theorem then tolerates an error of only 0.1667. For a failure probability of 0.01 it asks for at least 33,296 queries. That is about 33 per person, and the count per person grows with \(n\) because of the factor \(\ln(n + 1)\), which the union bound over the grid adds. Sharper analyses need only a number of queries proportional to \(n\). In practice, the least-squares decoder of the next section already works at errors of about \(0.2\sqrt n\) with \(4n\) queries. So don’t read the proved constants as a safety margin.
Two further results show that the attack does not depend on the assumptions of the proof. Requiring every answer to be within \(E\) fails if a single answer is wildly wrong. Dwork, McSherry and Talwar (2007) studied a variant that instead minimises the total absolute difference between the candidate’s answers and the published ones. It tolerates a constant fraction of answers with arbitrarily large errors. Random queries are not essential either, since Dinur and Nissim used them only to make the proof work. Real attacks use whatever queries a system answers. Cohen and Nissim (2020) ran a linear-programming reconstruction against a commercial query system that added noise to its answers, and recovered most of a secret column.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
section: 17.5 Least squares under worst-case and random error
text:
17.5 Least squares under worst-case and random error
The linear program needs a solver and a value of \(E\). A simpler decoder needs neither. Least squares picks the vector whose answers come closest to the published answers, measured by the sum of squared differences. Write \(\hat x\) for this estimate of the secret. It has a closed form, \[\hat x = (A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top a, \tag{17.5}\] and the decoder clips each entry to the range from 0 to 1 and then rounds it. The decoded vector is a linear function of the answers. Its error is therefore a linear function of the curator’s error, and you can analyse it exactly in two cases. In the first, an adversary chooses the errors. In the second, the errors are independent random noise.
How much least squares amplifies the curator’s error depends on how much the query matrix can shrink a vector. The smallest singular value \(s_{\min}(A)\) is the smallest length that \(A\) gives to a vector of length 1. It measures the direction that the queries see least clearly. The analysis assumes at least as many queries as people, and a query matrix whose columns are linearly independent, so that \(s_{\min}(A)\) is positive. Without this, some change to the secret would leave every answer unchanged, and no decoder could detect it.
Consider first errors chosen by an adversary. The closed form maps the error vector to the decoder’s error, and this map can stretch a vector by at most a factor \(1/s_{\min}(A)\). So the decoded vector is never farther from the secret than the length of the error vector times that factor. Clipping only moves an entry closer to its true bit, so it cannot make this worse. Each wrong bit is off by at least \(\frac12\), so it adds at least \(\frac14\) to the squared distance. If every error is at most \(E\), the squared length of the error vector is at most \(mE^2\), and the decoder gets at most \[\frac{4mE^2}{s_{\min}(A)^2} \tag{17.6}\] bits wrong.
For random subset queries, the theory of random matrices gives the approximation \[s_{\min}(A) \approx \tfrac12\big(\sqrt m - \sqrt n\big). \tag{17.7}\] With four times as many queries as people, this is about half of \(\sqrt n\), so its square is about \(m/16\) and the bound becomes about \(64E^2\). An error well below \(\sqrt n\) therefore leaves only a small fraction of the bits wrong, with only \(4n\) queries.
Now let the curator’s errors be independent normal draws with mean 0, and write \(\sigma\) for their standard deviation. Each entry of the decoder’s error is then normal too, with a variance of about \(4\sigma^2/(m - n)\). In words, the variance of the noise is divided by the number of equations beyond the \(n\) needed to determine the secret, because those extra equations average the noise down. The factor 4 appears because a random query includes each person only half the time.
The count is \(m - n\) rather than \(m\) because the inverse of a randomly fluctuating matrix is, on average, larger than the inverse of its average. The correction is exact for query rows drawn from a normal distribution. The rows here are zeros and ones, so the formula is only an approximation, which the simulations below check.
A bit comes out wrong when its error pushes it across \(\frac12\). Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function, so \(\Phi(t)\) is the probability that a standard normal draw is below \(t\). The expected fraction of bits that least squares recovers is then approximately \[\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{m - n}}{4\sigma}\right). \tag{17.8}\] The argument of \(\Phi\) is the distance \(\frac12\) to the wrong side, measured in units of the error’s standard deviation \(2\sigma/\sqrt{m - n}\).
Two consequences follow. The first is that only the ratio \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) matters when the number of queries is a fixed multiple of \(n\). Plotted against that ratio, the recovery curves for different numbers of people fall on top of each other (Figure 17.3), so \(\sqrt n\) is again the scale of the threat. But noise of that order is not automatically safe. With four queries per person and noise of a quarter of \(\sqrt n\), least squares recovers about 96% of the bits. Recovery degrades smoothly as the noise grows, and it does not switch off at a threshold.






Figure 17.3: Fraction of bits recovered by least squares from \(m = 4n\) noisy random subset sums, against the noise scale in units of \(\sqrt n\), for three database sizes. The black curve is Equation 17.8. The curves for different \(n\) coincide: the attack’s success depends on \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) only.



The second consequence is that more queries average independent noise away. At a fixed noise level, the predicted fraction tends to 1 as the number of queries grows. To hold the attack at a fixed accuracy, the noise must grow like \(\sqrt m\) (Figure 17.4). This is the second half of the Fundamental Law. A bound on the error of each answer is not enough when the number of answers is unbounded.






Figure 17.4: Fraction of bits recovered by least squares at \(n = 200\) as the number of queries grows, for three noise levels. Lines are Equation 17.8; dots are simulations. Near \(m = n\) the system is barely determined and the noise is amplified; beyond that, more queries average the noise away, and even at \(\sigma = 2\sqrt n\) the attack recovers most bits with \(64n = 12\,800\) queries.



Table 17.3 checks the prediction on 500 people with 2000 queries, averaged over four random secrets and query matrices. The prediction is within 0.013 of every simulated value.

The last column shows how a curator can look safe and still fail. With noise of twice \(\sqrt n\) and four queries per person, least squares recovers only 0.5875 of the bits. But suppose the same curator answers any number of queries at the same noise level. Solving Equation 17.8 for the number of queries, an attacker who asks \(m = 106.1n\) queries is predicted to recover 90% of the bits.
Errors chosen by an adversary hurt more than random errors of the same size. Least squares amplifies errors most along one direction of the secret’s space, the one belonging to the smallest singular value. Independent normal noise points in all directions equally, so only a small part of it falls along that direction. A worst-direction curator gives every answer an error of the full size \(E\). title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
section: 17.6 The Fundamental Law of Information Recovery
text:
17.6 The Fundamental Law of Information Recovery
The attacks so far say when answers are too accurate. Two questions remain. Is an error of order \(\sqrt n\) really enough to stop reconstruction, or is it just where the proofs stop? And how many queries does any attack need? This section answers both.
To show that an error of order \(\sqrt n\) can stop reconstruction, you need a curator whose errors are that small yet hide many bits completely. A sampling curator does this. It fixes a sampling probability \(p\) and draws a secret sample of the people, keeping each person independently with that probability. It answers every query from the people in the sample only, and divides by \(p\) so that each answer is correct on average. The error of one answer is then a sum of independent terms with mean zero, one per person, so it is of order \(\sqrt n\). Hoeffding’s inequality (Concentration inequalities) bounds that error for one query, and the union bound extends it to all \(m\) queries at once. With probability at least \(1 - \eta\), every answer has error at most \[\sqrt{\frac{n\ln(2m/\eta)}{2p^2}}. \tag{17.9}\]
People outside the sample never affect any answer, so the answers reveal nothing about their bits. Suppose the secret bits are uniformly random. To the attacker, the bit of a person outside the sample is then a fair coin, and any guess about it is right half the time. At best the attacker gets everyone in the sample right. The expected fraction it recovers is therefore at most \(p + \frac{1 - p}{2}\), which is three quarters when \(p = \frac12\).
This curator shows that an error of order \(\sqrt n\) can be enough. The full edition’s script runs it in the setting of Table 17.3, keeping each person with probability one half, and it keeps 250 people. The largest error over all the queries is 28.00, or \(1.25\sqrt n\). The Hoeffding bound Equation 17.9 at \(\eta = 0.05\) is 106.25, which is loose because it assumes the widest spread each term could have. Least squares on these answers recovers 0.7560 of the bits, right at the ceiling of three quarters. The sampling curator’s error is only a logarithmic factor above the error the attacks need. So an error of order \(\sqrt n\) is necessary to stop reconstruction, and it can be enough.
But stopping reconstruction is not privacy. The same curator’s answers are exact sums over its sample, scaled up by \(1/p\). An attacker with enough queries therefore learns every sampled person’s bit, because least squares recovers each such bit divided by \(p\). Half the people are fully exposed so that the other half can be fully hidden. Stopping blatant reconstruction is a much weaker goal than protecting everyone. The definition of differential privacy gives a guarantee that holds for every individual.
The sampling curator also shows why the source of the errors matters, not just their size. Compare it with a curator that adds an independent random error of the same size to each answer. That curator is not as safe. Its errors are independent across queries, so least squares averages them away as the attacker asks more. The sampling curator’s errors all come from one secret sample, shared by every answer, so asking more never reveals the people left out.
How few queries can any attack use? To answer, count bits of information, with the tools of Information theory. Suppose the secret is \(n\) uniformly random bits, so that it carries \(n\) bits of information. Write \(V\) for the largest number of different values that one answer can take, which is \(n + 1\) for exact counts of up to \(n\) people. An answer with that many values carries at most \(\log_2V\) bits, so the \(m\) answers together carry at most \(m\log_2V\) bits. The argument treats the queries as fixed in advance, so that only the answers carry information about the secret.
A guess that is wrong on some bits still leaves the attacker uncertain about the secret. The binary entropy \(h(\beta) = -\beta\log_2\beta - (1 - \beta)\log_2(1 - \beta)\) is the uncertainty, in bits, of a coin that comes up heads with probability \(\beta\). Fano’s inequality says how much a good guess can leave unknown. A guess that is wrong on an expected fraction \(\beta\) of the bits, with \(\beta\) at most one half, leaves at most \(n\,h(\beta)\) bits of uncertainty about the secret. The secret carries \(n\) bits, so the guess must carry the rest, at least \(n(1 - h(\beta))\) bits. The data processing inequality says that a guess computed from the answers cannot carry more information about the secret than the answers themselves. Combining the two counts, any attack needs at least \[m \ge \frac{n\,(1 - h(\beta))}{\log_2V} \tag{17.10}\] queries.
Take a thousand people and allow 5% wrong bits. The binary entropy of that fraction is 0.2864, so the answers must still supply 0.7136 bits per person. An exact count takes one of 1001 values, so it carries at most about 9.97 bits. Dividing one by the other, the bound asks for at least 71.6 queries. Coarser answers take fewer values and carry fewer bits each, so they raise the floor. Rounding every count to a multiple of 10 leaves about a hundred values and raises the floor to 106.9 queries. Rounding to multiples of 32 raises it to 141.5. These floors hold for any attack, whatever its running time. They are not a defence, though, because an attacker can simply ask more queries.
The bound also shows that the attacks use nearly as few queries as possible. With exact counts, the bound grows like \(n/\log n\), while least squares with exact answers uses \(n\) queries, only a logarithmic factor more. The bound needs answers that take finitely many values, because a real-valued answer could carry unlimited information in its low-order digits. Any published table has finite precision, so the condition holds in practice.
So a defence must control both halves of the law, the error scale and the number of answers. That is why the privacy definition of Part 3 tracks a budget spent across all the queries.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.7 Reconstructing a census block
National statistical offices publish many tables computed from the same confidential records. A table might give counts by age, sex and race for every block, or the same counts by household type, or medians and means. Each table cell is a query. Garfinkel, Abowd and Martindale (2019) built a toy block of seven people. They showed that a modest set of published statistics can determine every person’s age, sex, race and marital status, and that a constraint solver finds the solution in seconds. The full edition repeats this experiment with a block of its own, as a reconstruction game whose queries are the published tables.
The fictional block has seven people. Each person has a sex, a race that is Black or White, a marital status, and an age in whole years from 0 to 99. Nobody under 18 is married. Table 17.5 is everything the agency publishes about the block. The means are given to two decimals, which is enough to recover the sum of ages in each group exactly. A sum of ages is a whole number, and \(34.29 \times 7 = 240.03\), so the seven ages total 240.

The women’s and men’s medians and means leave 14,790 candidate age vectors, and the overall median keeps 12,906 of them. Each of these already splits into four women and three men, because it was built from their lists. The decoder then tests the other two splits separately. Only 387 vectors can be split into Black and White people who match the race statistics. Only 33 can be split into married and single people who match the marital statistics. In total, eighteen published numbers determine the age, sex, race and marital status of all seven people.
Withholding one number rarely helps. Figure 17.5 repeats the search with each of the twelve medians and means withheld in turn. Eight of the twelve leave the block uniquely determined, because the remaining statistics either imply the missing one or pin the block down without it. The female mean, for example, adds nothing, since the total and male sums imply it.






Figure 17.5: Number of seven-person blocks consistent with Table 17.5 when one median or mean is withheld (log scale). Blue bars: the block is still unique. Red bars: a few candidates remain, still far fewer than the possible blocks.



Withholding the married mean hurts the attacker most, because it is the only statistic about the single people’s ages. Without it, neither the married sum nor the single sum, which is the total minus the married sum, is known. Even so, only 45 blocks remain, and 51% of them have the true sex, race and marital pattern of all seven people.
Real publications are more exposed than this toy, not less, because their tables overlap. They cross-classify many variables at many geographic levels, so the same people appear in thousands of cells. That is exactly the “too many questions” half of the Fundamental Law. The usual protections also leave most constraints exact. The main protection of the 2010 Census swapped a small fraction of households between blocks, which changes some answers and leaves the rest exact. Coarsening ages into bands and suppressing small cells, common in other tables, have the same weakness. They remove some constraints, and the remaining ones still hold exactly.
The attack also works at full scale. Abowd (2021) described the Census Bureau’s own reconstruction of the 2010 Census. It rebuilt a record for each of the 308,745,538 people counted. Each record gave a block, sex, age, race and ethnicity, and about 46% of them matched a real person exactly on all five fields. Linking them to commercial data confirmed the identity of about 17% of the population. The Bureau responded by moving the 2020 Census to a method based on the privacy definition of Part 3.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.8 Code
To audit a query system or plan a release, three numbers come first. You want the fraction of bits that least squares would recover at your noise level, and how many queries per person push that fraction to a target. You also want the fewest queries any attack needs, and the snippet below computes all three. It uses the finite-sample variance \(4\sigma^2 n/((n + 1)(m - n - 1))\) from the full edition’s derivation, which is about \(4\sigma^2/(m - n)\).
from math import log2, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist

PHI = NormalDist()


def ls_recovered(n: int, m: int, sigma: float) -> float:
    """Predicted fraction of n secret bits that least squares recovers from m noisy random subset sums."""
    sd = 2 * sigma * sqrt(n / ((n + 1) * (m - n - 1)))  # spread of each decoded bit's error
    return PHI.cdf(0.5 / sd)  # a bit comes out wrong when its error crosses 1/2


def queries_per_person(target: float, sigma_over_sqrt_n: float) -> float:
    """m/n at which least squares recovers a fraction `target` of the bits, for noise sigma = c * sqrt(n)."""
    return 1 + (4 * sigma_over_sqrt_n * PHI.inv_cdf(target)) ** 2


def binary_entropy(p: float) -> float:
    return -p * log2(p) - (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)


def min_queries(n: int, wrong: float, values: int) -> float:
    """Fewest answers, each taking at most `values` values, from which any attack gets all but n * wrong bits."""
    return n * (1 - binary_entropy(wrong)) / log2(values)


n, m = 500, 2000
print(" ".join(f"{ls_recovered(n, m, c * sqrt(n)):.4f}" for c in (0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)))  # 1.0000 0.9585 0.8069 0.6676 0.5858
print(f"{queries_per_person(0.9, 2.0):.1f}")  # 106.1
print(f"{min_queries(1000, 0.05, 1001):.1f}")  # 71.6
print(f"{min_queries(1000, 0.05, 1000 // 10 + 2):.1f}")  # 106.9
print(f"{min_queries(1000, 0.05, 1000 // 32 + 2):.1f}")  # 141.5
The first line is the prediction row of Table 17.3. The last two lines count the values of an answer rounded to multiples of a width \(w\) as \(\lfloor n/w\rfloor + 2\), as the full edition’s script does. This may count one value too many, which only lowers the bound, so the floor stays valid. The full edition’s script, reconstruction.py, runs the attacks themselves.
uv run python code/part02-attacks/reconstruction.py

Rules of thumb

The threat scale of a random subset-sum query is \(\sqrt n\), and of the worst query \(n\). Errors well below that scale reveal the database.
Independent noise per answer is averaged away by more answers. Budget the error over all answers, not per answer.
Rounding, swapping and suppression are not noise, because an attacker can simulate them or work around them.
Stopping reconstruction is not privacy. Ask what the system guarantees for each individual.

text:
17.10 Further reading

Dinur & Nissim, “Revealing Information while Preserving Privacy” (PODS 2003): the original attacks and the notion of blatant non-privacy.
Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), ch. 8: the reconstruction attacks as lower bounds, and the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery.
Dwork, Smith, Steinke & Ullman, “Exposed! A Survey of Attacks on Private Data” (Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application, 2017): a readable survey of reconstruction and tracing attacks.
Garfinkel, Abowd & Martindale, “Understanding Database Reconstruction Attacks on Public Data” (CACM 2019): the seven-person block reconstructed with a solver.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter, except these, which it cites: the size of the smallest singular value of a random query matrix, the finite-sample correction to the least-squares variance (exact for normal query rows, an approximation checked by simulation in the full edition), Dinur and Nissim’s original proof with \(n(\log n)^2\) queries, the sharper analyses with a number of queries proportional to \(n\), the decoder of Dwork, McSherry and Talwar, the solver experiment of Garfinkel, Abowd and Martindale, the description of the 2010 Census swapping, and the reported attacks of Cohen and Nissim and of the Census Bureau.

title: Differential privacy foundations
text:
Who this part is for
The previous part showed that models and statistics leak: membership, attributes, training text, whole datasets. Each attack found a difference between what a system releases with your record and without it. This part introduces the defence the rest of the book is built on, differential privacy (DP), which makes that difference provably small, and takes it far enough for you to build a private release, check one somebody else built, and say what it costs. The finer tools for thousands of training steps come in the next part.
Read it if you build, review or audit a system that publishes statistics or trains models on personal data and claims a privacy guarantee. A claim such as “trained with \(\varepsilon = 8\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)” is only useful if you can say what it promises and to whom, check the noise behind it, and spot the mistakes that silently void it. The part assumes the attack games of Threat models and attacks and a little probability from the Prerequisites: the Laplace and normal distributions, and the error rates of a test.

title: Differential privacy foundations
text:
The common thread
A randomized algorithm is differentially private when changing one person’s record changes the probability of any output by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), up to a small slack \(\delta\). The whole part reads that sentence in three ways, each answering a practical question.
Read as a bound on every attack, it tells you what the guarantee is worth. An attacker asking whether you are in the data ends by saying yes or no, and the definition caps how much more often they can say yes when it is true than when it is false. So a membership attack’s true positive rate is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times its false positive rate, plus \(\delta\), whatever the attacker knows and however much they compute. That is how you turn \(\varepsilon\) into something a risk owner understands, and, run backwards, how an attack can prove a claimed \(\varepsilon\) wrong.
Read as a recipe for mechanisms, it tells you how to build a release. If one record can move an answer by at most some amount, its sensitivity, then noise that is wide compared with that amount makes the two worlds look alike. The size of the noise follows from the sensitivity and \(\varepsilon\), so most of the work is bounding how far one record can move the answer and choosing the cheapest noise that hides it.
Read as a budget to spend, it tells you how guarantees combine. Anything computed from a private output is free, because computing cannot add evidence the output didn’t contain. But every new look at the data adds its own evidence, so privacy losses add up over releases, and over the many records one person may own.

title: Differential privacy foundations
text:
How to read this part
The chapters follow the order in which those questions come up when you build something. The definition comes first, because every later claim is checked against it. Post-processing, group privacy and composition comes next: they let you prove each building block once and assemble a system from blocks. Then the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms give the two building blocks almost everything else uses. Advanced and optimal composition then revisits the budget, because adding up losses is safe but far too pessimistic for many releases; its exact accounting is what the next part builds on.
The next two chapters cover what noise on a number does not: selection, where the output is a choice among options, and data whose worst case is far from typical, where noise sized for the worst case would drown the answer. Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms is short and practical: a mechanism private on paper can leak through how a computer draws random numbers, so read it before implementing one. Local, shuffle and distributed trust models asks who sees the raw data. Lower bounds comes last because it closes the loop with the previous part’s attacks: it says how much accuracy any private release must lose, and so when a privacy target and an accuracy target cannot both be met.
Each chapter starts from the practical question, explains every result with the reason it holds and a worked example, and ends with a cheat sheet. The derivations are in the full edition, linked at the end of each chapter.

title: Differential privacy foundations
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
By the end of this part you will be able to state a DP guarantee with its neighbouring relation and unit of privacy, and translate a claimed \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) into a cap on what an attacker can achieve. You will be able to compute the sensitivity of a query, calibrate Laplace and Gaussian noise exactly, add up the cost of a pipeline, and choose a \(\delta\) that doesn’t hide a catastrophe. You will know which mechanism fits a selection problem or data with a heavy worst case, why naive floating-point noise is not private, what the local and shuffle models buy, and what accuracy no private mechanism can beat.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.1 Why this matters
Every attack in Threat models and attacks worked the same way. The attacker looked at what a system released and asked which of two worlds produced it: the one where a given person’s record was in the data, or the one where it was not. Membership inference asks this about a trained model, reconstruction asks it about a table of statistics, and each succeeded because the output looked different enough in the two worlds for a test to tell them apart.
So the defence has to make the two worlds look alike, not just to today’s attacks but to every test anyone could run. Differential privacy (DP) is that requirement written down. It is a property of the algorithm that produces the release, so you can check it before any data are touched, and it holds whatever the attacker knows or computes.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.2 What “one person” means
The guarantee compares two datasets that differ in one person, and the neighbouring relation says what that means. There are two standard choices. Under add/remove, the second dataset is the first with one record added or taken away. The attacker’s question is then “is this person in the data at all?”, which is exactly the membership question, and the dataset’s size is private too. Under replace, both datasets have the same size and one record’s value is swapped for another. Now the attacker is assumed to know who is in the data, and the guarantee only hides what their record says.
Replacing Alice’s record by Dan’s is removing Alice and then adding Dan: two add/remove steps, each allowed to shift the output by the guaranteed amount. So \(\varepsilon\) under add/remove becomes \(2\varepsilon\) under replace. The reverse fails, because a replace guarantee never compares datasets of different sizes: publishing the number of records is perfectly private under replace and not private at all under add/remove.
You can see the factor of 2 in a histogram of smokers and non-smokers, noised for \(\varepsilon = 1\) per record. Removing Carol changes one bar by one, and the largest privacy loss (defined in the next section) is 1.0000. Changing Alice’s answer from smoker to non-smoker moves two bars at once, one down and one up, and the loss doubles to 2.0000.
The second choice is what a record is. If each training example is a record, the guarantee protects each example. A person who wrote 200 messages is then 200 records, and hiding the person means hiding all 200 at once, which the guarantee covers only at a much higher price (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). So always ask of a claimed \(\varepsilon\): per what? The answer should be the unit you care about, usually the person.
Neighbours range over every record the data format allows, including a person aged 900. A mechanism must hide even that one, which is why private algorithms clip their inputs first.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.3 The definition
Run a randomized algorithm \(M\), called a mechanism, on neighbouring datasets \(D\) and \(D'\), and look at an output \(y\). The natural measure of what \(y\) reveals is how much more likely it is in one world than in the other. Its logarithm is the privacy loss, \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}, \tag{18.1}\] where \(p_{M(D)}(y)\) is the probability (or density) of output \(y\) on dataset \(D\). A loss of 0 tells the attacker nothing; a loss of 3 means the output is \(e^3 \approx 20\) times more likely with the record, which is strong evidence.
Why a ratio and not a difference? A change from 0.50 to 0.51 and one from 0 to 0.01 are the same difference, but the second creates an output possible only when the person is present, which identifies them with certainty. Only a ratio, infinite here, catches it.
Differential privacy bounds this ratio. \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differentially private if for every pair of neighbours and every set \(S\) of outputs, \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{18.2}\] The probabilities are over the mechanism’s randomness, with the data fixed. With \(\delta = 0\) this is pure DP: no event becomes more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times more likely, which is the same as saying the privacy loss of every single output is at most \(\varepsilon\). At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) an event of probability 0.5 in one world has probability at most \(0.5e^{0.1} = 0.553\) in the other, so the release barely moves anyone’s odds.
Pure DP is too strict for some useful mechanisms. With Gaussian noise, far-out outputs are much more likely in one world than the other, because the normal density falls off faster than any fixed ratio can follow. Those outputs are astronomically rare, and \(\delta\) is the allowance for them: the ratio bound may fail, but only on outputs whose total excess probability is at most \(\delta\). This is approximate DP.
The way \(\delta\) is counted matters in practice. The definition allows each output’s probability \(p\) in one world to be up to \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability \(q\) in the other, and only the excess, \(p - e^\varepsilon q\), has to be paid for by \(\delta\). An output with loss \(L\) has \(p = e^L q\), so the excess is a fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\) of its probability: close to zero when \(L\) is just above \(\varepsilon\), close to all of it when \(L\) is huge. The smallest valid \(\delta\), computed this way, is the hockey-stick divergence between the two output distributions. So \(\delta\) is not “the probability that privacy fails”: that probability is larger, because it counts outputs just over the line in full. For a count released with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), that probability is \(4.006\times10^{-2}\) while the true \(\delta\) is \(6.830\times10^{-3}\), nearly six times smaller (Figure 18.1). If you calibrate with the tail probability, you add noise you didn’t need.






Figure 18.1: The definition as a picture, for a count released with noise at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The shaded band runs from \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) to \(e^\varepsilon\) times the output density on \(D'\) (orange). Left: with Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\), the density on \(D\) (blue) stays inside the band, so the release is pure DP. Right: with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2, it leaves the band in the tail, and the red mass is what \(\delta\) must cover.



Ask for a larger \(\varepsilon\) and fewer outputs exceed it, so the required \(\delta\) shrinks: for the Gaussian count above, \(\delta\) falls from \(6.830\times10^{-3}\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) to \(3.401\times10^{-10}\) at \(\varepsilon = 3\). A mechanism therefore has a whole privacy curve \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), and any single pair you quote is one point on it. Report the mechanism’s parameters along with the pair, because the accountants of Part 4 combine curves, not points.
Never check approximate DP output by output: the slack is shared across a whole event. Two datasets whose outputs are spread over 1,000 disjoint values pass that check with \(\delta = 0.0010\), yet one look at any output reveals the dataset, and the true \(\delta\) is 1.0000.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.4 Randomized response
The oldest mechanism shows how privacy and useful statistics coexist. To learn what fraction of people did something embarrassing, ask each person to flip a coin in private: on heads, answer truthfully; on tails, flip again and answer “yes” on heads, “no” on tails. Any single “yes” might be a coin, so it proves nothing about the person. But the coins behave predictably over many people, so the fraction can be recovered.
This scheme reports the truth with probability \(t = 0.75\). A “yes” is then 0.75/0.25 = 3 times more likely from someone whose true answer is yes than from someone whose answer is no, and no report has a larger ratio, so this is pure DP with \(\varepsilon = \ln 3 = 1.0986\). In general, randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) tells the truth with probability \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), chosen so that the ratio is exactly \(e^\varepsilon\).
The lying pulls the share \(\bar y\) of “yes” reports towards one half by a known amount, and undoing that pull gives an unbiased estimate of the true fraction \(\pi\), \[\hat\pi = \frac{\bar y - (1 - t)}{2t - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) \approx \frac{1}{\varepsilon\sqrt n}\ \text{ for small } \varepsilon. \tag{18.3}\] The cost of privacy is visible in the denominator. When \(\varepsilon\) is small, \(t\) is close to one half, the reports are nearly pure coin flips, and \(2t - 1\) is small; dividing by it blows up the noise. Halving \(\varepsilon\) roughly doubles the error, and since error falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), you need four times as many people to win it back.
In a survey of 1,000 people with true fraction 0.3, the estimate’s standard deviation is 0.0274 at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\), about twice the 0.0145 of an ordinary survey of that size. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) it is 0.0626, and at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) it is 0.316, larger than the fraction being measured (Figure 18.2).






Figure 18.2: Left: randomized response at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) as output probabilities; each report is 3 times more likely under one true answer than under the other. Right: estimates of the fraction of “yes” from 4,000 simulated surveys of 1,000 people with true fraction 0.3, at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), with the normal curves the standard-deviation formula predicts.



Because each person randomizes before their answer leaves them, nobody needs to be trusted. That is the local model, and the large error is its price; a trusted curator who noises the aggregate once does far better, and Local, shuffle and distributed trust models compares the options.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.5 What \(\varepsilon\) means for an attacker
Whatever an attacker does, they end by deciding “in” or “out”, and the set of outputs on which they say “in” is an event. So the definition bounds how much more often they can say “in” when it is true than when it is false.
Write the attacker’s true positive rate (TPR) for how often they say “in” when the person is in, and their false positive rate (FPR) for how often they say “in” when the person is out. Applying Equation 18.2 to their “in” event gives, for every possible attack, \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta. \tag{18.4}\] This is the form to remember: an attacker who must rarely accuse wrongly keeps the FPR small, and the bound then caps the TPR at a small multiple of it. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), no attack reaches a TPR above 0.002728 at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\).
Read backwards, the same inequality turns an attack into an audit. If someone claims a model is \((2, 10^{-5})\)-DP and you run an attack that reaches a TPR of 0.05 at an FPR of 0.001, the claim cannot be right: the cap at that FPR is 0.0074. Solving for \(\varepsilon\) shows the attack proves \(\varepsilon \ge 3.91\) (Section 18.8). Audits use canaries, records planted to be as easy to detect as possible, because an ordinary record would give a much weaker bound.
Two other readings follow from the same bound. Averaged over a fair coin for “in” or “out”, an attacker’s advantage, \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\), is at most \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) under pure DP, about \(\varepsilon/2\) when \(\varepsilon\) is small. And because one output can change the likelihood ratio by at most \(e^\varepsilon\), it can multiply anyone’s odds that the person is in by at most \(e^\varepsilon\), whatever they believed before (Table 18.1).

These readings also show where the guarantee weakens. At \(\varepsilon = 5\) the advantage bound is 0.9866, an attacker right 99.3% of the time: a model trained at \(\varepsilon = 8\) may resist real attacks, but the guarantee no longer promises it. And the release bounds the change in a belief, not the belief: an adversary already 99% sure from other sources stays about that sure.
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.6 How small \(\delta\) must be
A deliberately terrible mechanism shows how small \(\delta\) must be. Publish each record, in full, with probability \(\delta\). Any one person is exposed only with probability \(\delta\), and otherwise the output ignores them, so this is \((0, \delta)\)-DP.
But it publishes \(n\delta\) records on average, and at least one with probability about \(1 - e^{-n\delta}\). With \(n = 10{,}000\) and \(\delta = 1/n\), someone’s record is published verbatim with probability 0.6321. So \(\delta\) must be much smaller than \(1/n\), where \(n\) counts people, not records. The common choice of \(10^{-5}\) for 60,000 training examples is only just below \(1/n\), and 10 million users need \(\delta\) well below \(10^{-7}\).
This usually costs little: reasonable mechanisms, like the Gaussian count, spread \(\delta\) over many outputs of moderate loss, so their privacy curve falls steeply and a slightly larger \(\varepsilon\) buys a much smaller \(\delta\).
crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.7 What differential privacy does not protect
text:
18.7 What differential privacy does not protect
The guarantee compares the world with your record to the world without it, so anything learned in both worlds is outside it. If a study shows that smokers often get cancer, beliefs about every smoker change, including those never in the data; that is the study doing its job.
It also treats records as separate. If five people in a household always answer alike, an attacker who learns one answer learns all five, and hiding the household means hiding five records at once. For a count released with Laplace noise at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per record, the household’s privacy loss can reach 5.0000, and an attacker asking whether the household took part can be right with probability up to 0.959. Match the unit of privacy to the unit of correlation: protect households or users, not rows.
Finally, a DP proof covers the algorithm, not the code: floating-point noise samplers can leak through their low-order bits (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms), and timing can leak. The implementation needs its own review.
