title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.1 Why this matters
A private mechanism is never the whole system. You round its output and train models on it, your users each contributed fifty records, and an analyst asks a hundred queries or a training run takes thousands of noisy steps. Which of these cost privacy, and how do the costs add up? Three properties of differential privacy (DP) answer that without a new proof for every pipeline: you prove each building block once, then add up the costs.
All three follow from one quantity, the privacy loss of The definition of differential privacy: the log of how much more likely an output is when the data are \(D\) than when they are a neighbouring dataset \(D'\), one record different. Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP keeps it between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\) for every output. The one idea of this chapter is that privacy losses add along a path of datasets or across a sequence of mechanisms, and only average under processing. Each section applies it to one situation.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.2 Post-processing
Suppose you transform a private output: round it, threshold it, fit a model to it. Several raw outputs can lead to the same processed one, and the probability of the processed output is the sum of theirs. So its likelihood ratio between the two datasets is a weighted average of their ratios. If every raw ratio lies between \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) and \(e^\varepsilon\), an average of them does too. Processing pools evidence, and pooling can only dilute it. This data processing inequality gives the rule: if \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP and \(f\) is any function that does not read the data, deterministic or with its own coins, then publishing \(f(M(D))\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP too. Its whole privacy curve \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) lies on or below that of \(M\).
Collect a randomized-response answer at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), which tells the truth with probability \(\frac34\), so each report is 3 times more likely under one true answer than under the other. Before publishing, flip it with probability \(\frac14\) using a fresh coin. A published 1 can come from a kept 1, whose ratio is 3, or from a flipped 0, whose ratio is \(\frac13\), and the two paths carry equal weight. The published 1 therefore has ratio \(\frac12(3 + \frac13) = \frac53\): it has probability 0.625 when the true bit is 1 and 0.375 when it is 0. The release is \(\ln\frac53 = 0.5108\)-DP, well below the original \(\ln 3 = 1.0986\), because the coin mixed outputs that pointed in opposite directions.
Processing you do for utility rarely mixes like that. Rounding a count with Laplace noise of scale 1 to an integer leaves its pure \(\varepsilon\) at 1.0000: a rounding cell that lies entirely below both possible counts holds outputs that all have the same loss, and an average of equal ratios is that ratio. Keeping only whether the noisy count exceeds \(\frac12\) merges outputs with losses of both signs, and lowers \(\varepsilon\) to 0.8318 (Figure 19.1). So report the guarantee of \(M\) and treat any gain from processing as a bonus you don’t count on.






Figure 19.1: Left: the privacy curve \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) of a count with Laplace noise of scale 1 (black), after rounding (blue), and after keeping only whether it exceeds \(\frac12\) (orange); processing only lowers the curve. Right: randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) followed by a fresh coin that flips the answer with probability \(f\); the dot is \(f = \frac14\), where \(\varepsilon = \ln\frac53\).



The argument has one condition. The averaging used the same processing under \(D\) and under \(D'\), and that holds only if \(f\) never looks at the data. “Take the noisy top category, then report its exact count” fails it: the second step reads the data, so it is a new mechanism, and a non-private one. Within it, the rule is powerful: a model trained on DP statistics, synthetic data from a DP model and a dashboard are all post-processing, and so is every attack of Threat models and attacks, since an attacker’s guess is a function of the output, so the definition’s bounds hold even against attacks invented later. That is why a DP system privatizes at one narrow point, such as noisy counts or noisy gradients, and treats everything after it as public.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.3 Group privacy
The definition protects one record, but a user may own fifty messages, and a household shares an address and an income. To cover datasets that differ in \(k\) records, walk from \(D\) to the other dataset one record at a time, through \(k\) neighbouring pairs. Each step can multiply an event’s probability by at most \(e^\varepsilon\), so \(k\) steps multiply it by at most \(e^{k\varepsilon}\): pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP becomes \(k\varepsilon\)-DP for the group.
The slack grows faster. Each step adds its own \(\delta\), and every later step multiplies everything accumulated so far, including the earlier \(\delta\)s, by \(e^\varepsilon\) again. So the \(\delta\)s pile up in a geometric sum. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is, for datasets \(k\) records apart, \[\Big(k\varepsilon,\ \delta_k\Big)\text{-DP}, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{19.1}\] Some mechanisms attain this bound exactly, so no better rule holds for every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism.
The price is steep. A per-record guarantee of \((0.5, 10^{-5})\) gives a user with 10 records \((5, 2.272 \times 10^{-3})\). A particular mechanism can do better than the general bound: for a count with Gaussian noise, ten records just shift the count by ten instead of one, and its exact guarantee for that user is \((5, 7.592 \times 10^{-4})\). That is still weak. At \(\varepsilon = 1\), a group of 10 multiplies \(\delta\) by 12818.3, and \(\delta\) had to be far below one over the number of people to begin with (The definition of differential privacy), so the group guarantee is often vacuous. Pure DP fares no better: \(0.1\)-DP per record is \(10\)-DP for a user with 100 records.
So if you care about users, don’t patch a per-record guarantee with group privacy: define neighbours as datasets that differ in one user’s records, bound each user’s contribution, and prove DP at that level directly. Group privacy is the fallback when you cannot.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.4 Sequential composition
Now run several mechanisms on the same data, each with fresh noise, and let the adversary see the whole transcript of outputs. Because the noise draws are independent, the probability of a transcript is the product of the probabilities of its parts, so its privacy loss, a logarithm, is the sum of theirs. So if each \(M_i\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP, releasing all their outputs is \[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\Big)\text{-DP}. \tag{19.2}\] This is basic composition. Unlike group privacy, the \(\delta\)s add plainly, because every mechanism compares the same pair of datasets: there is no chain of steps to multiply them through.
The argument only needed each mechanism to be private whatever the earlier outputs were, so the rule also covers adaptive composition, where an analyst picks each query after reading the last answer, as long as each query’s budget \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) is fixed in advance. If the budgets themselves depend on the answers (“keep going until the estimate looks good”), Equation 19.2 no longer applies in general; that needs privacy filters, covered in Advanced and optimal composition. Pure DP is the exception: each step’s privacy loss is at most its \(\varepsilon_i\) at every output, so the losses still add up to at most \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) whatever order the budgets were chosen in.
Basic composition is the true worst case, but that case is rare. Ask one person the same yes/no question \(k\) times, each with fresh randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\). The transcript in which every answer is truthful has loss exactly \(k\ln 3\), so no smaller pure \(\varepsilon\) holds. But that transcript has probability \((\frac34)^k\). Typical transcripts mix truthful answers, which add \(\ln 3\) to the loss, with lies, which subtract it, and the two partly cancel: the mean loss is half the bound (Figure 19.2). A sum of \(k\) independent bounded terms spreads only like \(\sqrt k\) around its mean, so if you allow a small \(\delta\) to write off the rare extreme transcripts, the \(\varepsilon\) you need is the mean plus a margin that grows like \(\sqrt k\). The mean per answer is \(\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\), about \(\varepsilon_0^2/2\) when \(\varepsilon_0\) is small, so for small per-step budgets the margin dominates and \(\varepsilon\) grows roughly like \(\sqrt k\) instead of \(k\). At \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\) and \(k = 1000\) answers, basic composition gives 100, while the exact \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) is 19.345. Ten counts with Gaussian noise, each \((0.5, 10^{-5})\)-DP, cost \((5, 10^{-4})\) by basic composition, while their exact \(\varepsilon\) at that \(\delta\) is 1.504.






Figure 19.2: Distribution of the privacy loss of 10 randomized-response answers at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) each, when the true bit is 1 (blue) or 0 (orange). The basic bound \(10\ln 3\) is reached, but only with probability \((3/4)^{10} = 0.056\); the mean under the first dataset is half of it.



So basic composition suits a handful of releases. It already overstates the ten Gaussian counts by a factor of 3.3, and for thousands of training steps it is useless: you need the accountants of Advanced and optimal composition and Part 4, which exploit exactly this cancellation.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.5 Parallel composition
If each mechanism sees a different, disjoint part of the data, one person’s record lands in only one part. The other parts get identical inputs in both worlds, so their outputs contribute zero privacy loss, and only the part that changed costs anything. Split the universe of possible records into disjoint parts by a rule fixed in advance, run \(M_i\) on the records in part \(i\) with independent noise, and suppose each \(M_i\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP under add/remove, where neighbours differ by one record added or removed. Then the whole release is \[\big(\max_i\varepsilon_i,\ \max_i\delta_i\big)\text{-DP under add/remove}. \tag{19.3}\]
This is why a histogram costs one \(\varepsilon\), not one per bin. Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on each bin is \(\varepsilon\)-DP however many bins there are; for two bins the full edition’s script finds exactly 1.0000 at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The same reasoning is why local randomized response stays \(\ln 3\)-DP however many people answer: each report depends only on its owner’s answer, so changing one person’s answer changes one report. That is a replace guarantee; under add/remove, the number of reports itself reveals who took part.
The neighbouring relation matters here. Under replace, where one record’s value is changed, a record can move from one bin to another, and then two parts see a difference: the two-bin histogram becomes 2.0000-DP. That is why a histogram’s sensitivity is quoted as 2 under replace (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). When each part is a fixed slot, as each person is in local randomized response, a replacement changes one slot only and the maximum applies again.
The argument also needs the partition to be fixed before the data are seen. “The top 10% of earners and the rest” moves its boundary when one high earner is added, which can shift other records across it and change both parts, so more than one mechanism sees a difference. Use fixed bins, or treat a data-dependent split as a mechanism of its own.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.6 What composes and what doesn’t
Each property rests on an assumption that its argument used: post-processing needs the processing to ignore the data, composition needs independent noise and the same neighbouring relation at every step, and both need budgets fixed in advance. Most real failures break one of them, and badly.
Shared noise is the clearest case. Release the number of smokers and the number of smokers aged 40 or over, adding the same Laplace draw \(Z\) to both. Each release alone is 1-DP. But subtracting one from the other cancels \(Z\) and leaves the exact number of smokers under 40, which changes when Alice, a smoker aged 30, is removed. Composition assumed the transcript’s probability is a product of independent parts; with one shared draw it is not, and one release can undo the other’s noise. In 200,000 simulated runs, an attacker who subtracts the two releases is right about Alice every time, an accuracy of 1.0000. With fresh noise for each count the same attack reaches 0.6206, and no attack can beat 0.6967.
In code, the bug hides in two mechanisms seeded with the same random seed, a cached noise value re-added to a related query, or noise reused across the shards of a distributed system. Returning the same noisy answer to a repeated identical query is fine, because that is post-processing of one release. An exact statistic published elsewhere is the same mistake in another form: it can be differenced against your DP release just as the two counts were, and the guarantee covers only what your mechanism released. Finally, a guarantee proved under add/remove costs up to twice as much under replace, because a replacement is a removal plus an addition, so mixing the two relations inside one accountant is a factor-2 bug.
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.7 Code
Group privacy is where hand calculations go wrong most often, because \(\delta\) does not simply scale by \(k\). This snippet computes the three budget rules of this chapter:
from math import exp


def group_privacy(eps: float, delta: float, k: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """The guarantee for a group of k records, from an (eps, delta) guarantee per record."""
    delta_k = delta * sum(exp(j * eps) for j in range(k))
    return k * eps, delta_k


def basic_composition(budgets: list[tuple[float, float]]) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """The guarantee of several mechanisms run on the same data with fresh noise."""
    return sum(e for e, _ in budgets), sum(d for _, d in budgets)


def parallel_composition(budgets: list[tuple[float, float]]) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """The guarantee of mechanisms run on disjoint parts of the data, under add/remove."""
    return max(e for e, _ in budgets), max(d for _, d in budgets)


eps_k, delta_k = group_privacy(0.5, 1e-5, 10)
print(f"{eps_k:.1f} {delta_k:.3e}")  # 5.0 2.272e-03
print(f"{group_privacy(0.5, 1e-5, 2)[1]:.3e}")  # 2.649e-05
print(f"{group_privacy(1.0, 1.0, 10)[1]:.1f}")  # 12818.3
print(basic_composition([(0.5, 1e-5)] * 10))  # (5.0, 0.0001)
print(parallel_composition([(0.5, 0.0)] * 50))  # (0.5, 0.0)
The third line is the factor by which \(\delta\) grows for a group of 10 at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Basic composition here is a valid upper bound only; for the exact cost of many Gaussian releases, use an accountant. The full edition’s script checks every number in this chapter by exact computation and simulation:
uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/properties.py

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.1 Why this matters
You want to publish a statistic with a differential privacy (DP) guarantee: a count, a mean, a histogram, or a gradient during training. The definition of differential privacy says what the release must satisfy: on two neighbouring datasets \(D\) and \(D'\), which differ in one person’s record, every set \(S\) of outputs must have \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta\). Almost every DP system builds such a release the same way: compute the exact answer \(f(D)\), add fresh random noise \(Z\), and publish \[M(D) = f(D) + Z. \tag{20.1}\]
The one idea of this chapter is what this does to the privacy loss, the log of how much more likely an output is under \(D\) than under \(D'\). On the two datasets the mechanism places the same noise around two different centres, \(f(D)\) and \(f(D')\). So the privacy loss is the log-ratio of the noise density and a copy of itself shifted by the change one record makes, and it depends on two things: how big that shift can be, and how the log of the noise density falls off. The Laplace density’s log falls off in a straight line, which bounds the loss everywhere and gives pure DP. The normal density’s log falls off like a parabola, which leaves the loss unbounded but large only on rare outputs, and gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. The sections follow the decisions in order: sensitivity, which noise, and how much.
crumbs: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.2 Sensitivity
To hide one record, the noise must cover the largest change one record can make to the answer, its sensitivity. Because the guarantee must hold for every pair of neighbours, it is a worst case over every dataset the domain allows, not a property of your data. So you can compute it before looking at the data, but it can be infinite: a sum of unbounded numbers changes by as much as one record likes, so you must clip every value to a fixed range first.
For a vector of answers, the two noises measure a change differently. The \(\ell_1\) norm adds up the absolute changes over all coordinates; the \(\ell_2\) norm is their straight-line length, the square root of the sum of squares. The \(\ell_p\) sensitivity is the largest change between neighbours, \[\Delta_pf = \max_{D \simeq D'}\big\|f(D) - f(D')\big\|_p, \qquad p \in \{1, 2\}. \tag{20.2}\] The two agree when one record moves a single coordinate, and they are furthest apart when it moves all \(d\) coordinates by the same amount: a change of 1 in each of \(d\) coordinates has \(\ell_1\) norm \(d\) but \(\ell_2\) norm only \(\sqrt d\). That gap decides, in Section 20.5, which noise to use.
The answer also depends on what “differ in one record” means. Under add/remove one dataset has an extra record, so its size is private. Under replace one record is swapped for another, so the size \(n\) is fixed and public. Each entry of Table 20.1 is the effect of the single worst record. A histogram has sensitivity 1 under add/remove, because the new record raises one bin by 1, but 2 under replace, because the swapped record leaves one bin and joins another. The count of all records has sensitivity 0 under replace, because \(n\) never changes; if the size of your dataset is itself sensitive, use add/remove. And a record at the top of the range raises every one of \(d\) threshold counts, which makes that query dense.

For example, a study releases the mean age of \(n = 1000\) patients, with ages clipped to \([0, 100]\), under replace neighbours. One patient’s age can move the sum by at most 100, and the mean by \(100/1000 = 0.1\): a tenth of a year, however old they are. Since the noise is proportional to the sensitivity, the same noise on a histogram gives an \(\varepsilon\) twice as large under replace, so always state the relation with \(\varepsilon\). Computing the sensitivity from your data, say from the largest value present, leaks information (Beyond global sensitivity).
crumbs: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.3 The Laplace mechanism
The Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) with scale \(b\) has density \(\frac1{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\), a two-sided exponential. Its log falls off in a straight line with slope \(1/b\) on each side, so sliding the density over by a distance \(\Delta\) changes its log at any point by at most \(\Delta/b\). Hence no output can be more than \(e^{\Delta/b}\) times as likely under one dataset as under its neighbour. With independent noise on \(d\) coordinates the log-ratios of the coordinates add, each bounded by its own shift divided by \(b\), so the total is bounded by the \(\ell_1\) norm of the shift. Setting the scale so that the worst shift gives exactly \(\varepsilon\), adding independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise to each coordinate with \[b = \frac{\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon} \tag{20.3}\] is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. No smaller scale works, and the worst case is not rare: for a count, every output below both true answers has privacy loss exactly \(\varepsilon\), and half the outputs land there (Figure 20.1, left).






Figure 20.1: Left column: a count released with \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) noise on neighbouring datasets with true counts 0 and 1, and the privacy loss \(L(y)\), the log of how much more likely the output \(y\) is under one dataset than the other. It equals \(+\varepsilon\) for every \(y \le 0\) and \(-\varepsilon\) for every \(y \ge 1\), never more. Right column: the same count with \(\mathcal N(0, 2^2)\) noise. The privacy loss is a straight line, and exceeds \(\varepsilon = 1\) on the shaded tail, which has probability 0.0401 under \(M(D)\). The exact \(\delta(1) = 0.0068\) is smaller, because the bound subtracts \(e^\varepsilon\) times the mass of \(M(D')\) on the same tail.



The error is the noise itself: \(b\) on average in each coordinate. Its exponential tail puts one coordinate within \(b\ln(1/\beta)\) with probability \(1 - \beta\); giving each of \(d\) coordinates a failure probability of \(\beta/d\) puts all of them within \(b\ln(d/\beta)\). Say 1,234 of a hospital’s 10,000 patients have diabetes. Released with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) under add/remove, the sensitivity is 1, so the noise is \(\mathrm{Lap}(10)\): the error is 10 on average and below \(10\ln 20 = 29.96\) with probability 0.95, a relative error of 2.4%. A histogram of diagnoses with 20 bins at \(\varepsilon = 1\) gets \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) in each bin, and every bin is within \(\ln(20/0.05) = 5.99\) of its true count with probability 0.95.
Notice what the scale does not contain: the size of the data. One record moves a count by 1 whether the database holds a hundred records or a hundred million, so the noise is the same, and the relative error of a count of \(n\) is about \(1/(n\varepsilon)\). Large populations are cheap to protect and small subgroups are expensive. The flip side is that the sensitivity must count every number one record can move: ten counts that each get \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\), and that one record can all change, have \(\Delta_1 = 10\) and form a \(10\varepsilon\)-DP release. Drawing the noise is another matter: textbook floating-point Laplace samplers break the guarantee through their low-order bits, as Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms shows, so use a vetted DP library rather than numpy.random.laplace.
crumbs: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.4 The Gaussian mechanism
Gaussian noise, the other natural choice, is calibrated to the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. Independent normal coordinates with equal variance look the same in every direction, so you can rotate the axes until the shift points along one of them; the other coordinates then carry no evidence, and only the shift’s straight-line length matters. The price is the parabola. The log of a normal density falls off like \(-z^2\), so the log-ratio of two shifted copies is a straight line in the output, and grows without limit far in the tail (Figure 20.1, right). Gaussian noise therefore cannot give pure DP. It gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, where \(\delta\) pays for the rare outputs whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\).
As the definition showed, \(\delta\) is not the probability of those outputs: only their excess over \(e^\varepsilon\) times their probability on the neighbour has to be paid for. For two normal distributions both terms are normal tail probabilities, which gives the exact answer in closed form (Balle & Wang 2018). Only the ratio \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\) enters, the number of noise standard deviations between the two answers, so doubling both the sensitivity and the noise changes nothing. Adding \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) noise to each coordinate is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta \ge \delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\), where \[\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) \tag{20.4}\] and \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The first term is the probability, on one dataset, of the outputs whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\); the second subtracts \(e^\varepsilon\) times their probability on the neighbour. Less noise means a larger \(\mu\) and a larger \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\), so exactly one noise level hits a target \(\delta\), and you find it by bisection (Section 20.6). That is the analytic calibration, the smallest \(\sigma\) that meets a target \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).
Many papers and libraries still use the classic calibration of Dwork & Roth, \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}, \tag{20.5}\] which is proved only for \(\varepsilon < 1\). Its proof bounds \(\delta\) by the probability of the bad outputs, dropping the subtracted term, then loosens that bound again into a simple formula, so at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the classic \(\sigma\) delivers a \(\delta\) about 240 times smaller than asked for. Below \(\varepsilon = 1\) the classic formula uses 1.3 to 1.7 times the necessary noise (Table 20.2). Above it, nothing in the proof applies: at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the formula happens to stay safe up to \(\varepsilon = 8.42\) and uses too little noise beyond, because the classic \(\sigma\) shrinks like \(1/\varepsilon\) while the exact one shrinks more slowly.

Back to the diabetes count, now at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The analytic calibration gives \(\sigma = 30.75\), and a normal variable stays within 1.96 standard deviations with probability 0.95, so the 95% error is 60.27, against 29.96 for Laplace noise with \(\delta = 0\). For a single count, the Laplace mechanism wins on both error and guarantee.
A Gaussian release has a whole curve of guarantees, one \(\delta\) for every \(\varepsilon\). At \(\sigma = \Delta_2f\) the curve passes through \(\delta = 0.1269\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and reaches \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) at \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\) (Figure 20.2). title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.5 Laplace or Gaussian?
The choice comes down to how many coordinates one record moves, because that is what separates \(\Delta_1f\) from \(\Delta_2f\). Compare the typical error per released number at the same \(\varepsilon\): it is \(\sqrt2\,\Delta_1f/\varepsilon\) for Laplace noise, its standard deviation, and \(\Delta_2f\,\sigma_1\) for Gaussian noise, where \(\sigma_1\) is the analytic \(\sigma\) for unit sensitivity at your \((\varepsilon, \delta)\): 3.7306 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
For a sparse query, where a record moves one coordinate, as in a histogram, the two sensitivities are equal, and Laplace noise wins at every \(d\): an error of 1.41 against 3.73 at those parameters, with a stronger guarantee besides. For a dense query, where a record moves all \(d\) coordinates, the Laplace error grows like \(d\) and the Gaussian error like \(\sqrt d\), so the Gaussian wins once \(d\) exceeds \((\varepsilon\sigma_1)^2/2\), which is 6.96 at those parameters (Figure 20.3). Threshold counts of ages are such a query, since one person’s age moves every count at or below it. At 100 thresholds Gaussian noise is 3.79 times more accurate, and at 1,000 thresholds 11.99 times (Table 20.3).

One example’s gradient moves every coordinate of a model with millions of parameters, the densest query there is, and clipping each gradient bounds its \(\ell_2\) norm, which is exactly what the Gaussian mechanism is calibrated to. The comparison is at equal \(\varepsilon\) only: the Gaussian release also carries a \(\delta\).

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.1 Why this matters
A differential privacy (DP) system rarely answers one query. A dashboard refreshes a hundred counts; a training run takes thousands of noisy gradient steps. Each step is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP: for any two neighbouring datasets \(D\) and \(D'\), which differ in one person’s record, the probability of any set of outputs changes by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), plus a small slack \(\delta\). You need one guarantee for the whole run, as small as the truth allows, because it sets how much noise each step can afford.
Post-processing, group privacy and composition gave the first answer, basic composition: \(k\) steps that are each \(\varepsilon\)-DP are together \(k\varepsilon\)-DP. It is correct, and for large \(k\) far too pessimistic. A hundred counts at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) give \(k\varepsilon = 10\), which lets the outputs multiply an attacker’s odds by up to \(e^{10} \approx 22{,}000\): nothing worth stating. Yet at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the same hundred counts are \((4.31, 10^{-5})\)-DP, and no analysis that knows only each step’s \(\varepsilon\) can say less.
Basic composition assumes that every step produces its most revealing output at once. But the evidence a run leaks about a person is a sum of the evidence each step leaks, and a sum of many small random terms almost never reaches its maximum. Every result in this chapter charges for the tail of that sum instead of its maximum, and pays for the rare outputs beyond it with \(\delta\).

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
section: 21.2 The privacy loss of a composition
text:
21.2 The privacy loss of a composition
Run a mechanism on \(D\) and look at its output \(y\). The log of how much more likely \(y\) was under \(D\) than under \(D'\) is the privacy loss of that output: positive when \(y\) favours \(D\), negative when it favours \(D'\), zero when it says nothing. Its distribution over random outputs is the privacy loss distribution. Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP says that its absolute value never exceeds \(\varepsilon\).
Now run \(k\) steps. The probability of the whole output sequence is the probability of the first output, times that of the second given the first, and so on. The ratio of two such products is the product of the step-by-step ratios, and its log is a sum: the total loss is the sum of the per-step losses. This needs no independence: each term is the loss of whatever step was run after the outputs seen so far.
The total loss tells you \(\delta\). The definition lets each output be up to \(e^\varepsilon\) times likelier under \(D\) than under \(D'\), with \(\delta\) covering the excess. An output whose loss \(L\) is at most \(\varepsilon\) costs nothing. An output with a larger loss costs the part of its probability above the allowed ratio, a fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\) of it: almost nothing just above \(\varepsilon\), all of it when the loss is infinite. Averaging over outputs, the smallest \(\delta\) that works at a given \(\varepsilon\) is \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big] \le \Pr[L > \varepsilon], \tag{21.1}\] where \((x)_+ = \max\{x, 0\}\). So a composition theorem only needs the right tail of the total loss.
Each step’s loss can reach \(\varepsilon\), but its average is much smaller. When \(\varepsilon\) is small, an output that favours \(D\) is only slightly more likely than one that favours \(D'\), so positive and negative losses nearly cancel, and what remains is of order \(\varepsilon^2\): at most \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), about \(\varepsilon^2/2\). It is never negative, because each step is a little more likely to point to the truth than away from it, so these averages add up to a steady drift.
Randomized response makes this concrete, and turns out to be the worst case. It reports a person’s bit truthfully with probability \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), so each report has loss exactly \(+\varepsilon\) (truthful) or \(-\varepsilon\) (a lie). Take the dashboard’s 100 counts at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), as randomized response: \(t = 0.5250\). The total loss has mean 0.4996 and standard deviation 0.9988. Basic composition’s \(k\varepsilon = 10\) needs all 100 reports to be truthful, which happens with probability \(t^{100} = 1.0\times10^{-28}\), 9.5 standard deviations above the mean. A sum of many small independent terms is nearly normal, and the optimal \(\varepsilon'\) at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), 4.31, sits 3.8 standard deviations above the mean, where only a sliver of the distribution remains (Figure 21.1).






Figure 21.1: The distribution of the total privacy loss of 100 rounds of randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\). The vertical lines mark its mean, the \(\varepsilon'\) of optimal composition at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), the \(\varepsilon'\) of advanced composition, and basic composition’s \(k\varepsilon = 10\), which the loss reaches with probability \(10^{-28}\).



Two consequences follow. The spread grows like \(\sqrt k\,\varepsilon\) but the drift like \(k\varepsilon^2/2\), so once \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\) is of order 1 or more the drift is comparable to the spread, and the savings over \(k\varepsilon\) shrink. And the trick needs \(\delta > 0\): with \(\delta = 0\) you must cover even the all-truthful output, which has positive probability, so you are stuck with \(k\varepsilon\).

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.3 Advanced composition
Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan (2010) turned this picture into a theorem. Split the total loss into the drift, the sum of the per-step averages, and a fluctuation around it. The fluctuation is a sum of \(k\) terms, each confined to a range of width \(2\varepsilon\) whatever happened before, and Azuma’s inequality, a version of Hoeffding’s inequality for terms that may depend on earlier terms, says it exceeds \(\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\) with probability at most \(\delta'\). Adding the drift gives the bound: \(k\) steps that are each \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, chosen adaptively, are together \((\varepsilon', k\delta + \delta')\)-DP with \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2). \tag{21.2}\] The original theorem uses a cruder drift, \(k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), about twice as large for small \(\varepsilon\); both are valid. The extra \(k\delta\) is the chance that some step uses its own slack.
The price of the \(\sqrt k\) is the factor \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta')}\), which is 4.80 at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), the cost of cutting far into the tail. So the bound beats \(k\varepsilon\) only once \(\sqrt k\) has outgrown that factor. At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) with the original drift, that is from \(k = 29\) on; at \(k = 10\) it gives 1.623 (1.567 with the \(\tanh\) drift), worse than basic composition’s 1, so always take the smaller of the two. Inverting the leading term gives a budget: to be \((\varepsilon_{\text{total}}, \delta')\)-DP after \(k\) steps, give each step roughly \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_{\text{total}}/\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\), much more than the \(\varepsilon_{\text{total}}/k\) basic composition allows.
For the 100 counts at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), the fluctuation term is 4.7985 and the drift \(100 \times 0.1\tanh(0.05) = 0.4996\), so \(\varepsilon' = 5.2981\); with the original drift, 5.8502. Table 21.1 and Figure 21.2 follow the bounds as \(k\) grows. At \(k = 10{,}000\), where \(\varepsilon\sqrt k = 10\), the drift has taken over: the original drift costs 105 of the 153, which is why the \(\tanh\) form is worth using.

The bound is conservative in three places. Azuma’s inequality assumes each step’s loss has the largest variance its range allows. The original drift is about twice the true average loss. And the tail bound in Equation 21.1 counts every output above \(\varepsilon'\) in full, ignoring the discount for outputs just above it. So the guarantee is far stronger than it claims: at \(k = 100\) the exact \(\delta\) at the advanced \(\varepsilon' = 5.85\) is \(1.96\times10^{-9}\), not \(10^{-5}\). Use it for quick estimates, not for the number you report.

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.4 Optimal composition
The best bound comes from asking which \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is worst. Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath (2015) answered with an argument built on post-processing: further randomized steps that do not look at the data can only make the two worlds harder to tell apart, so they never increase \(\delta(\varepsilon')\). They showed that every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism can be obtained by post-processing one particular mechanism, a four-output randomized response that spends both parameters to the full: with probability \(\delta\) it announces which dataset it ran on, and otherwise it runs randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\). So any composition of \(k\) steps, even an adaptive one, is a post-processing of \(k\) copies of it, and can be no worse than those copies, whose loss you already know.
Their \(\delta\) has two parts. Either some step announces the dataset, which happens with probability \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k\), and the output is impossible under \(D'\), so it counts in full. Or none does, and the run is \(k\) rounds of randomized response: exactly \(j\) of the reports are lies with binomial probability, and the loss is then \((k - 2j)\varepsilon\). Putting that loss into Equation 21.1 gives, for every composition of \(k\) steps that are each \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, adaptive or not, \[\delta(\varepsilon') \le 1 - (1 - \delta)^k\big(1 - \delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon')\big), \qquad \delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon') = \sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj t^{k-j}(1 - t)^j\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon' - (k - 2j)\varepsilon}\big)_+, \tag{21.3}\] with \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\). The \(k\) copies are themselves a valid composition, so the bound is attained: no better one holds for the whole class. To get the total \(\varepsilon'\) for a target \(\delta\), bisect on \(\varepsilon'\) (Section 21.6).
For the 100 counts, the optimal \(\varepsilon'\) at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\) is 4.3068: 19% below the \(\tanh\) advanced bound and 57% below basic composition. If each step also has \(\delta = 5\times10^{-8}\), the announcements use up \(5.0\times10^{-6}\) of a total \(10^{-5}\), and the optimal \(\varepsilon'\) is 4.4469. The one trap is numerical. Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath’s closed form divides numbers that overflow: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(k = 1{,}000\) the denominator \((1 + e)^{1000}\) is about \(10^{570}\), beyond any double. Summed in log space nothing overflows; the snippet gives \(\delta(550) = 6.094\times10^{-4}\) there.
“Optimal” means optimal for mechanisms you know only by their \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). A real mechanism usually does better, because its loss is not always at \(\pm\varepsilon\). Laplace noise on a count sometimes lands between the two true counts, where the loss is strictly between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\); those outputs carry less evidence, so its mean loss at \(\varepsilon = 1\) is 0.3679 against randomized response’s 0.4621. With different \(\varepsilon_i\) per step, computing the exact bound is #P-complete, the class of hard counting problems (Murtagh & Vadhan 2016), so use an accountant.
The bigger waste is summarizing a mechanism by one point at all. A Gaussian mechanism has a whole curve \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), and its privacy loss is itself normal, so \(k\) Gaussian steps with noise \(\sigma\) on a sensitivity-1 query compose exactly into a single Gaussian step with shift \(\sqrt k/\sigma\). With \(\sigma = 20\), 1,000 steps are exactly \((7.51, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Converting each step to its best \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) point and composing optimally gives 62.7, about 8 times worse (Figure 21.3): the point forgets how the curve continues. When you know the mechanisms, compose their curves with the accountants of Privacy accounting.






Figure 21.3: Total \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) after \(k\) Gaussian mechanisms with \(\sigma = 20\) on a query of sensitivity 1. The first three curves convert each step to one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) point, with the best split of \(\delta\), then compose with basic, advanced or optimal composition. The dashed curve composes the exact Gaussian curves, a single Gaussian with shift \(\sqrt k/\sigma\), and lies far below.

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.5 Adaptive composition
In practice the next query depends on the last answer: an analyst zooms into the largest bin of a noisy histogram, a training loop takes its next gradient at parameters set by earlier noisy gradients. This costs nothing extra, because every argument above looked at one step given the outputs so far, and once those are fixed, so is the choice of step. In the adaptive composition experiment of Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan, an adversary picks each \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism as any function of the earlier outputs, and basic, advanced and optimal composition all hold for what it sees.
An analyst who runs 100 steps at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), choosing a Laplace query after any output that pointed to \(D\) and a randomized-response query otherwise, shows it: in 100,000 simulated runs its \(\delta\) at \(\varepsilon' = 2\) is 0.0196, below the optimal bound of 0.0201, as it must be (Figure 21.4).






Figure 21.4: The privacy curve \(\delta(\varepsilon')\) of 100 steps at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\): the exact curve of composed randomized response (optimal composition), simulated curves for composed Laplace mechanisms and for the adaptive analyst, the advanced-composition pairs \((\varepsilon', \delta')\) for several \(\delta'\), and basic composition at \((10, 0)\). The three compositions nearly coincide; advanced composition lies far to the right.



The same reasoning shows where adaptivity breaks. The theorems fix \(k\), \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) in advance. If each \(\varepsilon_i\) is picked after seeing earlier outputs, the width of each term’s range depends on the history, and Azuma’s inequality, which needs those widths fixed, no longer applies. A rule such as “keep querying until the budget is spent” therefore needs its own theorem, a privacy filter, and reporting the spend so far at every moment needs a privacy odometer, which costs more (Adaptive composition). Pure DP under basic composition is the exception: each loss is bounded by its \(\varepsilon_i\) on every output, so \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) bounds the total whatever order the budgets came in.
Choices must also be made from the outputs, never from the raw data. A stopping rule that looks at the noisy answers is post-processing and free; one that looks at the raw data leaks: a system that answers private counts until the true count of some group crosses a threshold reveals that count through the number of answers it gives, and the run is not DP for any finite \(\varepsilon\), even though every answer is.

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.6 Code
The optimal bound needs only a binomial sum, evaluated in log space so that nothing overflows, and a bisection. This is the whole of it, with advanced composition alongside:
from math import exp, expm1, lgamma, log, log1p, sqrt, tanh


def advanced_epsilon(eps: float, k: int, delta_prime: float) -> float:
    """Advanced composition with the sharp drift term k * eps * tanh(eps / 2)."""
    return eps * sqrt(2 * k * log(1 / delta_prime)) + k * eps * tanh(eps / 2)


def optimal_delta(eps_total: float, eps: float, k: int, delta: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """Kairouz-Oh-Viswanath: the exact delta(eps_total) of k (eps, delta)-DP steps, in log space."""
    log_t, log_1mt = -log1p(exp(-eps)), -log1p(exp(eps))  # log of truthful / lying probability
    logs: list[float] = []
    for j in range(k + 1):  # j of the k reports lie
        loss = (k - 2 * j) * eps
        if loss <= eps_total:
            break
        log_binom = lgamma(k + 1) - lgamma(j + 1) - lgamma(k - j + 1)
        logs.append(log_binom + (k - j) * log_t + j * log_1mt + log(-expm1(eps_total - loss)))
    top = max(logs, default=0.0)
    delta_rr = exp(top) * sum(exp(x - top) for x in logs) if logs else 0.0
    return 1 - (1 - delta) ** k * (1 - delta_rr)


def optimal_epsilon(eps: float, k: int, target_delta: float, delta: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """The smallest total epsilon whose optimal delta is at most target_delta, by bisection."""
    lo, hi = 0.0, k * eps
    for _ in range(100):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if optimal_delta(mid, eps, k, delta) > target_delta else (lo, mid)
    return hi


print(f"{advanced_epsilon(0.1, 100, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 5.2981
print(f"{optimal_epsilon(0.1, 100, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 4.3068
print(f"{optimal_epsilon(0.1, 100, 1e-5, delta=5e-8):.4f}")  # 4.4469
print(f"{optimal_epsilon(0.1, 1000, 1e-5):.3f}")  # 17.787
print(f"{optimal_delta(550, 1.0, 1000):.3e}")  # 6.094e-04
It reproduces the numbers of Section 21.3 and Section 21.4, including the case where the closed form overflows. The full edition’s script, composition.py, checks the bound against brute-force enumeration and simulates the Laplace and adaptive compositions:
uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/composition.py

text:
21.8 Further reading

Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), §3.5: basic and advanced composition, the version most libraries cite.
Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015): the hypothesis-testing view, the worst-case mechanism and the optimal bound.
Rogers, Roth, Ullman & Vadhan, “Privacy Odometers and Filters: Pay-as-you-Go Composition” (NeurIPS 2016): why adaptively chosen privacy parameters need new theorems.
Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (JRSS Series B, 2022): composing whole privacy curves, and why the total loss looks normal.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.1 Why this matters
Many questions ask you to pick something rather than compute a number. Which of 50 hyperparameter settings scores best on the validation set? Which of a thousand monitored statistics first crosses an alarm level? The answer is a name from a list, and “model 7 plus noise” is not a model.
The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms of differential privacy (DP) add noise to numbers. You could release a noisy score for every candidate, but that is \(k\) releases, and if one record can move all \(k\) scores, their costs add up and the noise must grow with \(k\), which is often in the thousands. Yet you only wanted the winner, and you never have to pay for the losers.
The one idea of this chapter is to release the position, not the values. Each mechanism adds noise to scores it never publishes and releases only which candidate won. A candidate wins when its own noise clears a bar set by the best of the others, and a maximum of numbers that each move by at most \(\Delta\) moves by at most \(\Delta\), however many numbers there are. So the number of candidates never enters the privacy cost. It enters only the accuracy, and only as \(\ln k\).
crumbs: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.2 The exponential mechanism
Each of \(k\) candidates has a score \(u(D, r)\), how good candidate \(r\) is on dataset \(D\), and its sensitivity \(\Delta\) is the largest change in any one score between two neighbouring datasets, which differ in one person’s record. A deterministic argmax can jump to another candidate when one record moves a score across a tie, so a private selection must be random, tilted toward high scores. The question is how much tilt you can afford.
McSherry and Talwar (2007) answered by giving each candidate a weight that grows exponentially with its score, and picking it with probability equal to its share of the total weight. The exponential mechanism outputs candidate \(r\) with probability \[\Pr[M_E(D) = r] = \frac{\exp\big(\varepsilon\,u(D, r)/(2\Delta)\big)}{\sum_s\exp\big(\varepsilon\,u(D, s)/(2\Delta)\big)}, \tag{22.1}\] which is a softmax of the scores at temperature \(2\Delta/\varepsilon\). Why exponential, and why the 2? Changing one record moves each score by at most \(\Delta\), and an exponential turns that additive change into a multiplicative one: each weight changes by at most a factor \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\), whatever the score. The probability of \(r\) is its weight divided by the total, and both can move against you at once, one record raising \(r\)’s score while lowering its competitors’. Each costs at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\), so the ratio is at most \(e^\varepsilon\): the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and \(k\) appears nowhere in that argument.
The 2 can be dropped when the scores are monotone, meaning one record always pushes all scores the same way. Counts under add/remove neighbours are monotone; a histogram under replace neighbours is not, because moving a record from one bin to another raises one count and lowers another. With monotone scores, \(r\)’s weight and the total cannot both move against you, so weights \(e^{\varepsilon u/\Delta}\) are also \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Check this under your neighbouring relation before you drop the 2.
How much accuracy does the randomness cost? Call the gap the distance between the best score and the chosen one. A candidate whose score is at least \(c\) below the best has at most \(e^{-\varepsilon c/(2\Delta)}\) times the best candidate’s weight, so even if all \(k\) candidates were that bad, together they would be picked with probability at most \(k\,e^{-\varepsilon c/(2\Delta)}\). Setting that to \(e^{-t}\) gives, with probability at least \(1 - e^{-t}\), \[\text{gap} \le \frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}(\ln k + t), \tag{22.2}\] and an expected gap of at most \(\frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}(\ln k + 1)\). The \(\ln k\) comes from the factor \(k\) in front of an exponential: doubling the number of candidates adds only \(\frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}\ln 2\), and a lower bound shows that no \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism can avoid it.
Take 50 models scored on a private validation set of 1,000 examples: model \(r\) gets \(900 - r\) right, the score is the count of correct predictions, and \(\Delta = 1\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the mechanism picks the best model only 39% of the time, yet loses just 1.54 correct predictions on average, 0.15% accuracy: its mistakes are near-ties, which cost almost nothing (Table 22.1, Figure 22.1). Because the counts are monotone, the weights \(e^{\varepsilon u}\) cut the expected gap from 1.54 to 0.58.

The bound is loose here, 9.82 against 1.54, because it treats every candidate as if it sat just \(c\) below the best, while most of these are far below and nearly weightless. Use it to choose \(\varepsilon\), not to predict the result.
Two consequences follow from the proof. The candidate list must be fixed before you look at the data, because the argument compares the same list on both datasets; a candidate read off the data leaks through its mere presence. And never exponentiate scores in the thousands directly. Adding a constant to every score multiplies every weight by the same factor, which cancels, so subtract the largest score first, or use the Gumbel form of the next section.

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.3 Report-noisy-max and Gumbel noise
The other natural recipe adds noise to every score and reports the index of the largest, and only the index. Report-noisy-max outputs \(\arg\max_r\big(u(D, r) + Z_r\big)\) with independent \(Z_r \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\), and it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \(b = 2\Delta/\varepsilon\).
To see why the losers cost nothing, fix the noise of every other candidate. Their noisy scores are now fixed numbers, and candidate \(i\) wins exactly when its own noise clears a bar: the best of the others’ noisy scores minus \(i\)’s own score. One record moves the maximum by at most \(\Delta\), however many candidates it ranges over, and moves \(i\)’s score by at most \(\Delta\), so the bar moves by at most \(2\Delta\). Laplace noise of scale \(b\) pays for a shift \(s\) with a factor \(e^{s/b}\), so \(b = 2\Delta/\varepsilon\) makes the cost \(e^\varepsilon\). With monotone scores the maximum and \(i\)’s score move the same way, the bar moves by at most \(\Delta\), and \(b = \Delta/\varepsilon\) suffices: the same factor of 2, for the same reason, as in the exponential mechanism.
The proof also shows why you must release only the index. It holds the other noises fixed and averages over candidate \(i\)’s noise; publishing the winning noisy score publishes that very noise, and the guarantee is gone. If you need the winner’s score, spend extra budget on a fresh Laplace answer for that one query.
Accuracy follows from the same picture. If no noise exceeds \(b\ln(k/\beta)\), which happens with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the noise cannot reorder candidates more than twice that apart, so the gap is at most \(2b\ln(k/\beta)\). On the 50 models at \(\varepsilon = 1\), Laplace report-noisy-max with \(b = 2\) picks the best model with probability 0.4241, against 0.3935 for the exponential mechanism, and has expected gap 1.40 against 1.54. Neither dominates in general.
They become the same mechanism with a different noise. If you add Gumbel noise of scale \(2\Delta/\varepsilon\) instead of Laplace noise, the argmax picks each candidate with exactly the probability of Equation 22.1. This Gumbel-max trick gives the stable sampler promised above: it works in score units, with no normalizer to overflow. On five candidates, a million Gumbel draws land within 0.0008 of the exponential mechanism’s exact probabilities, about the sampling error, while Laplace noise of the same scale, with a different tail, is off by a total variation distance of 0.0216. Taking the \(c\) largest Gumbel-noised scores gives the same distribution as running the exponential mechanism \(c\) times and removing each winner (Durfee & Rogers 2019), at a cost of \(c\varepsilon\) by basic composition.
crumbs: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.4 The sparse vector technique
Now the candidates arrive one at a time and you want the first that is good enough, such as the first statistic to cross an alarm level. Answering each query with the Laplace mechanism would cost \(\varepsilon\) per query, mostly to learn “below”. The sparse vector technique (Dwork, Naor, Reingold, Rothblum & Vadhan 2009) compares every query with one noisy threshold and pays only for the one above it.
Its basic form, AboveThreshold (Dwork & Roth 2014, Algorithm 1), takes queries of sensitivity \(\Delta\), possibly chosen adaptively, a threshold \(T\), and budgets \(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon\). It draws the threshold noise \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon_1)\) once. For each query it draws fresh noise \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\); if \(f_i(D) + \nu_i \ge T + \rho\) it outputs \(\top\) (“above”) and halts, and otherwise outputs \(\bot\) (“below”) and continues. It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any number of \(\bot\) answers.
The same bar argument explains why. The output “stop at query \(k\)” says two things: the noisy threshold sits above every earlier noisy answer, and at or below the \(k\)-th. The first is a statement about one number, the largest earlier noisy answer, which moves by at most \(\Delta\) however many queries came before; sliding the threshold noise by that much keeps all the \(\bot\) answers in place, at a cost of \(e^{\varepsilon_1}\). The single \(\top\) is paid for by sliding its own fresh noise by at most \(2\Delta\), at a cost of \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\). With monotone queries that slide is at most \(\Delta\), and \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\) suffices (Lyu, Su & Li 2017).
The accuracy, unlike the privacy, depends on \(k\), because each of the \(k\) query noises could happen to be large. With the equal split and probability at least \(1 - \beta\), every \(\bot\) query has \(f_i(D) < T + \alpha\) and the \(\top\) query has \(f_k(D) \ge T - \alpha\), where \[\alpha = \frac{8\Delta\big(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}. \tag{22.3}\] Only queries within \(\alpha\) of \(T\) can go either way. Say you monitor \(k = 1000\) counting queries (\(\Delta = 1\)) with \(T = 500\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\). With \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\alpha = 84.77\), so with probability at least 0.95 no query below 415.23 fires and no query above 584.77 is skipped. If every count is 400 except query 700, which is 600, the output is query 700; in 10,000 simulated runs it always was (Figure 22.2 shows a smaller run). Answering all 1,000 queries with the Laplace mechanism instead would add noise of scale 1,000 to counts of a few hundred.






Figure 22.2: One run of AboveThreshold with \(\varepsilon = 1\) on 30 queries whose true answers rise from 8 to 22.5, with threshold \(T = 20\). Each query’s noisy answer is compared with the same noisy threshold. The first one above it is reported and the run halts.



AboveThreshold answers a yes/no question; to release the value of the query that fired, spend extra budget on a fresh Laplace answer. To find the first \(c\) queries above the threshold, restart it with fresh threshold noise after each \(\top\), at \(\varepsilon/c\) per run. Any split of \(\varepsilon\) is private; Lyu, Su & Li give a more accurate one than the equal split.

section: 22.5 When the sparse vector technique goes wrong
text:
22.5 When the sparse vector technique goes wrong
The proof has three ingredients, and each protects one step: the fresh noise \(\nu_i\) pays for the \(\top\), the halt limits the run to the one \(\top\) that was paid for, and the noisy values stay secret because the proof averages over them. Lyu, Su & Li (2017) surveyed published variants, each a seemingly harmless optimization that weakens one ingredient; several are not DP at all (Table 22.2).



Table 22.2: Variants of the sparse vector technique and their actual privacy, from Lyu, Su & Li (2017).

The no-halt variant is the instructive one, because it uses exactly AboveThreshold’s noise and only skips the halt. Each further \(\top\) would need another slide of its own noise, another factor \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\), and nothing pays for it. Take neighbours where the first \(m\) queries are 0 and the last \(m\) are 1 on \(D\), and the reverse on \(D'\). The output “\(m\) below, then \(m\) above” is a little more likely under \(D\) at every one of its \(2m\) answers, and without a halt these small factors multiply: the privacy loss is at least \(m\varepsilon/4\), which grows without bound. At \(\varepsilon = 1\), AboveThreshold’s largest loss levels off at exactly \(\varepsilon\), so its proof is tight, while the no-halt variant’s grows linearly in \(m\) (Figure 22.3, left).
A reviewer who checks only noise scales will miss this bug. An empirical audit catches it. If a mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, any event is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times as likely under \(D\) as under \(D'\), so the log-ratio of a test’s firing rates is a lower bound on the true \(\varepsilon\). The test “more \(\top\) answers in the second half than in the first” gives a log-ratio of 1.40 at \(m = 40\), which already proves the no-halt variant is not 1-DP (Figure 22.3, right). When you review an implementation, check the ingredients directly: fresh noise for every query (reusing one draw is Algorithm 5’s bug), one threshold noise per run, a halt after the allowed number of \(\top\) answers, and no published noisy values.






Figure 22.3: Left: privacy loss on the counterexample with \(\varepsilon = 1\), computed exactly. For the no-halt variant the loss of \(\bot^m\top^m\) grows linearly in \(m\), above the lower bound \(m\varepsilon/4\); for AboveThreshold the largest loss levels off at \(\varepsilon\). Right: the no-halt variant under the test “more \(\top\) answers in the second half”; once the probability under \(D\) exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) times that under \(D'\) (dotted), no \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism could produce it.

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.6 Code
Each mechanism fits in a few lines. Note where AboveThreshold draws its two noises:
import random
from math import exp, log
from typing import Sequence


def exponential_mechanism_probs(scores: Sequence[float], eps: float, sensitivity: float) -> list[float]:
    """Selection probabilities, proportional to exp(eps * u / (2 * sensitivity)), without overflow."""
    top = max(scores)
    weights = [exp(eps * (u - top) / (2 * sensitivity)) for u in scores]
    total = sum(weights)
    return [w / total for w in weights]


def gumbel_select(scores: Sequence[float], eps: float, sensitivity: float, rng: random.Random) -> int:
    """One draw of the exponential mechanism: add Gumbel noise of scale 2 * sensitivity / eps, take the argmax."""
    beta = 2 * sensitivity / eps
    noisy = [u - beta * log(-log(1 - rng.random())) for u in scores]
    return max(range(len(scores)), key=noisy.__getitem__)


def laplace(scale: float, rng: random.Random) -> float:
    return rng.expovariate(1 / scale) - rng.expovariate(1 / scale)


def above_threshold(
    answers: Sequence[float], threshold: float, eps: float, sensitivity: float, rng: random.Random
) -> int | None:
    """Index of the first answer whose noisy value reaches the noisy threshold; equal budget split."""
    noisy_threshold = threshold + laplace(2 * sensitivity / eps, rng)  # drawn once per run
    for i, answer in enumerate(answers):
        if answer + laplace(4 * sensitivity / eps, rng) >= noisy_threshold:  # fresh noise every query
            return i  # halt, and release only the index
    return None


def svt_margin(k: int, eps: float, sensitivity: float, beta: float) -> float:
    return 8 * sensitivity * (log(k) + log(2 / beta)) / eps


print([round(p, 4) for p in exponential_mechanism_probs([3, 2, 1, 0], 1.0, 1.0)])  # [0.4551, 0.276, 0.1674, 0.1015]
print(f"{svt_margin(1000, 1.0, 1.0, 0.05):.2f}")  # 84.77
counts = [600.0 if i == 699 else 400.0 for i in range(1000)]  # query 700 is the only high one
print(above_threshold(counts, 500.0, 1.0, 1.0, random.Random(0)))  # 699
The first line is a vote with counts \((3, 2, 1, 0)\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\); the last finds query 700 of the alarm stream. Floating-point samplers are fine for checking a calculation but not for production (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms): use a vetted DP library. The full edition’s script, selection.py, computes every number in this chapter and checks each mechanism by exact integration and simulation:

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.1 Why this matters
The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms set their noise by the global sensitivity: the most one record can move the answer, over every pair of neighbouring datasets that could exist, not just yours. For a count that is the right scale. For many statistics it is not. The median of ages in \([0, 100]\) has global sensitivity 100, because in a dataset of half zeros and half hundreds one person swings it from end to end. The mean of incomes has infinite sensitivity, and for an estimator fitted by an optimizer nobody knows it. Yet on a realistic sample of 1,001 ages, one person moves the median by about a tenth of a year, because the ages near the middle are packed tightly together.
Can you add noise on the scale of the data you hold and keep a differential privacy (DP) guarantee? Yes, if you respect one idea: the noise scale is itself a function of the data, so it must be private too. Each technique below makes the scale safe to reveal in a different way. Throughout, datasets have a fixed size \(n\) and neighbours differ by one replaced record.

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
section: 23.2 Local sensitivity, and why it leaks
text:
23.2 Local sensitivity, and why it leaks
The obvious fix is to take the maximum over your own dataset’s neighbours only, the local sensitivity: \[\mathrm{LS}_f(D) = \max_{D':\ d(D, D') = 1}|f(D) - f(D')|, \tag{23.1}\] where the Hamming distance \(d(D, D')\) counts the records in which two datasets differ. For the median of \(n\) sorted values (with \(n\) odd), one change can push the median at most one place up or down the sorted list, so the local sensitivity is the larger of the two gaps next to the median.
But noise of scale \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)/\varepsilon\) publishes the local sensitivity along with the answer, and one record can change it enormously. With ages in \([0, 100]\), the dataset \((0, 0, 0, 0, 100)\) has median 0 with gaps of 0 on both sides, so its “noisy” median is exactly 0. Its neighbour \((0, 0, 0, 100, 100)\) has the same median, but a gap of 100 above it, so its release is spread out and never exactly 0. An output of 0 identifies the first dataset with certainty, whatever \(\varepsilon\) you claim.
Nor does it need a degenerate dataset. The neighbours of Table 23.1 both have median 30, but at \(\varepsilon = 1\) their noise scales are 10 and 60. The narrow Laplace density falls off six times faster than the wide one, so the further an output lands from 30, the more it favours \(D'\): the privacy loss grows in a straight line with the distance and has no bound. It passes 1 beyond a distance of 33.50, which happens with probability 0.572 under \(D'\) and only 0.0351 under \(D\), and covering that would take \(\delta = 0.477\) (Figure 23.1).

The same leak hides in any scale computed from the private data, such as a clip bound set to the observed maximum. Each such number needs one of the repairs below or its own share of the budget.

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.3 Smooth sensitivity
The first repair, due to Nissim, Raskhodnikova and Smith (2007), uses a scale that cannot jump: an upper bound on the local sensitivity that changes by at most a factor \(e^\beta\) between neighbours. A bounded factor is the right kind of control because a privacy loss is a log-ratio, and stretching the noise by \(e^\beta\) shifts log-densities by about \(\beta\).
What is the smallest such bound? If some dataset \(k\) changes away has a large local sensitivity, the bound at yours can be smaller only by the factor \(e^{-\beta}\) per step on the way. So it must be at least that dataset’s local sensitivity discounted by \(e^{-k\beta}\), and the \(\beta\)-smooth sensitivity is exactly the largest of these discounted values: \[S^*_\beta(D) = \max_{D''}\ \mathrm{LS}_f(D'')\,e^{-\beta\,d(D, D'')}. \tag{23.2}\] For the median, \(k\) changes can at most empty the stretch between two sorted values \(k + 1\) ranks apart next to the median; calling the widest such gap \(A^{(k)}\), \(S^*_\beta\) is the largest \(e^{-k\beta}A^{(k)}\), an exact \(O(n^2)\) computation (Section 23.7).
The release stretches noise of a fixed shape \(Z\) by this bound, \(f(D) + (S^*_\beta(D)/\alpha)\,Z\), where \(\alpha\) sets how many noise scales one record’s shift is worth. Which shapes work depends on their tails, because between neighbours the loss contains the log-ratio of a density and a copy stretched by up to \(e^\beta\). For Laplace noise the log-density is linear in \(|z|\), so the stretch changes it by an amount proportional to \(|z|\): unbounded, exactly the leak of Table 23.1 in miniature. A power-law tail has a log-density that grows only like \(\ln|z|\), so a stretch changes it by a bounded amount everywhere. That is why pure DP needs heavy tails: with standard Cauchy noise and \(\alpha = \beta = \varepsilon/6\), releasing \(f(D) + \frac{6}{\varepsilon}S^*_{\varepsilon/6}(D)\cdot Z\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Laplace noise can still be used, if you pay for its rare large draws with a \(\delta\): the release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when \[\beta + e^\beta\alpha + (e^\beta - 1)\ln(1/\delta) \le \varepsilon. \tag{23.3}\] The last term charges the change of scale once for each unit of \(\ln(1/\delta)\), which forces \(\beta\) down to roughly \(\varepsilon/(2\ln(1/\delta))\), much smaller than the Cauchy’s \(\varepsilon/6\).
Release the median of 1,001 synthetic ages at \(\varepsilon = 1\). With global sensitivity the median absolute error is 69.31 years. The local sensitivity is 0.1386, and the Cauchy release’s smooth sensitivity, 0.1632, is barely above it, because with this many people even seven changes cannot open a wide gap near the middle; its error is 0.979. Laplace noise at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), with \(\alpha = 1/2\), allows only \(\beta = 0.0322\), so more distant datasets count and \(S^* = 0.5144\), but the lighter tails make up for it: error 0.713. Both are 70 to 100 times better than the global release, and the gain grows with \(n\), because the smooth bound follows the spacing of the data near the median (Figure 23.2). The same reasoning shows where it fails: for \(n \lesssim 20\), a few changes can open a gap across nearly the whole range, and smooth sensitivity loses to global sensitivity.
The heavy tail has its own cost: about one Cauchy release in 16 is off by more than ten times the typical error, and the Cauchy has no mean, so don’t average such values. And a bound you substitute for \(S^*\), for a statistic without an exact formula, works only if it is itself \(\beta\)-smooth.

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.4 Propose-test-release
Without a formula like the median’s, Dwork and Lei (2009) take a cruder route. Propose a bound \(b\) on the local sensitivity before looking at the data, then ask how many records would have to change before the local sensitivity could exceed \(b\); call that distance \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D)\). This count is safe to release with noise: a path from a neighbour to a bad dataset can always go through your dataset first, so one record moves the distance by at most 1. Propose-test-release adds \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) to the distance, outputs \(\bot\) (“no answer”) if the result is at most \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), and otherwise releases \(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(b/\varepsilon)\).
Why is that private? If the proposal is right for a pair of neighbours, so that their answers differ by at most \(b\), the release is an ordinary Laplace mechanism, and test plus release cost \(\varepsilon\) each: \(2\varepsilon\) in all. If it is wrong, both datasets have local sensitivity above \(b\), so both sit at distance 0, and the test passes only if the noise alone clears the threshold, which happens with probability \(\delta/2\). That lucky pass is what \(\delta\) pays for, so the mechanism is \((2\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. The noise scale is now your proposal, which reveals nothing, and \(\bot\) says only that the data were probably near an unstable point.
The threshold is demanding: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) it is \(\ln(10^6) = 13.82\), so the data must be stable against more than a dozen changes. On the 1,001 ages with \(b = 1\) year, the distance is 21, the test passes with probability 0.999621, and the release has median error 0.693 years at a total cost of 2. On 101 ages the distance is 1 and the test almost never passes: one year is far too optimistic there (Figure 23.2, right).






Figure 23.2: Left: median absolute noise when releasing the median age at \(\varepsilon = 1\), by global sensitivity, smooth sensitivity with Cauchy noise and with Laplace noise (\(\delta = 10^{-6}\)), and propose-test-release with \(b = 1\) when it passes, as the number of people grows. The dotted line is the non-private local sensitivity. Right: the probability that propose-test-release with \(b = 1\) answers.



A proposal taken from the data, such as twice the observed local sensitivity, brings back the leak of Section 23.2. Plan for \(\bot\): every retry with a larger \(b\) spends budget again.

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.5 Subsample-and-aggregate
When you cannot analyse \(f\) at all, such as a trained model, make the sensitivity small by construction. Split the records into \(B\) disjoint blocks by a partition fixed in advance (say, by a hash of a record identifier), run \(f\) on each block, clip each block answer \(z_j\) to \([0, R]\), and release \[M(D) = \frac1B\sum_{j=1}^B \operatorname{clip}_{[0,R]}(z_j) + \mathrm{Lap}\Big(\frac{R}{B\varepsilon}\Big). \tag{23.4}\] One record lives in one block, so it changes one clipped answer by at most \(R\) and the average by at most \(R/B\). That is the whole proof, and it never looks inside \(f\), so the release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any \(f\). It is also why the partition must not depend on the values: otherwise one record could reshuffle many blocks.
The number of blocks sets a trade-off. The noise falls like \(1/B\), because one record’s influence is diluted over more blocks. But each block sees only \(n/B\) records, and many estimators are biased on small samples, so the bias grows with \(B\). The sampling error hardly moves: each block estimate is noisier by a factor \(B\) in variance, and averaging \(B\) of them undoes it. Take the rate of \(n = 10{,}000\) exponential inter-arrival times, estimated by \(1/\bar x\), at \(\varepsilon = 1\) with \(R = 5\). Its global sensitivity is infinite. With 10 blocks the noise standard deviation is 0.7071 and swamps everything; with 1,000 blocks of 10 records the bias is 0.1111. At 250 blocks the two are of similar size and the error is 0.0396, about four times the non-private 0.0100, for an estimator whose sensitivity you never had to bound (Figure 23.3). Choose \(B\) from an error model, not by trying values on the data.






Figure 23.3: Root-mean-square error of subsample-and-aggregate for the exponential rate against the number of blocks \(B\), with its three components: the bias of the estimator on small blocks, the Laplace noise, and the sampling error.



The range \(R\) is still a global bound, now on the output of \(f\), and a loose \(R\) means large noise. With a noisy vote as the combiner, this is private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE), where models trained on disjoint shards vote.

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.6 Clipping
For the mean of unbounded data, clipping forces a bound: replace each value by \(\min(x, C)\), and one record moves the mean by at most \(C/n\), so \(\frac1n\sum_i\min(x_i, C) + \mathrm{Lap}(C/(n\varepsilon))\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for non-negative data. Every “assume the data lie in \([0, \Lambda]\)” of earlier chapters is a clip in disguise, and the same move on per-example gradients is the core of private model training.
The price is bias: clipping removes the part of each value above \(C\), so the estimate is low by the average excess \(\mathbb E[(X - C)_+]\). Adding the sampling variance of the clipped values and the noise variance gives the mean squared error, \[\operatorname{err}(C)^2 = \mathbb E[(X - C)_+]^2 + \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\min(X, C))}{n} + \frac{2C^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}. \tag{23.5}\] Raising \(C\) shrinks the first term and grows the last. The noise shrinks with \(n\) but the bias does not, so with more data you can clip further into the tail. Given a model of your data, minimize Equation 23.5 numerically before seeing any records.
Log-normal incomes, in thousands, with median 40 and mean 55.085, show the trade-off at \(n = 1000\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\) (Table 23.2). Clipping at the median cuts half the population back and leaves a bias of 23. The optimum, 331.34, touches only 0.4% of people and has error 1.666, just 1% above the 1.649 of the unclipped, non-private mean. And the optimum moves out as predicted: 177.5 at \(n = 100\), 557.3 at \(n = 10{,}000\) (Figure 23.4).

Three consequences follow. Choosing \(C\) from the data, say the empirical 99th percentile, makes the noise scale a statistic again and reopens the leak of Section 23.2; take it from domain knowledge, or spend budget on a private quantile with the exponential mechanism or the methods above. Clipping from above only ever lowers values, so it always underestimates, and clipping to \([-C, C]\) is unbiased only when the cuts on both sides cancel, as they do for distributions symmetric about 0. And under add/remove neighbours \(n\) itself is private, so release a noisy clipped sum and a noisy count, divide, and charge both to the budget (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).

title: 23  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
23.7 Code
The smooth sensitivity of the median is easy to get subtly wrong, mostly in the padding of the order statistics. The snippet computes it for \(D = (1, 3, 4, 6, 9)\) in \([0, 10]\) with \(\beta = 0.5\): the local sensitivity is 2, but one change opens a gap of 5, and \(e^{-0.5}\times 5 = 3.03\) wins. It also solves for the \(\beta\) of the age example.
from math import exp, log


def gap_within(xs: list[float], upper: float, k: int) -> float:
    """A(k): the widest gap next to the median that changing k records can open."""
    n, m = len(xs), (len(xs) + 1) // 2  # n odd; m is the rank of the median

    def x(i: int) -> float:  # order statistic i, padded with 0 below and `upper` above
        return 0.0 if i < 1 else upper if i > n else xs[i - 1]

    return max(x(m + t) - x(m + t - k - 1) for t in range(k + 2))


def smooth_sensitivity_median(values: list[float], upper: float, beta: float) -> float:
    """The beta-smooth sensitivity of the median of values in [0, upper]."""
    xs = sorted(values)
    return max(exp(-k * beta) * gap_within(xs, upper, k) for k in range(len(xs) + 1))


def laplace_beta(eps: float, delta: float, alpha: float) -> float:
    """The largest beta with beta + e^beta * alpha + (e^beta - 1) * ln(1/delta) <= eps."""
    lo, hi = 0.0, eps
    for _ in range(100):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        ok = mid + exp(mid) * alpha + (exp(mid) - 1) * log(1 / delta) <= eps
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if ok else (lo, mid)
    return lo


data = [1.0, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0, 9.0]
print(f"{gap_within(sorted(data), 10.0, 0):.2f}")  # 2.00
print(f"{smooth_sensitivity_median(data, 10.0, 0.5):.2f}")  # 3.03
print(f"{laplace_beta(1.0, 1e-6, 0.5):.4f}")  # 0.0322
The distance for propose-test-release is the first k with gap_within(xs, upper, k) > b. The full edition’s script computes every number in this chapter and checks the formula for \(A^{(k)}\) by brute force:
uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/sensitivity.py
