\(\bot\) if \(\operatorname{dist}_b + \mathrm{Lap}(\frac1\varepsilon) \le \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}\), else \(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(\frac b\varepsilon)\)
\((2\varepsilon, \delta)\)
Stable statistics without a smooth-sensitivity formula


Subsample-and-aggregate
Mean of \(B\) clipped block outputs \(+ \mathrm{Lap}(\frac{R}{B\varepsilon})\)
\(\varepsilon\)
Black-box estimators and models


Clipped mean
\(\frac1n\sum\min(x_i, C) + \mathrm{Lap}(\frac{C}{n\varepsilon})\); bias \(\mathbb E[(X - C)_+]\)
\(\varepsilon\)
Means and sums of unbounded data






Rules of thumb

Pure DP with a data-dependent scale needs heavy-tailed noise; Laplace noise needs a \(\delta\) and a \(\beta\) near \(\varepsilon/(2\ln(1/\delta))\).
Fix clip bounds, block counts and proposals before looking at the data, from an error formula or with a separate slice of the budget.

text:

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.1 Why this matters
The proof of the Laplace mechanism compares two densities on the real line. Your computer has no real numbers. It has floating-point numbers, a finite set with uneven gaps, and a source of random bits, and the function that “samples \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\)” produces some distribution on that finite set, about which the proof says nothing. Mironov (2012) showed that the textbook sampler, in double precision, leaks the true answer through the low-order bits of its output.
The one idea of this chapter is that differential privacy (DP) is a property of the output distribution the code actually produces, so the code must produce exactly the distribution the proof is about. There are two ways to get there. Keep floating point and repair the output, by rounding it to a coarse grid so that every output is reachable from every input. Or leave floating point behind: make the query integer-valued and sample integer noise exactly, with integer and rational arithmetic only. The second gives the discrete Laplace and discrete Gaussian mechanisms, whose samplers deliver exactly what their proofs assume.

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.2 Floating-point Laplace breaks differential privacy
Suppose some output can be produced from a dataset \(D\) but never from its neighbour \(D'\). Seeing that output tells an observer the data were \(D\), with certainty. The DP inequality \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta\), applied to the set \(S\) of such outputs, has a right-hand side of \(e^\varepsilon \cdot 0 + \delta\), and the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) is useless however large it is. So the whole probability of those outputs must be paid for by \(\delta\): \[\delta \;\ge\; \Pr[M(D) \in S] \tag{24.1}\] for every \(\varepsilon\). Any output reachable from one input only rules out pure DP, and this support check is the quickest audit of an implementation.
The textbook sampler fails it. It draws \(U\) uniform on \((0, 1)\) and a random sign \(\xi\), and outputs \(f(D) + \xi\cdot b\ln(1/U)\), rounding the logarithm and the sum to the nearest float. Floats are dense near 0 and sparse far from it: between \(2^e\) and \(2^{e+1}\) they are evenly spaced, and the spacing doubles with each power of 2. With \(f(D) = 0\), an output near 0 is a noise value as it is, on the fine grid of floats near 0. With \(f(D') = 1\), the same output must come from \(1\) minus a noise value near 1, which lies on the coarser grid there. So most of the fine-grained outputs of \(M(D)\) near 0 cannot come from \(M(D')\), and away from the inputs the two sets of outputs only partly coincide.
Suppose a hospital releases a count with this sampler at \(b = 1\), which would be 1-DP in exact arithmetic, and an analyst who knows the count is 0 or 1 checks whether the released float can be produced from 1. In a toy model with 12-bit floats, small enough to enumerate exactly, \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] = 0.4791\): the check identifies the count 0 with certainty 47.91% of the time, where the proof promised odds moved by at most a factor \(e\) (Figure 24.1).






Figure 24.1: The toy 12-bit floating-point Laplace sampler with \(b = 1\). Left: the outputs that \(f(D) = 0\) (top) and \(f(D') = 1\) (bottom) can produce in a narrow window, coloured by whether the other input can produce them too. Right: the probability that \(M(D)\) produces an output \(M(D')\) cannot, against the number of significand bits, for the textbook sampler (flat, near 48%) and the snapped one (zero).



More precision does not help, because extra bits refine both grids together and the mismatch stays: from 6 to 14 bits, about 48% of the mass sits on outputs the other input can’t produce. Mironov found the same effect at the 53 bits of a double in several DP libraries, and Jin et al. (2022) found such leaks in later ones. The tails leak as well: a 53-bit uniform is never below \(2^{-53}\), so the noise never exceeds about \(36.74\,b\), and the outputs just beyond that bound from one input are unreachable from the other. So numpy.random.laplace, or any f + scale * log(u), is not a DP mechanism, whatever \(\varepsilon\) the code claims.

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.3 The snapping mechanism
The leak lives in which float the output is, not in where it lands on the real line, and that is the idea of Mironov’s snapping mechanism. Round the noisy answer to a grid at least as coarse as the noise scale, and the bits that depend on the input are discarded; every input now reaches the same finite set of grid points, and the support argument has nothing to bite on.
Why does rounding cost no privacy? Each grid point collects all the noise values that round to it, an interval of the real line. In exact arithmetic its probability under \(D\) and under \(D'\) is the probability that a Laplace variable lands in one of two intervals shifted by at most one unit, and the Laplace density changes by at most a factor \(e^{1/\lambda}\) under such a shift. Rounding exact noise is just post-processing. What remains is the floating-point error, which moves the interval endpoints slightly. That error is a fraction \(\eta = 2^{-53}\) of the numbers involved, so the mechanism clamps the input and the output to \([-B, B]\) to keep those numbers, and the error, bounded.
Concretely, for a query with sensitivity 1 and noise scale \(\lambda\), let \(\Lambda\) be the smallest power of 2 at or above \(\lambda\). Clamp \(f(D)\) to \([-B, B]\), add floating-point Laplace noise of scale \(\lambda\), round to the nearest multiple of \(\Lambda\), and clamp again. For \(\lambda < B < 2^{46}\lambda\) the result is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \frac{1 + 12B\eta}{\lambda} + \frac{2^{-49}B}{\lambda}, \qquad \eta = 2^{-53}: \tag{24.2}\] the exact mechanism’s \(1/\lambda\) plus two terms that pay for the floating-point error and grow with the clamping range. For \(\lambda = 1\) and \(B = 10\) the excess is about \(3.1\times10^{-14}\). In the toy, snapping to integers and clamping to \([-10, 10]\) makes both inputs reach the same 21 outputs at every precision, and the largest privacy loss is 1.0010 at 12 bits and 1.0002 at 14, against 1 for the exact mechanism.
The costs follow from the construction. Rounding adds up to \(\Lambda/2 \le \lambda\) of error, and clamping biases answers near \(\pm B\), so choose \(B\) from the domain, knowing that \(\varepsilon\) grows with it. And because snapping post-processes a mechanism that is not DP, its proof rests on Mironov’s bookkeeping and on an ideal uniform and a correct logarithm: use a vetted implementation, not your own variant.

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.4 The discrete Laplace mechanism
Most DP queries are counts and histograms, integer-valued with sensitivity 1, and for them the natural noise is integer-valued too: the output has no low-order bits to leak, and the noise can be sampled exactly. Take the Laplace density, keep its values at the integers and renormalize: that is the discrete Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\), and adding it is the geometric mechanism of Ghosh, Roughgarden and Sundararajan (2009). Each step away from 0 multiplies the probability by \(r = e^{-1/b}\), as the continuous density drops by \(e^{-1/b}\) per unit, so its probability mass function (PMF) is \[\Pr[Z = z] = \frac{1 - r}{1 + r}\,r^{|z|}, \qquad z \in \mathbb Z, \qquad r = e^{-1/b}. \tag{24.3}\] The privacy guarantee is the continuous one. Shifting the input by one unit changes each output’s probability by at most the factor \(e^{1/b}\), and shifting by an integer only relabels the terms of the normalizing sum, so it doesn’t change the normalizer. For an integer-valued query with \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(\Delta_1 f\), adding independent \(\mathrm{Lap}_{\mathbb Z}(b)\) noise to each coordinate is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \(\varepsilon = \Delta_1 f/b\), the same calibration as before.
A count at \(\varepsilon = 1\) has \(b = 1\) and \(r = e^{-1} = 0.3679\). The exact count comes out with probability 0.4621, and the noise variance is 1.8413, slightly below the 2 of continuous \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\): same guarantee, a little less noise. For a single count nothing does better: every user, whatever their loss function and prior, can post-process the geometric mechanism’s output to do as well as with any other \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism.
The query must be integer-valued, since a non-integer shift moves the noise off the lattice and brings back the support problem. Rounding \(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(b)\) to an integer is no substitute: it would be private in exact arithmetic, but it needs the floating-point sampler of Section 24.2.

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.5 The discrete Gaussian mechanism
The Gaussian mechanism is the workhorse for dense vectors, because its noise follows the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020) define its integer analogue the same way: the discrete Gaussian \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2)\) gives each integer \(x\) probability proportional to \(e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\). The US Census Bureau used it for the 2020 Census, and it is the noise of choice before secure aggregation, which works with integers.
The discrete Laplace argument carries over. Integer shifts leave the normalizer unchanged, so the log-ratio of two shifted PMFs is the log-ratio of the two bell curves: the privacy loss is the continuous Gaussian’s, linear in the output, evaluated at integers. The outputs whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) therefore form a tail, and for a query whose value differs by \(\Delta\) between neighbours the smallest \(\delta\) at each \(\varepsilon\) has the same form as the continuous Gaussian’s analytic curve, with discrete tails in place of continuous ones: \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Pr\Big[X > \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta} - \frac\Delta2\Big] - e^\varepsilon\Pr\Big[X > \frac{\varepsilon\sigma^2}{\Delta} + \frac\Delta2\Big], \qquad X \sim \mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, \sigma^2). \tag{24.4}\] The first term is the probability of the outputs that favour \(D\) by more than \(e^\varepsilon\); the second subtracts the part of it that the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) already covers.
Same form does not mean same value. The privacy loss now takes only lattice values, one per integer output, so as \(\varepsilon\) crosses one of them a whole output enters or leaves the sum, and the discrete curve has a kink there and oscillates around the continuous one (Figure 24.2). For sensitivity 1 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), it gives \(\delta = 0.6032\) against 0.5099 for the continuous Gaussian at \(\sigma = 0.5\), 0.1414 against 0.1269 at \(\sigma = 1\), and 0.0072 against 0.0068 at \(\sigma = 2\); at other \(\varepsilon\), such as just past a kink, the discrete curve is below, so neither dominates. So don’t reuse the continuous formula to report the discrete Gaussian’s \(\delta\): it can understate it, and more so for small \(\sigma\). Compute Equation 24.4 directly, as Section 24.7 does. In Rényi divergence, which Rényi differential privacy uses for composition, the discrete Gaussian is never worse than the continuous one, so Gaussian accountants apply unchanged.






Figure 24.2: Discrete against continuous Gaussian for sensitivity 1: \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) of the discrete Gaussian (solid) and of the continuous Gaussian (dashed), for \(\sigma = 0.5\), 1 and 2. The discrete curve has a kink at each value of its lattice-valued privacy loss, and approaches the continuous one as \(\sigma\) grows.



Restricting the bell curve to integers also pulls a little mass towards 0, so the variance is below \(\sigma^2\), by a relative \(2.11\times10^{-7}\) at \(\sigma = 1\) but down to \(0.8601\,\sigma^2\) at \(\sigma = 0.5\).
Two consequences matter in machine learning. A real-valued query, such as a clipped gradient, must be scaled by \(1/\gamma\) for a small step \(\gamma\) and rounded to integers first. Randomized rounding (up with probability equal to the fractional part) keeps it unbiased, but the rounded query can have a slightly larger sensitivity, and that is the one to calibrate to. And unlike continuous Gaussians, a sum of discrete Gaussians is not exactly a discrete Gaussian; for \(\sigma \ge 1\) it is very close, which schemes where each client adds a share of the noise rely on.

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
section: 24.6 Sampling exactly, and choosing a library
text:
24.6 Sampling exactly, and choosing a library
Inverting a cumulative distribution function (CDF) needs the discrete Gaussian’s normalizer, which is irrational, and a floating-point uniform, which brings back every problem of Section 24.2. Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020) avoid both with samplers that use only integer and rational arithmetic and uniform random integers.
The building block is a coin that comes up 1 with probability \(e^{-\gamma}\), made from coins with rational probabilities. Flip coins with probabilities \(\gamma, \gamma/2, \gamma/3, \dots\) until one fails: the chance of surviving \(k\) flips is \(\gamma^k/k!\), a term of the power series of \(e^{-\gamma}\), and reporting whether the first failure came at an odd step adds those terms with alternating signs, giving exactly \(e^{-\gamma}\). Such coins yield an exact discrete Laplace sampler. The discrete Gaussian then comes by rejection: the discrete Laplace has heavier tails, so it can serve as a proposal, and each draw is kept with a probability, decided by one exact coin, chosen so that proposal times acceptance is proportional to the Gaussian weights. Rejection never needs the normalizer.
They are cheap. A discrete Laplace draw takes about 10 to 12 uniform integers. A discrete Gaussian draw is accepted with probability 0.5185 at \(\sigma^2 = \frac14\) and 0.7532 at \(\sigma^2 = 100\), so it takes fewer than two proposals on average. A histogram of 1,000 bins with \(\mathcal N_{\mathbb Z}(0, 100)\) noise per bin uses about 15.6 uniform integers per bin, about 15,600 in all, and no floating-point operation.
Exactness is not timing safety. The number of rejection rounds depends on the output, so the running time leaks information about the noise, and Jin et al. (2022) show such leaks are exploitable. So a review of a library or pipeline asks four questions. Is the noise drawn by an exact integer sampler or a snapping-style repair, with no floating-point exp, log or random() inside the sampler? Do the random bits come from a cryptographic source (in Python, secrets.SystemRandom()), not a seeded generator? Is the running time padded or fixed? And does the reported calibration match the mechanism used: the discrete Gaussian’s own \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), the rounded query’s sensitivity, the clamping range?

title: 24  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
24.7 Code
Take the noise itself from a vetted library. What you can check yourself is the calibration: that the \(\delta\) reported for a discrete Gaussian matches Equation 24.4. The snippet sums the PMF over the integers and compares it with the continuous Gaussian’s exact curve.
from math import ceil, erfc, exp, sqrt


def discrete_gaussian_delta(eps: float, sigma: float, sens: int = 1) -> float:
    """Exact delta(eps) of the discrete Gaussian mechanism, summed over the integers."""
    reach = ceil(40 * sigma) + sens  # the mass beyond 40 sigma is far below double precision
    weight = {y: exp(-y * y / (2 * sigma**2)) for y in range(-reach - sens, reach + 1)}
    total = sum(weight[y] for y in range(-reach, reach + 1))
    delta = 0.0
    for y in range(-reach, reach + 1):  # outputs of f(D) = 0 and f(D') = sens
        p, q = weight[y] / total, weight[y - sens] / total
        delta += max(p - exp(eps) * q, 0.0)
    return delta


def normal_cdf(x: float) -> float:
    return 0.5 * erfc(-x / sqrt(2))


def gaussian_delta(eps: float, sigma: float, sens: float = 1.0) -> float:
    """Exact delta(eps) of the continuous Gaussian mechanism, for comparison."""
    mu = sens / sigma
    return normal_cdf(mu / 2 - eps / mu) - exp(eps) * normal_cdf(-mu / 2 - eps / mu)


print(f"{discrete_gaussian_delta(1.0, 0.5):.4f} {gaussian_delta(1.0, 0.5):.4f}")  # 0.6032 0.5099
print(f"{discrete_gaussian_delta(1.0, 1.0):.4f} {gaussian_delta(1.0, 1.0):.4f}")  # 0.1414 0.1269
print(f"{discrete_gaussian_delta(1.0, 2.0):.4f} {gaussian_delta(1.0, 2.0):.4f}")  # 0.0072 0.0068
Floating point is fine here: this computes a guarantee, not a release. The full edition’s script implements the exact samplers with fractions.Fraction and integers, checks each against its exact distribution, and enumerates the toy floating-point sampler:
uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/discrete_mechanisms.py

text:

24.9 Further reading

Mironov, “On Significance of the Least Significant Bits for Differential Privacy” (CCS 2012): the floating-point attack and the snapping mechanism.

title: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.1 Why this matters
Every mechanism so far in this part assumed a trusted curator that holds the raw data and releases only a mechanism’s output. The guarantee of differential privacy (DP) covers that output, not the curator’s database, its engineers or a court order. Often the curator is exactly the party users don’t want to see their data: a browser vendor collecting usage statistics, a keyboard app learning new words. So what can you trust instead, and what does it cost in accuracy?
The answer turns on where the noise enters. The four models of Figure 25.1 all release a noisy statistic; they differ in who sees the data before the noise is added. The further upstream it enters, the fewer parties you trust and the more noise reaches the answer. A report randomized on a person’s device must hide its owner from everyone, so it carries about as much noise as a curator adds once to the whole answer. Sum \(n\) such reports and their variances add: the noise grows like \(\sqrt n\) while the count grows like \(n\). The shuffle and distributed models move the noise back downstream without handing the data to anyone: anonymity hides which report is whose, and cryptography hides everything but the sum.
crumbs: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text: Figure 25.1: The four trust models. Blue boxes hold one record each, green boxes must be trusted, and red boxes see what is released and are not trusted. Only the central model gives raw records to a single party.
crumbs: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.2 Central and local differential privacy
In the local model each person runs a local randomizer \(R\) on their own record and sends only the result. The receiver may know whose report it is, so the report must look about the same whatever the record: for any two records \(x, x'\) and any set \(S\) of reports, \[\Pr[R(x) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon_0}\Pr[R(x') \in S]. \tag{25.1}\] Changing one record changes one report, so the collection is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP against everyone, the collector included: a breach of its database reveals only reports, which are already private. The neighbours are replace neighbours, because the number of reports already shows who took part.
The basic local randomizer is randomized response: report your true bit with probability \(t = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), the flipped bit otherwise (The definition of differential privacy). The lying pulls the mean report towards one half by a known amount, and undoing the pull estimates the fraction of ones without bias, with standard deviation \[\operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0/2}}{(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\sqrt n}. \tag{25.2}\] Of \(n = 10{,}000\) people, say 3,000 hold a 1, and each answers at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\). The estimate’s standard deviation is 0.00866, or 86.6 people on the count. A trusted curator adding Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) to the count has standard deviation 1.287: same people, same \(\varepsilon\), and the local survey is 67.3 times noisier.
That is the model’s fault, not randomized response’s. Squeezing every report into a probability band \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) wide shrinks what it says about the population by a factor of order \((e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)^2\), about \(\varepsilon_0^2\), so you need that many times more people to learn the same thing. No local protocol beats error of order \(1/((e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\sqrt n)\) on a fraction (Duchi, Jordan & Wainwright 2018), and randomized response is within a constant of it. A curator’s error is of order \(1/(n\varepsilon)\), so the ratio grows like \(\sqrt n\) (Figure 25.2). For a standard deviation of 0.001 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), randomized response needs 920,674 people and the central Laplace mechanism 1,415.






Figure 25.2: Standard deviation of an estimated fraction at \(\varepsilon = 1\), against the number of people. Randomized response (line and simulated dots) falls like \(1/\sqrt n\) and stays a constant factor above the lower bound for any local protocol; the central Laplace mechanism falls like \(1/n\).



So local DP suits frequent items in very large populations, as in Google’s RAPPOR in Chrome and Apple’s telemetry. Since the guarantee is about a report’s content, a network address stored beside it still links it to the person. And \(\varepsilon_0\) is per report: a user who reports daily releases a new output about the same record each day, and by composition the losses add (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
crumbs: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.3 Frequency estimation
The workhorse of deployed local DP is frequency estimation: each person holds one of \(k\) values, and the analyst wants the fraction \(f_v\) holding each value \(v\). In every scheme in use, a frequency oracle, a report “supports” \(v\) with probability \(p\) if the person holds \(v\) and a smaller \(q\) otherwise. The share of supporting reports is then \(q + f_v(p - q)\) on average, so with \(C_v\) supporting reports, subtracting \(q\) and dividing by \(p - q\) gives an unbiased estimate, with exact variance \[\hat f_v = \frac{C_v/n - q}{p - q}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}\hat f_v = \frac{f_vp(1-p) + (1 - f_v)q(1-q)}{n(p - q)^2}. \tag{25.3}\] Design comes down to making the gap \(p - q\) large at a given \(\varepsilon_0\), since its square divides the variance.
\(k\)-ary randomized response reports the true value with probability \(p = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + k - 1)\) and each other value with \(q = 1/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + k - 1)\). The ratio \(p/q\) is the allowed \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\), but both shrink as \(k\) grows: with many values the report is nearly uniform, and a rare value’s variance grows linearly in \(k\). Optimized unary encoding (Wang et al. 2017) sends a one-hot vector of \(k\) bits, each randomized. Changing a person’s value changes only two bits, whatever \(k\) is, so the variance doesn’t depend on \(k\); the price is a \(k\)-bit report. It keeps a true 1 with probability \(p = \frac12\) but invents a 1 with only \(q = 1/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)\), because almost all bits are 0 and invented 1s are the noise that hurts most. Setting \(f_v \to 0\) in Equation 25.3 gives each scheme’s noise floor, \[k\text{-ary: } \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} + k - 2}{n(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)^2}, \qquad \text{optimized unary: } \frac{4e^{\varepsilon_0}}{n(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)^2}, \tag{25.4}\] and \(k\)-ary randomized response wins exactly when \(k < 3e^{\varepsilon_0} + 2\) (Figure 25.3).






Figure 25.3: \(n\) times the variance of a rare value’s estimated frequency, against the domain size \(k\), at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 3\). \(k\)-ary randomized response grows linearly in \(k\); the unary encodings are flat; the dotted line is the crossover \(k = 3e^{\varepsilon_0} + 2\).



A keyboard app wants the frequency of \(k = 128\) emoji at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) from \(10^6\) users. A rare emoji’s standard deviation is 0.0066 under \(k\)-ary randomized response and 0.0019 under optimized unary encoding. An estimate must stand about three standard deviations above zero to be seen, so emoji used by fewer than about 0.6% of users are lost either way: these oracles are optimal local protocols, and the \(\sqrt n\) gap remains. For large \(k\), hashing schemes (local hashing, Hadamard response) reach the unary variance with reports of about \(\log k\) bits. And because of composition, RAPPOR (Erlingsson, Pihur & Korolova 2014) memoizes one permanent randomized response per value and adds fresh noise around it in each report, so averaging a user’s daily reports recovers at most the permanent randomized value, not the value itself.
crumbs: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.4 The shuffle model
The local model loses \(\sqrt n\) because the analyst knows whose report is whose. In the shuffle model a shuffler strips identifiers and timing and forwards the reports in random order, so the analyst sees what was sent but not by whom. It is trusted only to unlink: it sees reports, which are already \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP.
Anonymity helps because of what Equation 25.1 says about everyone else. Another person’s report is at most \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) times less likely than if they held the target’s value, so with probability about \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) each of them sends a report that looks exactly like one the target might have sent. The target hides among about \(ne^{-\varepsilon_0}\) such clones, and more people means more clones (Amplification by shuffling and by iteration). Theorem 3.1 of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021) makes this a bound: shuffling \(n\) reports from \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP local randomizers is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP under replace neighbours with \[\varepsilon \le \ln\left(1 + \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\left(\frac{8\sqrt{e^{\varepsilon_0}\ln(4/\delta)}}{\sqrt n} + \frac{8e^{\varepsilon_0}}{n}\right)\right), \tag{25.5}\] provided \(\varepsilon_0 \le \ln\big(n/(16\ln(2/\delta))\big)\). The bracket falls like \(1/\sqrt n\), the clones at work. The proviso, rewritten as \(ne^{-\varepsilon_0} \ge 16\ln(2/\delta)\), demands enough expected clones; below it the theorem says nothing.
The payoff is that each report can be randomized weakly. For central \(\varepsilon = 1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), bisection on Equation 25.5 (Section 25.7) allows \(\varepsilon_0 = 3.504\) at \(n = 10^4\), 5.701 at \(10^5\) and 7.992 at \(10^6\). At 7.992 a single report is almost the truth, yet the shuffled collection is \((1, 10^{-6})\)-DP. Because the allowed \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) grows in proportion to \(n\), the error returns to the central rate up to a factor \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\). At \(n = 10^3\) there are too few clones: the proviso caps \(\varepsilon_0\) at 1.460.






Figure 25.4: Central \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) after shuffling, against \(n\), for \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 3\): the closed form of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (lines, drawn where its condition holds), their numeric bound (dots) and the exact \(\varepsilon\) of shuffled binary randomized response (crosses). The dotted lines mark \(\varepsilon_0\), the guarantee without shuffling.



The closed form is loose (Figure 25.4). The same paper computes the clone comparison numerically, and that bound is still valid for every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP randomizer: at \(n = 10^4\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) it gives 0.0530 where the closed form gives 0.2140. Reason with the closed form, deploy with a numerical accountant.
The amplification lasts only while the shuffler does its one job. If it colludes with the analyst, the guarantee falls back to the local \(\varepsilon_0\), which you just made large, so keep it reasonable. If the adversary controls \(m\) senders, it can remove their known reports, leaving \(n - m\) people to provide clones. And the theorem covers only the set of reports, so timing, message sizes and counts must not leak, which is why real shufflers batch and pad.

title: 25  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
25.5 Distributed DP
The distributed model adds the central amount of noise once, in pieces. Independent Gaussians add up to a Gaussian whose variance is the sum of theirs, so if each of \(n\) clients adds \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2/n)\), the sum carries exactly the \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) of the central Gaussian mechanism (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). A secure aggregation protocol (Bonawitz et al. 2017), built on additive secret sharing (Cryptography basics), shows the server nothing it couldn’t compute from the sum, so its view is as private as the central mechanism’s output.
Each client can’t add the full \(\sigma^2\) to be safe: the sum would then carry \(n\sigma^2\), the local model again. The small shares make the accuracy central, and they are also the weakness, since no share is enough noise alone. If the adversary knows the noise of \(t\) clients, because they collude or dropped out, it subtracts their shares, leaving a Gaussian mechanism with noise \[\sigma\sqrt{\frac{n - t}{n}}. \tag{25.6}\] So over-provision: to tolerate a fraction \(\rho\) of such clients, each adds variance \(\sigma^2/(n(1 - \rho))\), and the honest ones alone still supply \(\sigma^2\).
A server aggregates a histogram through 100 clients at \((1, 10^{-6})\)-DP. Under replace a changed value moves two counts by 1, so the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity is \(\sqrt2\), and the exact calibration gives total noise \(\sigma = 5.975\), or 0.597 per client. If 20% of clients collude with the server, the delivered guarantee is \(\varepsilon = 1.128\); at 50%, 1.455; with only 10% honest, 3.525 (Figure 25.5). Nobody outside can see how many are honest, so decide the fraction up front.






Figure 25.5: The actual \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) of distributed Gaussian noise calibrated for a target \(\varepsilon\), against the fraction of the total noise that the adversary does not know. At fraction 1 every client is honest and the target is met; below it, colluding or dropped clients leave less noise than planned.



Secret shares can be uniformly random only in a finite set, so secure aggregation works on integers modulo some \(q\), chosen large enough that the true sum never wraps around. Clients round their values and add integer noise whose sum still has a known distribution. Skellam noise, a difference of two Poisson variables, sums exactly to Skellam noise because Poissons add, and its privacy is close to a Gaussian’s (Agarwal, Kairouz & Liu 2021); discrete Gaussian shares sum approximately to a discrete Gaussian (Kairouz, Liu & Steinke 2021). Laplace noise doesn’t split: \(n\) shares of \(\mathrm{Lap}(b/n)\) sum to variance \(2b^2/n\), not \(2b^2\). And secure aggregation hides inputs without checking them: a malicious client can send a vector with no noise, and bounding that needs zero-knowledge proofs or verifiable aggregation.

title: 26  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
26.1 Why this matters
Someone hands you a design for a private release: a histogram over a million locations with a maximum error of five records at \(\varepsilon = 1\), say. Before reading their code, you can check whether that accuracy is possible at all. The earlier chapters gave upper bounds, what one mechanism achieves. A lower bound says that no mechanism satisfying differential privacy (DP) can do better. When it matches a known mechanism, that mechanism is optimal, and more accuracy can only come from more data or less privacy. When a claim beats a lower bound, the claim is wrong.
How can anything be said about every mechanism, when you can’t try them all? By using only the two things you know about it: it is accurate, and it is private. Accuracy is an attack: an accurate output reveals something about the data, which of many datasets was used, whether a person is in it, what their secret bits are. DP caps every attack. If an accurate mechanism would hand an attacker more than DP allows, it can’t be both, and solving that clash for the error or for the number of records \(n\) gives the bound. Throughout, the error is at most \(\alpha\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), and the examples use \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\beta = 0.05\) and, for approximate DP, \(\delta = 10^{-6}\).
crumbs: 26  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 26  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 26.2 Pure DP pays for the number of candidates
text:
26.2 Pure DP pays for the number of candidates
Suppose the output must point to one of \(m\) candidates, such as the most common of a million ZIP codes. For each candidate there is a dataset on which an accurate answer points to it with probability at least \(1 - \beta\). Now run the mechanism on one reference dataset instead, say the empty one. Its output probabilities add up to 1, so most candidates get only a small share. But pure DP extended to datasets \(k\) records apart (group privacy, Post-processing, group privacy and composition) says no event becomes more than \(e^{k\varepsilon}\) times less likely, so every candidate keeps a share of at least about \(e^{-k\varepsilon}\) on the reference. A budget of 1 can’t cover \(m\) such demands unless \(k\) is large. This counting argument is packing: if each candidate’s dataset is within \(k\) records of the reference, then \[k \ge \frac{\ln\big(m(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}. \tag{26.1}\]
Two consequences follow under add/remove neighbours. To report the mode of \(N\) elements reliably, the top element must lead by at least \(\ln(N(1 - \beta))/\varepsilon\) records. And a histogram accurate to \(\alpha\) in every bin can find a spike of height more than \(2\alpha\), so any \(\varepsilon\)-DP histogram over \(N\) bins has \[\alpha \ge \frac12\left(\frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} - 1\right). \tag{26.2}\] The Laplace histogram has error at most \(\ln(N/\beta)/\varepsilon\), since each of \(N\) noises exceeds \(\alpha\) with probability \(e^{-\alpha\varepsilon}\), and report-noisy-max (Selection) finds the mode at a lead of the same order. Both grow like \(\ln N/\varepsilon\), so both are optimal within a factor of about 2 (Figure 26.1). The factor is mostly slack in the argument: the argument counts only the reference output’s mass inside candidates’ regions, but for Laplace that output is pure noise around zero and almost none of it lands in any region. That wasted mass is the factor of 2.
For \(N = 10^6\) locations, the most common one must lead by at least 13.76 records before any \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism can report it reliably; report-noisy-max needs 18.44. Every \(\varepsilon\)-DP histogram has, at the 95% level, an error of at least 6.38 in some bin; Laplace has 16.79.






Figure 26.1: \(\ell_\infty\) error of \(\varepsilon\)-DP histograms over \(N\) bins at \(\varepsilon = 1\), failure probability 0.05. Orange: the Laplace mechanism, exact (line), union bound (dotted, indistinguishable) and simulated (dots). Blue: the packing lower bound; no \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism has an error in the shaded region. Both grow like \(\ln N\).



Packing needs \(\delta = 0\). With \(\delta > 0\), group privacy over \(k\) records carries an additive slack that grows with \(k\), while the share \(e^{-k\varepsilon}\) shrinks; past about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records (13.82 at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\)) the slack swamps it and the argument demands nothing. That is not a weak proof but a real escape. The stability-based histogram (Vadhan 2017) adds noise only to non-empty bins and releases one only if its noisy count clears a threshold of order \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\). Empty bins are never released, so nothing pays for the \(N\) bins, and its error doesn’t grow with \(N\). For a huge, mostly empty universe, approximate DP is how you escape the \(\ln N\).

title: 26  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
26.3 How many records privacy costs
An error of 6 records is large in a dataset of 50 and negligible in a million, so dividing by \(n\) turns a bound on error into a bound on records. That lets you compare privacy’s cost with one you pay anyway, sampling error. For a histogram, an error of \(\alpha\) in every frequency needs \[n \ge \frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big) - \varepsilon}{2\alpha\varepsilon} \tag{26.3}\] records under \(\varepsilon\)-DP, while sampling alone needs up to \(\ln(2N/\beta)/(2\alpha^2)\). The private term grows like \(1/\alpha\) and the statistical one like \(1/\alpha^2\), so privacy adds a term that dominates only for coarse answers at strong privacy, \(\alpha \gtrsim \varepsilon\). Over \(10^6\) cells to within \(\alpha = 0.1\), privacy needs at least 64 records and sampling up to 875; at \(\alpha = 0.01\), 638 and 87,522.
With many attributes, pure and approximate DP part ways. To release the means of \(d\) yes/no attributes, coded \(\pm1\), each within \(\alpha\), a pure-DP mechanism faces \(2^d\) candidates, one per corner of the cube, and packing charges \(\ln 2^d\): about \(d\ln 2/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) records, linear in \(d\). The Gaussian mechanism needs only \(2\sqrt d\,z/(\mu\alpha)\), where \(z\) is the normal quantile with tail \(\beta/(2d)\) and \(\mu\) is the largest ratio of sensitivity to noise the exact calibration allows (0.2367 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\); The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). The \(\sqrt d\) comes from calibrating to the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, \(2\sqrt d/n\), instead of the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity, \(2d/n\), which is possible only with \(\delta > 0\). There is no contradiction with packing, which stops working at \(\delta > 0\).
Is \(\sqrt d\) itself unavoidable, or could a cleverer mechanism do better? Packing can’t answer, so fingerprinting (Bun, Ullman & Vadhan 2014) looks only at neighbours, where \(\delta\) stays small. Draw a random dataset and release its means accurately. To follow the true means the release must follow the data, so it correlates with the records, by a total amount of order \(d\) shared among \(n\) records: each member’s correlation with the release is of order \(d/n\). A stranger’s correlation is random, with spread of order \(\sqrt d\). DP lets a member stand out from a stranger by only a constant multiple of that spread, so \(d/n \lesssim \sqrt d\), which is \(n \gtrsim \sqrt d\). The tight version is \(n\) of order \(\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) (Steinke & Ullman 2016): the Gaussian mechanism is optimal up to a logarithm.

In Table 26.1 the packing column grows tenfold with each tenfold increase in \(d\), the Gaussian column only about \(\sqrt{10}\)-fold, so it must cross below: from \(d = 2731\) attributes on, the Gaussian mechanism needs fewer records than any pure-DP mechanism (Figure 26.2). A model with a few thousand parameters is already past that point, which is one reason private machine learning uses the Gaussian mechanism.






Figure 26.2: Records needed to release \(d\) attribute means to \(\ell_\infty\) error 0.1 with probability 0.95, at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), on log–log axes. Orange: pure DP (Laplace upper bound, packing lower bound), both of slope 1. Blue: approximate DP (Gaussian upper bound, fingerprinting lower bound), both of slope ½. The constants of the fingerprinting bound are loose; the slopes are the point.



Use the fingerprinting bound for its rate, not its numbers: in the simple form the full edition proves, it says \(n \ge 5.0\) at \(d = 1000\), against 10,836 for the Gaussian mechanism. Its \(\delta\) term is harmless only for small \(\delta\), and that is no artefact: publishing each record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, so with \(\delta\) near \(1/n\) no bound of this kind could hold. And “privacy is only an additive term” fails for small subgroups, where \(n\) is the subgroup’s size.

title: 26  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 26.4 The lower bound is a membership inference attack
text:
26.4 The lower bound is a membership inference attack
The fingerprinting argument is an attack you can run. In 2008 Homer et al. showed that from the published allele frequencies of a genome-wide association study you could tell whether a given person’s DNA was in it, and their test is, up to details, the fingerprinting score. Given the released means \(\hat q\) of \(d\) attributes, with Gaussian noise \(\sigma\) per coordinate, the population means \(p\) and a target record \(y\), the attacker computes \(Z(y) = \langle\hat q, y - p\rangle\) and says “member” when it is large. Each member pulls the release towards its own record by \(1/n\) of its deviation from the population, so members’ scores are shifted up; a stranger’s record is independent of the release, so its score is centred at zero. With attribute means drawn uniformly, the shift and the spread of the scores are \[\text{gap} = \frac{2d}{3n}, \qquad \text{variance} = d\left(\frac2{15} + \frac{8}{15n} + \frac{2\sigma^2}3\right). \tag{26.4}\] The ratio of gap to spread decides the attack. Without noise it is of order \(\sqrt d/n\), so tracing works once \(d\) is large next to \(n^2\). Noise adds \(2\sigma^2/3\) to the variance per attribute, and the ratio becomes of order \(\sqrt d/(n\sigma)\), so the attack fails once \(\sigma \gg \sqrt d/n\). That is the order of noise the Gaussian mechanism adds, as it must be for a mechanism both private and as accurate as fingerprinting allows.
The full edition releases the means of \(n = 50\) records with \(d = 2000\) attributes. Without noise the gap is 26.67 and the spread 16.97, and a quarter of the members (a true positive rate (TPR) of 0.242) are identified at a false positive rate (FPR) of 1%. With the noise of a \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP Gaussian mechanism, \(\sigma = 6.67\), the TPR at 1% FPR drops to 0.014. DP guarantees no more: any test fires on members at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times as often as on strangers, plus \(\delta\), so \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta = 0.0272\). The attack fades around \(\sigma = \sqrt d/n = 0.89\) (Figure 26.3, Figure 26.4).






Figure 26.3: Tracing scores of members (blue) and non-members (orange) for \(n = 50\) records and \(d = 2000\) attributes. Left: exact means; the members’ scores are shifted by \(2d/(3n) = 26.7\). Right: means released with the Gaussian noise of a \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP mechanism; the two distributions nearly coincide.









Figure 26.4: Advantage of the tracing attack against the noise standard deviation, \(n = 50\), \(d = 2000\). Dots: simulation; solid line: the normal approximation; dashed: the worst-case bound on every attack. The attack fails once \(\sigma\) is well above \(\sqrt d/n\); the DP Gaussian mechanism adds \(\sigma = 6.7\).



So aggregates are not safe because they are aggregates: what protects members is the ratio of \(n\) to \(\sqrt d\), or noise. This is the attack of Membership inference on statistics instead of models, and it is reported the same way, as TPR at a low FPR, because identifying a few people with confidence is already a failure. When auditing with this score, take \(p\) from a separate reference sample: estimating it from the release itself subtracts part of each member’s own pull and weakens the signal.

title: 26  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
section: 26.5 Reconstruction: why answers must carry \(\sqrt n\) noise
text:
26.5 Reconstruction: why answers must carry \(\sqrt n\) noise
Reconstruction attacks recover almost all of \(n\) secret bits from about \(n\) random subset counts whose error grows more slowly than \(\sqrt n\) (Dinur & Nissim 2003): any set of bits that fits such accurate answers must agree with the truth almost everywhere. Read as a lower bound, this says such a release can’t be private. Guessing one person’s bit is a test between two neighbouring datasets, so DP caps how often any guess is right, and the fraction recovered, an average of such guesses, obeys the same cap: at most \((e^\varepsilon + \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\), 73.11% at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Turned around, recovering a fraction \(r\) proves \[\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{r - \delta}{1 - r}. \tag{26.5}\] So answers to that many counting queries need noise of order \(\sqrt n\), and the Gaussian mechanism matches: changing one bit moves each of \(k\) answers by at most 1, an \(\ell_2\) distance of at most \(\sqrt k\), so it adds noise of order \(\sqrt k\) per answer. Laplace, calibrated to the \(\ell_1\) distance \(k\), pays of order \(k\).
The full edition answers 800 random subset sums of 200 bits with Gaussian noise and decodes by least squares. Recovering 0.9607 of the bits proves \(\varepsilon \ge 3.20\). The attack recovers 0.8058 at noise \(0.5\sqrt n\), above the 73.11% an \(\varepsilon = 1\) mechanism allows, and 0.6710 at \(\sqrt n\), below it, so an \(\varepsilon = 1\) mechanism needs noise between the two (Figure 26.5).






Figure 26.5: Left: fraction of 200 secret bits recovered by least squares from 800 subset sums with Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\), against \(\sigma/\sqrt n\). The dotted line is the most that any \(\varepsilon = 1\) mechanism allows. Right: the \(\varepsilon\) that the reconstruction proves (blue) and the \(\varepsilon\) that the Gaussian mechanism guarantees (orange), at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\); the true privacy loss of the release lies between them.



An attack proves only a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\). Recovering 67% of the bits at \(\sigma = \sqrt n\) proves \(\varepsilon \ge 0.71\), but least squares is not the best attack, so it doesn’t make the release \((0.71, 10^{-6})\)-DP; the mechanism’s analysis guarantees only \(\varepsilon \le 11.00\). The true loss lies between, and stronger attacks narrow the gap, which is what privacy auditing does.

title: 26  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
26.6 Code
Checking a claimed accuracy is a few lines of arithmetic: the pure-DP histogram floor and the Laplace error, the records needed for \(d\) means under pure DP and with the Gaussian mechanism, and the \(\varepsilon\) a reconstruction proves.
from math import exp, log, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist

PHI = NormalDist().cdf


def histogram_error_floor(bins: int, eps: float, beta: float) -> float:
    """Smallest max-bin error any eps-DP histogram can have with probability 1 - beta (packing)."""
    return max(0.0, (log(bins * (1 - beta)) / eps - 1) / 2)


def laplace_histogram_error(bins: int, eps: float, beta: float) -> float:
    """Max-bin error the Laplace histogram reaches with probability 1 - beta (exact)."""
    return -log(1 - (1 - beta) ** (1 / bins)) / eps


def means_records_floor_pure(d: int, eps: float, alpha: float, beta: float) -> float:
    """Records any eps-DP release of d means in [-1, 1] needs for max error alpha (packing)."""
    return ((d * log(2) + log(1 - 2.0**-d) + log(1 - beta)) / eps - 1) / alpha


def gaussian_mu(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Largest sensitivity / sigma for which the Gaussian mechanism is (eps, delta)-DP."""
    lo, hi = 1e-6, 100.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mu = (lo + hi) / 2
        d = PHI(mu / 2 - eps / mu) - exp(eps) * PHI(-mu / 2 - eps / mu)
        lo, hi = (mu, hi) if d < delta else (lo, mu)
    return lo


def means_records_gaussian(d: int, eps: float, delta: float, alpha: float, beta: float) -> float:
    """Records the Gaussian mechanism needs for the same release (an upper bound)."""
    z = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - beta / (2 * d))
    return 2 * sqrt(d) * z / (gaussian_mu(eps, delta) * alpha)


def epsilon_proved(recovered: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Lower bound on epsilon from an attack that recovers this fraction of uniform secret bits."""
    return log((recovered - delta) / (1 - recovered))


print(f"{histogram_error_floor(10**6, 1.0, 0.05):.2f} {laplace_histogram_error(10**6, 1.0, 0.05):.2f}")  # 6.38 16.79
print(f"{means_records_floor_pure(1000, 1.0, 0.1, 0.05):.0f} {means_records_gaussian(1000, 1.0, 1e-6, 0.1, 0.05):.0f}")  # 6921 10836
print(f"{epsilon_proved(0.9607, 1e-6):.2f}")  # 3.20
Back to the opening claim: a pure \(\varepsilon = 1\) histogram over \(10^6\) locations with maximum error 5 at 95% confidence is impossible, since no mechanism goes below 6.38. Unless the design uses \(\delta > 0\) and exploits sparsity, ask what it is really doing. The full edition’s script, lower_bounds.py, computes every number in this chapter and runs the attacks:

title: Privacy accounting
text:
The common thread
The previous part defined differential privacy (DP), built the basic mechanisms and showed how \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees add up when mechanisms run one after another. That is enough for a handful of releases, not for training a model, which runs thousands of noisy steps, each on a random subset of the data, and must then state one \(\varepsilon\). No single theorem gives that number. It comes from an accountant, a procedure that tracks a summary of each step’s privacy loss, combines the summaries, and converts the result into the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) you report. Two accountants given the same training run can report values of \(\varepsilon\) that differ by a large factor, and both can be correct upper bounds; only the tighter one tells you what the noise bought.
Read this part if you train models with DP, or review or audit a model that claims an \(\varepsilon\). It assumes Differential privacy foundations: the definition, the privacy loss of an output, the Gaussian mechanism and its exact curve \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), and composition. Each chapter restates in a sentence what it uses.
The privacy loss of an output is the log of how much more likely that output is with your record than without it. Over a run, the per-step losses add, so for the loss itself composition is easy. For \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) it is hard, because a pair of numbers is one point of a whole curve and forgets almost everything about how the loss is distributed. Composing points pays for that lost information at every step. Every accountant in this part makes the same move instead: track a richer summary of the privacy loss, one that composes simply, and convert to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) only once, at the end.
The chapters differ in the summary they keep, and their order follows from it. The first two introduce Rényi differential privacy (RDP), the summary most libraries use: a curve of exponential moments of the loss that adds up step by step, and the conversion that turns the final curve into the reported pair. Every later chapter starts from that curve, so they come first. Concentrated DP then squeezes the curve into one number \(\rho\), which describes Gaussian noise exactly and many other mechanisms only loosely, and f-DP goes the other way, keeping the whole trade-off between an attacker’s false positives and missed detections, which reads directly as attack power.
None of these summaries yet explains why training is private at all. The differentially private version of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, clips each example’s gradient and adds Gaussian noise, and if every step used the whole dataset its guarantee would be useless. It is private because each step touches a random fraction of the records, so most steps don’t see a given record at all. Amplification by subsampling turns that into a much smaller per-step loss. It is a separate question from the summary, since it decides which pair of output distributions you account for, and it must match how the training code really samples its data. Numerical accounting then keeps the whole distribution of the loss and composes it with a discretization error it bounds, which makes it the tool that checks every other accountant. These two chapters are the practical core, in that order, because the numerical accountant takes the subsampled step as its input.
The last chapters handle departures from that setting. Shuffling instead of sampling, or releasing only the final model, can give extra privacy, but only under assumptions the code has to meet. Budgets chosen while training runs, or privacy spent differently per record, break the assumption that each step’s bound is fixed in advance, and need filters and odometers. The final chapter puts the pieces together.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
The running example
Every chapter that can compute it reports the same number: the \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of DP-SGD with Poisson sampling rate \(q = 0.01\), noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\) and up to \(k = 10{,}000\) steps. That is about one hundred epochs at a typical setting. A single Gaussian mechanism with \(\sigma = 1\) serves as the small example. Watching the same number move from chapter to chapter shows what each tool gains, and Choosing an accountant puts all the values side by side.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
How to read this part
Read the RDP and conversion chapters first, then subsampling and numerical accounting. The chapters on concentrated DP and f-DP explain the other summaries you will meet in papers and libraries. Read shuffling and iteration if your code shuffles instead of sampling or releases only the final model, adaptive composition if your budgets are chosen during training, and the last chapter last. The derivations are in the full edition.

title: Privacy accounting
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
By the end of this part you will be able to compute the RDP curve of a Gaussian training step, compose a run of them and convert the result with the right conversion. You will know what each summary keeps and loses, how much subsampling buys and which sampling scheme it assumes, and how to check any accountant against a numerical one. And for a DP-SGD run you will be able to pick an accountant, state its assumptions, and report \(\varepsilon\) in a way someone else can check.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.1 Why this matters
You train a model with 1000 steps of full-batch noisy gradient descent. Each step computes a quantity whose sensitivity is 1, meaning one person’s record moves it by at most 1, and adds Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is \(\sigma = 20\) times that sensitivity; \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier. What is the total differential privacy (DP) guarantee at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)?
Advanced composition turns each step into one \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) pair and composes the pairs; with the best split of \(\delta\) it gives \(\varepsilon = 68.01\). The true answer is \(\varepsilon = 7.51\), nine times smaller, and the damage is done in the first move. A Gaussian step has no single \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\): for every \(\varepsilon_0\) there is a smallest \(\delta_0\) that works, so it has a whole curve of valid pairs. Picking one point throws away the rest of the curve, which composition needs.
So keep a curve that is easy to compose. Rényi differential privacy (RDP) records, for each order \(\alpha > 1\), an exponential moment of the privacy loss. These curves add up over a run, with no \(\delta\) spent along the way, and you convert the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the end. For the 1000 Gaussian steps this gives \(\varepsilon = 8.84\), 18% above the exact 7.51.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.2 The RDP curve
Run a mechanism \(M\) on neighbouring datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) to get output distributions \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\). The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is \(L(y) = \ln\frac{p(y)}{q(y)}\), the log of how much more likely \(y\) is under \(D\) than under \(D'\). Over several steps the losses add, because the likelihood ratios multiply.
Which summary of a loss survives being summed? Not a tail probability, which is what \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) records. Exponential moments do: for independent losses, the average of \(e^{\lambda(L_1 + L_2)}\) is the product of the averages of \(e^{\lambda L_1}\) and \(e^{\lambda L_2}\), so their logarithms add. The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is the log of one such moment, scaled: \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\,dy. \tag{27.1}\] A mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP if \(D_\alpha(M(D)\|M(D')) \le \varepsilon\) for every pair of neighbours, and its RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is the smallest such \(\varepsilon\) at each order, the divergence of the worst pair.
The order sets how much large losses count, since an exponential moment is dominated by them, the more so the larger \(\alpha\). As \(\alpha \to 1\) the curve tends to the average loss, the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence; as \(\alpha \to \infty\) it tends to the largest loss of any output, so a mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP exactly when \(\varepsilon(\infty) \le \varepsilon\). In between it never decreases. A loss that is usually small but sometimes huge is caught only at large orders.
Randomized response shows both ends. It reports one person’s bit truthfully with probability \(p = 0.75\) and flips it otherwise, so the loss is \(\ln 3\) on an output that agrees with the bit and \(-\ln 3\) on one that doesn’t. The average loss is \((0.75 - 0.25)\ln 3 = 0.5493\), the curve’s value as \(\alpha \to 1\); it rises through 0.8473 at order 2 and 1.0666 at order 10 to the largest loss, \(\ln 3 = 1.0986\). A single point such as “\((2, 0.8473)\)-RDP” says nothing about higher orders, where the curve may keep rising, so accountants store the whole curve on a grid of orders.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
section: 27.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
text:
27.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
A mechanism that adds noise to a query’s answer produces the same noise centred at two different answers. Its curve is the divergence between the noise and a shifted copy, and since a larger shift makes the copies easier to tell apart, the worst pair is the one with the largest shift, the sensitivity.
For the Gaussian mechanism the log of the ratio of two normal densities is a difference of two squares whose quadratic terms cancel, so the loss is linear in the output and therefore itself normal. The log of a normal variable’s exponential moment is quadratic in \(\lambda\), and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) leaves a straight line. With sensitivity 1, \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{27.2}\] For a vector query only the Euclidean distance between the two answers matters, because the noise looks the same in every direction, so \(\sigma\) is the noise standard deviation in units of the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. In the differentially private version of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, which clips each example’s gradient and adds Gaussian noise, that sensitivity is the clipping norm, so the \(\sigma\) you plug in is the noise standard deviation divided by the clipping norm.
A linear loss has no maximum, so the curve grows without limit: the Gaussian mechanism is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\). It is RDP at every finite order, though, and that is all composition and conversion need. The Laplace mechanism, which adds noise of density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|y|/b}\), behaves differently. Its loss at \(y\) is \((|y - 1| - |y|)/b\), which the triangle inequality keeps between \(-1/b\) and \(1/b\), so its curve levels off at its pure-DP level \(1/b\); randomized response levels off at \(\ln\frac{p}{1-p}\) for the same reason. All three curves are exact (Mironov 2017); the closed forms are in Table 27.3, and Figure 27.1 and Table 27.1 compare them.

The Laplace and randomized response curves level off at their pure DP levels \(1/b\) and \(\ln 3\) (dotted); the Gaussian curve keeps growing.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.4 Composition adds curves
Training steps are not independent, since each gradient depends on the model so far, so the product argument of Section 27.2 needs one more idea. Fix the first output and look at the second step alone. Whatever the first output was, the second step is some mechanism with curve at most \(\varepsilon_2\), so its moment is at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_2(\alpha)}\); averaging over the first output leaves the first step’s moment times that constant. Taking the log, the curves add: \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \sum_{i=1}^k \varepsilon_i(\alpha) \qquad\text{for every } \alpha > 1, \tag{27.3}\] with equality for independent steps (Mironov 2017). The argument also shows the limit of adaptivity: each step’s bound must hold whatever the earlier outputs were, so it has to be fixed in advance. A noise level or step count chosen on the fly from the data needs the filters of Adaptive composition.
The smallest \(\delta\) for a given \(\varepsilon\) has no such product structure. It is the probability by which one output distribution exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) times the other, a positive part of a difference, which does not factor over steps. So never convert each step first and compose afterwards: that is where the factor of nine in the opening example comes from.
For Gaussian steps the sum has a picture. Each of \(k\) steps shifts its output by at most 1, and the \(k\) shifts together form a vector of length \(\sqrt k\); a shift of \(\sqrt k\) under noise \(\sigma\) is the same as a shift of 1 under noise \(\sigma/\sqrt k\). So \(k\) steps with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) have the curve \(k\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\), the curve of one Gaussian step with noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt k\). With \(\sigma = 20\) and 1000 steps that is one Gaussian with \(\sigma = 0.6325\).
The same picture shows why DP-SGD needs more than noise. If every step of the part’s running example, 10,000 steps with \(\sigma = 1\), used the whole dataset, the run would be one Gaussian with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{10{,}000} = 0.01\), and even the exact guarantee at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is \(\varepsilon = 5425.5\): no guarantee at all. DP-SGD is private only because each step touches a random 1% of the data, which Amplification by subsampling accounts for.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.5 Post-processing and group privacy
Anything computed from a private output without looking at the data again, such as a released model’s predictions, cannot raise the curve: \(\varepsilon_{g\circ M}(\alpha) \le \varepsilon_M(\alpha)\) for any map \(g\) that ignores the data. A processed output’s likelihood ratio is an average of the ratios of the outputs that could have produced it, and averaging can only lower an exponential moment.
Groups are harder. For pure DP a group of \(k\) records costs \(k\varepsilon\), because likelihood ratios along a chain of neighbours multiply. For RDP, bounding the average of that product needs higher moments of each factor, so a bound at order \(\alpha\) for one record buys one at only about order \(\alpha/2\) for two. Mironov’s (2017) Proposition 2: if \(M\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP with \(\alpha \ge 2^{c+1}\), then on datasets that differ in \(2^c\) records it satisfies the bound of order \(\alpha/2^c\) with \(3^c\varepsilon\) in place of \(\varepsilon\). This bound is loose, so use the mechanism when you can: a group of \(2^c\) records shifts a Gaussian answer by \(2^c\), so the exact group curve is Equation 27.2 with sensitivity \(2^c\), and at \(\sigma = 1\) the generic bound is 1.5 times too large for two records and 3.375 times for eight. A mechanism that is already \(\varepsilon\)-DP keeps the pure-DP bound \(k\varepsilon\) at every order, which can win: for Laplace with \(b = 1\), two records apart at order 2, the exact value is 1.5958, the generic bound 2.4411 and the pure-DP bound 2.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.6 The moments accountant is RDP
Abadi et al. (2016) trained neural networks with DP by tracking, for the worst pair of neighbours, the log of the moment generating function (MGF) of the privacy loss, \(K(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E_P[e^{\lambda L}]\): the moments accountant. The definition of Section 27.2 says that \((\alpha - 1)D_\alpha\) is exactly this log-MGF at \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), so the two are the same curve in different units: \[K(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon(\lambda + 1), \qquad \varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{K(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{27.4}\] For randomized response, \(K(1) = \ln(0.75 \times 3 + 0.25 \times \frac13) = 0.8473 = 1 \cdot \varepsilon(2)\). What was new in 2016 was not the bookkeeping but a bound on the curve of the subsampled step. So when a “moments accountant” and an “RDP accountant” disagree, look at that curve, the order grid or the conversion.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.7 From RDP to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)
After composing you hold a curve, but you report a pair. An output whose loss is at most some threshold \(c\) already satisfies the \(e^c\) bound of DP, so only outputs with loss above \(c\) can break it, and you can charge their total probability to \(\delta\). That probability is a tail of the loss, and Markov’s inequality bounds a tail by an exponential moment, which is exactly what each point of the curve provides. Setting the bound equal to \(\delta\) and solving for \(c\) gives Mironov’s conversion: an \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon_\delta, \delta)\)-DP for every \(0 < \delta < 1\), with \[\varepsilon_\delta = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{27.5}\] Every order gives a valid pair. The curve grows with the order and the tail term shrinks, so you minimize over the grid after composing. For a Gaussian curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) the minimum has a closed form, where the two order-dependent terms are equal: \[\alpha^* = 1 + \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}, \qquad \varepsilon_\delta = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}}{\sigma}. \tag{27.6}\] For \(k\) steps, put \(\sigma/\sqrt k\) in place of \(\sigma\).
For one Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), where \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.5129\), order 2 gives \(1 + 11.5129 = 12.5129\), dominated by the tail term, and the best grid order, 5.8, gives 5.2985. The exact \(\varepsilon\) is 4.3772, so the conversion is 21% too large, and at \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\) the true \(\delta\) is \(1.300 \times 10^{-7}\), 76.9 times smaller than promised. Advanced composition is 5 to 9 times the exact value, worse as \(k\) grows, because every step was collapsed to a point; RDP is 18% to 57% above, better as \(k\) grows. The best order falls as the run grows, because a steeper composed curve makes large orders expensive: one step with \(\sigma = 20\) wants \(\alpha \approx 97\), a thousand steps want \(\alpha \approx 4\), and the full-batch run of Section 27.4 wants 1.048, below the grid’s smallest order 1.1. The remaining gap is slack: the conversion charges the whole probability of every output above the threshold to \(\delta\), although an output just over the line breaks the bound only slightly, and Markov’s inequality then overestimates that tail. The slack depends on the composed \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\): 1.07 times exact at \(\mu = 10\), 1.21 at \(\mu = 1\) and 1.76 at \(\mu = 0.01\). Weak mechanisms pay most, because as \(\mu\) shrinks the exact \(\varepsilon\) falls faster than the tail bound. So don’t report this conversion; use the improved one of From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests, or a numerical accountant.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.8 Code
RDP accounting for full-batch Gaussian steps is a curve on a grid of orders, a sum over steps and a minimum over orders. This snippet uses the part’s grid of 154 orders.
from math import log

ORDERS = [1 + x / 10 for x in range(1, 100)] + list(range(12, 64)) + [128, 256, 512]


def gaussian_rdp(alpha: float, sigma: float, steps: int = 1) -> float:
    """RDP curve of `steps` Gaussian steps with noise multiplier sigma (sensitivity 1)."""
    return steps * alpha / (2 * sigma**2)


def mironov_eps(curve: list[float], delta: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Best (epsilon, order) from Mironov's conversion over the grid."""
    return min((eps + log(1 / delta) / (a - 1), a) for a, eps in zip(ORDERS, curve))


one = [gaussian_rdp(a, sigma=1.0) for a in ORDERS]
run = [gaussian_rdp(a, sigma=20.0, steps=1000) for a in ORDERS]
full_batch = [gaussian_rdp(a, sigma=1.0, steps=10_000) for a in ORDERS]
print("%.4f at order %g" % mironov_eps(one, 1e-5))  # 5.2985 at order 5.8
print("%.3f at order %g" % mironov_eps(run, 1e-5))  # 8.838 at order 4
print("%.1f at order %g" % mironov_eps(full_batch, 1e-5))  # 5615.1 at order 1.1
The last line shows the best order stuck at the bottom of the grid. The full edition’s script, renyi_dp.py, computes every number in this chapter, including the exact Gaussian values:
uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/renyi_dp.py

Rules of thumb

Compose in RDP and convert once at the end. Never convert each step to \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) first.

Report the noise multiplier, the number of steps and the sampling scheme along with \(\varepsilon\), so others can recompute it.

title: 27  Rényi differential privacy
text:
27.10 Further reading

Mironov, “Rényi Differential Privacy” (IEEE CSF 2017): the definition, composition, the curves of the basic mechanisms, group privacy and the conversion. Short and readable.
Abadi et al., “Deep Learning with Differential Privacy” (CCS 2016): DP-SGD and the moments accountant, with the experiments that made private deep learning practical.
Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism” (arXiv 2019): the curves of subsampled steps, and the reference behind most RDP accountants.

title: 28  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
28.1 Why this matters
A Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant adds up the curves \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) of a run’s steps, one value per order \(\alpha > 1\) (Rényi differential privacy). Nobody reports that curve. A paper, a model card or a regulator asks for an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) differential privacy (DP) guarantee, or for a statement about attacks, so every RDP analysis ends with a conversion, and the conversion decides the number you publish.
Ask what a conversion is allowed to know. The privacy loss of an output is the log of how much more likely it is under one neighbouring dataset than under the other, and the RDP curve records exponential moments of that loss and nothing else. A conversion must therefore give a \(\delta\) that is safe for every mechanism with that curve, not just for yours. Mironov’s conversion, the original one, uses the moments crudely. The improved conversion uses them almost as well as anything can, at no cost. What remains, 5 to 10% of \(\varepsilon\) for the Gaussian mechanism, belongs to the summary itself.
The running example is the Gaussian mechanism. A step adds noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\) times the sensitivity, and \(k\) such steps compose to one Gaussian whose two output distributions are \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\) noise standard deviations apart. Its RDP curve is \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2\), so every number below depends only on \(\mu\). All use \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and the part’s grid of 154 orders, from 1.1 to 512.

title: 28  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
section: 28.2 Mironov’s conversion and where it loses
text:
28.2 Mironov’s conversion and where it loses
Start from what \(\delta\) is. The smallest valid \(\delta\) at a given \(\varepsilon\) is an average over outputs: an output whose loss \(L\) exceeds \(\varepsilon\) breaks the \(e^\varepsilon\) bound only by its excess probability, which is the fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\) of its probability. An output just over the line contributes almost nothing, and one far over it contributes almost all of its probability.
Mironov’s conversion bounds that average in two steps. It first charges the whole probability of every output with \(L > \varepsilon\) to \(\delta\), which replaces \(\delta\) by the tail probability of the loss. It then bounds the tail with Markov’s inequality applied to \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\), whose average is what the RDP curve provides. Setting the result equal to \(\delta\) gives \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}, \tag{28.1}\] minimized over the orders of the grid.
Both steps lose on the Gaussian. Its loss is normal, and \(\varepsilon\) sits several standard deviations above the mean, where the density falls steeply; most of the tail lies just above \(\varepsilon\), exactly where each output’s true contribution is near zero, so the first step overcounts. The second step loses more. Markov’s inequality is tight only for a variable that puts all its mass at 0 and at the threshold, and a normal loss is nothing like that.
For a mean released with the Gaussian mechanism at \(\sigma = 1\), so \(\mu = 1\), the exact \(\varepsilon\) is 4.377. Charging the whole tail alone raises it to 4.765, and the Markov step to 5.299, at order 5.8. At \(\varepsilon = 5.299\) the true \(\delta\) is \(1.300\times10^{-7}\): you pay for \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and get far less. The conversion is valid, just loose: safe but overstated. Older code and papers, including the original moments accountant, use it, so check which conversion each side used before comparing your \(\varepsilon\) with a published one.

title: 28  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
28.3 The improved conversion
Taken together, the two steps replace each output’s contribution \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\) by an exponential in \(L\) that lies above it, and an exponential is used because it is the only function whose average the RDP curve tells you. Mironov’s exponential equals 1 at \(L = \varepsilon\), where the true contribution is still 0. A lower exponential still stays above the contribution, touching it just to the right of \(\varepsilon\). Using the lowest one is the whole improvement (Balle, Barthe, Gaboardi, Hsu & Sato 2020; Canonne, Kamath & Steinke 2020). An \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP mechanism is then \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}, \tag{28.2}\] again minimized over the grid, and reported as 0 if it comes out negative.
Compare the two formulas at the same order and both the curve and the \(\ln(1/\delta)\) term cancel. What is left, the saving, depends only on the order, not on the mechanism or \(\delta\): \[\Delta(\alpha) = \frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{28.3}\] It is large at small orders and fades at large ones (Table 28.1). That gives you a diagnostic. If two accountants report values about 0.4 apart from the same curve at a best order near 10, one of them is using Mironov’s conversion. Opacus and Google’s dp_accounting both use the improved one, and if you implement a conversion yourself, use Equation 28.2.

title: 28  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
28.4 Choosing the order
The converted \(\varepsilon'\) is the curve, which grows with the order, plus a term in \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), which shrinks with it, and the best order balances the two. For a composed Gaussian with curve \(\rho\alpha\), where \(\rho = \mu^2/2 = k/(2\sigma^2)\), setting the derivative to zero gives \(\rho(\alpha - 1)^2 = \ln\frac{1}{\alpha\delta}\), so roughly \[\alpha^* - 1 \approx \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho} = \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)/k}. \tag{28.4}\] The formula says how the best order moves. More steps or less noise make the curve steeper, so high orders get expensive and the best order moves toward 1. A smaller \(\delta\) pushes it up, but only through the square root of a logarithm, so \(\delta\) hardly matters: at \(\mu = 1\), going from \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-10}\) moves the best order only from 5.432 to 7.483.
Table 28.2 shows the range a grid must cover. One release at \(\sigma = 10\) wants order 40.525, a long run at \(\sigma = 1\) wants 1.048. At \(k = 10{,}000\) that order is below the grid’s smallest, 1.1, and the grid’s answer is 135.987 larger than the continuous optimum.

title: 28  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
28.5 The slack no conversion removes
The improved conversion still stays above the exact \(\varepsilon\). That is the summary’s fault, not the formula’s, and a counterexample shows why. Take a mechanism with only two outputs: almost all its probability sits on an output with loss close to 0, and a sliver on an output with loss 4.5956. This mechanism satisfies the Gaussian’s RDP curve at \(\mu = 1\) at every order, yet at \(\varepsilon = 4.377\), the Gaussian’s exact value, its \(\delta\) is \(4.4698\times10^{-5}\), not \(10^{-5}\). A certificate computed from the curve alone cannot tell the two mechanisms apart, so it must cover both, and it cannot certify 4.377. The best any method can certify from the curve is 4.7284 to four decimals, which is what the improved conversion gives at its best real order.
Across run lengths (Table 28.3, Figure 28.1), the best conversion from the curve and the improved conversion agree to three decimals, and both exceed the exact \(\varepsilon\) by 5 to 10%.
