Right: each divided by the exact value. The improved conversion is as good as any conversion from the curve; the remaining 5 to 10% belongs to the RDP summary itself.



So if a reviewer asks whether a better conversion would lower your \((4.729, 10^{-5})\) for a Gaussian with \(\mu = 1\), the answer is no. When the slack matters, change the summary, not the formula: track the trade-off function (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy) or the whole privacy loss distribution (Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions). The 5 to 10% is for the plain Gaussian. DP-SGD’s subsampled steps have a curve that is not a line, and the gap can be much larger; for the part’s running example (\(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(k = 10{,}000\)), RDP gives 7.43 with Mironov’s conversion and 6.71 with the improved one, and Choosing an accountant measures the gap.
The same reasoning governs mixing RDP with other guarantees. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP guarantee with \(\delta > 0\) implies no RDP bound at any order. A mechanism that publishes your record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, but it has an output that is impossible without you, an infinite likelihood ratio, and so an infinite exponential moment. Never feed an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) component into an RDP accountant as if it had a curve; you need to know how its \(\delta\) arises, for example from Gaussian noise. A pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP guarantee has no such outputs, and it implies \((\alpha, \min(\varepsilon, \alpha\varepsilon^2/2))\)-RDP at every order (Bun & Steinke 2016).

title: 28  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
section: 28.6 RDP as a bound on attacks
text:
28.6 RDP as a bound on attacks
A membership test looks at the output and decides “your record was used” or “it was not”. Whatever it computes, its verdict is a coin: it says “used” with probability \(a\), its false-positive rate, when the record was absent, and with probability \(1 - b\), its power, when it was present. The verdict is computed from the output, so it cannot be further apart in the two worlds than the output itself, and the Rényi divergence between the two coins is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) at every order (Balle et al. 2020). Each order thus constrains every test’s \((a, b)\).
The constraints of different orders bend differently. Large orders weigh the extreme outputs heavily, so they guard small false-positive rates; small orders guard the bulk. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair, by contrast, constrains every test by one straight line, power \(\le e^\varepsilon a + \delta\), which can touch the curved region the orders allow at only one point and lies far above it elsewhere.
The gap matters for audits. An auditor attacks the mean released at \(\sigma = 1\) with a false-positive rate of \(a = 10^{-3}\). The RDP curve guarantees that no test has power above \(2.4910\times10^{-2}\); the best test against the Gaussian actually reaches \(1.8298\times10^{-2}\). The \((4.729, 10^{-5})\) guarantee from the improved conversion only says power \(\le e^{4.729}\times10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.1131\), more than four times the curve’s bound. So when you translate an RDP result into attack risk, don’t go through one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair: at low false-positive rates, the ones that matter for membership attacks, it throws away most of what the curve says. Use the curve, or better, the trade-off function of f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy.

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.1 Why this matters
You run a pipeline of Gaussian releases, such as noisy counts, answers in a query system or noisy marginals for synthetic data, and you want to keep the differential privacy (DP) budget as one number that you add to as you go. Rényi DP describes each mechanism by a curve: its Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) gives, for each order \(\alpha > 1\), the largest Rényi divergence between the outputs on neighbouring datasets, which differ in one person’s record. Composition adds the curves. For the Gaussian mechanism with noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the noise standard deviation in units of the sensitivity, the curve is a straight line through the origin, \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/(2\sigma^2)\). A line through the origin is fixed by its slope, so for Gaussian noise one number already carries everything.
Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), the most widely used form of concentrated differential privacy (CDP), turns that observation into a definition: describe any mechanism by the slope of a line through the origin that lies above its RDP curve. Lines add to a line, so composition is addition of slopes, and converting a line to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) has a closed form. The rest of the chapter asks one question: how well does a line fit the curve? For the Gaussian, exactly. For pure DP mechanisms with large \(\varepsilon\), badly. For the subsampled steps of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD for short, it fits so badly that zCDP is the wrong tool.

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.2 The definition of zCDP
A mechanism \(M\) is \(\rho\)-zCDP if its RDP curve lies under the line of slope \(\rho\): for all neighbours \(D \simeq D'\) and all orders \(\alpha > 1\), \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le \rho\alpha. \tag{29.1}\] Because RDP curves add under composition, so do the lines above them: a \(\rho_1\)-zCDP step followed by a \(\rho_2\)-zCDP step is \((\rho_1 + \rho_2)\)-zCDP, even when the second step is chosen after seeing the first one’s output. Post-processing cannot increase a divergence, so it cannot increase \(\rho\) either.
The Gaussian mechanism, which adds \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) to a query with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta\), is \(\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\)-zCDP, and the line is its exact curve. The reason also explains the name. The privacy loss of an output is the log of how much more likely it is under \(D\) than under \(D'\). For two normal densities with the same variance, that log-ratio is a linear function of the output, and a linear function of a normal variable is normal: with \(\Delta = 1\) the loss has mean \(1/(2\sigma^2) = \rho\) and variance \(1/\sigma^2 = 2\rho\). zCDP in general says the privacy loss has tails no heavier than this normal variable, “concentrated” around a small mean.
With \(\sigma = 1\) one Gaussian step is \(0.5\)-zCDP and ten are \(5\)-zCDP; with \(\sigma = 2\) a step costs \(0.125\). Halving the noise multiplier multiplies \(\rho\) by four, because \(\rho\) goes with the square of the shift in units of the noise. The 2020 United States Census TopDown algorithm is built this way (Abowd et al. 2022): it measures many noisy queries with the discrete Gaussian mechanism (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms), adds up the \(\rho\)’s, and converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the end. For Gaussian noise the line loses nothing, so the only approximation is that final conversion.
Two warnings. \(\rho\) is not \(\varepsilon\): \(\rho = 0.5\) is about \(\varepsilon = 4.7\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) (Section 29.4). And the ledger covers only what passed through the noise: the Census Bureau released some statistics, the invariants, exactly; they were never charged to \(\rho\), and they sit outside the guarantee.

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
section: 29.3 Pure DP steps in a zCDP budget
text:
29.3 Pure DP steps in a zCDP budget
A Laplace count, a randomized-response bit or an exponential-mechanism selection is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and to put it in the same ledger you need its \(\rho\). Pure DP means every output’s probability changes by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), so its privacy loss is confined to \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\). A bounded random variable has light tails, at most as heavy as a normal’s, so the step should be zCDP with \(\rho\) of order \(\varepsilon^2\). Bun & Steinke (2016) show that every \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zCDP. The exponential mechanism does four times better, \(\varepsilon^2/8\), because its privacy loss lies in an interval of length \(\varepsilon\) rather than \(2\varepsilon\), and the tail bound goes with the square of the length (Cesar & Rogers 2021).
So a Laplace count at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) costs \(0.005\). The constant \(\varepsilon^2/2\) is the right one only as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). Randomized response, which reports a bit truthfully with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), is the worst \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism at every order, and its smallest valid slope is \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\): \(0.4621\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), against \(\varepsilon^2/2 = 0.5000\).
The trouble is at large orders. No Rényi divergence can exceed the largest log-ratio of probabilities, so the RDP curve of a pure DP step flattens at \(\varepsilon\), while a line keeps rising. The curve therefore lies under both, \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \min\Big(\varepsilon,\ \frac{\alpha\varepsilon^2}{2}\Big), \tag{29.2}\] and a zCDP accountant can keep only the line. For randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the line is close near \(\alpha = 1\), but at \(\alpha = 50\) it says 25 where the exact curve is 0.9936; the cap is within 1% there (Figure 29.1, left).






Figure 29.1: The RDP curve of randomized response (black) against the zCDP line \(\alpha\varepsilon^2/2\) (dashed), the sharp line \(\alpha\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) (dash-dotted) and the pure-DP cap \(\varepsilon\) (dotted), for \(\varepsilon = 1\) (left) and \(\varepsilon = 3\) (right). At \(\varepsilon = 3\) even the sharp line crosses the cap almost at once.



The larger \(\varepsilon\) is, the sooner the line crosses the cap, since it does so at \(\alpha = 2/\varepsilon\). At \(\varepsilon = 3\) the slope \(\varepsilon^2/2 = 4.5\) is already above the cap at \(\alpha = 1\), so the line is worse than plain \(\varepsilon\) at every order (Figure 29.1, right). Charging a large-\(\varepsilon\) step in \(\rho\) then makes it more expensive than it is: a \(5\)-DP step charged \(12.5\) converts to a worse \(\varepsilon\) than the 5 you started with. This is the usual situation in local DP, where each user randomizes their own data. Keep such steps as \(\varepsilon\) or as an RDP curve; an RDP accountant can charge them the exact curve of randomized response, below both bounds.

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.4 From zCDP to (ε, δ)
Whatever you account in, you report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). The conversion of From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) gives a valid \(\varepsilon\) at every order, and you take the best. Write \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\). For a line the conversion at order \(\alpha\) is \(\rho\alpha + \ell/(\alpha - 1)\): the first term grows with the order and the second shrinks, so the best order balances them, at \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\). Substituting gives the simple conversion (Bun & Steinke 2016), \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\,\ell}. \tag{29.3}\]
Modern accountants use the sharper improved conversion of Canonne, Kamath & Steinke (2020), which adds two correction terms at each order and is minimized numerically: \[\varepsilon = \min_{\alpha > 1}\left[\rho\alpha + \frac{\ell}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\Big(1 - \frac1\alpha\Big) - \frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\right]. \tag{29.4}\] How much do the two lose? For a Gaussian the line is the exact RDP curve, so any gap between the reported and the true \(\varepsilon\) comes from the conversion alone, and the true value is known in closed form (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy). One Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 1\) is \(\rho = 0.5\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), where \(\ell = 11.5129\), the simple formula gives 5.299, the improved conversion 4.728, and the exact value is 4.377: the simple formula is 21% too large and the improved one 8% (Table 29.1, Figure 29.2).

To calibrate, run the simple conversion backwards. A target \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is met by any \[\rho \le \Big(\sqrt{\varepsilon + \ell} - \sqrt{\ell}\Big)^2, \tag{29.5}\] and the noise multiplier is then \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{2\rho}\). Because the map from \(\rho\) to \(\varepsilon\) is not linear, \(\varepsilon\) does not add and there is no clean “\(\varepsilon\) left”: with a budget of \(\rho = 1\), the whole run is \(7.077\)-DP by the improved conversion however you split it. Add in \(\rho\), and convert once, at the end.

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.5 Group privacy
A household, or a user with several records, differs from a neighbouring dataset in \(m\) records rather than one. For the Gaussian, the group moves the query’s value \(m\) times as far, and its RDP grows with the square of the shift. zCDP inherits exactly this: a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \(m^2\rho\)-zCDP for datasets that differ in \(m\) records (Bun & Steinke 2016), with equality for the Gaussian.
Quadratic growth is the same price as pure DP’s \(m\varepsilon\), translated: with \(\rho \approx \varepsilon^2/2\), \(m^2\rho \approx (m\varepsilon)^2/2\). A user who contributes up to 4 records to a \(0.1\)-zCDP release is protected at \(\rho = 4^2 \times 0.1 = 1.6\). For the Gaussian with \(\sigma = 1\), a group of 2 costs \(\rho = 2\), or \(\varepsilon = 10.725\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), and a group of 8 costs \(\rho = 32\), or \(\varepsilon = 68.616\). If users contribute many records, bound each user’s contribution before adding noise and account at the user level.

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
section: 29.6 Subsampling: why DP-SGD is not accounted in zCDP
text:
29.6 Subsampling: why DP-SGD is not accounted in zCDP
DP-SGD runs each step on a Poisson sample: each record enters the batch independently with probability \(q\). A record is usually not in the batch, so the step’s RDP curve is tiny at small orders. For the part’s running example, \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), it stays around \(10^{-4}\alpha\) up to \(\alpha = 8\) (Figure 29.3).
High orders, however, weigh the rarest and most revealing outputs. For the subsampled step those come from the event that the record was in the batch, where it pays the full Gaussian loss. So at large orders the curve bends up, and its slope approaches that of the unsubsampled line \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) (Amplification by subsampling explains the bend). A line through the origin above the whole curve must be as steep as the curve at infinity. For the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian, at any \(q\), the smallest valid \(\rho\) is therefore \(1/(2\sigma^2)\), exactly what the step would cost without subsampling. zCDP throws away all of the amplification.






Figure 29.3: The RDP curve of one Poisson-subsampled Gaussian step with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), on integer orders (black), against the best zCDP line \(\rho\alpha\) with \(\rho = 0.5\) (red dashed), which is the unsubsampled Gaussian’s line, and the tCDP line on orders up to \(\omega = 8\) (blue). Both axes are logarithmic.



With \(k = 10{,}000\) steps and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), zCDP must charge \(\rho = 0.5\) per step, so \(\rho = 5000\) in total and \(\varepsilon = 5479.9\) by the simple formula, or \(5475.8\) with the improved conversion. RDP accounting of the same run, on integer orders, gives \(7.469\) with Mironov’s conversion and \(6.719\) with the improved one. Both are upper bounds, but RDP kept the part of the curve the conversion uses: the small orders. The composed curve is \(k\varepsilon(\alpha)\), and the conversion looks for the order where \(k\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ell/(\alpha - 1)\) is smallest. Below the bend the first term is small, so the conversion pushes the order up until the bend makes the curve expensive, and stops early: here the best integer order is 4. The large orders that set the zCDP slope are never used.
Truncated concentrated differential privacy (tCDP) keeps one number per step but asks for the line only on orders up to a cut-off \(\omega\) (Bun, Dwork, Rothblum & Steinke 2018). Steps compose to \((\sum_i\rho_i, \min_i\omega_i)\), and the conversion is the simple one when its best order lies below \(\omega\), otherwise order \(\omega\): \[\varepsilon = \begin{cases}\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\,\ell} & \text{if } \ell \le (\omega - 1)^2\rho,\\[2pt] \rho\omega + \dfrac{\ell}{\omega - 1} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases} \tag{29.6}\] On orders up to \(\omega = 8\), the per-step slope is \(1.1171 \times 10^{-4}\), against zCDP’s 0.5. With \(\omega = 4\), tCDP gives \(7.469\), the same as RDP with Mironov’s conversion, because both end up converting at order 4. But once \(\omega\) passes the bend near \(\alpha = 10\), the slope must cover the steep part, and tCDP collapses towards zCDP: 80.252 with \(\omega = 10\), 2228.027 with \(\omega = 16\).
So never account a subsampled mechanism in zCDP. If a pipeline mixes Gaussian releases with a DP-SGD run, keep it all in RDP: a \(\rho\)-zCDP step is just the RDP curve \(\rho\alpha\) and joins an RDP ledger without loss. Nor is tCDP a practical substitute: RDP does at least as well as any choice of \(\omega\), and tCDP’s general subsampling theorem is loose: with \(\sigma = \sqrt5\) and a 1% sample it gives \(\varepsilon = 9.037\) where RDP gives \(2.046\). That comparison is only indicative: the tCDP theorem assumes fixed-size batches and replace-one neighbours, while the RDP curve assumes Poisson sampling and add/remove (Amplification by subsampling).

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.7 Approximate zCDP
Some useful mechanisms, such as stability-based histograms, are \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP but cannot be zCDP at all: zCDP’s strong group privacy rules them out. Approximate zCDP lets zCDP fail on an event of probability \(\delta_a\), so one ledger holds two columns. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP step enters as \(\rho = \varepsilon^2/2\) and \(\delta_a = \delta\). The \(\rho\) column adds and converts as usual; the \(\delta_a\) column adds up to at most \(\sum_i\delta_i\), like \(\delta\) in basic composition. At the end the pipeline is \((\varepsilon, \delta_a + (1 - \delta_a)\delta')\)-DP, where \(\varepsilon\) is any zCDP conversion of \(\rho\) at \(\delta'\) (Bun & Steinke 2016).
The gain comes from the first column. Ten stability-based steps, each \((0.5, 10^{-7})\)-DP, and ten Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 1\) give \(\rho = 10 \times 0.125 + 10 \times 0.5 = 6.25\) and \(\delta_a = 1.0000 \times 10^{-6}\), so \(\varepsilon = 22.100\) at total \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Composing the stability steps separately, by basic composition, gives \(19.119 + 5 = 24.119\): in the unified ledger each \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) step costs \(\varepsilon^2/2\) in \(\rho\) rather than its full \(\varepsilon\). A Gaussian step put in the \(\delta_a\) column would waste \(\delta\) for nothing.

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.8 Code
The whole zCDP ledger is a few lines: charge each Gaussian step its \(\rho\), add, convert once. The improved conversion is minimized over the same grid of 20,001 orders that the full edition uses.
from math import log, sqrt


def zcdp_gaussian(sigma: float, sensitivity: float = 1.0) -> float:
    """rho of one Gaussian step; compose steps by adding their rho."""
    return sensitivity**2 / (2 * sigma**2)


def zcdp_to_eps_simple(rho: float, delta: float) -> float:
    return rho + 2 * sqrt(rho * log(1 / delta))


def zcdp_to_eps_improved(rho: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Improved conversion, minimized over 20,001 log-spaced orders in (1, 1 + 1e4]."""
    best = float("inf")
    for i in range(20001):
        alpha = 1 + 10 ** (-4 + 8 * i / 20000)
        eps = rho * alpha + log(1 / delta) / (alpha - 1) + log(1 - 1 / alpha) - log(alpha) / (alpha - 1)
        best = min(best, eps)
    return best


def rho_for_target(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Largest rho whose simple conversion stays within eps at delta."""
    return (sqrt(eps + log(1 / delta)) - sqrt(log(1 / delta))) ** 2


rho = 10 * zcdp_gaussian(sigma=1.0)  # ten Gaussian steps with sigma = 1
print(f"{rho:.1f}")  # 5.0
print(f"{zcdp_to_eps_simple(rho, 1e-5):.3f}")  # 20.174
print(f"{zcdp_to_eps_improved(rho, 1e-5):.3f}")  # 19.047
r = rho_for_target(1.0, 1e-5)
print(f"{r:.5f} {1 / sqrt(2 * r):.3f}")  # 0.02082 4.901
The full edition’s script, concentrated_dp.py, computes every number in this chapter, including the subsampled curve and the tCDP values:
uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/concentrated_dp.py

title: 29  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
29.10 Further reading

Bun & Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (TCC 2016): the definition, the Gaussian and pure-DP conversions, group privacy and approximate zCDP. Sections 1–3 are the core.
Canonne, Kamath & Steinke, “The Discrete Gaussian for Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2020): the discrete Gaussian with its zCDP guarantee, and the improved conversion with a stable way to compute it.
Bun, Dwork, Rothblum & Steinke, “Composable and Versatile Privacy via Truncated CDP” (STOC 2018): truncated CDP and its subsampling theorem.
Abowd et al., “The 2020 Census Disclosure Avoidance System TopDown Algorithm” (Harvard Data Science Review, 2022): zCDP accounting at national scale, and the role of invariants.

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.1 Why this matters
Every privacy guarantee answers one question: how well can an attacker who sees the output of a mechanism \(M\) tell whether it ran on a dataset \(D\) or on a neighbour \(D'\) that differs in one record? Differential privacy (DP) answers with two numbers \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), Rényi differential privacy (RDP) with a curve over orders \(\alpha\) (Rényi DP), and zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) with one number \(\rho\) (Concentrated differential privacy). But the question is a hypothesis test, and the complete answer to a test is its trade-off function \(T(P, Q)\) between \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\): for each rate \(a\) at which a test may wrongly claim \(D'\) (its type I error), the smallest rate \(b\) at which it must wrongly claim \(D\) (its type II error) (Hypothesis testing). (\(a\) and \(b\), because \(\alpha\) is the Rényi order in this part.)
The one idea is that this curve is the guarantee, and every other notion is a summary of it that throws something away. Gaussian noise makes the curve practical: it produces a one-parameter family of curves \(G_\mu\) that stays in the family under composition, so a pipeline of Gaussian steps has an exact guarantee in one number. And a central limit theorem (CLT) says that many small steps compose to a curve close to some \(G_\mu\), which gives a quick estimate, though not a guarantee, for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD for short.
crumbs: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.2 f-DP
A privacy guarantee should say what an attacker cannot do. In testing terms, the strongest statement of that kind is a floor under the attacker’s type II error at every type I error: however it tunes its test, it must miss at least this often. A floor at every \(a\) is a curve, so the definition takes a curve \(f\) as its parameter. A mechanism is \(f\)-differentially private (\(f\)-DP) if \(T(M(D), M(D')) \ge f\) for all neighbours \(D \simeq D'\) (Dong, Roth & Su 2022). Processing an output can only make two distributions harder to tell apart, because any test on the processed output is also a test on the raw one, so the curve can only rise and \(f\)-DP survives post-processing.
The familiar \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP is one such floor, made of two straight lines: \[f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(a) = \max\big(0,\; 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon a,\; e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - a)\big). \tag{30.1}\] The first line is the definition read as a test. A test that fires with probability \(a\) under \(D\) may fire with probability at most \(e^\varepsilon a + \delta\) under \(D'\), so it misses \(D'\) with probability at least \(1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon a\). The second line is the same statement with the roles of \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped. The floor starts at \(1 - \delta\), not at 1: \(\delta\) is a free shot, a chance to catch \(D'\) at no type I cost (Figure 30.1).
Two lines are a crude floor. Three mechanisms carry the label “\(\varepsilon = 1\)” in Table 30.1. Randomized response, which reports a bit truthfully with probability \(e/(1 + e)\), sits exactly on \(f_{1,0}\): it is the worst \((1, 0)\)-DP mechanism. The Laplace mechanism matches it at small \(a\) but is more private in the middle, 0.3679 against 0.3204 at \(a = 0.25\). The label cannot tell them apart; the curves can. The floor is set by the worst neighbouring pair; most records are better protected.

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.3 Gaussian differential privacy
The Gaussian mechanism’s curve takes two steps to find, neither of which changes any test’s errors. Divide the output by the noise standard deviation and subtract the mean under \(D\): both maps can be undone, so a test on the new output is a test on the old one. What is left is telling \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) from \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), where \(\mu\) is the distance between the two output means in units of the noise. For a vector output only the direction of the shift carries evidence, since the noise in every other direction looks the same under both hypotheses, so the problem is always one-dimensional. The best test fires when the output exceeds a threshold. At type I error \(a\) the threshold is \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function, and a draw from the shifted normal stays below it with probability \[G_\mu(a) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - a) - \mu\big). \tag{30.2}\] A mechanism is \(\mu\)-Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) if it is \(G_\mu\)-DP. The Gaussian mechanism with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) (the noise standard deviation in units of the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity) shifts the mean by at most one sensitivity, so it is \(1/\sigma\)-GDP, and the bound is exact for a pair that attains the sensitivity. For Gaussian noise, \(\mu\) is the curve, not a bound with slack.
It reads as attack errors. A count released with \(\sigma = 1\) is 1-GDP, so at a 1% false-positive rate, whatever the attacker knows about the rest of the data, it detects the presence of a record at most 9.24% of the time (\(G_1(0.01) = 0.9076\)); at a 10% false-positive rate its power is at most 0.3891. Dong et al. suggest that \(\mu \le 0.5\) is a reasonable guarantee and \(\mu \ge 6\) promises almost nothing.
To report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) without losing anything, use the shape of the curve. A trade-off curve is convex, and a convex curve is the upper envelope of the straight lines that touch it. Each touching line is one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) floor, so a symmetric curve is the same guarantee as being \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP for every \(\varepsilon \ge 0\) at once. That function, the privacy profile, has a closed form for \(G_\mu\): \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\Big). \tag{30.3}\] In words, take the test whose curve has slope \(-e^\varepsilon\); the first term is its power and the second is \(e^\varepsilon\) times its type I error, so \(\delta\) is how far that test beats what pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP would allow. This is the same formula as the analytic Gaussian calibration of The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms. \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) falls as \(\varepsilon\) grows, so to report \(\varepsilon\) at a target \(\delta\) you solve by bisection (Table 30.2).

The profile also explains what a small \(\delta\) costs. \(\delta\) is set by the first term, a normal tail, and a normal tail falls like \(e^{-x^2/2}\), so reaching \(\delta\) needs \(x = \varepsilon/\mu - \mu/2\) of about \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\), and \(\varepsilon\) grows roughly like \(\mu\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\). Each decade of \(\delta\) therefore costs extra \(\varepsilon\) in proportion to \(\mu\), a little less with each decade: at \(\mu = 1\), going from \(\delta = 10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-6}\) raises \(\varepsilon\) from 3.8044 to 4.3772 to 4.8866, and at \(\mu = 2\) the steps are about twice as large.

Right: \(G_1\) and six of its \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\) curves; their upper envelope is \(G_1\), so the whole profile loses nothing, while one pair keeps a single touching line.



The whole profile loses nothing, but one point of it does. “1-GDP” implies “\((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP”, but the single pair is one touching line and permits far more: at \(a = 0.1\) it allows \(b = 0.0113\), while \(G_1(0.1) = 0.6109\) (Figure 30.2, right). Report \(\mu\), or the noise multiplier, along with any pair.

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
30.4 Composition
An attacker who sees two outputs with independent noise faces the joint distributions, and their trade-off curve is the composed guarantee. For two Gaussian releases the joint problem is a shift in two dimensions, by \(\mu_1\) along one axis and \(\mu_2\) along the other. Only the direction of the shift carries evidence, as before, so this is a one-dimensional shift by the length of that vector, \(\sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \mu_2^2}\) (Figure 30.3). Repeating the argument, \(k\) steps compose to \[G_{\mu_1} \otimes \dots \otimes G_{\mu_k} = G_\mu, \qquad \mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2}, \tag{30.4}\] even when each step is chosen after seeing the earlier outputs, and no better bound holds in general (Dong et al. 2022). \(\mu^2\) adds, just as the variances of independent noises add. Full-batch noisy gradient descent with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) for \(k\) steps is therefore exactly \(\sqrt k/\sigma\)-GDP. zCDP does the same arithmetic with \(\rho = \mu^2/2\), but ends with an RDP bound on the curve rather than the curve.






Figure 30.3: Left: 400 draws each from \(\mathcal N(0, I_2)\) and \(\mathcal N((1, 1), I_2)\), the outputs of two Gaussian releases on \(D\) and \(D'\); the best test thresholds the projection on the shift. Right: \(G_1\) for one release, \(G_{\sqrt 2}\) for two, and simulated errors of the projected test.



Two 1-GDP releases compose to \(G_{1.4142}\), four to \(G_2\), and 100 releases with \(\sigma = 10\) each to \(G_1\). Four 1-GDP releases are therefore \(\varepsilon = 9.9973\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Suppose instead you first turn each release into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) point, giving each a quarter of the \(\delta\) budget, \((4.6902, 2.5\times10^{-6})\), and then add the points by basic composition. You get \(\varepsilon = 18.7607\), almost twice as large, because each point had already dropped most of its curve. Compose curves, not points.
For curves that are not Gaussian there is no closed form, and composing \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees exactly is computationally intractable when the steps differ. Numerical accountants instead compose the distribution of the privacy loss by convolution (Numerical accounting). A subsampled step’s curve is not Gaussian either, which is where the CLT comes in.

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
section: 30.5 The central limit theorem and DP-SGD
text:
30.5 The central limit theorem and DP-SGD
The privacy loss of an output is the log of how much more likely it is under \(D\) than under \(D'\). Independent outputs have densities that multiply, so the loss of a composition is the sum of the per-step losses. A sum of many small independent terms is nearly normal, and a normal privacy loss is exactly what a Gaussian curve has. So many small steps compose to roughly some \(G_\mu\), whatever the steps were.
DP-SGD is the case that matters. Each step runs on a Poisson sample that includes each record with probability \(q\), clips each gradient and adds Gaussian noise with noise multiplier \(\sigma\). When \(q\) is small the record is usually absent, so each step leaks little. To leading order in \(q\), one step’s privacy loss has mean \(q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)/2\) and variance \(q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), and a loss whose variance is twice its mean is exactly the shape of a Gaussian curve’s loss, whose variance is \(\mu^2\). Adding \(k\) steps adds the variances, which gives, under add/remove neighbours, as \(k \to \infty\) with \(q\sqrt k\) held fixed, \[\mu = q\sqrt{k\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)} \tag{30.5}\] (Bu, Dong, Long & Su 2020). Compared with full-batch training, \(\sqrt k/\sigma\), subsampling multiplies \(\mu\) by about \(q\sigma\sqrt{e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1}\), which is \(q \times 1.3108\) at \(\sigma = 1\).
This is a limit, used at finite \(k\) as an approximation. It is not a bound, and for the running example, \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), it errs on the unsafe side. Table 30.3 turns each \(\mu\) into \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and compares it with a numerical accountant’s bracket, whose lower end is a lower bound on the true \(\varepsilon\), exact up to a small quadrature error. At \(k = 10{,}000\) the CLT says 6.0071; the true \(\varepsilon\) is at least 6.1377 (Figure 30.4).

The reason it under-reports is where \(\delta\) lives. A CLT controls the bulk of the loss distribution, but a \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\) is decided by rare, large values of the loss, in the tail, where the normal approximation has no control. The error is worst for short runs, furthest from the regime the limit describes: 0.4575 against at least 0.7175 at \(k = 100\). Plugging exactly computed per-step moments into the CLT does not help, and gives an even smaller \(\varepsilon\), 5.9184 at \(k = 10{,}000\). A more exact \(\mu\) is not a more conservative one; only a certified accountant is. Plan with the CLT; report an accountant’s number.
Two more cautions. The formula is specific to Poisson sampling under add/remove neighbours: Dong et al.’s version for fixed-size batches under replace-one neighbours has a different constant, \(\mu = 1.7101\) at \(k = 10{,}000\) here, and the two must not be mixed (Amplification by subsampling). And \(\mu\) is very sensitive to \(\sigma\) through \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\), which is 3.7707 at \(\sigma = 0.8\), 1.7183 at \(\sigma = 1\) and 0.5596 at \(\sigma = 1.5\).

title: 30  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
section: 30.6 RDP as a lossy summary of the curve
text:
30.6 RDP as a lossy summary of the curve
The curve also shows where RDP accounting leaves slack. An RDP curve records the exponential moments of the privacy loss, one per order. Different loss distributions can share those moments, so the best trade-off curve that the RDP values alone can certify, \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), has to allow the worst of them. It lies below the true curve even for the Gaussian, whose RDP curve is exact. The best \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) any RDP conversion can report is the profile of \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ)).
So the slack of RDP accounting has two parts: the conversion, which a better formula removes, and the gap between \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) and the true curve, which no conversion removes. For 1-GDP, whose RDP curve is \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\), the RDP summary allows an attacker an advantage of 0.4830 where the best possible is 0.3829, and the best \(\delta(1)\) it can certify is 0.2149, 1.69 times the exact 0.1269. For Gaussian noise on the full data, then, account in GDP, where \(\mu^2\) adds and the profile at the end is exact.

30.9 Further reading

Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, 2022): \(f\)-DP, GDP, duality, composition and the CLTs. The discussion sections explain why the curve is the right object.
Bu, Dong, Long & Su, “Deep Learning with Gaussian Differential Privacy” (Harvard Data Science Review, 2020): the CLT for Poisson-subsampled DP-SGD, with experiments.
Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz, “Numerical Composition of Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2021): an accountant with error bounds, and examples where the CLT under-reports \(\varepsilon\).
Balle & Wang, “Improving the Gaussian Mechanism for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2018): the exact \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) profile of the Gaussian mechanism and its use for calibration.

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
text:
31.1 Why this matters
Differential privacy (DP) for deep learning would be useless without one trick. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, runs ten thousand steps or more. Each step clips every example’s gradient, sums them and adds Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) times the clipping norm. If every record paid at every step, ten thousand steps with \(\sigma = 1\) would cost \(\varepsilon = 5425.5\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), a number nobody would report. The trick is that each step looks only at a small random batch. If a record is in the batch with probability \(q\), an attacker must first guess whether it was used at all; with \(q = 0.01\) that uncertainty turns a step that costs \(\varepsilon = 1\) into one that costs about \(0.017\).
The one idea: the output with the record is a mixture, “used with probability \(q\), unused otherwise”, and mixing pulls every likelihood ratio towards 1. How much a step is worth depends on how far the mixture pulls, and because the mixture comes from how the batch was drawn, an accountant that assumes one sampler while the training code runs another reports a number that does not apply.

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
section: 31.2 Amplification for (ε, δ)-DP under Poisson sampling
text:
31.2 Amplification for (ε, δ)-DP under Poisson sampling
Under Poisson sampling each record enters the batch by its own independent coin flip with probability \(q\). Take add/remove neighbours, \(D\) and \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\), and fix which other records were drawn. On \(D\) the step outputs some distribution \(P_0\). On \(D'\) it outputs \(P_1\) if \(x\) was drawn and \(P_0\) otherwise, so it outputs the mixture \((1 - q)P_0 + qP_1\). Divide by \(P_0\) and the likelihood ratio \(P_1/P_0\) becomes \((1 - q) + q\,P_1/P_0\), a weighted average of 1 and the old ratio. If the step was \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the old ratio was at most \(e^\varepsilon\) outside the \(\delta\) slack, so the new one is at most \(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), and the slack only matters when the record was drawn. The result (Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi 2018) is \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big), \qquad \delta' = q\delta, \tag{31.1}\] for add/remove neighbours, and randomized response shows it cannot be improved. Randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 1\), sampled at \(q = 0.1\), has its likelihood ratio pulled from \(e = 2.718\) to \(1.1718\), so \(\varepsilon' = 0.1586\).
For small \(\varepsilon\), \(e^\varepsilon - 1 \approx \varepsilon\) and the logarithm is nearly linear, so \(\varepsilon' \approx q\varepsilon\): a 1% sample makes the step a hundred times cheaper. For large \(\varepsilon\), once \(qe^\varepsilon \gg 1\), the 1 inside the logarithm is negligible and \(\varepsilon' \approx \varepsilon - \ln(1/q)\): sampling only subtracts. The reason is the worst case: with probability \(q\) the record was drawn, and sampling can make that event rare but not less revealing. At \(q = 0.01\) a step with \(\varepsilon = 1\) costs 0.0170, but one with \(\varepsilon = 5\) still costs 0.9059, not 0.05, and one with \(\varepsilon = 10\) costs 5.3993, close to \(10 - \ln 100 = 5.395\) (Table 31.1). The switch happens near \(\varepsilon \approx \ln(1/q)\), where \(qe^\varepsilon\) reaches 1 (Figure 31.1).

Since the amplification is the attacker’s uncertainty about whether the record was used, each record’s coin must be independent of the rest of the sample, and the sample must stay secret. And Equation 31.1 is tight for one step only; composing per-step pairs over thousands of steps is hopeless (Section 31.4).

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
section: 31.3 The sampling scheme must match the neighbouring relation
text:
31.3 The sampling scheme must match the neighbouring relation
Poisson sampling gives batches of random size, and most training code draws fixed-size batches instead, either a fresh random batch of \(m\) out of \(n\) records at each step or a random permutation cut into consecutive batches each epoch (shuffle and partition). A fixed batch size pairs naturally with replace-one neighbours, datasets of the same size that differ in one record’s value, because adding a record would change the size. For a uniformly random batch, a record is used with probability \(m/n\), and Equation 31.1 holds with \(q = m/n\), provided the base guarantee is for replace-one neighbours (Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi 2018).
That proviso is where the cost hides. Replacing a clipped gradient can move the gradient sum twice as far as adding one: the old gradient, of norm up to \(C\), leaves, and a new one, possibly pointing the opposite way, comes in. Twice the shift with the same noise is the same as half the noise multiplier. Table 31.2 lists what to account for under each combination, for DP-SGD’s sum of gradients clipped to norm \(C\) with noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\).

Halving the noise multiplier is not a small change: for the part’s running example, \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(10{,}000\) steps and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), fixed-size batches give \(\varepsilon = 47.42\) against \(6.71\) for Poisson sampling, both by Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accounting, the first with noise multiplier 0.5.
Shuffle and partition is worse, because the source of amplification is missing altogether. In one epoch the record is in exactly one batch, never absent, so no step’s output is a mixture with “not used”. The only uncertainty is which batch held it, and the other records can give that away; Chua et al. (2024) build such a case, with a test that gives a lower bound on the true \(\varepsilon\). For one epoch of 100 batches, Table 31.3 compares that lower bound with the Poisson accountant’s upper bound and with deterministic batches, where the epoch is a plain Gaussian mechanism and its \(\varepsilon\) is exact. At \(\sigma = 1\), shuffled training has \(\varepsilon \ge 4.06\), while the Poisson accountant reports at most 1.21 (Figure 31.2), and shuffling buys almost nothing over a fixed batch order (4.38). At \(\sigma = 3\) the order flips, which says only that this particular test is too weak there to show a gap.

If it shuffles and partitions, the Poisson number does not apply at all: switch to Poisson sampling, or say plainly that the reported \(\varepsilon\) assumes a sampler you did not run. Always state the neighbouring relation with \(\varepsilon\).

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
text:
31.4 The RDP accountant for DP-SGD
A mechanism’s RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) bounds the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\) between its outputs on neighbours, and under composition the curves of the steps add (Rényi DP). So you need the curve of one subsampled Gaussian step. The other records contribute the same to both outputs and can be subtracted, and Mironov, Talwar & Zhang (2019) show that the worst case is one coordinate in which the record moves the clipped sum by the full sensitivity: a Gaussian \(P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) against the mixture \(P_q = (1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). Of the two orders of the pair, the one with the mixture first is always the larger.
The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is an average of the likelihood ratio raised to the power \(\alpha\). The ratio is \((1 - q) + q\,r\), with \(r\) the ratio of the shifted Gaussian to \(P_0\), and for an integer \(\alpha\) the binomial theorem expands its power into a finite sum. With sensitivity 1 and add/remove neighbours, \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \ln A_\alpha/(\alpha - 1)\), where \[A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{j^2 - j}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{31.2}\] Term \(j\) is the case in which \(j\) of \(\alpha\) imagined copies of the record’s contribution are present, weighted by its chance. At \(\alpha = 2\), with \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), the sum has three terms, \(0.9801 + 0.0198 + 0.0001e\), so \(A_2 = 1 + q^2(e - 1) = 1.00017183\) and \(\varepsilon(2) = 1.7181 \times 10^{-4}\), against 1 without sampling. Fractional orders need numerical integration.
After \(k\) steps the curve is \(k\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\), and you convert once, at the best order: \[\varepsilon = \min_{\alpha}\Big[k\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\Big] \ \text{(Mironov)}, \qquad \varepsilon = \min_\alpha\Big[k\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big] \ \text{(improved)}. \tag{31.3}\] Table 31.4 compares this with the per-step route, which amplifies each step by Equation 31.1 and composes the pairs. After 10,000 steps the RDP accountant with the improved conversion gives \(\varepsilon = 6.71\); per-step amplification followed by basic composition gives 11296.93 (Figure 31.3).

The per-step route fails because of the shift regime of the previous section. To end at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) after 10,000 steps, basic composition can give each step only a tiny \(\delta\), and a tiny \(\delta\) forces a large per-step \(\varepsilon\), here 5.35. That is above \(\ln(1/q)\), where sampling only subtracts, so the amplified step costs 1.130, only about five times less, and basic composition multiplies that by 10,000. The RDP accountant avoids the trap: each step costs almost nothing at moderate orders, and the conversion term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) is paid once.
That one-time term is also why RDP loses for a single step, 0.96 against 0.20. RDP wins from \(k = 4\) here. The best order falls from 9.9 to 4.1 as \(k\) grows, because a larger \(k\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\) pulls the minimum towards smaller orders, where the curve is lower; make sure the accountant’s grid includes small and fractional orders, since removing orders can only raise \(\varepsilon\). The improved conversion saves 9.6% at 10,000 steps (6.71 against 7.43). And 6.71 is an upper bound with slack, from the conversion and from the RDP curve itself; Numerical accounting computes the tight value and Choosing an accountant compares them.

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
section: 31.5 Small q and the moments accountant
text:
31.5 Small q and the moments accountant
The sum Equation 31.2 also explains the shape of the curve. If every exponential in it were 1, the sum would be \(((1 - q) + q)^\alpha = 1\), and the terms \(j = 0\) and \(1\) have exponential exactly 1, so the excess over 1 starts at \(j = 2\). For small \(q\) that term dominates and gives \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac{\alpha q^2\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}{2} \approx \frac{\alpha q^2}{2\sigma^2}\ \text{for large } \sigma. \tag{31.4}\] The cost is quadratic in \(q\), where the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) amplification was linear. That gives a design rule: \(E\) epochs are \(k = E/q\) steps, so the total RDP is about \(E\,q\,\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\), and at a fixed number of epochs smaller batches are cheaper, as long as the orders used stay in the quadratic regime. Abadi et al. (2016), who introduced DP-SGD with the moments accountant (RDP in disguise), used a bound of this shape with about twice the constant, valid on a limited range of orders. Their headline example, \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 4\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and 10,000 steps, reports \(\varepsilon \approx 1.26\). The exact curve with Mironov’s conversion gives 1.2586, at \(\alpha = 20\), and the improved conversion 1.0355.
The quadratic term fails at high orders. The last term of the sum, the event that the record was in every one of the \(\alpha\) imagined copies, has a tiny weight \(q^\alpha\) but the full Gaussian cost, which grows like \(e^{\alpha^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), and eventually it wins. That happens near \(\alpha \approx 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\), about 9.2 at \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\). The exact curve is 1.30 times the quadratic term at \(\alpha = 8\) and 44.54 times at \(\alpha = 10\), then rises towards the unsubsampled line (Figure 31.4). In the tail, as at large \(\varepsilon\), sampling saves only about \(\ln(1/q)\).






Figure 31.4: The RDP curve of the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) (black), against the unsubsampled Gaussian \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\), the small-\(q\) term and the leading term of Abadi et al.’s bound. The exact curve stays near the quadratic term up to about \(\alpha = 8\), then rises towards the unsubsampled line.



So use Equation 31.4 for estimates, never inside an accountant: beyond the breakdown it is 2246 times too small at \(\alpha = 16\) for \(\sigma = 1\), and an accountant using it there would under-report \(\varepsilon\).

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
text:
31.6 Other mechanisms
For \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), Equation 31.1 is one tight formula for every mechanism, because randomized response is the worst case for every \(\varepsilon\). For RDP there is no such formula: mechanisms with the same RDP curve can subsample differently. Zhu & Wang (2019) bound the subsampled curve of any mechanism under Poisson sampling with the same binomial expansion, each term bounded by the mechanism’s own curve and a factor 3 on the terms from \(j = 3\) on, and Wang, Balle & Kasiviswanathan (2019) do the same for fixed-size batches. Applied to the Gaussian at \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), the general bound is exact at \(\alpha = 2\), where there are no terms beyond \(j = 2\), but 1.57 times the exact value at \(\alpha = 8\), near the best orders for 100 to 1,000 steps. So accountants special-case the Gaussian with the exact sum. For other mechanisms, a numerical accountant must also check its worst-case pair of datasets: Lebeda et al. (2024) show that the worst pair for one step need not be the worst for many.

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
text:
31.7 Code
An RDP accountant for DP-SGD fits in a few lines. This one uses Equation 31.2 in log space, so large orders do not overflow, and the integer orders 2 to 63 only. With fractional orders, as in Table 31.4, the improved value drops slightly, from 6.719 to 6.71.
from math import exp, lgamma, log


def amplify(eps: float, delta: float, q: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """(eps, delta) of an add/remove-DP mechanism run on a Poisson sample with rate q."""
    return log(1 + q * (exp(eps) - 1)), q * delta


def subsampled_gaussian_rdp(alpha: int, q: float, sigma: float) -> float:
    """RDP at integer order alpha of one Poisson-subsampled Gaussian step (sensitivity 1)."""
    logs = [
        lgamma(alpha + 1) - lgamma(j + 1) - lgamma(alpha - j + 1)
        + (alpha - j) * log(1 - q) + j * log(q) + (j * j - j) / (2 * sigma**2)
        for j in range(alpha + 1)
    ]
    top = max(logs)
    log_a = top + log(sum(exp(t - top) for t in logs))  # log-sum-exp avoids overflow
    return log_a / (alpha - 1)


def dpsgd_eps(q: float, sigma: float, steps: int, delta: float, improved: bool = True) -> tuple[float, int]:
    """Compose the RDP curve over the steps, convert to (eps, delta) at the best integer order."""
    best = (float("inf"), 0)
    for alpha in range(2, 64):
        rdp = steps * subsampled_gaussian_rdp(alpha, q, sigma)
        if improved:
            eps = rdp + log((alpha - 1) / alpha) - (log(delta) + log(alpha)) / (alpha - 1)
        else:
            eps = rdp + log(1 / delta) / (alpha - 1)
        best = min(best, (eps, alpha))
    return best


print(f"{amplify(1.0, 0.0, 0.01)[0]:.4f}")  # 0.0170
print(f"{subsampled_gaussian_rdp(2, 0.01, 1.0):.4e}")  # 1.7181e-04
print("%.3f %d" % dpsgd_eps(0.01, 1.0, 10_000, 1e-5))  # 6.719 4
print(f"{dpsgd_eps(0.01, 1.0, 10_000, 1e-5, improved=False)[0]:.3f}")  # 7.469
print("%.4f %d" % dpsgd_eps(0.01, 4.0, 10_000, 1e-5, improved=False))  # 1.2586 20
print("%.4f %d" % dpsgd_eps(0.01, 4.0, 10_000, 1e-5))  # 1.0355 17
The last two lines reproduce Abadi et al.’s example. To account for fixed-size batches, call dpsgd_eps with half the noise multiplier. In production, use a maintained library and check it against a second one (Choosing an accountant). The full edition’s script, subsampling.py, computes every number in this chapter, including the fractional orders and the sampler comparisons:
uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/subsampling.py

title: 31  Amplification by subsampling
text:
31.9 Further reading

Balle, Barthe & Gaboardi, “Privacy Amplification by Subsampling: Tight Analyses via Couplings and Divergences” (NeurIPS 2018): tight \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) amplification for each sampling scheme and neighbouring relation.
Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism” (2019): the subsampled Gaussian’s RDP curve and its stable computation, the basis of most RDP accountants.
Lebeda, Regehr, Kamath & Steinke, “Avoiding Pitfalls for Privacy Accounting of Subsampled Mechanisms under Composition” (IEEE SaTML 2025): fixed-size against Poisson sampling, and worst-case pairs that fail under composition.
Chua, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar, Manurangsi, Sinha & Zhang, “How Private are DP-SGD Implementations?” (ICML 2024): why shuffle-and-partition batching can be much less private than the Poisson accountant reports.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.1 Why this matters
You trained a model with differential privacy (DP): 10,000 steps of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), each on a Poisson sample of the data with rate \(q = 0.01\), with clipped gradients and Gaussian noise of multiplier \(\sigma = 1\). This is DP-SGD, the running example of this part, and you need the smallest \(\varepsilon\) for which the whole run is \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Rényi differential privacy (RDP), from Rényi DP, gives an upper bound that loses an unknown amount in its conversion. The Gaussian central limit theorem (CLT) of f-DP and Gaussian DP gives an approximation that may err in either direction.
This chapter computes the answer itself. \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) depends on a mechanism only through the distribution of its privacy loss, a distribution on the real line, and composing steps adds losses, so a whole run’s distribution is a convolution that a computer can evaluate on a grid. Rounding in a chosen direction gives the grid’s error a known sign: you get a certified upper bound and a lower bound whose distance you know in advance.
crumbs: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.2 The privacy loss distribution
Let \(P\) be the distribution of the output on your dataset \(D\) and \(Q\) on a neighbour \(D'\). The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is \(L(y) = \ln\frac{P(y)}{Q(y)}\) (Composition). Draw \(y\) from \(P\) and the loss is a random variable; its distribution is the privacy loss distribution (PLD).
Why should this one-dimensional distribution carry everything? The definition lets each output’s probability under \(P\) be up to \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability under \(Q\), and \(\delta\) pays only for the excess. An output with loss \(\ell\) has \(P(y) = e^\ell Q(y)\), so its excess is a fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell}\) of its probability when \(\ell > \varepsilon\), and nothing otherwise. That fraction depends on the output only through its loss, so \(\delta\) is an average over the PLD: \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big] = P[L > \varepsilon] - e^{\varepsilon}\,Q[L > \varepsilon], \tag{32.1}\] where \((x)_+ = \max\{x, 0\}\). The second form reads it as a gap: the chance under \(P\) that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), minus \(e^\varepsilon\) times that chance under \(Q\). An output impossible under \(D'\) has infinite loss and counts fully. So the output space never enters: a run with millions of parameters and a one-dimensional mechanism with the same PLD have the same privacy curve.
The weight is 0 up to \(\ell = \varepsilon\) and rises slowly towards 1, so \(\delta\) is the PLD’s upper tail with losses just above \(\varepsilon\) discounted (Figure 32.1). That is why the plain tail \(P[L > \varepsilon]\) is a loose bound: it counts the barely-over outputs in full.
For the Gaussian mechanism, with \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\) the sensitivity in noise standard deviations, the two densities have the same shape, so their log-ratio is linear in the output and the loss is itself Gaussian, \(\mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\). Its two tails give the closed form of The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, with \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function: \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^{\varepsilon}\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{32.2}\] With sensitivity 1 and \(\sigma = 1\), the PLD is \(\mathcal N(0.5, 1)\); at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the formula gives \(\Phi(-0.5) - e\,\Phi(-1.5) = 0.3085 - 0.1816 = 0.1269\), and solving \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) gives \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\).






Figure 32.1: The Gaussian PLD for \(\mu = 1\) (blue), the weight \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - \ell})_+\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (orange, scaled by 0.4 to fit), and their product (green). The green area is \(\delta(1) = 0.1269\): only losses above \(\varepsilon\) count, and those just above it count little.

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.3 Composition is convolution
For independent steps the probability of the tuple of outputs is a product, its log is a sum, and so the privacy loss of the run is the sum of the step losses. The distribution of a sum of independent variables is the convolution of their distributions, so the PLD of \(k\) steps is the \(k\)-fold convolution of the per-step PLDs.
This step is exact, which sets it apart from the theorems of Composition: they see each step only through its \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) and must cover the worst step with those values, while convolution uses each step’s actual shape. All the error in a PLD accountant comes from computing it. Gaussian steps give a check, since means and variances add: \(k\) steps with shift \(\mu\) behave like one Gaussian mechanism with \(\mu_k = \sqrt k\,\mu\). Ten steps with \(\sigma = 1\) are \((17.8566, 10^{-5})\)-DP and a hundred \((91.8173, 10^{-5})\)-DP, values any accountant must reproduce at \(q = 1\). The same picture explains why the CLT is plausible, since long sums look Gaussian; the PLD accountant computes the sum instead.
DP-SGD steps are adaptive: each gradient depends on the model, so the losses are not independent. The repair is a dominating pair, a fixed pair at least as easy to tell apart as the step, whatever came before; convolving the dominating pairs’ PLDs bounds the adaptive run (Zhu, Dong & Wang 2022). The bound is exactly as tight as the pair. For the Gaussian mechanism, \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) is produced by real datasets, so nothing is lost; for a subsampled mechanism the pair depends on how batches are drawn and must match your training code.

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.4 Pessimistic and optimistic discretization
A computer convolves vectors, so the loss goes on a grid of width \(h\). The rounding can still give a guarantee, because the weight in Equation 32.1 never decreases as the loss grows: move every loss up and \(\delta\) can only rise, move every loss down and it can only fall.
The pessimistic PLD rounds every loss up to the next grid point and sends any truncated upper tail to \(+\infty\). The optimistic PLD rounds every loss down and drops the truncated lower tail. In any run, each step’s rounded-up loss is at least its true loss, which is at least its rounded-down loss, and adding over \(k\) steps keeps that order for the totals. So at every \(\varepsilon\) \[\delta_{\text{optimistic}}(\varepsilon) \;\le\; \delta(\varepsilon) \;\le\; \delta_{\text{pessimistic}}(\varepsilon). \tag{32.3}\] The same argument gives the width: each step’s two roundings are at most \(h\) apart, so the totals, and the two values of \(\varepsilon\) at your \(\delta\), are at most \(kh\) apart. For a continuous PLD the gap is almost exactly \(kh\): the error grows linearly in \(k\).
The two sides are not equally strong. Raising losses keeps the pessimistic distribution the PLD of a real pair that dominates the original, so the upper bound holds for adaptive composition too. Lowering them can produce a distribution no pair has, so the optimistic value bounds the mechanism from below only when real datasets produce the pair, as for the Gaussian and the subsampled Gaussian.
Randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), composed three times on the coarse grid \(h = 0.5\), has exact \(\delta(1) = 0.4190\) between the pessimistic 0.6758 and the optimistic 0.3648 (Figure 32.2). For Gaussian steps with \(\mu = 1\) on \(h = 10^{-3}\) (Table 32.1), the width is exactly \(kh\) and the exact value sits in the middle, because a loss spread evenly within a cell moves up by about \(h/2\) when rounded up and down by as much when rounded down. The midpoint, like rounding to the nearest point, is a good estimate, but only the two sides are guarantees.

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.5 Composition by FFT
On a common grid, adding two losses adds their grid indices, so composing two discretized PLDs is a discrete convolution of their mass vectors. A fast Fourier transform (FFT) turns it into a pointwise product of transforms, at a cost of order \(N\log N\) for length \(N\), and repeated squaring composes \(k\) steps in at most \(2\log_2k\) convolutions.
The FFT has one trap, which follows from how it works: it attaches to each index a power of an \(N\)-th root of unity, so indices add modulo \(N\), and mass that falls off one end of the window reappears at the other. Ten Gaussian steps with \(\mu = 1\) on \(h = 10^{-3}\) give a pessimistic \(\delta(1) = 0.81891018\), against the exact 0.81851782. On a circular window from loss 0 to 10, the same computation gives 0.83478562, wrong in the second decimal: negative losses, which should count nothing, wrap to the top of the window where they count almost fully. Width 40 gets it right. The error from wraparound can go either way, so a wrapped result is no bound at all; pad every convolution to the sum of its inputs’ lengths. Truncating tails at a tiny mass such as \(10^{-15}\) is safe only if the pessimistic side moves the cut mass up, to \(+\infty\).
Each tenfold refinement of \(h\) makes the vectors ten times longer. The privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant (Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz 2021) rounds to the nearest point and shifts the grid to preserve the mean loss, so the per-step errors have mean zero and grow like \(\sqrt k\,h\) instead of \(kh\); a grid of \(h \approx 1/\sqrt k\) then suffices, with explicit error bounds. Connect the dots (Doroshenko et al. 2022) builds the best pessimistic PLD on a given grid.

title: 32  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
32.6 The subsampled Gaussian
A DP-SGD step with Poisson sampling includes each record with probability \(q\). Without the record in question, the noisy sum is a Gaussian centred at 0; with it, the record is sampled with probability \(q\) and shifts the centre by 1, so the output is a mixture (Amplification by subsampling). Under add/remove neighbours the pair’s two orders differ. With \(D'\) the dataset that holds the record, the remove direction puts it first, \(P = M(D')\) and \(Q = M(D)\): \[P = (1 - q)\,\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2), \qquad Q = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2), \tag{32.4}\] and the add direction swaps them (Zhu, Dong & Wang 2022). Dividing the mixture by the base gives the remove loss, \(L_{\mathrm{rem}}(y) = \ln\big((1 - q) + q\,e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}\big)\), and the add loss is its negative.
The formula explains the asymmetry (Figure 32.3). For an ordinary output the exponential is small, so the remove loss never falls below \(\ln(1 - q)\); but a large output is far likelier from the shifted component, and there the loss grows without limit: a rare large gradient betrays that the record was used. The add loss is the mirror image, bounded above by \(-\ln(1 - q) = 0.0101\), and since \(\delta\) counts only losses above \(\varepsilon\), one add step costs nothing beyond that. For \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), one step is \((0.1995, 10^{-5})\)-DP in the remove direction and \((0.0091, 10^{-5})\)-DP in the add direction.






Figure 32.3: Left: the densities of \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and of the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) for \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), on a log scale; they differ only in the far right tail. Right: the privacy loss as a function of the output for the remove pair (red) and the add pair (blue).



Composition narrows the gap, since many small add losses add up: after 10,000 steps the add direction’s upper bound is 5.6615. The remove direction stays larger here, but that is an observation, not a theorem, so compose both and report the larger \(\varepsilon\); an accountant using only the remove pair covers half of the add/remove relation. The pair also assumes Poisson sampling: if your loader shuffles and partitions instead, the mixture is the wrong model and these numbers do not apply.

32.10 Further reading

Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz, “Numerical Composition of Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2021): the PRV accountant, with explicit error bounds and a running time of order \(\sqrt k\); read it when you need a fast accountant with certified error bars.
Doroshenko, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar & Manurangsi, “Connect the Dots: Tighter Discrete Approximations of Privacy Loss Distributions” (PoPETs 2022): the cleanest account of why the pessimistic bound is valid, and the best discretization on a given grid.
Zhu, Dong & Wang, “Optimal Accounting of Differential Privacy via Characteristic Function” (AISTATS 2022): dominating pairs, adaptive composition and the two directions of Poisson subsampling.

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
33.1 Why this matters
Amplification by subsampling showed that uncertainty is worth privacy: if an adversary cannot tell whether a step used your record, the step leaks far less than its noise alone suggests. Two other kinds matter in practice. In the shuffle model, \(n\) users randomize their own data and a trusted shuffler strips identities and mixes the order, so the analyst does not know which report is yours. Each report alone satisfies local differential privacy (DP) at a level \(\varepsilon_0\), usually large to keep reports useful, yet the bag of reports is central DP with an \(\varepsilon\) that falls like \(1/\sqrt n\). And when noisy gradient descent (GD) on a convex loss releases only its final model, the adversary does not see what happened inside training: later steps add fresh noise and pull the parameters together, hiding early records better than composition says.
One idea gives every result. Show that what the adversary sees can be generated from a much simpler pair of distributions by a procedure that does not depend on your record. Anything the adversary learns from the real output, it could then have learned from the simple pair, so that pair’s privacy carries over. For shuffling the simple pair is a pair of counts; for iteration, a pair of Gaussians. Throughout, neighbouring datasets differ by replacing one record. The shuffling results are about anonymous, locally randomized reports, not the shuffle-and-partition batching used to train models in the central model, where no comparable theorem applies (Amplification by subsampling).

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
33.2 Shuffled randomized response, exactly
Start with the simplest randomizer, whose exact answer is the yardstick for every general bound. Each user reports a bit with binary randomized response: the true bit with probability \(\theta = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), the flipped bit otherwise. Once the order is gone, a bag of bits can tell the analyst only how many of them are 1. Your report moves that count by at most one, while the other users’ random flips spread it over a range of about \(\sqrt{n\theta(1 - \theta)}\), and that spread is what hides you.
Let your bit be 0 in \(D\) and 1 in \(D'\), and let the others all hold 0, so their number of 1-reports is binomial, \(\mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, 1 - \theta)\), with probability mass function \(b\). A count of \(y\) arises either when your report is 0 and the others sent \(y\) ones, or when your report is 1 and they sent \(y - 1\), so \[P(y) = \theta\,b(y) + (1 - \theta)\,b(y - 1), \qquad Q(y) = (1 - \theta)\,b(y) + \theta\,b(y - 1). \tag{33.1}\] The exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the larger of the two hockey-stick divergences between \(P\) and \(Q\), one per order, which takes milliseconds to compute (Section 33.6). Strictly, this is exact for the case where all the others hold 0 and a lower bound on the worst case; the other configurations the full edition scans come within \(10^{-4}\) of it, so the book treats it as exact.
Why \(1/\sqrt n\)? The count is a sum of many independent bits, so it is nearly normal. Your report shifts its mean by \(2\theta - 1\), and its standard deviation is \(\sqrt{n\theta(1 - \theta)}\) under both datasets. A pair of normals is a Gaussian mechanism whose \(\mu\) is the shift divided by the standard deviation, and simplifying gives \[\mu \approx \frac{2\sinh(\varepsilon_0/2)}{\sqrt n}. \tag{33.2}\] More users mean more noise to hide one bit in, hence \(1/\sqrt n\); a larger \(\varepsilon_0\) means more faithful reports and a less noisy count, hence the growth like \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2}\). A company that asks 10,000 users whether they used a feature, with \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\), gets reports that are each the truth with probability 0.8808, a weak local guarantee; the shuffled bag is \((0.0870, 10^{-6})\)-DP.






Figure 33.1: Left: the number of 1-reports among \(n = 30\) shuffled randomized-response reports with \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\), when you hold 0 (blue) and 1 (orange); your report moves the count by at most one. Right: the exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for one unshuffled report and for \(n = 10, 100, 1000\) shuffled reports. Every curve reaches 0 only at \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\), but for large \(n\) it is negligible far earlier.



Shuffling never improves pure DP, as the count of zero shows. If nobody reports a 1, you most likely hold 0, and the likelihood ratio of that outcome is \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) whatever \(n\) is. What shuffling changes is how often it happens: rarely, for large \(n\). So amplification moves the bad outcomes into \(\delta\) (Figure 33.1), and a shuffled guarantee always needs \(\delta > 0\). The normal approximation fails for the same reason it works: it needs many 1-reports to hide among. At \(n = 1000\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) the others send about 18 on average, the count is far from normal, and the approximation gives 0.9667 against the exact 1.6910.

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
section: 33.3 The clone bound for any local randomizer
text:
33.3 The clone bound for any local randomizer
Users often send histograms or noisy vectors, so you need a bound for every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP local randomizer. The argument of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021) finds a hidden randomized response inside any of them. Being \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP means no output is more than \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) times likelier for one input than for another. Read the other way, any user’s report keeps at least a fraction \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) of each output’s probability under your \(D\)-version, and likewise under your \(D'\)-version. So every other user’s report can be generated by a coin: with probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) it is a clone, a draw distributed exactly like your report could be, half the time like your \(D\)-version and half like your \(D'\)-version; otherwise it is a draw that depends only on that user’s own data.
After shuffling, nobody can tell a clone from your report, so the adversary can do no better than count how many reports look like each version of you. That count is the simple pair, and its exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the numeric clone bound, valid for every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP randomizer, even adaptively chosen ones. The clones supply the noise: about \(ne^{-\varepsilon_0}\) of them, whose split between the two versions has standard deviation \(\sqrt{ne^{-\varepsilon_0}}/2\). That again gives \(1/\sqrt n\) with a constant growing like \(e^{\varepsilon_0/2}\). The analytic form (their Theorem 3.1) bounds the count pair with Chernoff bounds: \[\varepsilon \le \ln\left(1 + \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\left(\frac{8\sqrt{e^{\varepsilon_0}\ln(4/\delta)}}{\sqrt n} + \frac{8e^{\varepsilon_0}}{n}\right)\right), \qquad\text{valid when } \varepsilon_0 \le \ln\frac{n}{16\ln(2/\delta)}. \tag{33.3}\] The condition says there must be enough clones to hide among: it is \(ne^{-\varepsilon_0} \ge 16\ln(2/\delta)\). At \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) it caps \(\varepsilon_0\) at 1.460 for \(n = 1000\) and 6.066 for \(n = 10^5\).

Table 33.1 shows the cost of generality. The numeric clone bound is 1.44 to 2.36 times the exact value for randomized response, for a clear reason: in randomized response every other report is a bit that could be yours, while the clone argument counts only the \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) fraction guaranteed to look like yours. No general bound can beat the exact column, since randomized response is one of the randomizers it must cover. To collect a bit from \(10^5\) users with central \(\varepsilon \le 0.2\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), the closed form allows \(\varepsilon_0 = 2\) (0.1862), the numeric clone bound allows \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) (0.1698), and the exact value at \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) is 0.0847. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\) the noise adds only \(0.0190/n\) to the variance of the estimated proportion, against up to \(0.25/n\) from sampling alone.
