title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
33.4 Amplification by iteration
Projected noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD) makes one pass over the data, using record \(x_t\) at step \(t\). If every iterate is released, \(x_t\) is protected only by the noise of its own step. If only the final model is released, the noise of every later step also covers it, and Feldman, Mironov, Talwar & Thakurta (2018) turned this into a guarantee.
The step that uses your record pushes the two runs apart. Each later noisy step can “pay off” part of that gap, and the price of paying an amount \(a\) is quadratic in \(a\), like the Rényi divergence of two Gaussians shifted by \(a\). Paying a gap \(s\) in \(m\) equal instalments costs \(m(s/m)^2 = s^2/m\), so spreading the payment over every remaining step is cheapest. This only works if the later steps never push points apart, if they are contractions; a gradient step on a convex, \(\beta\)-smooth loss with step size \(\eta \le 2/\beta\), followed by projection onto a convex set, is one. For convex, Lipschitz, smooth losses and noise multiplier \(\tilde\sigma\) (noise per unit of the gradient’s replace-one sensitivity), releasing only the last iterate gives the record used at step \(t\) of \(n\) the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve \[\varepsilon_t(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\tilde\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{1}{n - t + 1}: \tag{33.4}\] one Gaussian step’s curve divided by the number of noisy steps from \(t\) to the end.
Take one pass over \(n = 10{,}000\) records with \(\tilde\sigma = 1\), converted to \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\) (Rényi DP). The first record gets \(\varepsilon = 0.0481\), the one in the middle 0.0707, and the one used 100 steps before the end 0.4849. The last record gets 5.2985, exactly what it would get if every iterate were released: no later step pays anything for it.






Figure 33.2: The \(\mu\) of the last iterate against the step \(t\) at which your record is used, for a one-pass run of \(T = 100\) steps with per-step shift equal to the noise standard deviation. Releasing all iterates gives \(\mu = 1\) for every record (dotted). The bound Equation 33.4 (red) is exact in the worst case; for typical contractions (blue, orange) the true value is smaller.



So a report must state the worst record’s value, which gets no amplification at all; randomizing the stopping time spreads the benefit across records. The bound is exact in the worst case, when the step that uses your record wipes out all earlier noise, and loose for typical runs, where earlier noise and strict contraction also help (Figure 33.2). It covers one pass in a fixed order; several passes or subsampling need other theorems (Altschuler & Talwar 2022). And it needs convexity, because a non-contractive step can stretch a small gap faster than the noise pays it off.
crumbs: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
section: 33.5 Hidden state: privacy that stops growing
text:
33.5 Hidden state: privacy that stops growing
Full-batch noisy GD uses every record at every step, and composition charges every step, so the privacy loss grows linearly in the number of steps \(T\), and amplification by iteration alone does not help: each step opens a fresh gap, and paying each one off as it comes is composition again. Two properties can change that when only the final model is released. If the parameters live in a bounded convex set, the two runs can never be further apart than its diameter, however long they run, so only the last stretch of steps has to hide that gap and the cost stops depending on \(T\). If the loss is strongly convex, each step is a strict contraction that shrinks the gap for free.
Altschuler & Talwar (2022) prove the bounded-domain version: the last iterate’s RDP grows like composition up to a number of steps proportional to the diameter, then stays flat, and their lower bound shows the shape is right. For a quadratic loss the answer is exact. With contraction factor \(c < 1\) per step, your record’s per-step shift \(s\) reaches the end damped, so the total signal saturates at \(s/(1 - c)\); the noise saturates the same way, at a standard deviation of \(\sigma/\sqrt{1 - c^2}\). Their ratio is the limiting Gaussian mechanism, \[\mu_\infty = \frac{s}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{1 + c}{1 - c}}, \tag{33.5}\] reached after about \(1/(1 - c)\) steps, the time it takes \(c^T\) to become small; for a gradient step of size \(1/\beta\) on a \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, \(\beta\)-smooth loss, that is the condition number \(\beta/\lambda\). With \(c = 1\) the signal grows like \(T\) and the noise only like \(\sqrt T\), so there is no plateau: without contraction, hiding the state buys nothing.
Run 10,000 steps of full-batch noisy GD with \(\sigma/s = 10\) on a quadratic with \(c = 0.99\). Releasing every iterate is a Gaussian mechanism with \(\mu = 10\), which is \(\varepsilon = 91.8173\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\): no guarantee at all. Releasing only the final model is at the plateau, \(\mu = 1.4107\), which is \(\varepsilon = 6.5534\), with the same noise. The bounded-domain bound is looser: for a linear loss on the unit interval (Figure 33.3, right), after 2000 steps composition charges an RDP of 20.0000 at \(\alpha = 2\) and the bound 4.0000, while a hard instance reaches 0.3786. The shape is right; the constant is loose.






Figure 33.3: Left: the exact \(\mu\) of the last iterate of one-dimensional full-batch noisy GD against the number of steps \(T\), for \(c = 1\) (on top of composition), \(c = 0.99\) and \(c = 0.9\); with contraction it plateaus. Right: the Rényi divergence of order 2 of the last iterate for a linear loss on \([0, 1]\): composition, the bounded-domain bound, and the exact value for two projected random walks.



Both conditions are load-bearing. The argument needs only the last iterate released, because the adversary must not see the run before it has forgotten: checkpoints, logged intermediate models, a model published after each epoch, or the best of several checkpoints put you back to composition. It also needs contractive steps, which require convexity. For non-convex losses, Annamalai (2024) built a loss for which the last iterate of DP-SGD leaks as much as all iterates together. That attacks seeing only the final model have fallen short of the DP-SGD bound (Nasr et al. 2021) is an observation about attacks, not a guarantee. Do not report a hidden-state \(\varepsilon\) for deep learning.

title: 33  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
33.6 Code
This standard-library snippet builds Equation 33.1 in log space, takes the larger hockey-stick divergence over both directions, and bisects for \(\varepsilon\):
from math import exp, lgamma, log


def log_binom_pmf(k: int, n: int, p: float) -> float:
    return lgamma(n + 1) - lgamma(k + 1) - lgamma(n - k + 1) + k * log(p) + (n - k) * log(1 - p)


def shuffled_rr_pair(n: int, eps0: float) -> tuple[list[float], list[float]]:
    """Distribution of the number of 1-reports when you hold 0 (P) or 1 (Q); the n - 1 others hold 0."""
    theta = exp(eps0) / (1 + exp(eps0))
    b = [exp(log_binom_pmf(y, n - 1, 1 - theta)) for y in range(n)] + [0.0]
    P = [theta * b[y] + (1 - theta) * (b[y - 1] if y else 0.0) for y in range(n + 1)]
    Q = [(1 - theta) * b[y] + theta * (b[y - 1] if y else 0.0) for y in range(n + 1)]
    return P, Q


def hockey_stick(P: list[float], Q: list[float], eps: float) -> float:
    return sum(max(p - exp(eps) * q, 0.0) for p, q in zip(P, Q))


def shuffled_rr_epsilon(n: int, eps0: float, delta: float) -> float:
    P, Q = shuffled_rr_pair(n, eps0)
    lo, hi = 0.0, eps0  # shuffling never does worse than the local eps0
    for _ in range(50):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        worst = max(hockey_stick(P, Q, mid), hockey_stick(Q, P, mid))
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if worst > delta else (lo, mid)
    return hi


print(f"{shuffled_rr_epsilon(10_000, 2.0, 1e-6):.4f}")  # 0.0870
print(f"{shuffled_rr_epsilon(100_000, 4.0, 1e-6):.4f}")  # 0.0847
print(f"{shuffled_rr_epsilon(1_000, 4.0, 1e-6):.4f}")  # 1.6910
It reproduces the exact column of Table 33.1. The full edition’s script, shuffling_iteration.py, also computes the numeric clone bound and every iteration result:
uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/shuffling_iteration.py

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.1 Why this matters
You train a model with differential privacy (DP) using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped per-example gradients and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD. You may want to stop when the validation loss stalls, lower the noise mid-run, or let well-fitted records keep training. Every composition theorem so far assumes the opposite: the per-step budgets \(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_k\) and the number of steps \(k\) are fixed before the run (Advanced and optimal composition). Once they depend on what the run released, they are random, and plugging the values you happened to use into a fixed-parameter theorem afterwards is not valid.
So the question splits in two. A privacy filter answers “may I run one more step without exceeding a budget fixed in advance?” A privacy odometer answers “how much have I spent so far?”, and since you may stop at any moment, its answer must hold at every step at once. Both rest on one fact about Rényi differential privacy (RDP): at an order fixed before the run, adding up the spends as you go is as safe as if they had been fixed. That makes a filter free, an odometer cheap, and per-record accounting possible.
crumbs: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
section: 34.2 Why plugging in the realized parameters fails
text:
34.2 Why plugging in the realized parameters fails
Advanced composition is a high-probability statement: at a time \(t\) fixed in advance, the total privacy loss exceeds a bound \(U_t\), its mean plus a spread growing like \(\sqrt t\), only with probability \(\delta\). It says nothing about a time chosen by watching the outputs. An analyst who stops when the loss happens to be high picks exactly the paths on which the bound fails, and so does stopping on anything correlated with it, such as “these answers look unusual”.
Ask randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) about one person’s bit at every step. Each report moves the privacy loss up or down by 0.1, so the loss is a random walk with a slight upward drift. At any single step up to 1,000, the plug-in bound at \(\delta = 0.01\) fails with probability at most 0.0016. Now stop at the first crossing and report \(U_T\). The bound is narrow early, when \(\sqrt t\) is small, so a few walks cross it early and are frozen there (Figure 34.1). By \(10^4\) steps a fraction 0.0318 of runs have crossed (Table 34.1): “\(\varepsilon = U_T\) with \(\delta = 0.01\)” is wrong 3.18 times as often as it claims. A smaller \(\delta\) does not save it (Table 34.1, last row).

The probability keeps growing because a random walk eventually wanders further than any fixed multiple of \(\sqrt t\) (its reach grows like \(\sqrt{t\ln\ln t}\)), so given time it crosses with certainty. A valid running bound must be wider, and Rogers et al. (2016) showed that every odometer pays at least an extra \(\ln\ln n\) inside the logarithm for \(n\) steps.
Basic composition escapes the problem: the sum of the realized \(\varepsilon_t\) bounds the loss of every output, so there is no bad event for a stopping rule to select. A filter escapes it too, because it makes no running claim to catch at a bad moment; it only asks whether the next step fits a budget fixed in advance.
crumbs: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.3 The Rényi filter
RDP describes each step by a curve \(\varepsilon_t(\alpha)\) over orders \(\alpha > 1\), and with fixed parameters the curves of a run add (Rényi DP). This survives adaptivity at one fixed order. Fix an order \(\alpha\) and an RDP budget \(B\) before the run. Let step \(t\) be \((\alpha, \varepsilon_t(\alpha))\)-RDP whatever happened before it, with \(\varepsilon_t(\alpha)\) known before the step runs. Run step \(t\) only if the spends so far, its own included, fit: \[\sum_{j \le t}\varepsilon_j(\alpha) \le B. \tag{34.1}\] Then the stopped run is \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP, as if the spends had been fixed.
The reason is a betting argument. Treat \(e^{(\alpha - 1)(\text{loss} - \text{spend})}\) as your wealth in a game. RDP at order \(\alpha\) bounds the average of \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\times\text{loss}}\), so a step charged its RDP spend cannot make this wealth grow on average: the game is fair or tilted against you. In such a game no quitting rule raises your expected final wealth, as long as you decide whether to play each round before seeing its result. If the total spend is at most \(B\) on every path, the average of \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\times\text{loss}}\) at the end is at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)B}\), which is exactly what \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP says.
Each condition is a step of that argument. A step’s price must be known before it runs: a mechanism allowed to charge little on exactly the outputs that reveal most would make the game a winning one. The budget must hold on every path, not on average, because the paths that spend most may be those where the loss is high. And the order must be fixed in advance. You may track several orders and halt when any one is exhausted, since then each held on every path; continuing while some order still fits, chosen after seeing the spends, is not free (Section 34.5 prices it).
You train with full-batch noisy gradient descent towards \((5.299, 10^{-5})\) at order \(\alpha = 5.8\). Mironov’s conversion turns \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP into \((B + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1), \delta)\)-DP, so run backwards it sets \(B = 5.299 - \ln(10^5)/4.8 = 2.900\). A full-batch Gaussian step with noise multiplier \(\sigma_t\) spends \(\alpha/(2\sigma_t^2)\). With \(\sigma_t = 10\) each step spends \(5.8/200 = 0.0290\) and you get 100 steps. If training plateaus at step 60 and you drop to \(\sigma_t = 5\), each later step costs \(5.8/50 = 0.1160\), and the filter allows \((2.900 - 60\times0.0290)/0.1160 = 10\) more. Either way the run is \((5.8, 2.900)\)-RDP, whatever rule decided the switch.
At a fixed order the filter costs nothing. It can even beat fixed-curve composition, which charges every step its worst branch, while the filter charges what each path spent.
crumbs: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.4 Filters for pure differential privacy
An interactive query system has a global budget \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\), and each query brings a pure-DP \(\varepsilon_t\) chosen after earlier answers. Summing the \(\varepsilon_t\) is valid but grows like the number of queries \(k\); you want advanced composition’s \(\sqrt k\) without the failure of Section 34.2.
The Rényi filter delivers it. An \(\varepsilon_t\)-DP step spends at most \(\alpha\varepsilon_t^2/2\) at every order \(\alpha\) (Concentrated differential privacy). So a rule that keeps \(\frac12\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2\) below a fixed level is a Rényi filter at every order at once, and because the rule does not mention the order, the conversion may pick the best one afterwards. Doing that conversion gives the Whitehouse filter (Whitehouse et al. 2023): continue while \[\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)\textstyle\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2} + \tfrac12\textstyle\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2 \le \varepsilon_g, \tag{34.2}\] with sums over every step so far. It reads like advanced composition, the first term the spread of the total loss and the second its mean, and the stopped run is \((\varepsilon_g, \delta)\)-DP.
At \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) and \(\varepsilon_g = 1\), the filter allows 349 steps of 0.01, slightly more than the 337 of advanced composition with \(k\) fixed in advance (Table 34.2). It wins, despite allowing adaptivity, because its mean term, \(\varepsilon_t^2/2\) per step, is tighter than the \(\varepsilon_t(e^{\varepsilon_t} - 1)\) of the fixed-\(k\) form. From the budget side, 1,000 steps of 0.01 need 1.712 under the Whitehouse filter, 1.763 under fixed-\(k\) advanced composition and 10.000 under the basic filter \(\sum_t\varepsilon_t \le \varepsilon_g\).

The older Rogers et al. (2016) filter has the same shape, but its inequality must hold for every value of \(\sum_t\varepsilon_t^2\) at once, and that costs 1.40 to 1.51 times the budget and fewer than half the steps; use the Whitehouse form. Check it before each step, with that step’s \(\varepsilon_t\) included, since the guarantee is about the decision to run it. For steps with \(\delta_t > 0\), add a second rule, \(\sum_t\delta_t \le \delta''\), and the guarantee becomes \((\varepsilon_g, \delta + \delta'')\).

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.5 Odometers
Early stopping and open-ended analyses need a running “how much have I spent?” that is true whenever the run stops. Return to the betting game of Section 34.3. Markov’s inequality says that the wealth, which starts at 1, reaches \(c\) at one given time with probability at most \(1/c\). Ville’s inequality extends this to reaching \(c\) at any time, because “stop the first time you reach \(c\)” is itself a quitting rule and cannot raise the mean. Unpacked, at one order fixed in advance, Mironov’s conversion of the running spend holds at every step at once, for free.
The cost comes from the order: the best order for 10 steps is not the best for 1,000. To choose it late, fix a grid \(\Lambda\) of \(|\Lambda|\) orders, track the spend \(S_t(\alpha) = \sum_{j\le t}\varepsilon_j(\alpha)\) at each, and give each order a share \(\delta/|\Lambda|\) of the failure probability. The Ville odometer reports the best order’s conversion, \[U_t = \min_{\alpha\in\Lambda}\Big[S_t(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(|\Lambda|/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\Big], \tag{34.3}\] and with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) the loss stays below \(U_t\) at every step. It is Mironov’s conversion with \(\delta\) replaced by \(\delta/|\Lambda|\); that union bound is the whole price.
For full-batch Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 10\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the part’s 154 orders raise \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.513\) to 16.550, and the odometer costs 15–19% over the fixed-time value: 6.253 against 5.299 at \(t = 100\) (Table 34.3). A single order chosen in advance, 5.8, is free at \(t = 100\), its design point, and poor elsewhere: 31.399 at \(t = 1000\). On the part’s running example (DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(10^4\) steps, \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)), the fixed-time RDP value is 7.43, and an odometer valid whenever the run stops costs 8.82 (Ville) or 9.08 (the slightly looser odometer of Lécuyer 2021).

Read an odometer for what it is: “\(\varepsilon = U_T\)” says the loss exceeds the random number \(U_T\) with probability at most \(\delta\), a tail bound rather than an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP guarantee. title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.6 Individual privacy accounting in DP-SGD
DP-SGD’s usual analysis charges every record at every step as if its clipped gradient had norm \(C\), the clipping norm. But once the model fits a record, its gradient shrinks and it moves the noisy sum less, so the same noise hides it better.
That cost is exact. With full-batch steps and noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) on the summed clipped gradients, removing record \(i\) shifts the output by its clipped gradient \(\bar g_{i,t}\), so its spend is the Gaussian RDP for that shift: \[\varepsilon_{i,t}(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha\|\bar g_{i,t}\|^2}{2\sigma^2C^2} \le \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{34.4}\] It depends only on the record and the current model, which depends only on earlier releases, so it is known before the step: what the Rényi filter needs. The individual filter (Feldman & Zrnic 2021) runs one Rényi filter per record. Record \(i\) joins the sum only while its own spends total at most \(B\); once dropped, it no longer changes the output and spends nothing. Neighbouring datasets differ in one record, whose filter held, so the run is \((\alpha, B)\)-RDP. No step costs more than the worst case, so every record trains at least as long as in the worst-case run.
The full edition simulates 10,000 records (\(C = 1\), \(\sigma = 10\), full batch): 90% typical records whose gradients shrink as the model fits them, 10% hard records it never fits. The worst-case run has 100 steps and \(\varepsilon = 5.299\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), best at order 5.8, where \(B = 2.900\). Converting each record’s own spend after 100 steps (Table 34.4) gives a typical median of 3.17 and a hard median of 5.02, near the worst case. Run the individual filter for 300 steps and hard records reach the budget and are dropped from step 101 (the median one at step 111), while no typical record ever is: their median spend at step 300 is 0.778, a quarter of the budget (Figure 34.4).

The filter certifies one guarantee for everyone, \((5.8, 2.900)\)-RDP. The per-record values in the table are estimates: each is a fixed-time conversion of a random spend, the mistake of Section 34.2, and at a fixed order none can fall below the conversion’s toll \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1) = 2.399\). They are also sensitive, since a small spend says “the model fits this record well”: show a value to the record’s owner, never publish them all. There is a fairness cost too: records the model fits worst, often from under-represented groups, keep large gradients, exhaust their budget first and are dropped first, so the model sees even less of them. With Poisson subsampling the argument still works, using the subsampled Gaussian at noise multiplier \(\sigma C/\|\bar g_{i,t}\|\) (Amplification by subsampling), but you need every record’s gradient norm at every step, sampled or not.

title: 34  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
34.7 Code
Filters and odometers are a sum of spends and a comparison. This snippet implements the Whitehouse filter, the Rényi filter for a noise schedule and the Ville odometer for full-batch Gaussian steps, and reproduces the numbers above.
from math import log, sqrt


def whitehouse_statistic(eps_steps: list[float], delta: float) -> float:
    """Advanced composition of pure-DP budgets with mean term eps^2 / 2: valid under adaptivity."""
    v = sum(e * e for e in eps_steps)
    return sqrt(2 * log(1 / delta) * v) + v / 2


def steps_allowed(eps_step: float, eps_global: float, delta: float) -> int:
    """Run steps of eps_step while the Whitehouse filter, checked before each step, says continue."""
    spent: list[float] = []
    while whitehouse_statistic([*spent, eps_step], delta) <= eps_global:
        spent.append(eps_step)
    return len(spent)


def gaussian_rdp(alpha: float, sigma: float) -> float:
    """RDP at order alpha of one full-batch Gaussian step with noise multiplier sigma."""
    return alpha / (2 * sigma**2)


def renyi_filter(sigmas: list[float], alpha: float, budget: float) -> int:
    """Number of steps of a noise schedule that a Renyi filter at order alpha lets through."""
    spent, steps = 0.0, 0
    for sigma in sigmas:
        cost = gaussian_rdp(alpha, sigma)
        if spent + cost > budget + 1e-12:  # tolerance for floating-point sums
            break
        spent, steps = spent + cost, steps + 1
    return steps


ORDERS = [1 + x / 10 for x in range(1, 100)] + [float(x) for x in range(12, 64)] + [128.0, 256.0, 512.0]


def ville_odometer(t: int, sigma: float, delta: float, orders: list[float]) -> float:
    """Running epsilon after t full-batch Gaussian steps, valid whenever the run stops."""
    return min(t * gaussian_rdp(a, sigma) + log(len(orders) / delta) / (a - 1) for a in orders)


print(f"{whitehouse_statistic([0.01] * 1000, 1e-6):.3f}")  # 1.712
print(steps_allowed(0.01, 1.0, 1e-6))  # 349
alpha, budget = 5.8, 2.9
print(renyi_filter([10.0] * 1000, alpha, budget))  # 100
print(renyi_filter([10.0] * 60 + [5.0] * 1000, alpha, budget) - 60)  # 10
print(f"{budget + log(1 / 1e-5) / (alpha - 1):.3f}")  # 5.299
print(len(ORDERS))  # 154
print(f"{ville_odometer(100, 10.0, 1e-5, ORDERS):.3f}")  # 6.253
print(f"{ville_odometer(100, 10.0, 1e-5, [alpha]):.3f}")  # 5.299
print(f"{ville_odometer(1000, 10.0, 1e-5, [alpha]):.3f}")  # 31.399
ORDERS is the part’s grid of orders. The full edition’s script, adaptive_composition.py, also computes the plug-in failure exactly, checks the Rényi filter by simulation and runs the individual-accounting experiment:

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.1 Why this matters
You trained a model with differential privacy (DP), using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipping and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD: each record joined each batch independently with probability \(q = 0.01\) (Poisson sampling), gradients were clipped to norm \(C\), and noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) was added to their sum, with noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\), for \(k = 10{,}000\) steps. Now you must write “the model is \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP” in a model card. The procedure that bounds or estimates \(\varepsilon\) is an accountant. On this run, composing per-step guarantees gives 11296.93, Rényi differential privacy (RDP) gives 7.4287 or 6.7127 depending on the conversion, the Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) central limit theorem (CLT) gives 6.0071, and a privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant gives the interval \([6.1377, 6.2377]\). Which do you report, and what else must you say?
The numbers differ because they are different kinds of statement. An upper bound comes with a proof that the run is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP; it may be loose, but it is true. An approximation has no proof, and if it lands below the truth, the claim it supports is false. A certified lower bound says the true \(\varepsilon\) is at least this large: not a guarantee, but a referee for every other number. Hence the rule this chapter unpacks: report the tightest upper bound whose assumptions hold for the code you ran, with enough detail that someone else can recompute it.

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.2 Every accountant on one run
Every accountant starts from what one step reveals about one record. Along that record’s clipped gradient, in units of \(C\), the output is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) without the record. With it, the record is sampled with probability \(q\) and then shifts the output by 1, giving the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). Accountants differ in how much of this pair they keep before combining \(k\) copies, and whatever they throw away must be replaced by a worst case. So the more they keep, the tighter they are.
The crudest keeps two numbers per step, an amplified \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair (Amplification by subsampling), and composes them. That is a valid bound, but composition must assume every step leaks its worst case, while in reality the losses of different steps mostly cancel. It is right at \(k = 1\) and over a thousand times too large at \(k = 10{,}000\) (Table 35.1); advanced composition is even worse here.
RDP keeps a whole curve, the Rényi divergence of the pair at every order \(\alpha\) (Rényi DP). Curves add exactly under composition, and a conversion then turns \(k\) times the curve into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests). Mironov’s, the improved and the optimal conversion are each proved for every pair of distributions with that curve, so all three are upper bounds, ordered Mironov \(\ge\) improved \(\ge\) optimal \(\ge\) true \(\varepsilon\). The improved conversion beats Mironov’s at every order, so never use the older one.
RDP’s excess has two sources, and the run’s length decides which dominates. One is the conversion’s toll, \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), about \(11.5/(\alpha - 1)\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), paid however small the curve is. After one step the curve is tiny, the toll is most of the answer, and RDP with the improved conversion overstates the PLD by 379.1%. In a long run the toll is negligible, but the curve itself keeps only moments of the privacy loss, not its distribution: that costs the last 7.6% at \(k = 10{,}000\), and no conversion can remove it.
The GDP CLT treats the run as \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = q\sqrt{k(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy), since a sum of many small losses should be nearly Gaussian. But that is a large-\(k\) limit with no error bound, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is read far in the tail, where a Gaussian approximation is least reliable. On this run it falls below the certified lower bound at every \(k\).
The PLD accountant keeps everything: the whole distribution of the privacy loss on a grid of width \(h\), composed numerically (Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions). Rounding every loss up describes a pair that leaks at least as much as the real one, which stays true through composition, so the result is an upper bound; rounding down gives a lower bound. Each step’s rounding moves the loss by less than \(h\), so after \(k\) steps the two are at most \(kh\) apart: 0.1 here, with \(h = 10^{-5}\).

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
section: 35.3 Calibrating the noise for a target ε
text:
35.3 Calibrating the noise for a target ε
In practice you fix the budget, the steps and the batch size, and ask how much noise to add. Then a loose accountant costs utility: it overstates \(\varepsilon\) at every \(\sigma\), so it asks for more noise to meet the same target. The averaged gradient’s noise has standard deviation \(\sigma C/(qn)\) for \(n\) records, so every percent of \(\sigma\) is a percent of gradient noise.
The noise accountant \(A\) requires for a target \(\varepsilon^*\) is the smallest \(\sigma\) at which its reported \(\varepsilon_A(\sigma)\) meets the target: \[\sigma_A(\varepsilon^*) = \min\{\sigma > 0 : \varepsilon_A(\sigma) \le \varepsilon^*\}. \tag{35.1}\] More noise never raises a correct accountant’s \(\varepsilon\): a noisier run can be made from a less noisy one by adding independent noise, without looking at the data, and that cannot reveal more. So this is where a decreasing function crosses a level, and bisection finds it. Return the end of the final bracket where \(\varepsilon_A \le \varepsilon^*\) was actually checked, never the midpoint, which may miss the target.

It asks for 2.0 to 4.8% less noise than the certified bound needs, and at \(\varepsilon = 8\) that is provably too little: at its \(\sigma = 0.8676\) the optimistic PLD already gives 8.2594. At small targets the PLD’s fixed width \(kh\) is a large fraction of \(\varepsilon\): at \(\varepsilon = 1\) it brackets \(\sigma\) only to \([3.654, 3.988]\), so refine \(h\).

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.4 Where each accountant is tight
The ranking changes with the mechanism, by the principle above: an accountant is tight when its summary describes the mechanism’s privacy loss exactly.
For the plain Gaussian mechanism, with no subsampling, the composed pair is exactly Gaussian, and GDP describes it with one number, \(\mu\), whose squares add. GDP is then exact. A team that releases 100 noisy counts at \(\sigma = 10\) has exactly \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\); an old RDP accountant with Mironov’s conversion reports 5.2985, 21.0% too high, and the improved conversion 4.7285, because RDP keeps this curve exactly but still pays in the conversion.
For pure-DP steps such as randomized response, the privacy loss takes only a few values, so the PLD needs no rounding and is exact. For 100 steps of randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), the exact PLD gives 4.3068, RDP 4.6154, zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) 4.7263, advanced composition 5.8502 and basic composition 10.0000: each summary that keeps less pays more.
For DP-SGD, subsampling makes each step a mixture that no closed form describes exactly, and only the PLD is both certified and tight. zCDP is the wrong tool here: its single line \(\rho\alpha\) must lie above the RDP curve at every order, and at high orders the subsampled curve’s slope approaches the unsubsampled one, so the line cannot express the gain from subsampling. When the noise, the stopping time or per-record budgets are chosen during training, the per-step pair is no longer fixed in advance as the PLD accountant assumes; an RDP filter at a fixed order loses nothing to that adaptivity (Adaptive composition).

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
section: 35.5 Matching the accountant to the code
text:
35.5 Matching the accountant to the code
An accountant takes \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(k\) and trusts that the code does what its theorem assumes. A mismatch makes the number a statement about a different algorithm.
The sampling scheme is the most expensive mismatch, for a mechanical reason. With fixed-size random batches, adding a record must push another one out, so the batch sum can move by up to \(2C\) instead of \(C\), and such a run is covered by the Poisson accountant only at noise multiplier \(\sigma/2\) (Lebeda et al. 2024). With shuffle and partition, each record is used exactly once per epoch, in a batch fixed by the shuffle, and no amplification theorem holds for every dataset. What remains certain is one unamplified Gaussian step per epoch, for zero-out neighbours (one record’s gradient replaced by zero).
In a code review: a script uses a data loader with shuffle=True and batch_size=500 on 50,000 records for 100 epochs, and calls an RDP accountant with sample_rate=0.01, which reports 6.71. That sampler is shuffle and partition, so what holds is 100 unamplified steps at \(\sigma = 1\): \(\mu = 10\) GDP and \(\varepsilon = 91.8173\), or 284.39 under replace-one, where the sum moves by \(2C\). Fixed-size random batches, accounted correctly, would give 47.42 (RDP) and 43.42 (PLD). Switching to Poisson sampling makes the PLD’s 6.24 honest. The factor of 6.96 from fixed-size batches dwarfs the factor of at most 1.19 between RDP and PLD at 10,000 steps: check the sampler before arguing about accountants.
Other assumptions fail quietly. If you tune 10 configurations on the private data and release the best, which one is best depends on all 10 runs, so the release costs all 10 composed: \(\varepsilon = 27.23\) with RDP. The guarantee protects whatever differs between neighbours, so example-level DP protects each example, not a person who contributed many. And the theorems assume exact real-valued Gaussian noise; floating-point sampling can break a mechanism that is correct on paper (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.6 What to report
An \(\varepsilon\) without its assumptions cannot be checked or compared. NIST SP 800-226 (2025) and Ponomareva et al. (2023) ask for the setting (who is trusted), what is covered (one run, or tuning too), the unit of privacy, the neighbouring relation, the accountant and whether its assumptions hold, and, for DP-SGD, everything needed to recompute \(\varepsilon\): sampling scheme, \(q\), \(k\), \(\sigma\), \(C\), and the accountant’s version and discretization.
Choose \(\delta\) with its meaning in mind: it is the probability with which the promise may fail. A mechanism that publishes one randomly chosen record in full meets a \(\delta\) of about \(1/n\) with \(\varepsilon = 0\), while exposing someone completely. So \(\delta\) must be much smaller than \(1/n\) for \(n\) units of privacy (The definition of differential privacy): Ponomareva et al. suggest \(n^{-1.1}\), and NIST gives \(1/n^2\) as a common recommendation and calls values above \(10^{-5}\) suspicious. For \(n = 50{,}000\), \(1/n = 2.0\times10^{-5}\), so the customary \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is only half of it.
Report \(\varepsilon\) at several \(\delta\), not one pair. Many different mechanisms share a single \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair and behave differently at smaller \(\delta\), so a reader cannot convert your pair to the \(\delta\) they care about. One composed PLD gives the whole profile cheaply (Table 35.5). For the same reason, give the parameters behind any conversion: the RDP accountant’s is its curve, \(\varepsilon(4.1) = 3.7336\) at the best order 4.1, which the improved conversion turns into 6.7127.

A filled-in statement:

Privacy guarantee. The model was trained with DP-SGD in the central model: the training server is trusted to run the code below, and the guarantee covers every intermediate noisy gradient, hence every checkpoint and the final model. Unit of privacy: one training example; each person contributes at most one example. Neighbouring relation: add or remove one example. Training: Poisson sampling with rate \(q = 0.01\) (\(n = 50{,}000\) examples, expected batch size 500), \(k = 10{,}000\) steps (100 epochs), per-example clipping norm \(C = 1\), Gaussian noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\). Accountant: privacy loss distributions, pessimistic discretization on the grid \(h = 10^{-5}\), both add and remove directions. Guarantee: \((6.24, 10^{-5})\)-DP and \((9.06, 4.0\times10^{-10})\)-DP. The optimistic discretization gives 6.1377 and 8.9378, so the accountant’s own error is at most 0.1000 and 0.1124. For comparison, the RDP accountant with the improved conversion gives 6.7127 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Not covered: hyperparameters were tuned on a public proxy dataset; no tuning on the private data was performed. If the sampling assumption failed (for example, shuffled fixed-size batches), the guarantee without amplification is \((91.82, 10^{-5})\)-DP for zero-out neighbours.

Three habits in it follow from what an upper bound is. It is rounded up: 9.0502 becomes 9.06, because 9.05 would be a claim the accountant has not certified. The optimistic value is its error bar, which an RDP number cannot have, since RDP has no matching lower bound. And where an assumption is in doubt, the statement gives the fallback guarantee that does not rely on it.

title: 35  Choosing an accountant
text:
35.7 Checking an accountant
Test an accountant on cases whose answers you know. With \(q = 1\) there is no subsampling, so \(k\) steps are exactly \(\sqrt k/\sigma\)-GDP, and every upper bound must lie above that closed form. For \(\sigma = 1\) and \(k = 10\) the exact \(\varepsilon\) is 17.8566, and the RDP accountant gives 19.0536, above it as it must be. The CLT formula at \(q = 1\) gives \(\mu = 4.1452\) instead of 3.1623 and \(\varepsilon = 25.5853\): it fails, because its derivation assumes small \(q\). The PLD bracket for the plain Gaussian must contain the same closed form, and it does: \([17.8516, 17.8616]\) at \(h = 10^{-3}\).
Two properties hold for every correct accountant, so a violation is a bug, not slack. The orderings of Section 35.2 must hold at every \(k\), with no reported upper bound below the optimistic PLD. And \(\varepsilon\) must never decrease with \(k\), because what the first \(k\) steps release is part of what \(k + 1\) steps release.
Then compare against an independent library: Google’s dp_accounting (RDP and PLD), Opacus (RDP, GDP, and a privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant, its default), or Microsoft’s prv_accountant. When two RDP accountants disagree, the size of the gap says why: the improved conversion beats Mironov’s by \(\frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\) at order \(\alpha\) (0.3612 at order 10); on the running example it is what separates Mironov’s 7.43 from the improved 6.71. Certified PLD and PRV brackets from different libraries each contain the truth, so they must overlap; if they do not, one has a bug.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
The common thread
The previous parts built the guarantee and the tools to account for it. This part trains models with it, and asks the questions that decide whether a private model is worth deploying: how do you train with differential privacy (DP), how much accuracy does it cost, which knobs move that cost, and how do you check that the trained model is as private as the accountant claims? The answers are mostly about one algorithm, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD, and about everything around it.
Read this part if you train, review or sign off on a model that claims an \(\varepsilon\). It assumes the Gaussian mechanism and clipping from Differential privacy foundations, and amplification by subsampling and the accountant for DP-SGD from Privacy accounting. Each chapter restates what it uses.
A private training algorithm has two halves. The privacy half says which quantity has bounded sensitivity, meaning how far one record can move it, and how much noise covers that move; it is a theorem, and the accountants of Part 4 turn it into a number. The utility half says how much the noise and the bounding cost in accuracy; it is mostly measured, rarely proved. Every chapter moves one of the two, and keeping them apart is the most useful habit here: a choice that only affects accuracy can be tuned freely, one that touches the privacy half must be accounted for.
The first two chapters build the algorithm. Private empirical risk minimization compares three places to put the noise, on the final weights, inside the objective and on every gradient, and shows that only noise on the gradients survives non-convex models, because it needs nothing but a bound on each record’s gradient. DP-SGD supplies that bound by clipping, adds random minibatches and an accountant, and works out what each knob does. Every later chapter uses it, so these two come first.
The next three ask what else spends the budget, or could spend it better. Hyperparameter tuning shows that picking the best of several private runs is itself a computation on the data, and how to pay for it honestly. Mechanisms built on the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) algorithm, DP-FTRL and matrix factorization, replace the random batches that DP-SGD’s amplification relies on with correlated noise, for settings where sampling cannot be trusted or controlled. Private prediction privatizes answers instead of weights, which can be cheaper when you only need a limited number of predictions.
The next three change the setting rather than the algorithm. Public data and private fine-tuning explains why a public pretrained model helps so much: the noise grows with the number of parameters you train, so fine-tuning fewer of them can be more accurate. User-level differential privacy changes the unit of protection from one record to one person, which is usually what you meant to promise. Disparate impact asks who pays for the noise and the clipping, and finds that small groups and hard examples pay most.
The last two close the loop between theory and practice. Choosing ε turns a budget into what it means for an attacker and asks how to justify one. Auditing private training runs attacks with planted records against a trained model and turns their success into an empirical lower bound on \(\varepsilon\), which catches implementations that do not deliver what the accountant says. It comes last because it checks what the others claim.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
The running examples
Two models recur. The first is ridge-regularized logistic regression in ten dimensions on synthetic data, where the exact minimizer can be computed, so every private method can be compared with the non-private optimum. The second is a small neural network trained with DP-SGD on synthetic data, small enough that every experiment runs on a laptop in seconds, yet non-convex, so clipping and noise behave as they do in deep learning. It runs exactly the configuration whose \(\varepsilon\) Part 4 computed, so you can see what that number costs in accuracy.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
How to read this part
Read the first two chapters in order. Hyperparameter tuning and DP-FTRL change how the algorithm is run and can be read in either order. The chapters on private prediction, public data, user-level privacy and disparate impact are independent of each other. Read choosing \(\varepsilon\) after them, and auditing last. The derivations are in the full edition.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
By the end of this part you will be able to train a convex model privately and predict what it costs, and run DP-SGD knowing which knobs set \(\varepsilon\) and which only set accuracy. You will be able to check an implementation for the details that silently break its guarantee, account for tuning, decide when correlated noise, private prediction or a public pretrained model is the better route, and state the privacy unit you protect. And you will be able to say who pays for the noise, choose an \(\varepsilon\) you can defend, and audit a trained model to test whether it is as private as claimed.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.1 Why this matters
Most of machine learning is empirical risk minimization (ERM): choose the weights \(w\) that minimize the average loss on the training data, usually plus a ridge penalty \(\frac\lambda2\|w\|^2\). The trained weights are a function of every record, and Membership inference showed that they give some of those records away. Differential privacy (DP) promises that the distribution of whatever you release changes by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), plus a slack \(\delta\), when one record changes. To keep that promise for a trained model, randomness has to enter somewhere between the data and the released weights, and there are three natural places: on the final weights (output perturbation), inside the objective (objective perturbation), or on every gradient during training (gradient perturbation).
The one idea that organizes all three is that privacy needs a bound on how far one record can move what you release. That bound is the sensitivity, and the noise is sized to hide a move of that length. The three methods differ only in which quantity they bound, and each step back toward the data needs fewer assumptions. Output perturbation needs an exact, unique minimizer of a strongly convex objective. Objective perturbation needs that and a loss with bounded curvature. Gradient perturbation, for its privacy, needs only that each record’s gradient is bounded, with no convexity and no exact solution, which is why it is the one that survives in deep learning, as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD.
Throughout, neighbouring datasets differ by replacing one record, so both have \(n\) records; \(L\) bounds the length of every record’s loss gradient. The running example is ridge-regularized logistic regression in \(d = 10\) dimensions with \(\lambda = 0.01\), features on the unit sphere (so \(L = 1\)), and a target of \(\varepsilon = 1\), with \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for the methods that need one. Quality is measured by the excess risk, how much worse the private weights fit the training objective than the exact minimizer.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.2 Output perturbation
The simplest private trainer treats training as a black box: compute the exact minimizer \(w^*\), then add noise. For that you need the minimizer’s sensitivity. Replacing one record changes the average loss by one term in and one out, so the objective’s gradient changes by at most \(2L/n\) anywhere. The ridge makes the objective \(\lambda\)-strongly convex: its gradient grows by at least \(\lambda\) per unit of distance, so a point where the gradient is \(g\) long lies within \(g/\lambda\) of the minimizer. At the new minimizer, the old objective’s gradient is at most \(2L/n\), hence the minimizer moves by at most \[\|w^*(D) - w^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{36.1}\] Add Gaussian noise to that, and you have the Gaussian mechanism (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Its privacy depends only on the ratio \(\mu\) of the sensitivity to the noise standard deviation, and the exact calibration (Balle & Wang 2018) gives the largest admissible ratio \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(\mu = 0.2681\), so the noise must be \(\sigma = 3.7306\) times the sensitivity. The classic formula \(\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilon\) asks for 4.8448 times, 30% more noise for the same guarantee, so always calibrate exactly.
The noise must hide the worst case, not the actual move. In one dimension with \(n = 20\) records and \(\lambda = 0.5\), replacing one record moves the minimizer by 0.0832, but the bound is \(2/(0.5 \times 20) = 0.2\), and the noise is sized for 0.2 (Figure 36.1).






Figure 36.1: Left: two neighbouring regularized logistic objectives in one dimension (\(n = 20\), \(\lambda = 0.5\)), their minimizers (vertical lines) 0.083 apart, below the bound \(2L/(\lambda n) = 0.2\). Right: the released weight’s density under each dataset with Gaussian noise for \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\); the noise must hide a shift as large as the bound, not the actual shift.



What does the noise cost? Near the minimizer the objective is a bowl whose curvature is the Hessian \(H\), so a random displacement \(Z\) raises it by about \(\frac12 Z^\top HZ\), and for Gaussian noise that averages to \[\mathbb E\big[J(\tilde w) - J(w^*)\big] \approx \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\operatorname{tr}H. \tag{36.2}\] Notice the mismatch: the noise is calibrated to the curvature the ridge guarantees, \(\lambda\), but the damage is weighed by the actual curvature \(H\), data included. A small ridge buys a better non-private fit and costs a lot of noise, since \(\sigma \propto 1/\lambda\). In the running example at \(n = 10{,}000\), the sensitivity is \(2/(0.01 \times 10{,}000) = 0.02\), so \(\sigma = 0.07461\) per coordinate, next to a minimizer of length 2.886. The Hessian has trace 0.3129, and Equation 36.2 predicts an excess risk of \(8.711 \times 10^{-4}\); 20 simulated releases average \(9.274 \times 10^{-4}\). Because the noise falls like \(1/n\), the excess risk falls like \(1/n^2\), faster than the \(1/n\) statistical error of the non-private model, so in this convex, low-dimensional setting privacy eventually costs less than sampling does.
The weak point is that the sensitivity bound holds for the exact minimizer. If the optimizer stops at a point whose gradient has length \(g\), each output may sit \(g/\lambda\) from its exact minimizer, and the sensitivity becomes \(2L/(\lambda n) + 2g/\lambda\). In the running example a tolerance of \(g = 10^{-3}\), which looks tight, gives a sensitivity of 0.22 instead of 0.02: eleven times the noise and roughly 121 times the excess risk. To keep the extra term small you need \(g\) well below \(L/n\), which shrinks with the dataset. And the stopping rule must be a gradient check, not a step count: the privacy proof needs the bound on every pair of datasets, and “50 Newton steps” only guarantees it on datasets where 50 steps happen to be enough.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.3 Objective perturbation
Output perturbation wastes the data’s curvature: it pays for the worst case \(\lambda\) and is judged on the actual \(H\). Chaudhuri, Monteleoni & Sarwate (2011) put the noise inside the optimization instead. They add a random linear term \(\frac1n\langle b, w\rangle\) to the objective and minimize exactly. A linear term acts like a constant force pushing the minimizer, and all of the objective’s curvature resists it, so where the data add curvature the minimizer moves less.
The privacy argument is subtler, because the output is no longer “something fixed plus noise”, and its result says where the budget goes. Each noise vector \(b\) produces exactly one output, so the output’s density is the noise density at the matching \(b\) times a stretching factor from the change of variables. Both factors differ between neighbours, and each consumes part of \(\varepsilon\). The stretching factor is governed by how much one record can change the objective’s curvature, which needs a loss of the form \(g(y\langle w, x\rangle)\) with \(|g'| \le 1\), curvature \(0 \le g'' \le c\) and \(\|x\| \le 1\); logistic regression qualifies with \(c = \frac14\). What is left for the noise is \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon - 2\ln\Big(1 + \frac{c}{n\lambda}\Big), \tag{36.3}\] and \(b\) is drawn with density proportional to \(e^{-\varepsilon'\|b\|/2}\). The result is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The stretching share shrinks as \(n\lambda\) grows: at \(n = 10{,}000\) in the running example it is 0.0050, so \(\varepsilon' = 0.9950\), while at \(n = 100\) the noise would get only \(\varepsilon' = 0.5537\). If \(\varepsilon'\) comes out non-positive, the method raises the ridge until the stretching takes only half the budget.
The benefit shows in the excess risk. To first order the minimizer moves by \(-H^{-1}b/n\), so the damage is weighed by \(H^{-1}\) rather than \(H\). If every eigenvalue of \(H\) is close to some \(h\), objective perturbation beats output perturbation by about \((h/\lambda)^2\). When the ridge supplies all the curvature the two are the same; when the data add curvature, objective perturbation wins quadratically. In the running example the curvature lies between 0.0263 and 0.0330, about three times the ridge, and the measured excess risk at \(n = 10{,}000\) is \(8.156 \times 10^{-5}\), against \(8.321 \times 10^{-4}\) for pure-DP output perturbation at the same \(\varepsilon\): ten times better, close to the \(3^2 = 9\) the rule of thumb predicts.
The analysis is safe, not tight. In one dimension the output densities can be computed exactly, and over 500 random datasets of 5 records with \(\lambda = 0.1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), the largest log ratio is 0.3779 (Figure 36.2). The noise part never exceeds 0.0992 of its budget of 0.1891, and the stretching part never exceeds 0.3395 of its budget of 0.8109, because the worst cases each factor assumes cannot happen together for logistic loss. The bound has to cover every dataset, so you cannot spend that slack, but for logistic loss the guarantee is conservative.






Figure 36.2: Objective perturbation in one dimension, \(n = 5\), \(\lambda = 0.1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\). Left: the exact densities of the released weight under a dataset and its neighbour, computed by change of variables. Right: their log ratio, the privacy loss, which stays well inside \(\pm\varepsilon\).



The price is in the requirements: exact minimization (the change of variables needs a unique minimizer), a twice-differentiable loss (a support vector machine’s hinge loss must be smoothed first) and a known curvature bound. Kifer, Smith & Thakurta (2012) extend it to Gaussian noise and constraints, and Iyengar et al. (2019) give a version that tolerates approximate solvers by adding a little output noise on top.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.4 Gradient perturbation: noisy gradient descent
Real training is iterative and stops early. Gradient perturbation, analysed by Song, Chaudhuri & Sarwate (2013) and Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014), makes each step of the optimizer private and composes the steps. Its simplest form is full-batch gradient descent with Gaussian noise added to the mean gradient at each of \(T\) steps.
Each step is a Gaussian mechanism. Given the current weights, which are public at that moment because they were computed from earlier noisy outputs, replacing one record moves the mean gradient by at most \(2L/n\), whatever the weights are. Gaussian steps compose exactly: \(T\) steps, each with ratio \(\mu_{\text{step}}\), are as private as one Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(\sqrt T\,\mu_{\text{step}}\) (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy). Setting that equal to \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) gives the noise on the mean gradient, \[\sigma = \frac{2L}{n}\cdot\frac{\sqrt T}{\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}. \tag{36.4}\] Releasing every iterate is covered. Nothing in this argument used convexity, a minimizer or smoothness: only the gradient bound at the points the algorithm visits.
The consequence for practice is that the step count is a privacy parameter. Every step spends budget, so the per-step noise grows like \(\sqrt T\). For a strongly convex objective, the excess risk is an optimization error that shrinks geometrically with \(T\) plus a noise floor, roughly \(d\sigma^2/(4\beta)\) for a step size \(1/\beta\) set by the largest curvature \(\beta\), that grows in proportion to \(T\). Too few steps leave optimization error; too many drown the solution in noise (Figure 36.3).






Figure 36.3: Excess risk of noisy gradient descent at \(n = 10{,}000\), \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (1, 10^{-5})\), against the number of steps \(T\), averaged over datasets, with the same steps without noise (dashed). The noiseless error falls geometrically and reaches machine precision; the noisy run is limited by noise that grows with \(T\), so its error is smallest near \(T = 50\).



You cannot pick \(T\) by trying several and keeping the best validation score for free: that choice is itself a computation on the data (Hyperparameter tuning). One honest option is a rule that uses only public quantities, the ridge, a curvature bound, the dimension, \(n\) and the budget, and minimizes the predicted excess risk. For \(n = 10{,}000\) it picks \(T = 218\), with per-step noise \(\sigma = 0.01102\) and a predicted excess risk of \(1.301 \times 10^{-3}\); simulated runs average \(1.384 \times 10^{-3}\). The rule is pessimistic, because it only knows that the curvature is at least \(\lambda\). With the data’s actual curvature the best \(T\) is near 50, with \(2.875 \times 10^{-4}\), five times less, but you may only use that knowledge if you obtained it privately or from similar public data.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.5 Which to use
Each method is private by its own argument, so the choice is about accuracy. Theory says that for strongly convex problems the best achievable excess risk under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP falls like \[\frac{L^2\,d\,\ln(1/\delta)}{\lambda\,(n\varepsilon)^2}, \tag{36.5}\] up to logarithmic factors in \(n\) (Bassily, Smith & Thakurta 2014), and that a version of noisy gradient descent attains it; no method can do better, by the fingerprinting lower bounds of Lower bounds. Two practical readings follow. The cost grows with the dimension \(d\), so more parameters cost more privacy. And \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\) appear only as the product \(n\varepsilon\), because every sensitivity is proportional to \(1/n\) and every noise to sensitivity over \(\varepsilon\): to keep the same accuracy at half the budget, you need twice the data.
All methods share the rate; the constants differ, and the constant is what you choose by. Table 36.1 measures them on the running example.

The first three columns fall like \(1/n^2\); noisy gradient descent falls slightly slower, because its step count grows with \(\ln n\). Objective perturbation is about ten times better than output perturbation throughout (Figure 36.4), and noisy gradient descent with the public step rule is the worst for \(n \ge 10{,}000\); tuned privately to \(T \approx 50\) it would sit between the two perturbation methods.






Figure 36.4: Excess risk of the four private releases against the dataset size on the running example, log-log, with a line of slope \(-2\). All fall like \(1/n^2\); objective perturbation is about ten times better than output perturbation throughout.



The pure-DP column is slightly better than the Gaussian one here only because \(d = 10\) is small. The pure-DP noise has a length that grows faster with the dimension than the Gaussian’s: at \(d = 10\) their mean squared lengths are \(110\,\Delta^2\) against \(139.2\,\Delta^2\), but at \(d = 100\) they are \(10{,}100\,\Delta^2\) against \(1{,}392\,\Delta^2\). Pure DP costs a factor that grows like \(d\), the price of \(\delta = 0\), which Lower bounds shows is unavoidable; in high dimension a small \(\delta\) is much cheaper.
Excess risk is a fine measure, but you care about predictions, and those are forgiving. On held-out data the non-private model has accuracy 0.747 at \(n = 1{,}000\); output perturbation drops it to 0.681, noisy gradient descent to 0.695 and objective perturbation only to 0.736. By \(n = 10{,}000\) all four are within 0.002 of the non-private 0.753. A low-dimensional convex model on ten thousand records can be made private almost for free.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
section: 36.6 When the model is not convex
text:
36.6 When the model is not convex
A neural network’s loss is not convex, and that breaks the first two methods outright. Without strong convexity the minimizer need not be unique or move continuously with the data. Take a one-dimensional loss with two wells near \(\pm1\), where the empirical minimizer sits in the well favoured by the majority label: with 501 labels of one kind and 500 of the other, changing one label flips the majority and moves the minimizer by 2.0010. No \(1/n\) appears, so output perturbation would need \(\sigma = 7.465\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), more than three times the distance between the wells, whatever the dataset size. Objective perturbation fails at its first step, since the map from noise to output is no longer invertible.
Gradient perturbation keeps its guarantee, because its argument only used the gradient bound at the visited points. What it loses is the accuracy guarantee: whether it learns anything becomes an empirical question. For a neural network there is no bound \(L\) either, since gradients can be arbitrarily long, but you can force one by clipping: rescale each record’s gradient to length at most \(C\) before averaging, as Beyond global sensitivity clips a value before averaging it. The mean of clipped gradients moves by at most \(2C/n\), and the privacy argument goes through with \(L = C\). Clipping has a cost of its own: the mean of clipped gradients is no longer the gradient of the objective, so the algorithm optimizes something slightly different.
Full-batch steps are also too slow for large datasets. Using a random minibatch at each step makes steps cheap and, by amplification by subsampling, more private, since each record is used only with a small probability. Clipping, noise, minibatches and a subsampled-Gaussian accountant together are DP-SGD.

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.7 Code
The calibrations of this chapter take a few lines: find the largest admissible Gaussian ratio by bisection on the exact \(\delta\), then size the noise for each method.
from math import erfc, exp, log, sqrt


def phi(x: float) -> float:
    """Standard normal cumulative distribution function."""
    return 0.5 * erfc(-x / sqrt(2))


def gaussian_delta(eps: float, mu: float) -> float:
    """Exact delta of a Gaussian mechanism with sensitivity-to-noise ratio mu."""
    return phi(mu / 2 - eps / mu) - exp(eps) * phi(-mu / 2 - eps / mu)


def gaussian_mu(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Largest ratio mu for which the Gaussian mechanism is (eps, delta)-DP."""
    lo, hi = 1e-6, 50.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (lo, mid) if gaussian_delta(eps, mid) > delta else (mid, hi)
    return lo


mu = gaussian_mu(1.0, 1e-5)
print(f"{mu:.4f} {1 / mu:.4f}")  # 0.2681 3.7306
print(f"{sqrt(2 * log(1.25 / 1e-5)):.4f}")  # 4.8448
# Output perturbation: sensitivity 2L/(lambda n), L = 1, lambda = 0.01, n = 10,000.
print(f"{2 / (0.01 * 10_000) / mu:.5f}")  # 0.07461
# Objective perturbation: the share of eps left for the noise, c = 1/4.
print(f"{1 - 2 * log(1 + 0.25 / (10_000 * 0.01)):.4f}")  # 0.9950
# Noisy gradient descent: noise on the mean gradient for T = 218 steps.
print(f"{2 / 10_000 * sqrt(218) / mu:.5f}")  # 0.01102
The full edition’s script implements the three methods for logistic regression with exact Newton solves, computes the exact one-dimensional densities of objective perturbation, and runs the comparison:

title: 36  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
36.9 Further reading

Chaudhuri, Monteleoni & Sarwate, “Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization” (JMLR 2011): output and objective perturbation with their excess-risk bounds.
Bassily, Smith & Thakurta, “Private Empirical Risk Minimization: Efficient Algorithms and Tight Error Bounds” (FOCS 2014): noisy gradient methods that attain the optimal rates, and the matching lower bounds.
Iyengar, Near, Song, Thakkar, Thakurta & Wang, “Towards Practical Differentially Private Convex Optimization” (IEEE S&P 2019): objective perturbation that tolerates inexact solvers, and a benchmark of the three methods.

Derivations. Every result in this chapter is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 37  DP-SGD
text:
37.1 Why this matters
Private empirical risk minimization ended with one method left standing for non-convex models: gradient descent with Gaussian noise on every step, made safe for any model by clipping each record’s gradient. Two more changes make it practical for differential privacy (DP) at scale. Each step uses a random minibatch, which makes steps cheap and, by amplification, more private. And an accountant composes thousands of such steps into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). The result is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD (Abadi et al. 2016), which nearly every private deep-learning system runs. Privacy accounting computed its \(\varepsilon\) without running it; this chapter runs it, and asks what the noise and the clipping cost and how to set the knobs that control them.
The one idea is that the privacy analysis never looks inside the model. Each step releases a noisy sum of clipped per-example gradients. Clipping caps each record’s contribution at length \(C\), so adding or removing one record moves the sum by at most \(C\), whatever the network, the loss or the current weights, and the proof stops there. That splits the knobs in two. The noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the sampling rate \(q\) and the number of steps \(T\) set \(\varepsilon\), and nothing else does. The clipping norm \(C\) and the step size \(\eta\) do not change \(\varepsilon\) at all; they decide how much of the gradient survives and how far the noise pushes the weights. The cost of privacy then comes in two forms: a bias from clipping, which changes the direction of the average gradient, and a variance from the noise.
The running example is a network with one hidden layer of 64 units, \(p = 3{,}329\) weights, trained on \(n = 10{,}000\) synthetic records and tested on 20,000 more, with \(q = 0.01\) (expected batch \(B = 100\)), \(C = 0.5\), \(\eta = 0.5\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps: Part 4’s running example, now actually trained.

title: 37  DP-SGD
section: 37.2 The algorithm and what its guarantee assumes
text:
37.2 The algorithm and what its guarantee assumes
Each step of DP-SGD does five things, and each is an assumption of the proof:

Sample: put each record in the batch independently with probability \(q\) (Poisson sampling).
Per-example gradients: compute each sampled record’s gradient \(g_i\) separately.
Clip: rescale each to length at most \(C\), \(\bar g_i = g_i\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\).
Noisy sum: add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to each coordinate of \(\sum_i\bar g_i\).
Step: divide by the expected batch size \(B = qn\), a public constant, and take a gradient step.

Why is this private? With the weights and the other records fixed, the record in question adds at most one term of length \(C\) to the sum, so a step on which it is drawn is a Gaussian mechanism with shift \(C\) and noise \(\sigma C\), so its ratio of shift to noise is \(1/\sigma\); the clipping norm cancels. Under Poisson sampling it is drawn with probability \(q\) independently of everyone else, so its effect on a step is a mixture of “shifted” and “not there”, which is the subsampled Gaussian of Amplification by subsampling. Dividing by a public \(B\) is post-processing. The steps depend on earlier outputs only through the weights, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curves add even for such adaptive sequences (Rényi DP), so the accountant adds the \(T\) per-step curves and converts once (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ)). Neighbours differ by adding or removing a record, which is the relation Poisson sampling pairs with. For the running example the accountant gives \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), attained at order \(\alpha = 4.1\), and Table 37.1 gives the noise multiplier other budgets need with the same \(q\) and \(T\).

Because the proof rests on these steps, an implementation can break the guarantee by changing a detail, with no visible symptom. Batch normalization computes statistics over the batch, so one record changes every other record’s gradient and the sum can move by much more than \(C\); private models use normalizations that act on one example at a time, such as group or layer normalization. Choosing \(C\) from the current batch, say as its median gradient norm, makes the noise scale depend on the data; fix \(C\) in advance, from public data or a private estimate. Shuffling the data and cutting it into fixed batches is a different mechanism, which can be much less private than the Poisson accountant reports. Dividing by the actual batch size \(|S_t|\) reveals how many records were drawn, which changes when one is added, so it is not post-processing; divide by \(B\). The accountant must see every step, including the steps of runs discarded during tuning (Hyperparameter tuning). And the guarantee is per record: a person with many records needs user-level privacy, and preprocessing that uses the data, such as normalizing features by their mean, must itself be private or use public statistics.
How large is the noise in practice? The averaged update carries noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C/B = 1 \times 0.5/100 = 0.005\) per coordinate. A Gaussian vector of \(p\) such coordinates has length close to \(0.005\sqrt p\), which is about 0.288 for 3,329 weights. The averaged clipped gradient is 0.070 long at the first step and between 0.015 and 0.027 from step 1,000 on, so every step’s noise is about ten times longer than its signal. Training works anyway because the signal points in roughly the same direction from step to step while the noise is independent: over \(k\) steps the signals add to about \(k\) times their length and the noise to about \(\sqrt k\) times, since independent vectors add in squares. Signal overtakes noise when \(k \cdot 0.026 > \sqrt k \cdot 0.288\), after about 123 steps. The final model reaches test accuracy 0.9589, against 0.9627 for non-private SGD.

title: 37  DP-SGD
section: 37.3 Clipping: bias, noise and the choice of C
text:
37.3 Clipping: bias, noise and the choice of C
The clipping norm does not affect privacy, but it controls both forms of cost. Averaged over the sampling and the noise, the update direction is \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big)g_i, \tag{37.1}\] the average gradient with each record weighted by \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\). Each record is in the batch with probability \(q\) and the noise has mean zero, so dividing the noisy sum by \(B = qn\) cancels the \(q\) exactly; that is why the denominator is the expected batch size. The weights are where the bias lives. Records the model fits badly, such as rare examples, members of small groups or mislabelled points, have large gradients and are down-weighted, while well-fitted records keep their full weight. So DP-SGD follows the gradient of a reweighted loss whose weights change during training, and Disparate impact measures who pays for this.
Two regimes follow from the formula. When \(C\) is below every per-example gradient norm, every gradient is clipped to exactly length \(C\), so the clipped sum is \(C\) times a sum of unit vectors, and the noise is \(C\) times \(\sigma\) times a standard normal vector. The whole update is then \(\eta C/B\) times something that does not depend on \(C\): DP-SGD becomes normalized SGD plus noise, and depends on \(\eta\) and \(C\) only through their product \(\eta C\). Lowering \(C\) further changes nothing once \(\eta\) is scaled up to match, which is why practitioners often clip aggressively and tune only the step size (De et al. 2022 report that small clipping norms work well). When \(C\) is above most gradient norms, the clipped average stops growing with \(C\) but the noise \(\sigma C/B\) keeps growing, so the signal-to-noise ratio falls like \(1/C\). A large \(C\) is never better than the smallest \(C\) that clips almost nothing.
Table 37.2 shows both regimes on the running example at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\), once with \(\eta\) fixed and once with \(\eta C\) fixed at 0.25.

title: 37  DP-SGD
section: 37.4 Batch size at a fixed budget
text:
37.4 Batch size at a fixed budget
Suppose the budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) and the number of epochs \(E\) are fixed. Each epoch is \(1/q\) steps, so should you take many small steps or few large ones? Recall from Amplification by subsampling that for small \(q\) a step’s RDP is about \(\frac\alpha2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), close to \(\alpha q^2/(2\sigma^2)\) when \(\sigma\) is well above 1. Over \(E/q\) steps that adds up to about \(\alpha Eq/(2\sigma^2)\), so \(\varepsilon\) stays fixed when \(q/\sigma^2\) does: the noise multiplier must grow like \(\sqrt q\). The noise on the averaged gradient, \(\sigma C/B\) with \(B = qn\), then falls like \(1/\sqrt B\). Larger batches give cleaner gradients.
Small batches are worse than that law says. They need small \(\sigma\), and when \(\sigma\) is near or below 1, \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\) is much larger than \(1/\sigma^2\), so each step costs more than the approximation assumes, by the factor \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\). Steps with little noise are expensive per unit of signal because sampling buys little in the tail of the privacy loss. In training runs of the example, the best of three step sizes goes from 0.25 at \(B = 30\) to between 1 and 2 from \(B = 100\) to \(B = 1{,}000\), and at their best step sizes the batch sizes tried reach between 0.9544 and 0.9591, with the two largest doing best. (Picking the best step size by test accuracy is itself a leak; it is done here only to compare batch sizes.) De et al. (2022) and Anil et al. (2022) train with batches of thousands to hundreds of thousands and report that large batches are a main ingredient of accurate private models. They also parallelize well.

title: 37  DP-SGD
section: 37.5 Per-example gradient norms without per-example gradients
text:
37.5 Per-example gradient norms without per-example gradients
Ordinary backpropagation computes the gradient of the batch’s summed loss, never each record’s. Forming all \(B\) per-example gradients costs \(B\) times the model’s gradient memory, which is prohibitive for large models. Ghost clipping avoids it for dense layers. A dense layer’s gradient for one record is an outer product \(\delta_ia_i^\top\) of the error flowing back into the layer and the layer’s input, and the length of an outer product is the product of the lengths, \(\|\delta_i\|\,\|a_i\|\). So one backward pass gives every record’s gradient norm, layer by layer, without forming any gradient; the clipped sum then comes from rescaling each record’s error by its clipping factor and doing the usual batch product. For a sequence of \(T\) tokens, the squared norm is a sum over pairs of tokens of input dot products times error dot products, which costs two \(T \times T\) Gram matrices per record. That beats forming the gradient only when \(2T^2 < p_{\text{in}}p_{\text{out}}\), so long sequences in narrow layers favour explicit gradients, and Bu, Mao & Xu (2022) choose per layer.

title: 37  DP-SGD
text:
37.7 Code
Before a long run, check how the noise compares with the signal. This snippet computes the noise on the averaged gradient and the number of steps after which a steady signal overtakes it, for the running example at \(\sigma = 1\) and at \(\sigma = 4.13\) (\(\varepsilon = 1\)), using the signal length of about 0.026 measured in the run:
from math import sqrt


def noise_length(sigma: float, clip: float, batch: float, params: int) -> float:
    """Approximate length of the noise on the averaged clipped gradient."""
    return sigma * clip / batch * sqrt(params)


def break_even_steps(noise: float, signal: float) -> float:
    """Steps after which a steady signal (adds like k) overtakes independent noise (adds like sqrt k)."""
    return (noise / signal) ** 2


print(f"{1.0 * 0.5 / 100:.3f}")  # 0.005
print(f"{noise_length(1.0, 0.5, 100, 3329):.3f}")  # 0.288
print(f"{break_even_steps(0.288, 0.026):.0f}")  # 123
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, 3329):.2f}")  # 1.19
print(f"{break_even_steps(1.19, 0.026):.0f}")  # 2095
