title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, run once with a fixed step size, clipping norm, batch size and number of steps, satisfies differential privacy (DP) with the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) its accountant reports; this is DP-SGD, and its guarantee covers one training run. Nobody trains once. You try a grid of step sizes, score each model on a validation set and ship the best, and every run and every score touched private data. How much does the search leak, and how do you pay for it honestly?
Releasing the best of \(k\) private runs can cost as much as releasing all \(k\), and composition, which charges for every run, turns a grid of 10 DP-SGD runs of this part’s running example from \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) into 27.23. But one change to the procedure changes the answer: draw the number of runs at random, from a suitable distribution, before the search starts. Then the best-of release costs a constant multiple of one run plus a term that grows only with the logarithm of the expected number of runs. For 10 runs in expectation, the cost falls from 27.23 to between 10.08 and 13.67, depending on the distribution, and for 1,000 runs from 1,035.93 to 13.46.
The one idea: the model you ship depends on every run, and a fixed number of runs lets an attacker test for the event “every run came out badly”, whose likelihood ratio is the product of the per-run ratios. A random number of runs explains that event mostly by “there happened to be few runs”, which does not depend on the data.
crumbs: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 38.2 The best of k runs costs k runs
text:
38.2 The best of k runs costs k runs
A choice among eight step sizes carries at most three bits, so why charge for it? Because the released model is not just the choice: it is a whole private run, picked because of how it came out. The worst case is easy to build. Let one run be randomized response on two outcomes, “good” and “bad”: on a dataset \(D\) it comes out good with probability \(1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), on its neighbour \(D'\) with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), so one run is exactly \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The best of \(k\) runs is bad only if every run is bad. The runs are independent, so the probability of that event is a product of \(k\) per-run probabilities on each dataset, and its likelihood ratio is the product of \(k\) ratios of \(e^\varepsilon\) each: \[\frac{P_D[\text{best of } k \text{ is bad}]}{P_{D'}[\text{best of } k \text{ is bad}]} = e^{k\varepsilon}. \tag{38.1}\] Here the best of \(k\) is exactly \(k\varepsilon\)-DP, no better than releasing all \(k\) runs. With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(k = 10\), the whole loss sits on one rare event: the privacy loss is \(-0.0446\) with probability 0.9564 and 10 with probability 0.0436 (Figure 38.1, right). An attacker who checks whether the released model is bad gets a likelihood ratio of \(e^{10}\) whenever the test fires.






Figure 38.1: Left: the exact \(\varepsilon\) of releasing the best of \(K\) randomized-response runs, each \(1\)-DP, against the expected number of runs, for a fixed number of runs, a Poisson, a geometric and a logarithmic number. A fixed number grows linearly; the geometric and logarithmic numbers stay below their bounds \(3\varepsilon\) and \(2\varepsilon\). Right: the privacy loss of the released outcome under \(D\) for one run, the best of 10 runs and the best of a Poisson number with mean 10; the best of 10 puts a loss of 10 on an event of probability 0.0436.



This is not a contrived corner: a DP-SGD run that sometimes diverges is a run with a “bad” outcome whose probability depends a little on the data, and best-of-\(k\) multiplies those small dependences. A particular search may leak much less, but no analysis that knows only each run’s guarantee can promise it, so a cheaper guarantee needs a different procedure.
Tuning without noise and then training once privately does not help: the winning hyperparameters are a non-private function of the data, which the final run’s \(\varepsilon\) does not cover. Papernot & Steinke (2022) build a model whose best regularization weight alone reveals whether a few outliers were in the training set.
The safe baseline is composition: charge every run. For DP-SGD this is simple, because the accountant charges each step the same whatever weights it is applied to, so \(k\) runs of \(T\) steps cost exactly one run of \(kT\) steps. Table 38.1 applies it to the running example (\(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), 10,000 steps, one run at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)).

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.3 Random stopping
Liu & Talwar (2019) found the change that breaks the \(k\varepsilon\) barrier. After each run, flip a coin and stop with probability \(\gamma\); then release the best run seen. The number of runs is geometric with mean \(1/\gamma\), and if each run is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, the release is \(3\varepsilon\)-DP whatever \(\gamma\) is.
Why a constant, and why 3? Write \(p\) for the probability that one run produces outcome \(y\), \(p_>\) for the probability that it produces something strictly better, and \(p_\ge = p_> + p\). Averaging the best-of-\(k\) probabilities over the geometric number of runs gives \[P[\text{release} = y] = \frac{\gamma\,p}{\big(\gamma + (1 - \gamma)p_>\big)\big(\gamma + (1 - \gamma)p_\ge\big)}. \tag{38.2}\] Each of \(p\), \(p_>\) and \(p_\ge\) is the probability of an event about one run, so each moves by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) between neighbours. The constant \(\gamma\), which does not depend on the data, cannot amplify those moves. Three factors, each moving by at most \(e^\varepsilon\): the ratio is at most \(e^{3\varepsilon}\). Compare the fixed-\(k\) case, where the ratio was a \(k\)-th power. The event “every run was bad” is now mostly the event “the coin stopped early”.
The 3 can be approached: on a three-outcome mechanism that is exactly 1-DP, the release reaches 2.9987. With two outcomes, as in randomized response, nothing is better than the best outcome, so only two factors move: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the exact value rises from 1.7957 at \(\gamma = 0.1\) to 1.9977 at \(\gamma = 0.001\) (Figure 38.1, left).
The price is paid in runs. The release misses the top fraction \(\pi\) of a single run’s outcomes with probability at most \(\gamma/\pi\). With a grid of 8 and \(\gamma = 1/8\), a mean of 8 runs, the chance of never trying the best eighth is 0.4667; it takes \(\gamma = 1/80\), a mean of 80 runs, to bring it to 0.0805. The geometric distribution is spread out, stopping after one run with probability 1/8 at \(\gamma = 1/8\), and that spread is what buys the privacy.
crumbs: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.4 Rényi bounds for DP-SGD
DP-SGD is not usefully \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any small \(\varepsilon\). Its guarantee is a curve in Rényi differential privacy (RDP): a bound \(\varepsilon(\lambda)\) on the Rényi divergence of order \(\lambda\) between its outputs on neighbours, where curves add under composition and are converted to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the best order (Rényi differential privacy). Papernot & Steinke (2022) extended random stopping to RDP and to a family of distributions for the number of runs \(K\), the truncated negative binomial with a shape parameter \(\eta > -1\). The geometric distribution is \(\eta = 1\); \(\eta = 0\) is the logarithmic distribution. For a run with RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\lambda)\), the best of \(K\) runs has curve at most \[\varepsilon(\lambda) + (1 + \eta)\Big(1 - \frac1{\hat\lambda}\Big)\varepsilon(\hat\lambda) + \frac{(1 + \eta)\ln(1/\gamma)}{\hat\lambda} + \frac{\ln\mathbb E[K]}{\lambda - 1}, \tag{38.3}\] for any second order \(\hat\lambda \ge 1\) you choose, where \(\gamma\) is the distribution’s other parameter, set by the mean.
Each term pays for something. The first is one run, the floor, since the release is a run. The last is the number of runs, and it is logarithmic: ten times more runs adds \(\ln 10/(\lambda - 1)\). The middle terms pay for the tail of \(K\), how well an attacker can tell “many runs, all bad” from “few runs”, as a constant multiple of the run’s own privacy at another order. For a pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP run the bound becomes \((2 + \eta)\varepsilon\): \(3\varepsilon\) for the geometric, as before, and \(2\varepsilon\) for the logarithmic.
For a Poisson number of runs with mean \(\mu\), the bound is \[\varepsilon(\lambda) + \mu\hat\delta + \frac{\ln\mu}{\lambda - 1}, \tag{38.4}\] where the run must be \((\hat\varepsilon, \hat\delta)\)-DP with \(e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le 1 + 1/(\lambda - 1)\). The tail term \(\mu\hat\delta\) is linear in \(\mu\), but it is multiplied by the run’s \(\hat\delta\) at a small \(\hat\varepsilon\), so it is small only when one run is very private.
On the running example (Table 38.2, Figure 38.2), the logarithmic distribution costs 10.08 for 10 runs in expectation, 1.5 times one run, and going to 1,000 runs adds only 3.38. The Poisson bound starts well but grows nearly linearly, because one run at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) is far from private enough at the small \(\hat\varepsilon\) the condition demands.

And the score that ranks the runs must itself be part of each run’s private output.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 38.5 The validation score, and selecting among fixed candidates
text:
38.5 The validation score, and selecting among fixed candidates
That last condition is easy to miss: ranked by an exact validation accuracy, the validation records are not protected at all. Score each run instead by its count of correct predictions on a held-out validation set, plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma_{\text{val}}\). The count is the right score because adding or removing one validation record changes it by at most 1, while an accuracy divides by the number of records, itself private. The noisy count is a Gaussian mechanism with RDP curve \(\lambda/(2\sigma_{\text{val}}^2)\).
It also need not add to the cost. Each record sits in exactly one of the training and validation sets, and a pair of neighbours differs in one record, so the procedure’s cost is the larger of the cost in training records and the cost in validation records, not their sum, and the scores add nothing as long as their cost stays below the training cost. With \(\sigma_{\text{val}} = 20\) correct predictions, one noisy count alone has \(\varepsilon = 0.182\) and eight composed \(0.546\). In the experiment below, eight DP-SGD runs at \(\sigma = 2.07\) cost 1.994 together, and adding the eight noisy counts leaves the total at 1.994, because the counts’ curve stays below the training curve at the orders that matter.
When the candidates do not depend on the private training data, such as public pretrained checkpoints, only the choice is private. That is a pure selection problem, and the exponential mechanism of Selection solves it: pick candidate \(r\) with probability proportional to \(e^{\varepsilon u(r)/2}\), where \(u(r)\) is its count of correct predictions. It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and its expected shortfall from the best count among \(k\) candidates is at most \(2(\ln k + 1)/\varepsilon\) correct predictions, logarithmic in \(k\) with no linear privacy cost. Table 38.3 runs it on eight trained models whose counts out of 5,000 range from 4,123 to 4,694, the best beating the second by 13.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 38.7 What to do and what to report
text:
38.7 What to do and what to report
The cheapest fix is upstream. In Table 38.4, the two strategies that spend the whole budget on one private run beat every honest search. That will not always hold, since a poor guess can be far worse than a noisy search, but it says where to start: get hyperparameters from public data, proxy data or similar tasks, and shrink what is left. Below the typical gradient norm only the product of step size and clipping norm matters (DP-SGD), so one of the two need not be searched.
Search the rest privately, and fix the search before touching the data: candidates, distribution of the number of runs, score, validation set. The random-\(K\) theorems are about a procedure, and an engineer who looks at the first results and decides to “try a few more” has changed it. Then account for the whole search: compose for a few candidates; for more, use random search with Equation 38.4 when each run is already very private and the search is moderate, or Equation 38.3 for many runs. Every run on the private data counts, including crashed runs, debugging runs and evaluations used for early stopping.
Finally, report two numbers: the \(\varepsilon\) of the released run, and the \(\varepsilon\) of the whole procedure with how it was computed. For the Poisson row of Table 38.4 a complete report reads: “DP-SGD with Poisson sampling rate 0.01, clipping norm 0.5, noise multiplier 1.53, 1,000 steps; one run satisfies \((0.98, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The step size was selected by random search over \(\{0.0625, 0.125, \dots, 8\}\) with a Poisson number of runs with mean 8, scored by correct predictions on a disjoint validation set of 5,000 records with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 20; the whole procedure satisfies \((1.99, 10^{-5})\)-DP by the Rényi bound of Papernot & Steinke (2022, Theorem 6), add/remove neighbours, record level.”
An audit will not catch a missing tuning charge: it tests the released model, not how it was chosen.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.8 Code
The best-of-\(K\) formula is one line once you have the generating function \(f(x) = \mathbb E[x^K]\) of the number of runs: the best of \(K\) runs is bad exactly when all runs are bad, with probability \(f(P[\text{bad}])\). This snippet computes the exact \(\varepsilon\) for randomized response with a fixed and a geometric number of runs:
from collections.abc import Callable
from math import exp, log


def best_of_rr_epsilon(eps: float, f: Callable[[float], float]) -> float:
    """Exact epsilon of releasing the best of K randomized-response runs, f(x) = E[x^K]."""
    bad_d = exp(eps) / (1 + exp(eps))  # one run comes out bad on D
    bad_d2 = 1 / (1 + exp(eps))  # ... and on its neighbour D'
    # The best is bad only if every run is bad: probability f(P[bad]).
    out_d = [f(bad_d), 1 - f(bad_d)]
    out_d2 = [f(bad_d2), 1 - f(bad_d2)]
    return max(abs(log(a / b)) for a, b in zip(out_d, out_d2))


def fixed(k: int) -> Callable[[float], float]:
    return lambda x: x**k


def geometric(gamma: float) -> Callable[[float], float]:
    """Stop after each run with probability gamma; the mean number of runs is 1/gamma."""
    return lambda x: gamma * x / (1 - (1 - gamma) * x)


print(f"{best_of_rr_epsilon(1.0, fixed(10)):.4f}")  # 10.0000
print(f"{best_of_rr_epsilon(1.0, geometric(0.1)):.4f}")  # 1.7957
print(f"{best_of_rr_epsilon(1.0, geometric(0.001)):.4f}")  # 1.9977
For DP-SGD, the full edition’s script, hyperparameter_tuning.py, has the bounds: tuned_epsilon(q, sigma, steps, strategy) gives the total \(\varepsilon\) of a search, with strategy one of ("fixed", k), ("poisson", mean) or ("tnb<η>", mean), and sigma_for_tuning(q, steps, eps, strategy) the noise multiplier for a budget. Running it reproduces every number in this chapter (two to four minutes):
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/hyperparameter_tuning.py

38.10 Further reading

Papernot & Steinke, “Hyperparameter Tuning with Renyi Differential Privacy” (ICLR 2022): the Poisson and truncated negative binomial bounds for DP-SGD, the lower bound for a fixed number of runs, and an experiment that recommends the Poisson distribution for small searches.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), the DP-SGD of this part, gets much of its privacy from Poisson sampling: each record enters a batch only with probability \(q\), and the accountant credits the run for the attacker’s uncertainty about whether the record was used at all (Amplification by subsampling). Many pipelines cannot honestly claim it: data loaders shuffle and cut fixed batches, streams arrive in order, and a federated server cannot choose which phones check in. The Poisson accountant can then understate \(\varepsilon\) considerably, and giving up amplification is expensive: on this part’s running example, for \(\varepsilon = 2\) over five passes through the data, the noise multiplier has to grow from 0.928 to 4.458, and test accuracy falls from 0.9460 to 0.8941.
How do you train privately without random batches, and can correlated noise beat independent noise? It can, by a lot. The first algorithm to show it ran the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) optimizer on noisy gradient sums released through a binary tree, and is called DP-FTRL. Its modern form, the matrix factorization mechanism, contains the tree as a special case, and on the running example it closes nearly all of the gap to amplified DP-SGD without any sampling.
The one idea: training releases running sums of gradients, so put the noise where the running sums need it. Noise added at one step may partly cancel the noise added before it; the price is that each record’s gradient then has to be hidden in several noisy quantities at once.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
section: 39.2 Training is a stream of prefix sums
text:
39.2 Training is a stream of prefix sums
Plain gradient descent, without momentum, adds up its steps. If \(x_t\) is the sum of the clipped gradients of the batch at step \(t\), each of length at most the clipping norm \(C\), and \(\hat x_t\) is its noisy version, then after \(t\) steps with step size \(\eta\) and batch size \(B\) \[w_{t+1} = w_0 - \frac\eta B\hat S_t, \qquad \hat S_t = \hat x_1 + \dots + \hat x_t. \tag{39.1}\] Every model along the way is a fixed function of the noisy prefix sums \(\hat S_t\), so releasing those privately makes every model private, and the noise in a model is the noise in its prefix sum. FTRL with a quadratic regularizer produces the same weights. All \(T\) prefix sums must be released, not just the last, because training is adaptive: the gradient at step \(t\) is computed at \(w_t\), which depends on the earlier sums.
Two mechanisms suggest themselves. Independent noise on each step, which is DP-SGD without amplification, hides a record’s single gradient with noise of the size of one gradient, but the noise in \(\hat S_t\) is a sum of \(t\) independent terms, a random walk whose standard deviation grows like \(\sqrt t\). Independent noise on each prefix sum keeps every error the same size, but a record at step 1 appears in all \(T\) sums, so the noise must be \(\sqrt T\) times larger to hide it, and every sum is as bad as the worst sum of the first mechanism. Neither uses the structure of the problem.
Take one epoch of the running example, \(T = 100\) steps, at \(\varepsilon = 2\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Independent noise needs a noise scale of 1.994 per step, in units of \(C\), so the final prefix sum carries noise of standard deviation 19.94. DP-SGD with Poisson sampling at \(q = 0.01\) and the same \(\varepsilon\) needs only \(\sigma = 0.827\), and its final prefix sum carries 8.27: amplification buys a factor of 2.4. The rest of the chapter shows that correlated noise can beat even that without sampling.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.3 The matrix mechanism
Releasing all prefix sums is a linear map, \(S = Ax\), where \(A\) is the \(T \times T\) lower-triangular matrix of ones and \(x\) stacks the \(x_t\) as rows. The matrix mechanism splits \(A\) into two factors, \(A = LR\), adds Gaussian noise \(z\) in the middle, and releases \[\hat S = L(Rx + z) = Ax + Lz, \tag{39.2}\] where \(z\) has independent entries with standard deviation \(sC\), and \(s\) is the noise scale, the analogue of DP-SGD’s noise multiplier. The encoder \(R\) decides what gets noised; the decoder \(L\) recovers the prefix sums from it.
Privacy lives in the columns of \(R\). A record that takes part in step \(\tau\) changes row \(\tau\) of \(x\) by a gradient \(g\) of length at most \(C\), which moves \(Rx\) by column \(\tau\) of \(R\) times \(g\). Recall that the privacy of a Gaussian mechanism depends only on one ratio, the sensitivity divided by the noise standard deviation, called \(\mu\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). So the mechanism has \[\mu = \frac{\operatorname{sens}(R)}{s}, \qquad \operatorname{sens}(R) = \max_j\|r_j\|, \tag{39.3}\] the length of the longest column \(r_j\). To meet an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) target, find the largest admissible ratio \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) from the exact Gaussian calibration, for example \(\mu(2, 10^{-5}) = 0.502\) and \(\mu(8, 10^{-5}) = 1.666\), and set \(s = \operatorname{sens}(R)/\mu\).
Error lives in the rows of \(L\). The error in \(\hat S_t\) is row \(t\) of \(L\), written \(\ell_t\), times the noise, a weighted sum of independent normals, so its standard deviation in each coordinate is \(sC\|\ell_t\|\). At a fixed privacy level that is \((C/\mu)\,e_t\), with \[e_t = \operatorname{sens}(R)\,\|\ell_t\| \tag{39.4}\] the error per unit of privacy. Multiplying \(R\) by 2 and dividing \(L\) by 2 changes nothing, so only the product matters, and the best factorization balances short columns against short rows. Independent noise on each step is \(R = I\), \(L = A\): columns of length 1, rows of length \(\sqrt t\). Noise on each prefix sum is \(R = A\), \(L = I\), the opposite extreme.
Does this survive adaptive training, where later gradients depend on earlier outputs? Yes, if both factors are lower-triangular (Denisov et al. 2022, Theorem 2.1). Then row \(j\) of \(Rx + z\) depends only on steps up to \(j\) and can be released at step \(j\). Before the record’s step the outputs have the same distribution on both datasets, and from then on the record shifts the remaining rows by column \(\tau\) times \(g\), so the accounting is the same as for inputs fixed in advance. A factor with entries above the diagonal would need noise or data from future steps.
When \(R\) is square and invertible, the mechanism is noisy SGD with correlated noise: it adds \(\zeta = R^{-1}z\) to the gradients, each step’s noise a fixed combination of the noise drawn so far. Neighbours here leave the record’s slot in the public data order empty; if they replace the record instead, every sensitivity doubles.
How good can a factorization be? No factorization can push the root-mean-square of \(e_t\) over a run below the trace norm of \(A\) (the sum of its singular values) divided by \(T\): 2.18 at \(T = 100\) and 3.63 at \(T = 10{,}000\). title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.4 Tree aggregation and DP-FTRL
The first mechanism with error far below \(\sqrt T\) was the binary tree, from the theory of private running counts (Dwork, Naor, Pitassi & Rothblum 2010; Chan, Shi & Song 2010). Build a tree over the steps: each leaf is one step, each node above covers a block of \(2, 4, 8, \dots\) consecutive steps. Release every node’s gradient sum with independent noise. Any prefix \(1, \dots, t\) is the union of one node for each 1 in the binary expansion of \(t\): \(7 = 4 + 2 + 1\) uses the nodes covering steps 1 to 4, 5 and 6, and 7. So a prefix sum collects at most \(\log_2 t + 1\) noise terms instead of \(t\). The price is that each step sits in one node per level, so its column in \(R\) has length \(\sqrt{L_T}\), with \(L_T = \lceil\log_2 T\rceil + 1\) levels, and the noise must be that much larger.
That trade is a large win for long runs: at \(T = 10{,}000\) the root-mean-square error is 9.84 against 70.71 for independent noise. But the error jumps around: the prefix \(127 = 1111111_2\) uses seven nodes and \(128\) uses one (Figure 39.2, left). And the encoder is wasteful: few prefixes use the top nodes, yet every step pays for being in them.
Kairouz et al. (2021) ran FTRL on prefix sums released by the tree, with momentum and periodic restarts, and called it DP-FTRL. They report that it compares favourably with amplified DP-SGD in their experiments while allowing much more flexible data access, and Xu et al. (2023) used it to train production keyboard language models in federated learning.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.5 The square-root factorization
A natural symmetric choice is \(L = R\), a lower-triangular matrix whose square is \(A\). It exists and has a closed form, because lower-triangular matrices that are constant along each diagonal multiply like power series in a variable \(x\), coefficient by coefficient. \(A\), all ones, is the series \(1 + x + x^2 + \dots = 1/(1 - x)\), so its square root is the series \((1 - x)^{-1/2}\), whose coefficients are \[r_k = \binom{2k}k4^{-k}: \qquad r = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac38, \tfrac5{16}, \tfrac{35}{128}, \dots, \tag{39.5}\] computed by \(r_0 = 1\), \(r_k = r_{k-1}(2k - 1)/(2k)\). The first column of \(R\) is the longest and the last row of \(L = R\) the longest, both with squared length \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2\), so that sum is both \(\operatorname{sens}(R)^2\) and the largest error per unit of privacy. It grows like \(\ln(T)/\pi\): logarithmic, like the tree’s error, but much smaller than the tree’s at both horizons of Table 39.1, and far below \(\sqrt T\). At \(T = 100\), \(\sum r_k^2 = 2.531\), so \(\operatorname{sens}(R) = 1.591\) and the final prefix sum’s error is 2.53, a quarter of independent noise’s 10.
Seen as noisy SGD, the noise added to step \(t\)’s gradient comes from \(R^{-1}\), the series \((1 - x)^{1/2} = 1 - \frac12x - \frac18x^2 - \frac1{16}x^3 - \dots\): \[\zeta_t = z_t - \tfrac12z_{t-1} - \tfrac18z_{t-2} - \tfrac1{16}z_{t-3} - \dots, \tag{39.6}\] fresh noise minus a decaying share of the noise already injected. Each step’s noise is slightly larger than independent noise, with standard deviation tending to \(\sqrt{4/\pi} = 1.128\) times the noise scale, but the negative coefficients pull the accumulated noise back towards zero, so the running sums no longer drift like a random walk (Figure 39.1).






Figure 39.1: Left: one coordinate of the noise added to each of the first 60 steps’ gradients, independent (identity factorization) and square-root correlated, both calibrated to \(\mu = 1\) for one participation. Right: the noise in the prefix sums over 1,000 steps, for independent noise, the binary tree and the square root, with bands of two standard deviations. Independent noise drifts like a random walk; the square root’s stays within a narrow band.



The square root is close to optimal: its root-mean-square error, 2.37 at \(T = 100\) and 3.84 at \(T = 10{,}000\), is within 9% and 6% of the lower bound. The best factorization, computed by a fixed-point iteration (Denisov et al. 2022), reaches 2.24 at \(T = 100\), but each iteration costs cubic time in \(T\), so the square root, free and nearly as good, is the usual default for long runs (Figure 39.2). The two even look alike (Figure 39.3).






Figure 39.2: Left: standard deviation of the error of each released prefix sum \(S_t\) for \(T = 256\), one participation, at \(\mu = 1\) and \(C = 1\), for five factorizations. Right: the root-mean-square error over a run against its length \(T\), with the trace-norm lower bound dotted; the optimal factorization is computed up to \(T = 256\).









Figure 39.3: The encoder \(R\) (top) and decoder \(L\) (bottom) of three factorizations of the \(16 \times 16\) prefix-sum matrix. The tree’s encoder has one row per node (31 rows), and its decoder picks the nodes of each prefix. The square root uses the same matrix for both; the optimal factorization’s encoder has columns of length exactly 1.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.6 Several participations
Training for \(E\) epochs puts a record’s gradient into \(E\) steps, each through a different column of \(R\), and the shifts add before the norm is taken. When all inner products between columns are nonnegative (as for any \(R\) with nonnegative entries: the identity, the tree, the square root), the worst case is the same gradient every time, and the sensitivity is the length of the sum of the record’s columns, maximized over the possible participation patterns.
For independent noise the columns are orthogonal, so \(E\) participations cost \(\sqrt E\), the usual composition of Gaussian mechanisms. For the square root, columns of nearby steps overlap and point in similar directions, so a record that appears again lands on top of its earlier contribution and the sensitivity grows faster than \(\sqrt E\). The tree is worse still: a node covering many steps holds several participations of the same record, and their contributions add inside it.
Banding fixes this. Keep only the first \(b\) diagonals of the square-root encoder, and make sure any two participations of a record are at least \(b\) steps apart (\(b\)-min-separation). Then the columns of different participations do not overlap at all, the cross terms vanish, and the sensitivity is back to at most \(\sqrt E\) times the longest column. The banded decoder, \(L = AR^{-1}\), is less accurate than the square root’s for a single participation, because the band no longer spreads the noise across the whole run, but with many participations the sensitivity saving dominates. Table 39.2 uses the running example’s order: 100 steps per epoch, each record exactly 100 steps apart, band \(b = 100\).

So the data order is part of the mechanism. A fixed permutation, drawn independently of the data and repeated every epoch, guarantees a separation of exactly \(n/B\) steps; reshuffling every epoch can put a record at the end of one epoch and the start of the next, one step apart, which breaks the banded bound. The order must be fixed in the analysis, but need not be random. Banded factorizations can also use amplification by sampling when it is available (Choquette-Choo et al. 2023).

Without amplification, correlated noise is essential. At \(\varepsilon = 2\), independent noise loses 2.8 points to DP-SGD after one epoch and 8.5 points after ten, and gets worse with more epochs, because its per-step noise grows like \(\sqrt E\) and then accumulates like a random walk. The tree recovers between a quarter and a half of the gap. The square root and the banded square root recover nearly all of it: at ten epochs the banded encoder reaches 0.9491, within 0.0002 of DP-SGD.
For short runs and large \(\varepsilon\), matrix mechanisms can beat amplified DP-SGD outright, because amplification gains little there. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) and one epoch, DP-SGD needs \(\sigma = 0.501\) and independent noise without sampling 0.600, barely more, while the square root’s final prefix sum carries 1.52 against DP-SGD’s 5.01, and it reaches 0.9461 against 0.9371. DP-SGD keeps its lead at small \(\varepsilon\) over many epochs, where amplification is strongest: at \(\varepsilon = 2\) its per-step noise grows only from 0.827 to 1.03 between one and ten epochs, while every fixed-order mechanism pays for ten participations. There the full square root falls behind, 0.9398 against 0.9493, because its overlapping columns make repeated participation expensive, and only banding keeps up. Across the table, the method with the least final-prefix noise is the most accurate, or within the run-to-run spread of the most accurate, in every row: that number is a good guide when choosing.






Figure 39.4: Test accuracy of the running example after 5 epochs (500 steps of batch 100) at step size 1, against \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), one run per point. DP-SGD uses Poisson sampling; the other four use a fixed data order and differ only in how their noise is correlated.



Three caveats. The RDP accountant overstates DP-SGD’s \(\varepsilon\) somewhat compared with a numerical accountant (Choosing an accountant), so a tighter one would lower its noise somewhat. The step size was picked per method by test accuracy, a leak that Hyperparameter tuning charges for; here it only compares methods at their best. And the runs are short, at most 1,000 steps; the noise gaps of Table 39.2 keep widening with epochs, so longer runs should separate the methods more, not less. Figure 39.4 shows the same pattern across budgets at five epochs.
This is what makes matrix mechanisms the tool for federated learning. The server cannot sample devices independently with a known rate, so the Poisson accountant does not apply, but it can enforce that a device contributes at most once every \(b\) rounds. With that min-separation, a banded mechanism has a provable guarantee, and on the running example’s scale it is as accurate as DP-SGD with sampling would be. That is why production federated training of language models uses DP-FTRL (Xu et al. 2023); the privacy unit there is a user, not an example, which User-level differential privacy treats.

title: 39  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
39.8 Code
A correlated-noise mechanism is a few lines on top of noisy SGD; what takes care is the sensitivity, which depends on the data order and must be computed for the order you actually use. This snippet computes the square root’s coefficients, its single-participation errors, the multi-epoch sensitivities of Table 39.2 and the resulting noise scale:
from math import ceil, erfc, exp, log2, sqrt


def sqrt_coeffs(t: int) -> list[float]:
    """r_k = C(2k, k)/4^k: the first column of the lower-triangular square root of A."""
    r = [1.0]
    for k in range(1, t):
        r.append(r[-1] * (2 * k - 1) / (2 * k))
    return r


def toeplitz_sensitivity(c: list[float], t: int, sep: int, epochs: int) -> float:
    """Length of the sum of the encoder columns a record touches, worst slot (entries of c >= 0)."""
    best = 0.0
    for offset in range(sep):
        steps = range(offset, t, sep)[:epochs]
        col = [sum(c[i - p] for p in steps if 0 <= i - p < len(c)) for i in range(t)]
        best = max(best, sqrt(sum(v * v for v in col)))
    return best


def tree_sensitivity(t: int, sep: int, epochs: int) -> float:
    """A record's contributions to one tree node add up before the norm is taken."""
    best = 0.0
    for offset in range(sep):
        steps = range(offset, t, sep)[:epochs]
        total = 0
        for level in range(ceil(log2(t)) + 1):
            counts: dict[int, int] = {}
            for p in steps:
                counts[p >> level] = counts.get(p >> level, 0) + 1
            total += sum(n * n for n in counts.values())
        best = max(best, sqrt(total))
    return best


def phi(x: float) -> float:
    return 0.5 * erfc(-x / sqrt(2))


def gaussian_mu(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Largest sensitivity-to-noise ratio for which a Gaussian mechanism is (eps, delta)-DP."""
    lo, hi = 1e-9, 100.0
    for _ in range(200):
        mu = (lo + hi) / 2
        if phi(mu / 2 - eps / mu) - exp(eps) * phi(-mu / 2 - eps / mu) > delta:
            hi = mu
        else:
            lo = mu
    return lo


T = 100
r = sqrt_coeffs(T)
sens = sqrt(sum(v * v for v in r))  # the first column is the longest
rows = [sqrt(sum(v * v for v in r[:t])) for t in range(1, T + 1)]  # row t of L = R
print(f"{sens:.3f} {sens * rows[-1]:.2f}")  # 1.591 2.53
print(f"{sens * sqrt(sum(x * x for x in rows) / T):.2f}")  # 2.37
print(f"{sqrt(sum(range(1, T + 1)) / T):.2f}")  # 7.11

E = 20  # epochs of 100 steps, each record exactly 100 steps apart
print(f"{toeplitz_sensitivity(sqrt_coeffs(T * E), T * E, T, E):.3f}")  # 17.191
print(f"{toeplitz_sensitivity(r, T * E, T, E):.3f}")  # 7.115
print(f"{tree_sensitivity(T * E, T, E):.3f}")  # 30.430
print(f"{toeplitz_sensitivity(r, T * 10, T, 10) / gaussian_mu(2.0, 1e-5):.3f}")  # 10.031
The banded encoder is the square root cut to its first 100 coefficients, which is why it reuses r; the last line is its noise scale for \(\varepsilon = 2\) over ten epochs, as in Table 39.3. The full edition’s script, matrix_mechanisms.py, builds every factorization, including the optimal one, and trains the running example with each:
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/matrix_mechanisms.py

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
40.1 Why this matters
Training with differential privacy (DP) by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped, noisy gradients, called DP-SGD (DP-SGD), makes the weights private, and after that every use of the model is free: answering a query is post-processing of the weights. But you pay during training, and you must own the training loop. Sometimes you cannot. The model may be a large language model (LLM) you can prompt but not train, a model without gradients such as a decision forest, or a tool that will answer a few dozen questions in its whole life, for which a private training run is overkill.
The alternative is to train ordinary models, never release them, and make each answer private instead. The idea that makes this work is one record, one vote. Split the private records into \(k\) disjoint shards and train one model, a teacher, on each. To answer a query, let every teacher vote for a label, add noise to the vote counts, and release only the winning label. A record lives in one shard, so it can change one teacher and so one vote, however that teacher was trained and however badly it overfits. That is the whole privacy argument. The accuracy argument is about the gap between the top two vote counts against the noise, and the noise must grow with the number of answers. Private prediction is therefore cheap for a few queries on which the teachers agree, and expensive otherwise. The method that turns those answers into a releasable model is private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE), due to Papernot et al. (2017).

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 40.2 The noisy vote and its cost
text:
40.2 The noisy vote and its cost
Fix the partition before looking at the data, by a hash of a record identifier rather than by position. Then adding or removing a record changes exactly one shard and one teacher, and that teacher’s vote can move from one label to another: one count goes down by 1 and another goes up by 1. The vote histogram moves by at most \(\sqrt2\) in Euclidean length. If shards were cut by position, inserting one record at the front would shift every later record into the next shard and could change every teacher; the guarantee would be gone.
Two mechanisms release the label. LNMax adds Laplace noise of scale \(b\) to each count and releases the index of the largest noisy count. It is report-noisy-max (Selection) on scores that one record moves by at most 1 each, in opposite directions, so each answer is \((2/b)\)-DP. GNMax adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) to each count instead. Adding the noise is the Gaussian mechanism on a vector of sensitivity \(\sqrt2\), and taking the argmax is post-processing, so in Rényi differential privacy (RDP), the accounting whose curves simply add under composition (Rényi DP), each answer costs \(\alpha/\sigma^2\) at order \(\alpha\) (Papernot et al. 2018). \(Q\) answers cost \(Q\alpha/\sigma^2\), even when each query is chosen after seeing the earlier answers. That curve is a line whose slope is \(Q/\sigma^2\), and a line converts to an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) that depends only on its slope. Call \(\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)\) the largest slope that still converts to your budget; then the noise you need is \[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{Q}{\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)}}. \tag{40.1}\] At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(\rho = 0.0306\) for \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(0.3731\) for \(\varepsilon = 4\).
Three consequences follow from this formula. First, the noise grows like \(\sqrt Q\): a hundred times more answers need ten times more noise. Second, neither \(k\) nor anything about the teachers appears in it. A teacher can be a network trained without noise, a decision forest or a human annotator who saw one shard; only the noise and the number of answers set the cost. The noise can be large in absolute terms because the counts are large: with 250 teachers, noise of standard deviation 40 is noticeable but not overwhelming. Third, release only the label. Publishing the noisy counts too would release a whole vector, and the data-dependent analysis below needs the label alone.

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 40.3 When a noisy vote is accurate
text:
40.3 When a noisy vote is accurate
On two labels, GNMax returns the plurality label when the noise difference between the two counts does not overturn the gap \(g\). The difference of two independent Gaussians of standard deviation \(\sigma\) is a Gaussian of standard deviation \(\sqrt2\sigma\), so the plurality wins with probability \(\Phi(g/(\sqrt2\sigma))\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. With more labels, the probability of losing to any competitor is at most the sum of the probabilities of losing to each, a union bound that is exact on two labels and loose when several labels are nearly tied with the winner.
The part’s running example makes this concrete: 50-dimensional Gaussian inputs labelled \(\pm1\) by a fixed random network, 10,000 private records, teachers that are regularized logistic regressions on one shard each. With \(k = 100\) teachers and the noise for 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 4\), \(\sigma = 51.8\), a query on which 98 teachers vote one way, a gap of 96, gets the plurality label with probability 0.9051. One split 70 to 30 gets it with probability 0.7076, and one split 52 to 48 with probability 0.5218, barely better than a coin (Figure 40.1).






Figure 40.1: Left three panels: the votes of 100 teachers on three public queries, with bars of one noise standard deviation (\(\sigma = 51.8\), the GNMax noise for 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 4\)); the title gives the probability that the noisy vote returns the plurality label. Right: across all 10,000 public queries, the fraction of the 100 teachers voting \(+1\).



How many teachers? More teachers multiply the gap by \(k\) while the noise stays fixed, but each teacher sees fewer records and agrees less with the others. On the running example the second effect is weaker than you might fear. Going from 25 teachers of 400 records to 500 teachers of 20, each teacher’s accuracy falls from 0.8954 to 0.6459, but the noiseless plurality vote hardly moves, staying between 0.9336 and 0.9403: a majority of many weak, nearly independent voters is right far more often than any one of them. The median gap grows in absolute terms, from 25 to 138, and since the noise does not depend on \(k\), more teachers win. With 100 answers at \(\varepsilon = 4\), 500 teachers answer with accuracy 0.9237, about a point below their noiseless vote. With 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 1\), even 500 teachers fall to 0.6987. Note the ceiling: noise can only pull answers towards a coin flip, so no private answer beats the noiseless vote, and on queries the teachers find hard any noise makes the answer close to random.

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 40.4 Private answers against a private model
text:
40.4 Private answers against a private model
You have one budget. Spend it on DP-SGD, and the model’s accuracy is fixed however many queries it answers. Spend it on answers, and accuracy starts near the noiseless ensemble and, on this task, falls towards a coin flip as \(Q\) grows, because \(\sigma\) grows like \(\sqrt Q\). A falling curve crosses a constant at most once, so there is a break-even number of queries \(Q^*\) below which private answers win.

On the running example (Table 40.2), at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), where DP-SGD reaches only 0.8164, 500 teachers answer up to 58 queries more accurately than the private model, and at \(\varepsilon = 1\) up to 18. From \(\varepsilon = 2\) on, DP-SGD beats even a single noiseless vote, because the ensemble’s ceiling is below DP-SGD’s 0.9438 (Figure 40.2). The pattern is general: private prediction wins at small budgets, where DP-SGD loses much, and for few queries. Two things the comparison leaves out cut the other way. If you cannot run DP-SGD at all, because the model is behind an interface or the data cannot be pooled, the comparison is with nothing. And private prediction runs \(k\) models on every query, while DP-SGD trains once.

section: 40.5 PATE: from answers to a model
text:
40.5 PATE: from answers to a model
Answers cost budget forever; a model costs it once. PATE spends the budget on labelling \(Q\) public, unlabelled inputs with GNMax, then trains a student on them and releases only the student. The student’s training reads public inputs and the \(Q\) noisy labels and nothing else, so it is post-processing: its weights and every prediction it ever makes cost exactly the \(Q\) answers, whatever its size, training algorithm or number of predictions. The student may choose which inputs to have labelled after seeing earlier labels, since the composition allows adaptive queries.
Three things limit the student: it learns from \(Q\) examples rather than \(n\), some of its labels are wrong, and the plurality vote has its ceiling. More labels mean more noise per label, so for each \(\varepsilon\) there is a best \(Q\). On the running example, with 250 teachers and the part’s network as student, the best student reaches 0.8238 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.8898 at \(\varepsilon = 4\), against 0.9128 and 0.9573 for DP-SGD, which wins at every budget. The best \(Q\) was chosen by looking at test accuracy, itself a leak that Hyperparameter tuning shows how to pay for. The reasons PATE loses here are the conditions under which it wins elsewhere: the task is binary, so a wrong label is as damaging as it can be; the teachers are weak and often disagree; the student needs thousands of labels; and DP-SGD does well even at \(\varepsilon = 1\). On a handwritten-digit benchmark (MNIST), where teachers agree on most inputs, Papernot et al. (2018) report a student with 98.5% accuracy against a non-private 99.2%, at \(\varepsilon = 1.97\) with 286 answered queries.
PATE needs public inputs from the same distribution as the private data, which are plentiful for images or text and absent for medical records, and they must really be public: an input that is someone else’s private record is protected by nothing. And the teachers are non-private models that must stay secret. An attacker who steals one can attack its shard directly, so PATE moves the trust from the training algorithm to the server that holds the teachers.

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 40.6 Paying less when the teachers agree
text:
40.6 Paying less when the teachers agree
The cost \(\alpha/\sigma^2\) is a worst case over vote histograms, including ties that one teacher decides. When 249 of 250 teachers agree, one record cannot realistically change the answer, and the data-dependent analysis of Papernot et al. charges such a query less: its cost is roughly proportional to the probability that the noise overturns the plurality. Figure 40.3 shows it for one answer with \(\sigma = 40\) at order 8. Up to a gap of about 100 the bound is no better than the data-independent 0.005; then it falls steeply, to \(1.23 \times 10^{-3}\) at a gap of 150. The bound is valid but not tight: the exact cost on two labels is five times lower at that gap.






Figure 40.3: The RDP cost at order 8 of one GNMax answer with \(\sigma = 40\), against the gap between the two vote counts, on a log scale: the data-independent \(\alpha/\sigma^2\), the data-dependent bound of Papernot et al. (2018), and the exact data-dependent cost on two labels.



The total saving depends on how many queries have large gaps. On the running example only 0.2879 of the public queries have a gap of at least 150 with 250 teachers, so 1,000 answers with \(\sigma = 40\) cost \(\varepsilon = 4.37\) instead of 5.38 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), about 20% less. On tasks where nearly every teacher agrees on nearly every input, almost every answer is nearly free. Confident-GNMax exploits this by design: it first checks, with a noisy maximum count of large noise \(\sigma_1\), whether the consensus clears a threshold, and answers with GNMax only if it does. The check costs a little on every query, the answer only on the confident ones, which are also the ones more likely to be right. The price is that the student never sees labels near the decision boundary. On the running example it answered 459 of 1,000 queries and trained a student to 0.8894 at a data-independent \(\varepsilon = 3.59\), about what plain GNMax reached at \(\varepsilon = 4\).
There is a trap. The data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) is computed from the votes, so it is itself private information, and its sensitivity is large: one record changes one teacher, whose votes may change on every query. Papernot et al. publish it only after adding noise calibrated to its smooth sensitivity, and pay for that release; on MNIST their data-dependent \(\varepsilon = 2.00\) becomes \(2.52 \pm 0.385\) once sanitized. Until it is sanitized, a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) is a measurement, not a guarantee. Report the data-independent value, or pay for the release.

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
40.7 Private in-context learning
An LLM learns a task from a few labelled examples, the exemplars, placed in its prompt. If the exemplars are private, every answer is computed from them. Duan et al. (2023) showed a membership inference attack (MIA) on GPT-3 prompted with one private example: the model’s probability for the correct label is markedly higher on the example in the prompt. The script’s stand-in learner shows the same: the attack’s area under the curve (AUC), the chance a member scores above a non-member, is 1.000 against a 1-shot learner and 0.889 against a 16-shot one. Putting private exemplars in a prompt that answers users directly protects nothing.
The fix is PATE with prompts as teachers (Wu et al. 2024; Duan et al. 2023). Split the exemplars into disjoint groups by a fixed rule, prompt the model once per group with the query, and release the GNMax label. One exemplar changes one prompt and so one vote, whatever the LLM computes, and the cost is exactly that of GNMax. Wu et al. also draw a fresh Poisson sample of the exemplars for each query, each record kept with probability \(r\); a record is then absent from most queries, and the cost is that of the subsampled Gaussian of Amplification by subsampling with rate \(r\) and noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt2\), the same accountant DP-SGD uses. The \(\sqrt2\) is the vote histogram’s sensitivity. Within one query the groups must still be disjoint, or a record in two groups moves two votes. PromptPATE (Duan et al.) instead labels a few public inputs this way and deploys them as the exemplars of one public prompt, the student in prompt form, free to use forever.
This is where private prediction is strongest. A prompted LLM knows most of the task from pretraining, so its votes with different exemplars agree far more than independently trained small models do, and high agreement is exactly what makes answers accurate and data-dependent costs small. The papers report, on a movie-review sentiment task with GPT-3 models, 92.7% accuracy at \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (0.147, 10^{-6})\) with PromptPATE against 95.2% without privacy (Duan et al.), and 91.97% at \(\varepsilon = 1\) for 10,000 queries each answered by ten 4-shot prompts, against 91.89% for one non-private 4-shot prompt (Wu et al.). The script’s stand-in learner has no pretraining at all, so it shows the accounting, not the accuracy. Subsampling makes its noise small: 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 1\) need \(\sigma = 7.39\) with \(r = 0.04\), against 181 without, yet with only 25 voters its accuracy still falls from 0.8090 to 0.6800 (Figure 40.4).






Figure 40.4: Accuracy of private answers from the stand-in in-context learner against the number of queries answered at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 4\) (\(\delta = 10^{-5}\)), with 25 groups of about 16 exemplars drawn per query at rate 0.04. The dashed line is the vote without noise and the dotted line a single 16-shot learner.

title: 40  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
40.8 Code
This snippet answers the two questions to ask before deploying a noisy vote: how much noise \(Q\) answers need (Equation 40.1, with \(\rho\) found by searching the RDP conversion over orders), and how often a vote with a given gap survives it.
from math import erfc, log, sqrt


def eps_of_line(rho: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """(eps, delta) of the RDP line rho * alpha, by the improved conversion at the best order."""
    orders = [1 + j / 100 for j in range(1, 6_000)]
    return min(rho * a + log((a - 1) / a) - (log(delta) + log(a)) / (a - 1) for a in orders)


def largest_slope(eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """The largest rho whose RDP line rho * alpha converts to (eps, delta), by bisection."""
    lo, hi = 1e-6, 10.0
    for _ in range(60):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if eps_of_line(mid, delta) <= eps else (lo, mid)
    return lo


def gnmax_sigma(answers: int, eps: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Noise per vote count so that `answers` GNMax answers cost (eps, delta) in total."""
    return sqrt(answers / largest_slope(eps, delta))


def p_plurality(gap: float, sigma: float) -> float:
    """Probability that a two-label GNMax vote returns the plurality label."""
    return 1 - 0.5 * erfc(gap / (2 * sigma))


print(f"{largest_slope(1.0, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 0.0306
print(f"{gnmax_sigma(100, 1.0, 1e-5):.1f}")  # 57.2
print(f"{gnmax_sigma(10_000, 1.0, 1e-5):.0f}")  # 572
sigma = gnmax_sigma(1000, 4.0, 1e-5)
print(f"{sigma:.1f}")  # 51.8
print(f"{p_plurality(96, sigma):.4f}")  # 0.9051
print(f"{p_plurality(4, sigma):.4f}")  # 0.5218
The full edition’s script trains the teachers, students and DP-SGD baselines, implements the data-dependent accountants and Confident-GNMax, and simulates in-context learning:
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/private_prediction.py

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.1 Why this matters
Training with differential privacy (DP) from random weights, by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD (DP-SGD), costs little on the part’s running example at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and a great deal at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and below. The most accurate private models are not trained that way. They start from a model pretrained non-privately on a large public dataset and only fine-tune it privately on the sensitive data, and at the same \(\varepsilon\) they are far more accurate than the same models trained privately from scratch (Tramèr & Boneh 2021; Yu et al. 2022; Li et al. 2022; De et al. 2022). A second practice helps on top of that: fine-tuning only a small part of the model often beats fine-tuning all of it under DP, although without privacy it would usually be the other way round.
Both follow from one idea: the noise is paid per trainable direction, the signal is not. DP-SGD adds noise of the same size to every coordinate it updates, while the useful part of the gradient is bounded in length however many coordinates there are, and usually concentrated in a few directions. A coordinate the task does not need only collects noise. Public data helps twice: it moves the starting point close to a good model, so little remains to be learned privately, and it tells you, for free, which few directions that remainder lies in. What it does not do is protect the people in the public data.
crumbs: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 41.2 Why dimension costs, and when it does not
text:
41.2 Why dimension costs, and when it does not
Each step of DP-SGD adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to a sum of per-example gradients clipped to length \(C\), where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier, and divides by the expected batch size \(B\). Nothing in the privacy proof depends on which weights the gradient is taken with respect to, so whatever you train, the accountant gives the same \(\varepsilon\). What changes is the noise. Over \(k\) trainable coordinates, a Gaussian vector with standard deviation \(s = \sigma C/B\) in each coordinate has length about \(s\sqrt k\), because its squared length is a sum of \(k\) terms of mean \(s^2\): \[\text{noise length} \approx \frac{\sigma C\sqrt k}{B}. \tag{41.1}\]
The signal, the average clipped gradient, is at most \(C\) long whatever \(k\) is, and it can be longer when \(k\) is smaller, because each record’s gradient restricted to fewer coordinates is shorter and less often clipped. The part’s running example shows both effects: 50-dimensional Gaussian inputs labelled by a fixed random network, \(n = 10{,}000\) private records, a student network with 3,329 weights pretrained on a related public task (Section 41.6), and DP-SGD with sampling rate \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\) and 10,000 steps, which needs \(\sigma = 4.13\) for \(\varepsilon = 1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). From the pretrained weights, the signal is 0.0130 long when all weights are trained, 0.0207 for a rank-4 adapter with the last layer, and 0.0250 for the last layer alone. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the noise is 92.0 times the signal for all weights, 22.9 times for the adapter and 6.7 times for the last layer (Table 41.1, Figure 41.1). A signal of constant direction outgrows a random walk of noise after about \((\text{noise}/\text{signal})^2\) steps: 8,455, 523 and 44 steps.

Right: their ratio. The noise grows like \(\sqrt k\) while the signal shrinks, because longer gradient vectors are clipped more.



Yet large language models with hundreds of millions of weights are fine-tuned privately with good results, so the count \(k\) cannot be the whole price. It is not, because noise only hurts in directions the loss cares about. Model the loss near the starting point as a quadratic. In a direction with curvature \(h\), noise kicks the weights around and the curvature pulls them back. A curved direction reaches a steady state and charges a fixed amount for it; a nearly flat direction keeps accumulating kicks but charges almost nothing for them, because moving along it barely changes the loss. Adding this up over \(T\) steps of step size \(\eta\) gives a loss increase of about \[\Delta \approx \frac{\eta s^2}{4}\,d_{\text{eff}}, \qquad d_{\text{eff}} = \sum_{j=1}^k\Big(1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^{2T}\Big), \tag{41.2}\] where \(h_j\) are the curvatures of the trainable directions. Each term is close to 1 for a direction whose curvature is above about \(1/(2\eta T)\) and close to 0 below it. So the effective dimension \(d_{\text{eff}}\) roughly counts the directions the noise has time to fill, and it is at most \(k\). Li, Liu et al. (2022) give this kind of explanation for why private fine-tuning of large models does not suffer from their size.
On the running example, at the pretrained weights with \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\), only 406 of the 3,329 directions have curvature above \(1/(2\eta T) = 5 \times 10^{-4}\), and \(d_{\text{eff}} = 451\); for the last layer, \(d_{\text{eff}} = 60.2\) of 65. Full fine-tuning’s noise is 7.2 times longer than the last layer’s, and by Equation 41.2 it costs only about 7.5 times more, not the 51 times that the ratio of weight counts suggests. Freezing weights can only lower \(d_{\text{eff}}\), but it adds bias: a frozen direction the task needs can never be learned. And \(d_{\text{eff}}\) grows with \(\eta T\), so a larger step size fills more flat directions with noise, one reason private fine-tuning wants smaller step sizes than training from scratch. The quadratic is a local model and loss is not accuracy, so use Equation 41.2 to compare strategies, not to predict accuracy.

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.3 The last layer: linear probing
The simplest strategy freezes everything except the last layer and trains a linear classifier on the frozen features, linear probing. Since the features come from public data, they are a fixed transformation of each record, and the problem becomes private convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) in \(k\) dimensions, where the methods and rates are known (Private ERM). Tramèr & Boneh (2021) showed that this beats end-to-end private training on standard image benchmarks at moderate budgets, even with handcrafted features.
A probe’s error splits in two. The feature gap is the distance from the best linear model on these features to the best model of any kind; it is paid even with infinite data and no privacy. The privacy cost is private convex ERM’s, which falls like \(\sqrt k/(n\varepsilon)\) up to logarithmic factors (Bassily, Smith & Thakurta 2014). So features cap the accuracy, and privacy only decides how close you get to the cap. On the running example, the pretrained network labels 0.9035 of the private test inputs correctly without any private data. Fitting its last layer exactly and non-privately on the 10,000 private records raises this to 0.9536, the probe’s ceiling, against 0.9606 for a network trained non-privately from scratch, a feature gap of 0.007. The private probe reaches 0.9478 at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and 0.9514 at \(\varepsilon = 8\): within 0.006 of its ceiling at every budget, and unable to pass it at any.
That makes the probe the safe first baseline: convex, with few hyperparameters, and if it meets your accuracy target there is little reason to train more.
crumbs: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.4 Low-rank adapters
When the features are not quite right for the new task, the probe stops at its ceiling, and training all weights pays for every weight. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al. 2022) sits in between. It freezes each pretrained matrix \(W_0\), of size \(d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}\), and learns a correction \(W = W_0 + UV^\top\) with \(U\) of size \(d_{\text{out}} \times r\) and \(V\) of size \(d_{\text{in}} \times r\), starting from \(U = 0\) so that training begins exactly at the pretrained model. It trains \[k = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}) \tag{41.3}\] weights instead of \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\). A rank-8 adapter on a \(768 \times 768\) projection of a transformer trains 12,288 weights instead of 589,824, 48 times fewer, so its noise is 6.9 times shorter. Its per-example gradients are outer products of short vectors, so their norms can be computed without forming them, the ghost clipping of DP-SGD; on the running example the ghost norms agree with explicitly formed gradients to a relative difference of \(3.3 \times 10^{-16}\). The privacy guarantee is DP-SGD’s with the same \(q\), \(\sigma\) and number of steps.
What the restriction costs is direction. At the start, with \(U = 0\) and \(V\) random, the update projects the true gradient onto a random \(r\)-dimensional subspace of the layer’s inputs, which captures little of it. As training proceeds \(V\) moves and the subspace aligns with the useful directions. Adapters work when the change the new task needs is itself close to low rank, and the rank trades bias against noise. Yu et al. (2022) found that private fine-tuning of language models with LoRA matches or beats private full fine-tuning; Li, Tramèr, Liang & Hashimoto (2022) found full fine-tuning matching or beating the parameter-efficient methods once it had large batches and a tuned step size, which Equation 41.2 allows, since full fine-tuning pays \(d_{\text{eff}}\), not \(k\). The published evidence goes both ways. The adapter’s other advantages are certain: it stores only \(k\) numbers per task and clips much smaller gradients.
crumbs: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.5 Gradients near a public subspace
If noise costs little in directions the loss does not use, you could add noise only in the directions it does use, if you knew them. Public data gives an estimate: compute per-example gradients on public records, find their top principal directions, and project the private clipped gradient sum and its noise onto those \(m\) directions. Projection never lengthens a vector, so the sensitivity is still \(C\), and because the subspace is fixed before any private data are read, the guarantee is unchanged. This is projected DP-SGD (Zhou, Wu & Banerjee 2021).
The trade is between noise and bias. The noise falls by \(\sqrt{p/m}\), where \(p\) is the number of weights. The signal keeps only the fraction \(f_m\) of its energy that lies in the subspace, and the lost part is a bias that no number of steps recovers. If the public data resemble the private task, \(f_m\) is close to 1 for small \(m\) and the trade is excellent. If they do not, the subspace is no better than a random one, \(f_m \approx m/p\), and the projection removes as much signal as noise. On the running example, a single direction of 500 public per-example gradients holds 60% of the private gradient’s energy, and 64 directions, 2% of the dimensions, hold 73%, against 2.2% for 64 random directions. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the kept signal outgrows the noise after 222 steps in the 64-dimensional subspace, against 8,455 for all weights; the price is the 27% outside it, which a fixed projection never learns, so methods recompute the subspace as training proceeds. The same concentration is what makes \(d_{\text{eff}}\) small for full fine-tuning (Figure 41.2).






Figure 41.2: Left: eigenvalues of the Gauss–Newton curvature of the private loss at the pretrained weights, estimated from 2,000 private records, on log scales, with the thresholds \(1/(2\eta T)\) for \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(0.5\) and \(T = 10{,}000\); directions below a threshold contribute little noise cost. Right: the fraction of the energy of the private average clipped gradient that lies in the top \(m\) principal directions of 500 public per-example gradients (solid), and in \(m\) random directions (dashed).

section: 41.6 Pretraining and fine-tuning the running example
text:
41.6 Pretraining and fine-tuning the running example
The public task labels 50,000 inputs from the private input distribution with a related teacher: the private teacher’s hidden units, each slightly perturbed, read out with weights turned partly towards a random vector. It agrees with the private teacher on 0.9004 of the private test inputs, so pretraining helps without solving the private task. The student is pretrained on it non-privately and then fine-tuned with DP-SGD in four ways: all weights from a random start (scratch), all weights from the pretrained ones (full), the last layer only, and a rank-4 adapter on the first layer plus the last layer. Each method’s step size was chosen at \(\varepsilon = 1\) on half of the private test set, without paying for that choice (Hyperparameter tuning shows how to), and accuracy is reported on the other half.

On this task pretraining is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\) (Table 41.2). Every fine-tuning method at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) beats training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 1\), and the adapter at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 0.9616, matches training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and the non-private model trained from scratch.
Which weights to train depends on the budget, as the noise lengths and the ceiling explain together. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the last layer is best: its noise is 7.2 times shorter than full fine-tuning’s, and its ceiling, 0.9536, is not yet binding. From \(\varepsilon = 1\) on it is stuck near that ceiling, while the adapter and full fine-tuning keep improving, because they can correct the features and the noise is now small enough to let them. The adapter is never more than 0.0022 below the best method at any budget, so it is the robust middle choice. Do not over-read the small differences: two runs estimate the spread only roughly, a repeat of the adapter at \(\varepsilon = 1\) gave a standard deviation of 0.0023, and differences between the pretrained methods below about 0.005 are not rankings (Figure 41.3, a separate set of single runs, orders them differently at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and 1). Step sizes matter as much as the method: full fine-tuning lost 1.3 points at a step size three times too large, and the best step size for full fine-tuning and the adapter, 0.1, was 2.5 times smaller than from scratch, as the effective-dimension argument predicts.

The pretrained methods are far ahead of training from scratch at small budgets; the last layer stays near its ceiling from \(\varepsilon = 1\) on, and training from scratch passes it at larger budgets.

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 41.7 What public data does not buy
text:
41.7 What public data does not buy
The guarantee treats the public data as a fixed input. For every fixed public dataset, the map from the private dataset to the fine-tuned model is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, because the DP-SGD proof holds for any starting weights chosen independently of the private data. With respect to the public data there is no guarantee at all: non-private pretraining can memorize individual records (Memorization and extraction), and the fine-tuned model inherits whatever the pretrained weights encode.
This matters most for a person whose record is in both datasets. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), any test of whether a record was in the private set that has a false positive rate of 0.01 has a true positive rate of at most \(e \times 0.01 + 10^{-5} = 0.0272\). If the same record is also in the public set, a membership test against the pretrained model, such as the likelihood-ratio attack of Membership inference, is bounded by nothing; it may fail in practice, but no theorem says it will. Compare a record that appears twice in the private set: group privacy gives the two copies \((2\varepsilon, 2e^\varepsilon\delta) = (2, 5.44 \times 10^{-5})\), weaker but real. A copy in the public set is worse than a duplicate in the private set. Web-scale “public” data contain posts, profiles and leaked documents, so overlap with private medical notes or emails is a real risk, and Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini (2024) argue that “differentially private” should be used with care for such models. Deduplication against the private set is the minimum check, and exact matching protects copies, not people: paraphrases and other records about the same person survive it.
Two further caveats. Benchmarks whose “private” set resembles curated public data can overstate what the method does on genuinely sensitive data, which is often unlike anything public. And any choice made by looking at private data, such as which public model to start from or the step size, is part of the private computation and must be paid for; choosing on public validation data is free. When you report \(\varepsilon\), say what the public data are, how they were obtained, whether overlap was checked, and that the guarantee covers the private data given the pretrained model.

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.8 Code
Before choosing what to fine-tune, count: the noise length for each candidate set of trainable weights, at the \(\sigma\) your accountant gives, is the first number to compare with the signal.
from math import sqrt


def noise_length(sigma: float, clip: float, batch: float, trainable: int) -> float:
    """Length of DP-SGD's noise on the averaged gradient over `trainable` coordinates."""
    return sigma * clip * sqrt(trainable) / batch


def lora_weights(rank: int, d_in: int, d_out: int) -> int:
    """Trainable weights of a rank-r adapter W0 + U V^T on a d_out x d_in matrix."""
    return rank * (d_in + d_out)


adapter = lora_weights(4, 51, 64) + 65  # first-layer adapter plus the 65-weight last layer
print(adapter)  # 525
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, 3329):.3f}")  # 1.191
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, adapter):.3f}")  # 0.473
print(f"{noise_length(4.13, 0.5, 100, 65):.3f}")  # 0.166
big = lora_weights(8, 768, 768)
print(big, 768 * 768 // big)  # 12288 48
print(f"{sqrt(768 * 768 / big):.1f}")  # 6.9

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.1 Why this matters
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee in this part so far protects one record. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, reports \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for the part’s running example, and that number says an adversary who sees the model learns little about whether any single training example was used. But people do not contribute one record each. A user of a messaging app writes hundreds of messages, a patient has dozens of visits, a photographer uploads thousands of photos. Each record is protected; the person behind all of them is not, because what an adversary learns from all of a person’s records together can be far more than what they learn from one.
The one idea: the neighbouring relation is the privacy unit. DP compares outputs on two datasets that differ in one unit, and whatever differs between them is what is protected. If neighbours differ in one record, records are protected; if they differ in all of one person’s records, people are. Nothing else in the definition changes. So there are two ways to protect a person. You can keep the record as the unit and pay for the person afterwards, which is cheap to build and expensive in privacy. Or you can make the person the unit from the start: sample people, bound each person’s total contribution, and run the usual accountant with people in place of records. On the running example the first route gives a useless model at any reasonable budget, and the second a model within a few points of the non-private one.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
text:
42.2 The privacy unit
A mechanism is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if the definition of DP holds for every pair of datasets that differ by adding or removing all the records of one user; it is example-level DP if it holds for datasets that differ in one record. User-level DP is not a new privacy notion, only a coarser neighbouring relation, so post-processing, composition and every accountant of Part 4 hold for it unchanged. What changes is the sensitivity: how far one unit can move the computation. Records, users, households, devices and organizations are all possible units, and the right one answers the question “whose participation do I want to hide?” A guarantee that does not name its unit leaves that question open.
What does an example-level guarantee promise a person with \(k\) records? Adding that person’s records one at a time walks from one dataset to the other in \(k\) example-level steps. Group privacy applies the one-record guarantee at each step (Post-processing, group privacy and composition): each step multiplies the probability bound by \(e^\varepsilon\), so the person gets \(k\varepsilon\), and each step’s slack \(\delta\) is multiplied by the \(e^\varepsilon\) of every later step, \[\delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{42.1}\] Some mechanisms attain this bound, so nothing better holds for a mechanism known only to be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. The \(\varepsilon\) part is linear in \(k\), already weak: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per record, a person with 10 records gets \(\varepsilon = 10\). The \(\delta\) part is worse, because it grows exponentially in \(k\varepsilon\).
Read naively, the running example’s \((6.71, 10^{-5})\) gives a user with two records \(\varepsilon = 13.42\) and \(\delta_2 = 10^{-5}(1 + e^{6.71}) = 0.0082\): a chance of almost one in a hundred that the guarantee fails outright, which is no guarantee. You can do better for DP-SGD, because its accountant converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at any \(\delta\): pick the per-record \(\delta\) that makes \(\delta_2 = 10^{-5}\) exactly. That gives a per-record \(\varepsilon\) of 9.30 and a user-level \((18.61, 10^{-5})\). For five records the same procedure gives a user-level \(\varepsilon\) of 118.12. For ten it gives nothing at all. Shrinking the per-record \(\delta\) raises the per-record \(\varepsilon\), and \(\delta_k\) is a race between a falling \(\delta\) and a rising \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\); beyond a few records the rising term wins at every \(\delta\), and no choice brings \(\delta_{10}\) down to \(10^{-5}\). In the running example’s population of 1,000 users, 244 have at least ten records.

title: 42  User-level differential privacy
section: 42.3 What a record-level model gives a heavy user
text:
42.3 What a record-level model gives a heavy user
Group privacy treats DP-SGD as a black box, and it is not one: you know exactly how a user’s records enter each step. Recall that DP-SGD draws each record into the batch independently with probability \(q\) (Poisson sampling), clips each record’s gradient to norm \(C\), sums them and adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\), where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier. A user with \(k\) records therefore has a random number of them in each batch, between 0 and \(k\), binomially distributed, and the worst case is that all the drawn ones push the sum by the full \(C\) in the same direction. So, in units of \(C\), one step compares the noise alone, \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), with a mixture of Gaussians shifted by \(m = 0, 1, \dots, k\), each weighted by the probability that \(m\) of the user’s records were drawn. Charles et al. (2024, Theorem 3) prove that this pair, composed over the steps, bounds the user’s privacy loss, and that some loss function, one that aligns the user’s gradients, attains it. An accountant built on the pair computes the user’s guarantee directly, the same way the subsampling accountant does for one record.
The result has a simple reading while \(kq\) is small: a user with \(k\) records looks like one record sampled at rate \(kq\). Amplification by subsampling works because the unit is usually absent from the batch, and what matters is the probability that some record of the user is present, about \(kq\). Halving the sampling rate exactly compensates doubling the user’s records. So the quick estimate is to rerun the record-level accountant with \(q\) replaced by \(kq\). It errs on the low side, because it drops the steps in which several of the user’s records are drawn together, and those steps shift the sum by several clipping norms at once, a mechanism with noise multiplier \(\sigma/m\) whose tail no amount of rarity can hide at high orders.

The direct accountant beats group privacy for every user with more than one record and stays finite where group privacy gives up (Figure 42.1).
